question: Israel's most famous psalm, beginning 'The LORD is my shepherd, I shall not want,' is traditionally attributed to which king?
context: Psalm 23. The Hebrew psalter collects 150 poems. David is named author of about half. Read at deathbeds and funerals across the Christian world.

question: Jesus's first public miracle, recorded in John 2, turned six stone jars of water into wine at a wedding feast in which town?
context: Mary told him 'they have no wine'. He produced the best wine last — about 150 gallons. The Gospel of John calls this the first of his 'signs'.

question: Paul was shipwrecked on his journey to Rome as a prisoner and spent the winter on which Mediterranean island?
context: Acts 27-28. A viper bit him on the beach and he shook it off unharmed. The Maltese still call themselves a Christian people since Paul's visit.

question: The first ecumenical council, called by Constantine in 325 AD to settle the Arian controversy, met in which city?
context: Now Iznik, Turkey. About 300 bishops attended. They condemned Arius's view that the Son was created and produced the Nicene Creed — still recited weekly.

question: Augustine's autobiographical account of his early years and conversion is regarded as the first true Western autobiography. What is it called?
context: Written c. 397-400 AD. 'Late have I loved thee.' Augustine's prose voice — direct address to God — invented Western interiority.

question: A scholar in his Bethlehem cell translated the Bible into Latin from Hebrew and Greek originals; his translation became the standard Western Bible for over a millennium. Who?
context: The Vulgate. Completed c. 405 AD. Trent declared it authentic in 1546. Jerome's translation shaped Latin Christendom's reading of Scripture.

question: An English missionary cut down a sacred oak of the Germanic thunder god in 723 AD to demonstrate the powerlessness of pagan deities. Who?
context: Apostle of the Germans. The Oak of Donar (Thor) at Geismar. He was martyred at Dokkum in 754 — Frisian raiders found him reading a gospel.

question: In 1054 papal legates and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, dividing Christendom into Catholic West and Orthodox East. The dispute included a phrase added to the creed. Which phrase?
context: Latin 'and from the Son' — the West said the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son. The East rejected the addition. Mutual excommunications were lifted only in 1965.

question: The Fourth Crusade never reached Jerusalem; in 1204 it sacked which Christian city instead?
context: Venetian-led. Three days of pillage shattered the Byzantine Empire. The Hagia Sophia was looted. Pope Innocent III had forbidden the attack but accepted its results.

question: A thirteenth-century Dominican friar wrote a vast unfinished synthesis of Christian theology that became the standard text of Catholic doctrine. What is it called?
context: Thomas Aquinas, c. 1265-1274. After a mystical experience on December 6, 1273 he stopped writing — 'all that I have written seems like straw to me'. He died months later.

question: Aquinas's Summa offers five rational arguments for God's existence — from motion, causation, contingency, gradation, and design. They are commonly called the what?
context: Latin 'Quinque Viae'. Drawn from Aristotle by way of Avicenna and Averroes. The cosmological and teleological arguments remain debated today.

question: A twelfth-century German abbess wrote of mystical visions, composed liturgical music, and corresponded with popes and emperors. Who?
context: 1098-1179. Scivias records her visions. Her music — Ordo Virtutum, Symphonia — survives. Benedict XVI named her a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

question: The Spanish Inquisition, established in 1478 by Ferdinand and Isabella, had its first Grand Inquisitor — a Dominican friar whose name became infamous. Who?
context: Grand Inquisitor 1483-1498. Targeted conversos suspected of secretly practicing Judaism. The Spanish Inquisition was abolished only in 1834.

question: In 1633 the Roman Inquisition condemned which astronomer for teaching that Earth moves around the Sun?
context: Forced to recant on his knees; tradition records him muttering 'and yet it moves'. Sentenced to house arrest at his villa near Florence. Died 1642.

question: A fourteenth-century Oxford theologian translated the Bible into English and inspired a movement of preachers called Lollards. Who?
context: c. 1330-1384. The Wycliffe Bible was translated from the Latin Vulgate. The Council of Constance condemned him posthumously in 1415 — his bones were dug up and burned.

question: Hidden at the Wartburg Castle, Luther translated the New Testament into which language in just eleven weeks (1522)?
context: The complete Luther Bible appeared in 1534. It shaped modern German prose as the King James would shape English. Luther's hymn A Mighty Fortress dates from the same period.

question: A fiery Scottish reformer confronted Mary, Queen of Scots in personal audiences during the 1560s and founded Presbyterian Scotland. Who?
context: c. 1514-1572. His First Blast Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women attacked female monarchs. He spent time as a French galley slave before returning to Scotland.

question: A British evangelical Anglican led the parliamentary fight that abolished the slave trade in 1807. Who?
context: Converted to evangelical Christianity in 1785. The 1807 act ended the trade; the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act ended slavery itself, days before he died.

question: Twenty people were executed and many more imprisoned during a 1692 witch panic in which Massachusetts town?
context: 19 hanged, 1 pressed to death (Giles Corey), several died in jail. Cotton Mather defended the trials; Increase Mather later turned against them. The colony apologized in 1697.

question: Pope John XXIII opened a major council in 1962 that introduced vernacular liturgy and modernization to the Catholic Church. What is it called?
context: Met 1962-65 with about 2,500 bishops. The Mass moved from Latin to vernacular languages. Dei Verbum, Lumen Gentium, Gaudium et Spes were its key documents.

question: What event does Christianity hold as the decisive vindication of Jesus, the founding event of the Church, and the basis of Christian hope?
context: On the third day after his crucifixion. Paul writes that without it 'our preaching is in vain' (1 Cor 15:14). Easter is the central feast of the Christian year.

question: The Reformation is summarized in five Latin 'solas': sola scriptura, sola fide, sola gratia, solus Christus, and which fifth?
context: 'To God alone be glory'. The five solas express the core Protestant claim against medieval Catholicism: salvation by Scripture, faith, grace, Christ, and to God's glory alone.

question: Which short creed, traditionally attributed to the apostles, summarizes Christian belief in three articles on Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
context: The text crystallized in Gallic baptismal liturgies of the eighth century. It is used in Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican, and many other Western liturgies.

question: Laban swapped which elder daughter for the younger one Jacob expected on his wedding morning?
context: Genesis 29. Veiled bride. She bore six of the twelve tribes, including Judah and Levi — ancestors of Jesus and Moses respectively.

question: Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams of seven fat cows and seven thin cows as a prophecy of how many years of famine following plenty?
context: Genesis 41. Joseph stockpiled grain through the fat years and saved Egypt. The famine drove his own brothers down from Canaan to buy food — the family reunion follows.

question: A Syrian commander with leprosy was healed by washing seven times in the Jordan River at the word of which prophet?
context: 2 Kings 5. Naaman first refused — the rivers of Damascus were better than the muddy Jordan. His servants persuaded him. Jesus references the story in Luke 4.

question: Nebuchadnezzar's army destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem and exiled the Jewish people to Babylon in what year?
context: Solomon's Temple stood about four centuries. The exile lasted about seventy years (Jer 25). The book of Lamentations was written in its aftermath.

question: A Jewish revolt against the Seleucid Antiochus IV recaptured Jerusalem and rededicated the temple in 164 BC. The family who led it bears what name?
context: Their dynasty (the Hasmoneans) ruled until Roman annexation. Hanukkah commemorates the rededication. Books of Maccabees are deuterocanonical/apocrypha.

question: Jesus called how many men to be his closest disciples — the inner circle who would become the foundation of the early church?
context: Mark 3 lists Peter, James, John, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot. Matthias replaced Judas (Acts 1).

question: A Roman centurion in Caesarea became the first Gentile convert when Peter, prompted by a rooftop vision, visited and baptized his household. Who?
context: Acts 10. The vision of unclean animals lowered in a sheet broke down the dietary wall. The Jerusalem church then debated and accepted Gentile inclusion.

question: A late-second-century bishop of Lyon wrote a five-volume work refuting Gnosticism and articulating apostolic tradition. Who?
context: c. 130-202 AD. A disciple of Polycarp, who had known John. Against Heresies systematized the New Testament canon and Trinitarian thinking decades before Nicaea.

question: A third-century Alexandrian biblical scholar wrote thousands of works and reportedly castrated himself in youth over Matthew 19:12. Who?
context: c. 184-253 AD. His Hexapla aligned six versions of the Old Testament. Some teachings (universal salvation, soul pre-existence) were condemned in 553.

question: The last and worst Roman persecution of Christians, ordered by an emperor in 303 AD, included burning of scriptures and demolition of churches. Which emperor?
context: Lasted to 311 in the East. Eusebius records the martyrdoms in Palestine. The persecution ended with Galerius's deathbed Edict of Toleration.

question: A fourth-century Egyptian organized the first communal Christian monasteries in upper Egypt around 320 AD. Who?
context: c. 292-348 AD. He brought hermits under a common rule and roof. By his death, his federation governed thousands of monks. Coenobitic monasticism begins with him.

question: The bishop of Milan baptized Augustine on Easter Eve 387 AD and defied Theodosius after the Thessalonica massacre. Who?
context: c. 340-397 AD. A Roman governor elected bishop by acclamation while still unbaptized. His allegorical preaching softened Augustine's Manichean objections to the Bible.

question: Augustine's North African mother followed him to Italy, prayed for his conversion for decades, and died at Ostia in 387 AD. Who?
context: She converted his pagan father Patricius on his deathbed. Her vision of a measuring rod and Augustine on the same plank as her sustained her hope through his Manichean years.

question: A Northumbrian monk's 731 AD Ecclesiastical History of the English People is our principal source for early Anglo-Saxon Christianity. Who?
context: c. 672-735 AD. 'The Venerable Bede'. Dates events 'AD' (Anno Domini) — popularizing the modern dating system. Doctor of the Church.

question: A twelfth-century Cistercian abbot preached the Second Crusade, mentored a pope, and shaped medieval Marian devotion. Who?
context: 1090-1153. Founded Clairvaux Abbey at 25. The Cistercians multiplied through his influence. His writings on the Song of Songs are mystical classics.

question: After a mystical experience on December 6, 1273 Aquinas stopped writing the Summa, saying his work seemed like what?
context: 'Mihi videtur ut palea' — 'it seems to me like straw'. He died three months later traveling to the Council of Lyon. The Summa was completed posthumously from his notes.

question: A late-thirteenth-century Franciscan from Scotland defended the Immaculate Conception and was nicknamed the 'Subtle Doctor'. Who?
context: c. 1266-1308. His ideas on the univocity of being and the formal distinction shaped later Catholic thought. The word 'dunce' comes from his name through anti-scholastic ridicule.

question: An early-fourteenth-century English Franciscan gave us a principle of parsimony — 'entities should not be multiplied without necessity'. Who?
context: c. 1287-1347. Defended Franciscan poverty against Pope John XXII. His nominalism — that universals are mere names — set the stage for early modern philosophy.

question: A fifteenth-century Dutch devotional book, after the Bible the most translated Christian text, is attributed to a member of the Devotio Moderna. Who?
context: c. 1380-1471. Written c. 1418-27. 'A humble peasant who serves God is better than a proud philosopher who studies the heavens and neglects himself.'

question: A Dutch humanist wrote a satirical 1509 essay narrated by Folly herself, mocking superstitions and corruption inside the Church. Who?
context: c. 1466-1536. The Praise of Folly was dedicated to Thomas More — its Greek title Moriae Encomium puns on More's name. Erasmus also produced a Greek New Testament in 1516.

question: Calvin's signature doctrine that God has from eternity elected some to salvation and passed by others bears what name?
context: Articulated in Institutes Book III. Calvin called it the 'horrible decree'. Reformed orthodoxy refined it in the five points of Dort (1618-19).

question: A sixteenth-century Spanish nun reformed the Carmelite order and wrote mystical classics including The Interior Castle. Who?
context: 1515-1582. Doctor of the Church (1970, with Catherine of Siena — the first women so named). Bernini's ecstasy sculpture freezes her vision of an angel piercing her heart.

question: John Wesley traveled an estimated 250,000 miles on horseback preaching across Britain. He is regarded as founder of which movement?
context: 1703-1791. The name 'Methodist' began as a Oxford nickname for his Holy Club. His brother Charles wrote thousands of hymns. The Methodist Church grew huge in America.

question: An eighteenth-century revival movement in colonial America associated with Whitefield, Edwards, and the Tennents is called the First what?
context: 1730s-40s. Reshaped American Protestantism, dividing 'Old Light' traditionalists and 'New Light' revivalists. Princeton, Brown, and Rutgers grew from Awakening colleges.

question: A nineteenth-century English missionary adopted Chinese dress and founded the China Inland Mission in 1865. Who?
context: 1832-1905. His Chinese-style queue and gown shocked Western missionaries. By his death the CIM had 800 missionaries and 125,000 Chinese converts.

question: A nineteenth-century English Baptist cobbler-turned-missionary translated the Bible into multiple Indian languages from Serampore. Who?
context: 1761-1834. 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.' He campaigned against sati. Bengali, Sanskrit, and Marathi Bibles among his many translations.

question: A formerly enslaved Methodist preacher delivered a famous 1851 speech at an Ohio women's convention. Who?
context: Born Isabella Baumfree c. 1797. She took her preaching name in 1843. 'Ain't I a Woman?' as transmitted by Frances Gage; the original speech text differs.

question: A formerly enslaved Methodist conductor on the Underground Railroad earned the nickname 'Moses' for leading dozens of slaves to freedom. Who?
context: c. 1822-1913. Bounty on her head; never lost a passenger. Devoutly Christian; said God spoke to her directly. Worked as a Union scout and nurse during the Civil War.

question: Bonhoeffer's smuggled-out reflections from a Berlin prison cell were published after the war under what title?
context: He wrote of 'religionless Christianity' and the 'world come of age'. His pivotal idea: 'only the suffering God can help.' Edited by his friend Eberhard Bethge.

question: Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity began their work in 1948 by gathering the dying from the streets of which Indian city?
context: Now Kolkata. She had served at a Loreto convent school there for two decades before her 1946 'call within a call' on a train to Darjeeling.

question: A North Carolina Baptist evangelist preached to an estimated 215 million people across crusades from 1947 to 2005. Who?
context: 1918-2018. Spiritual counselor to presidents from Eisenhower to Obama. His son Franklin Graham continues the organization.

question: Most Protestant traditions recognize how many sacraments instituted by Christ?
context: Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Catholics and Orthodox recognize seven (baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing of the sick, holy orders, matrimony).

question: Catholic theology counts how many sacraments?
context: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Reconciliation (confession), Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, Matrimony. The Council of Trent (1547) defined the number against the Reformers.

question: Christianity's central feast celebrates the resurrection of Jesus on what day?
context: Dating: first Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. The 325 Nicaea fixed the formula. Greek and Russian Orthodox follow the Julian calendar — often a different date.

question: The Thursday before Easter, commemorating Christ's Last Supper and the washing of feet, is called what in Anglican usage?
context: 'Maundy' from Latin 'mandatum' ('a new commandment') in Jesus's foot-washing words (John 13:34). British monarchs distribute Maundy money to the poor on this day.

question: The fourth commandment requires Israelites to remember and keep holy which day?
context: Exodus 20:8-11. Hebrew 'Shabbat'. Most Christians shifted observance to Sunday — the Lord's Day, day of the resurrection — though Seventh-Day Adventists keep Saturday.

question: Revelation 6 unveils four riders on white, red, black, and pale horses, often identified with conquest, war, famine, and what fourth?
context: The pale horse's rider is named Death; Hades follows. Albrecht Durer's 1498 woodcut is the most famous artistic depiction. Modern usage applies the phrase to any quartet of evils.

question: Tradition makes which Gospel writer the founder of the church in Alexandria, where his successors became the Coptic Pope?
context: His Gospel — the shortest and likely earliest — was the source for Matthew and Luke. Tradition has him martyred in Alexandria c. 68 AD by being dragged through the streets.

question: Tradition identifies the 'beloved disciple' of John's Gospel with the apostle John, who is also said to have written Revelation and three letters. Who outlived the other apostles?
context: He cared for Jesus's mother Mary after the crucifixion (John 19:27). Exiled to Patmos under Domitian. Tradition has him dying peacefully at Ephesus in extreme old age.

question: A late-seventh-century BC prophet of Anathoth wept over Jerusalem's fall and authored Lamentations (by tradition). Who?
context: Witness to the 586 BC destruction. Drawn down to Egypt by fellow refugees after the fall. Tradition has him stoned to death there. His book is the longest in the Bible by word count.

question: Which prophet closes the Christian Old Testament with a prophecy of the messenger who will prepare the way of the Lord?
context: Malachi 3:1; 4:5-6 — the return of Elijah. Christian readers identify the messenger with John the Baptist. 'Malachi' means 'my messenger' in Hebrew.

question: The opening line 'vanity of vanities, all is vanity' comes from which Old Testament book?
context: Traditionally attributed to Solomon — 'the Preacher' (Qoheleth). Hebrew 'hevel' translated 'vanity' means 'breath' or 'vapor'. A wisdom-book meditation on the limits of meaning.

question: The book of pithy sayings — 'fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom' — is traditionally attributed to which king?
context: Proverbs 9:10. Solomon was said to have spoken 3,000 proverbs (1 Kings 4:32). Later collections (Agur, Lemuel, the sayings of the wise) are appended.

question: When asked which is the greatest commandment, Jesus quoted Deut 6: love God with all your heart. He paired it with which second commandment from Leviticus?
choices: Be holy as I am holy
context: Mark 12:29-31, citing Deut 6:4-5 and Lev 19:18. 'On these two commandments depend all the law and the prophets'. The Shema is Judaism's central daily prayer.

question: An early-twentieth-century American study Bible popularized dispensational premillennialism in fundamentalism. By whom?
context: Published 1909. Built on John Nelson Darby's dispensationalism — distinguishing Israel and the Church and predicting a literal millennium after Christ's return. Hugely influential.

question: Around 49 AD an apostolic council in Jerusalem decided that Gentile converts need not be circumcised or keep the Mosaic law. Who presided?
context: Acts 15. Peter spoke for the Gentile mission; Paul and Barnabas reported their work; James pronounced the decision. The first major doctrinal council of the Christian church.

question: Jeremiah prophesied that the Babylonian exile of Judah would last roughly how many years?
context: Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10. From 605 BC (first deportation) to 538 BC Cyrus's decree is about 70 years. Daniel 9 reckons from these years toward the seventy weeks of years prophecy.

question: Genesis 6-9's flood narrative parallels a Mesopotamian flood story whose survivor is named in the Epic of Gilgamesh. Who?
context: Atrahasis and Ziusudra are alternate names in earlier Sumerian/Akkadian versions. The literary parallels — pitch-coated ark, raven and dove, sacrifice afterward — are striking.

question: The Apostles' Creed states that between his death and resurrection Christ 'descended into' what?
context: Latin 'descendit ad inferos'. Some translations say 'into hell' — meaning the realm of the dead, not the place of damnation. The doctrine is rooted in 1 Peter 3:19; 4:6 and Ephesians 4:9.

question: The 1906 Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles, often considered the birth of modern Pentecostalism, was led by which African-American preacher?
context: Son of Louisiana slaves, blind in one eye. The revival drew black and white worshipers together for three years — radical for Jim Crow America. Pentecostalism is now over 600 million globally.

question: Modern American fundamentalism takes its name from a series of essay pamphlets distributed free to clergy from 1910-1915 by Lyman and Milton Stewart. What were they called?
context: 12 volumes of essays by Reformed, dispensationalist, and other conservative theologians. Defending biblical inerrancy, virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, resurrection, and miracles.

question: The 1870 capture of Rome by the forces of Italian unification ended over a thousand years of which papal territory?
context: Pope Pius IX became the 'prisoner of the Vatican' in protest. The states had stretched from Rome north to Bologna and Ravenna. Their loss freed the papacy to focus on spiritual leadership.

question: The principal Lutheran statement of faith, presented to Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, was authored largely by which Reformer?
context: Luther read and approved it; he was at the Coburg Fortress, unable to attend himself. Twenty-eight articles. The defining doctrinal text of Lutheranism, with the Book of Concord (1580).

question: The 1646 Westminster Confession of Faith became the doctrinal standard of English-speaking Presbyterianism. Where was the assembly held?
context: Convened by the Long Parliament during the English Civil War. The Shorter and Larger Catechisms were also produced. Charles I rejected it; the Scottish Kirk adopted it as their confession.

question: Luther's 1517 95 Theses were specifically directed against the sale of what?
context: Latin 'Disputatio pro declaratione virtutis indulgentiarum'. They were addressed to Albrecht of Mainz; Luther probably also nailed them to the church door. Within weeks they were printed across Europe.

question: The First Vatican Council in 1869-70 defined a doctrine of papal infallibility. The pope is infallible only when speaking how?
answer: Ex cathedra on faith and morals
choices: Ex cathedra on faith and morals
context: 'From the chair' of Peter, on matters of faith and morals, intending to bind the whole church. Only one definition since 1870 fits the criteria: Pius XII's 1950 Assumption of Mary.

question: The Ethiopian (Aksumite) kingdom officially adopted Christianity in the fourth century under which king?
context: Aksum's Bishop Frumentius (a Tyrian captive) helped bring Christianity in. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the oldest continuous Christian bodies, with about 50 million members today.

question: Prince Vladimir of Kiev converted his realm to Christianity in 988 by mass baptism in the Dnieper, choosing Greek Orthodoxy after sending envoys to several religions. Which capital?
context: His envoys reported of Hagia Sophia: 'we knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth'. Vladimir married a Byzantine princess. Russian Orthodoxy dates from this moment.

question: Egyptian Christianity (the Coptic Church) traces its founding to which evangelist?
context: Tradition has him as bishop of Alexandria in the 40s AD, martyred c. 68. The Coptic Pope sits in his apostolic chair. Egypt had a Christian majority into the late medieval period.

question: In Hesiod's Theogony, the first thing to come into being — from which all else emerged — was a yawning void. What was it?
context: From Chaos came Gaia (Earth), Tartarus, Eros, Erebus (Darkness), and Nyx (Night). 'Chaos' in Greek means 'chasm' or 'yawning gap' more than disorder.

question: The primordial earth-goddess of Greek myth, mother of the Titans and grandmother of the Olympians, is called what?
context: Roman Tellus or Terra. Her union with Uranus (the sky) produced the twelve Titans. She also brought forth the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers.

question: The primordial sky-god of Greek myth was castrated by his own son with a sickle of adamant. Who was the sky-god?
context: Hesiod, Theogony. Gaia gave the sickle to Cronus. From the blood sprang the Furies, the Giants, and the Meliae nymphs; from the foam where his genitals fell, Aphrodite rose.

question: The Titan who castrated his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle and ruled the cosmos until his own son overthrew him is named what?
context: Roman Saturn. He swallowed his children to prevent the prophecy of being overthrown. His son Zeus escaped this fate and made him vomit the others back up.

question: Warned that his own son would overthrow him, Cronus swallowed his children at birth — until his wife hid one infant. Who was the wife?
context: Rhea wrapped a stone in swaddling clothes and gave it to Cronus, who swallowed it. The hidden child was Zeus, raised on Crete by the nymphs.

question: The infant Zeus was hidden on Crete and suckled by which goat-mother?
context: She lived in the Idaean cave. The Curetes clashed their shields to drown out the baby's cries. From her horn comes the cornucopia, the horn of plenty.

question: A ten-year war between the Olympians and the older generation of gods is known as what?
context: Zeus freed the Cyclopes (who made him the thunderbolt) and the Hundred-Handers from Tartarus to fight beside him. The defeated Titans were imprisoned in Tartarus.

question: After their defeat, the Titans were chained in a pit beneath the earth, said to be as far below earth as earth is below heaven. What was the pit called?
context: Hesiod: a bronze anvil falling from heaven would take nine days to reach earth, and another nine to reach Tartarus. The Hundred-Handers were stationed as guards.

question: The Titan who stole fire from Olympus and gave it to humanity was chained to a rock where an eagle ate his liver daily. Who?
context: Greek 'forethought'. The liver regenerated each night. Heracles eventually shot the eagle with an arrow. Prometheus also tricked Zeus over the division of sacrifice.

question: Some traditions credit Prometheus with shaping the first humans from what material?
context: Other accounts have him as patron rather than creator. Athena breathed life into his clay figures. Pandora was Zeus's counter-creation — the first woman.

question: Zeus's revenge against humanity for Prometheus's gift of fire was a beautiful woman sent to Earth with a sealed container. Who was she?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days. She opened the jar (not box — Latin mistranslation by Erasmus) and released all evils. Only hope remained inside.

question: Pandora was given as a 'gift' to which of Prometheus's brothers, whose name means 'afterthought'?
context: Prometheus had warned him to accept no gifts from Zeus. Epimetheus accepted Pandora anyway. The disaster that followed defines the human condition in Hesiod.

question: In Greek myth a flood drowned humanity, but one righteous couple survived in a wooden chest and repopulated earth by throwing stones over their shoulders. Who were they?
context: Deucalion was son of Prometheus; Pyrrha was daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora. His stones became men, hers became women. Parallel to Noah and the Mesopotamian flood myths.

question: Hesiod's Works and Days describes five successive ages of humanity. Which was the first and best?
context: Under Cronus's reign. No toil, no aging, no death — only sleep. Followed by Silver, Bronze, the Age of Heroes (the Trojan War generation), and the present Iron Age of toil and suffering.

question: The king of the Olympians wielded a weapon forged by the Cyclopes in gratitude for their freedom from Tartarus. What weapon?
context: Cyclopes forged it; Hephaestus reforged it after each use. Zeus also wore the aegis — a goatskin shield with Medusa's head — passed to his daughter Athena.

question: Zeus seduced the Spartan queen Leda in the form of a bird. Which bird?
context: Leda laid two eggs. From one came Helen of Troy and Polydeuces (Pollux); from the other, Clytemnestra and Castor. Yeats's poem 'Leda and the Swan' is the famous modern treatment.

question: Zeus seduced a Phoenician princess in the form of a white bull and carried her across the sea to a continent named for her. Who?
context: Mother of Minos of Crete by Zeus. The continent of Europe bears her name. She was the daughter of King Agenor of Tyre.

question: Zeus impregnated the imprisoned princess Danae as a shower of gold falling through her tower's roof. Her son became the hero who slew Medusa. Who?
context: Her father Acrisius had locked her in a bronze tower to thwart a prophecy that her son would kill him. Klimt's 'Danae' is the famous painting.

question: Zeus, smitten with a beautiful Trojan prince, took the form of an eagle and carried him off to Olympus to be cupbearer of the gods. Who was the prince?
context: Made immortal. The constellation Aquarius bears him. The story is openly cited in classical Greek and Roman texts on pederasty.

question: The queen of Olympus and goddess of marriage was famous for her implacable jealousy against Zeus's mortal lovers. Who?
context: Roman Juno. She drove Io across continents as a gadfly-tormented cow. She delayed the birth of Heracles to humiliate his mother Alcmene.

question: The rainbow goddess who served as Hera's swift messenger across the cosmos is called what?
context: Daughter of Thaumas and the ocean nymph Electra. Hermes serves the same messenger role for Zeus; Iris is for Hera. Her name gave the iris flower and the iris of the eye.

question: Zeus's elder brother, ruler of the sea, wielded a three-pronged spear. Who?
context: Roman Neptune. The trident, like Zeus's thunderbolt, was forged by the Cyclopes. He could call up storms, earthquakes, and horses — he was father of horses.

question: Athena won the contest with Poseidon for the patronage of a great city by gifting its first olive tree. Which city?
context: Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident and produced a saltwater spring. Athena's olive — useful for oil, food, and wood — won the citizen vote. The city's name follows.

question: Zeus's other brother ruled the underworld and the wealth beneath the earth. Who?
context: Roman Pluto (the rich one — wealth comes from beneath the soil). His helm, given by the Cyclopes, granted invisibility. Perseus borrowed it to approach Medusa.

question: Hades's guard-dog at the gates of the underworld has how many heads?
context: Some accounts give more — Hesiod says fifty. Heracles dragged him up as the twelfth labor and put him back. Orpheus charmed him with music; Aeneas drugged him with honey-cakes.

question: Hades kidnapped Demeter's daughter and trapped her in the underworld by feeding her how many pomegranate seeds?
context: Each seed bound her to a month underground — accounting for winter. Her name was Persephone (Kore, the maiden). Demeter's grief stopped the crops from growing.

question: The grain-goddess who searched the world for her abducted daughter Persephone, withholding harvest until she was returned, was called what?
context: Roman Ceres — root of 'cereal'. The Eleusinian Mysteries celebrated her search and the daughter's return. Persephone returns each spring, descends each autumn.

question: The Greek mystery cult centered on Demeter's grief and the return of Persephone was based at which Attic town?
context: About 14 miles from Athens. The Mysteries ran for over a thousand years. Initiates kept the secrets so well that we still do not know the central revelation.

question: The eldest of the Olympians, goddess of the hearth, gave up her seat on Olympus to Dionysus. Who?
context: Roman Vesta. The hearth-fire of every Greek and Roman home was her shrine. The eternal flame of the temple of Vesta in Rome was tended by virgin priestesses.

question: Athena was born fully grown and armed, springing directly from Zeus's forehead after Hephaestus split it open with an axe. Who first split the head?
context: Some accounts name Prometheus. Athena's mother Metis (Cunning) had been swallowed by Zeus, who had been warned her child would overthrow him.

question: Athena's two main attributes — gifts to Athens and symbols of wisdom — are her sacred bird and her sacred tree. Name them.
context: Roman Minerva. The owl appeared on Athenian coins for centuries. The olive she planted on the Acropolis is the gift that won her the city against Poseidon.

question: A mortal weaver challenged Athena to a contest and was transformed into a spider for her presumption. Who?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6. Her tapestry depicted the affairs of the gods so accurately that Athena tore it. The Greek word for spider — 'arachne' — and 'arachnid' come from her.

question: The Gorgon whose gaze turned men to stone was killed by Perseus, who used a polished shield as a mirror. Who?
context: Only Medusa was mortal of the three Gorgons. Pegasus and Chrysaor sprang from her severed neck. Perseus gave her head to Athena, who set it on her aegis.

question: Apollo's twin sister was born on the same day on the floating island of Delos to which Titaness mother?
context: Hera persecuted Leto until Delos — a floating rock — gave her refuge. Artemis was born first and helped deliver Apollo. The twins together became patrons of the Letoides.

question: Apollo killed a great serpent at Delphi and made it the seat of his oracle. What was the serpent called?
context: Delphi had earlier been an oracle of Gaia and Themis. The priestess (Pythia) sat over a chasm where Python's body was said to rot.

question: Apollo's amorous pursuit of a nymph ended when her father transformed her into a tree. What tree?
context: Daphne — the name means 'laurel' in Greek. Apollo wore the laurel ever after; Pythian Games victors received laurel crowns. Bernini's sculpture captures the transformation.

question: Apollo's beloved Spartan companion was killed by a discus deflected by the jealous wind-god Zephyrus. A flower sprang from his blood. Who?
context: The hyacinth flower bears his name. The Spartans held the Hyacinthia festival annually. One of several Greek myths of male love (eromenos relationships).

question: Apollo's oracle at Delphi spoke through a priestess seated on a tripod over a chasm. What was the priestess called?
context: She inhaled vapors (possibly ethylene from the rock) and prophesied in ecstatic verse. Croesus, Oedipus, Socrates, Alexander the Great all consulted Delphi.

question: Two famous maxims inscribed at Delphi: 'know thyself' and 'nothing in...' what?
context: Greek 'gnothi seauton' and 'meden agan'. The first was attributed to various sages; the second is Spartan economy of phrase. Socrates took 'know thyself' as his motto.

question: Apollo's twin sister, virgin huntress of the wild and moon-goddess, was called what?
context: Roman Diana. She demanded perpetual virginity at age three. She killed Niobe's daughters; turned Actaeon into a stag for seeing her bathe; took Iphigenia's place at Aulis.

question: The war-god of brutal slaughter, despised by his own father Zeus as the most hateful of the gods, was called what?
context: Roman Mars — significantly more dignified in Roman religion. Hated by most Greeks who preferred the more strategic Athena. Loved Aphrodite, caught in Hephaestus's golden net.

question: The goddess of love was born from the sea foam where Uranus's severed genitals fell. Where did she first step ashore?
context: Hence 'Cyprian' or 'Cytherean'. Botticelli's Birth of Venus shows her arrival on Cyprus. Roman Venus. Her sacred animal was the dove.

question: Three goddesses asked a Trojan prince to judge which of them was most beautiful, bribing him with gifts. Who won by promising the most beautiful woman?
context: Hera offered power; Athena offered wisdom in war; Aphrodite offered Helen of Sparta. Paris's choice triggered the Trojan War. The golden apple was inscribed 'to the fairest'.

question: Aphrodite's son hid his identity from his mortal wife and required her never to look at him by daylight. The wife's name became Greek for 'soul'. Who was she?
context: Greek 'breath, soul'. Apuleius's Golden Ass tells the fullest version. She broke the prohibition, was set tasks by Aphrodite, and was eventually reunited with Eros.

question: The lame smith-god, thrown from Olympus, forged the gods' weapons in his Lemnos forge. Who?
context: Roman Vulcan. Thrown by Hera (or by Zeus during a quarrel). His Cyclopes assistants. He forged the armor of Achilles, the necklace of Harmonia, and Pandora.

question: Hephaestus caught his wife Aphrodite and her lover Ares in a magical golden net while they slept together. Then he summoned the other Olympians to watch. Where?
context: Homer, Odyssey 8. Hermes whispered he would gladly trade places. Poseidon mediated the eventual release. One of the few openly comic scenes among the Olympians.

question: Zeus's herald, god of thieves, travelers, and souls of the dead, wore winged sandals and carried a herald's staff. Who?
context: Roman Mercury. The caduceus — two serpents entwined around a staff — became (incorrectly) the symbol of medicine. His name gave 'hermetic' (sealed) and 'hermeneutics'.

question: The infant Hermes stole his brother Apollo's cattle on his first day of life, then gave him the lyre to mollify him. Whose lyre?
context: Hermes had just invented the lyre from a tortoise shell, sheep gut, and reeds. The story is in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes. Apollo, charmed, became the lyre's eternal patron.

question: Twice-born from Zeus's thigh after his mother Semele died, the god of wine, theater, and ecstatic frenzy was called what?
context: Roman Bacchus. His ecstatic worshipers — maenads — tore his enemies apart. He gave wine to Icarius of Athens, who was killed by his neighbors when they thought they had been poisoned.

question: Pirates kidnapped a young Dionysus from a beach; he turned the ship's mast into a vine, set lions loose on the deck, and transformed the leaping pirates into what?
context: Homeric Hymn 7. Only the helmsman, who had warned the crew, was spared. The dolphin in Greek myth was a sacred animal of Apollo and Poseidon as well.

question: Dionysus drove the women of Thebes mad and they tore apart the king of Thebes, who had banned the god's worship. Who was the king?
context: Euripides, The Bacchae. His own mother Agave led the dismemberment, thinking him a lion. She returned to her senses still holding his head.

question: The ecstatic female followers of Dionysus, who ran wild on mountainsides and tore apart wild animals, were called what?
context: Greek 'mainomai' (to rage). Carried the thyrsus — a fennel staff topped with a pine cone. Suckled wolf-cubs and fawns. Euripides treats them in The Bacchae.

question: The goat-footed god of shepherds, whose terror in lonely places gave us the word 'panic', was called what?
context: Played reed pipes (the syrinx, from a nymph he chased). He helped panic the Persians at Marathon. The only Greek god whose death was reportedly announced — in Plutarch.

question: The goddesses who inspired the arts, daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, numbered how many?
context: Calliope (epic), Clio (history), Erato (love poetry), Euterpe (music), Melpomene (tragedy), Polyhymnia (sacred hymn), Terpsichore (dance), Thalia (comedy), Urania (astronomy).

question: The Theban hero Heracles performed how many labors set by King Eurystheus as penance for killing his wife and children?
context: Hera drove him to madness; the labors were Apollo's prescribed penance. They form a journey across the known Greek world and into the underworld. Roman Hercules.

question: Heracles's first labor was to strangle a great lion whose skin no weapon could pierce. Where did the lion live?
context: He wore the skin afterward — using the lion's own claws to skin it. The Nemean Lion became the constellation Leo.

question: Heracles's second labor was to kill a multi-headed swamp serpent whose heads grew back two for every one lopped off. What was it called?
context: His nephew Iolaus cauterized each stump with a torch. One head was immortal — Heracles buried it under a rock. He dipped his arrows in the Hydra's venom — fatal forever.

question: Heracles cleaned thirty years of dung from a vast cattle-stable in a single day by diverting two rivers through them. Whose stables?
context: The fifth labor. Augeas refused to pay the promised tithe; Heracles later killed him. The Alpheus and Peneus rivers were the diverted streams.

question: Heracles's eleventh labor was to fetch golden apples from a garden at the edge of the world, where three nymphs and a dragon guarded them. They were daughters of what god?
context: Heracles either tricked Atlas into fetching them or killed the dragon Ladon himself. The apples were a wedding gift from Gaia to Hera. Returned afterward.

question: Heracles's twelfth and final labor was to bring up alive from Hades the three-headed hound. The hound was named what?
context: Hades permitted it on condition Heracles use no weapons. He wrestled the dog into submission and dragged it up. Eurystheus hid in a jar; Cerberus was returned to Hades.

question: A dying centaur tricked Heracles's wife Deianira into preserving his blood as a love charm; she later anointed Heracles's robe with it and killed him. Who was the centaur?
context: Nessus had tried to abduct Deianira; Heracles shot him with a Hydra-poisoned arrow. The poisoned robe burned Heracles to death; he was apotheosized to Olympus.

question: Theseus killed a half-bull monster in a labyrinth and escaped with the help of a thread given by the king's daughter. Whose daughter?
context: The Minotaur was Pasiphae's son by a bull. Daedalus built the labyrinth. Athens had to send seven youths and seven maidens every year as tribute, until Theseus.

question: After fleeing Crete with Ariadne, Theseus abandoned her on a small Aegean island while she slept. Which island?
context: Dionysus found her there and married her. He set her crown in the sky as the Corona Borealis. Theseus's fault — and the curse it brought — leads to his father's suicide.

question: Perseus killed Medusa by looking at her reflection in a polished shield. Who lent him the shield?
context: Athena had cursed Medusa originally (for Poseidon raping her in Athena's temple — or for her vanity, depending on the source). Hermes lent the sickle.

question: Perseus rescued a princess chained to a sea-cliff to be devoured by a monster, then married her. Who was she?
context: Daughter of Cassiopeia and Cepheus of Ethiopia. The monster Cetus was sent by Poseidon. Andromeda's family became the Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, and Cetus constellations.

question: A Corinthian hero tamed the winged horse Pegasus and used him to kill a fire-breathing monster. Who?
context: The Chimera — lion in front, goat in the middle, serpent behind — terrorized Lycia. Bellerophon later tried to fly to Olympus; Zeus's gadfly stung Pegasus, and he fell.

question: Jason and his crew sailed the Argo to Colchis to retrieve a magical ram's-fleece. The crew was called what?
context: Heracles, Orpheus, Castor and Pollux, Atalanta, Theseus, Peleus (father of Achilles), and Telamon (father of Ajax) all sailed. The Argo was the first long-voyage ship.

question: Jason abandoned Medea for the princess of Corinth; she took revenge by killing what?
context: Euripides, Medea. She had also killed her brother Apsyrtus during their escape from Colchis, and tricked Pelias's daughters into murdering their own father. A monster of vengeance.

question: A monstrous sphinx outside Thebes asked riddles and devoured those who could not answer. Oedipus solved her riddle; she threw herself from the cliff. The riddle's answer was what?
context: 'What goes on four legs in the morning, two at noon, three in the evening?' — crawling baby, walking adult, cane-using elder. Oedipus's prize was Thebes — and his unknown mother as bride.

question: Oedipus killed his father at a crossroads and married his mother, all without knowing them. His mother and wife was named what?
context: Sophocles, Oedipus Rex. When the truth came out, Jocasta hanged herself and Oedipus blinded himself with her brooches. Their children: Antigone, Ismene, Eteocles, Polynices.

question: A swift huntress refused all suitors who could not outrun her. She was beaten by a suitor who dropped three golden apples to slow her. Who?
context: Hippomenes or Melanion (sources vary) was the suitor. Aphrodite gave him the apples from the Hesperides. He won; the couple was later turned into lions for impiety in her temple.

question: Tantalus offered his son Pelops in a stew to the gods; his eternal punishment in Tartarus was to stand in water and beneath fruit, both forever just out of reach. From his name we get the word what?
context: He had been a favored mortal at Zeus's table. His descendants formed the cursed house of Atreus: Agamemnon, Menelaus, Orestes, and Electra.

question: A nymph who had only the power to repeat the last words she heard pined away for Narcissus until only her voice remained. Who?
context: Hera had cursed her for distracting her with chatter while Zeus dallied with other nymphs. From her come 'echo' in English. Ovid pairs her with Narcissus in Metamorphoses 3.

question: A Cypriot sculptor fell in love with a statue he carved, and Aphrodite brought it to life. Who?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 10. The statue is later named Galatea. Shaw's play and the musical My Fair Lady are modern descendants.

question: Dionysus granted a king the wish that everything he touched turn to gold; he had to beg to have the gift removed when his food and daughter turned to gold. Who?
context: He bathed in the Pactolus river to wash off the curse. The river was said to run gold ever after. Midas also got donkey ears in a separate myth, for judging Pan over Apollo.

question: A musician descended to the underworld to retrieve his dead wife, charmed Hades and Persephone with song, and was permitted to lead her out — on condition he not look back. Who?
context: He looked. Eurydice vanished forever. Orpheus was later torn apart by maenads. His head floated singing down the Hebrus to Lesbos. The Orphic mysteries took him as founder.

question: Paris, prince of Troy, eloped with the queen of Sparta — wife of Menelaus — triggering the Trojan War. Who was she?
context: The 'face that launched a thousand ships'. Born of Leda and Zeus the swan. After Troy's fall she returned to Sparta with Menelaus — peacefully, says Homer.

question: The wooden horse that brought the Trojan War to an end was the idea of which Greek hero?
context: Built by Epeius. Filled with Greek warriors. The Trojans brought it inside their walls thinking it a gift to Athena. Virgil's Aeneid 2 gives the dramatic account from the Trojan side.

question: Achilles was made invulnerable as an infant when his mother Thetis dipped him in a sacred underworld river. Which river?
context: Only his heel — by which she held him — remained vulnerable. He died at Troy from an arrow shot by Paris, guided by Apollo, into that heel. Hence 'Achilles heel'.

question: Achilles killed the Trojan champion Hector in revenge for Patroclus's death and dragged his body around the walls behind his chariot. Who was the champion?
context: Eldest son of Priam. The duel and its aftermath occupy Iliad 22. Priam later came alone to Achilles's tent to ransom his son's body — the moral climax of the poem.

question: On the last night of the Iliad, an old king came to Achilles's tent to redeem his son's body. Whose son did he redeem?
context: Priam, king of Troy. Hermes guided him through the Greek camp. Achilles wept; Priam wept; they ate together. The first humane peace in the poem.

question: Achilles's closest companion borrowed his armor and rallied the Greeks before being killed by Hector. Who?
context: Iliad 16. Achilles's grief — and rage — drove the rest of the poem. The two have been read as lovers from Plato onward; Homer is more ambiguous.

question: Achilles's wrath in the Iliad began when which Greek commander seized his captive woman Briseis?
context: King of Mycenae, brother of Menelaus, commander of the expedition. Agamemnon had to surrender his own captive Chryseis to end Apollo's plague. The Iliad's first line names Achilles's rage.

question: Agamemnon sacrificed his own daughter at Aulis to obtain winds for the fleet to sail to Troy. Who was she?
context: Some traditions have Artemis snatch her away to Tauris at the last moment. The act drove Clytemnestra to murder Agamemnon on his return — and her son Orestes to murder her.

question: Apollo cursed a Trojan prophetess so that her true prophecies would never be believed. Who?
context: Daughter of Priam. She foretold the fall of Troy. Agamemnon took her as a concubine after the sack and brought her home to be murdered with him.

question: A Trojan prince fled the sack of Troy carrying his aged father on his shoulders and leading his son by the hand. Who fled?
context: Son of Anchises and Aphrodite. Virgil's Aeneid traces his journey to Italy — destined founder of the Roman race. His son Iulus (Ascanius) became ancestor of the Julian family.

question: Odysseus blinded a one-eyed giant with a sharpened stake after the giant ate several of his men, then escaped under the bellies of his sheep. Who was the giant?
context: Son of Poseidon. Odysseus told him his name was 'Nobody'. When Polyphemus called for help his neighbors thought 'Nobody is killing me'. Poseidon's wrath delayed Odysseus's return.

question: An island enchantress turned Odysseus's men into pigs with her magic potion. Odysseus resisted thanks to a herb given by Hermes. Who was she?
context: Aeaea was her island. Odysseus shared her bed for a year before continuing his voyage. She advised him on the path through the underworld and the dangers ahead.

question: Odysseus had himself tied to his ship's mast to hear the song of dangerous singers without being lured to his death. What were they?
context: His crew's ears were plugged with wax. Half-bird, half-woman in Homer; Roman art reimagined them as half-fish, ancestor of modern mermaid imagery.

question: Odysseus navigated a strait flanked by a six-headed monster on one side and a deadly whirlpool on the other. Name the monster and the whirlpool.
context: Often identified with the Strait of Messina between Italy and Sicily. To pass 'between Scylla and Charybdis' became proverbial for an unavoidable choice between two evils.

question: A nymph kept Odysseus on her island for seven years, offering him immortality if he would remain. Who?
context: Her island Ogygia. Hermes finally brought Zeus's order to release him. He chose mortal Penelope over immortal Calypso — the choice that defines the Odyssey.

question: After his shipwreck, Odysseus washed up naked on the shore of the Phaeacians and was discovered by a princess doing laundry on the beach with her handmaids. Who?
context: Daughter of King Alcinous. She fed him, clothed him, and led him to her father's palace. The Phaeacians took him home to Ithaca on a magical ship.

question: Odysseus's wife held off her suitors by promising to choose one when she finished weaving a shroud — but unraveled her day's work each night. Who?
context: She maintained the trick for three years before a treacherous maid revealed it. The shroud was for her father-in-law Laertes — who fortunately had not yet died.

question: When Odysseus returned to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, who recognized him first — and died of joy at the recognition?
context: Argos had waited twenty years. He wagged his tail once and died. Eurycleia later recognized the scar on his thigh while washing his feet.

question: The Iliad and the Odyssey are each divided into how many books?
context: One book per letter of the Greek alphabet, in the Alexandrian division. The Iliad treats about fifty days of the war's tenth year. The Odyssey treats Odysseus's ten-year return.

question: A Boeotian poet contemporary with Homer wrote a Theogony — a 'genealogy of the gods' — and Works and Days. Who?
context: c. 700 BC. Theogony narrates the rise of the Olympians. Works and Days addresses his brother Perses on farming, justice, and the five ages of man.

question: The home of the Olympian gods, traditionally a mountain in northern Greece, was called what?
context: About 2,917 meters, in Thessaly. Twelve principal Olympians: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, and Dionysus (or Hestia).

question: The Olympic Games, held every four years at Olympia in honor of Zeus, were traditionally founded in what year?
context: Other Panhellenic games: Pythian (Delphi, Apollo), Isthmian (Corinth, Poseidon), Nemean (Nemea, Zeus). Theodosius I abolished the Olympics in 393 AD. Revived in 1896.

question: The Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis (447-432 BC) housed a colossal chryselephantine statue of which goddess by Phidias?
context: About 12 meters tall, of gold and ivory. Lost in antiquity. The Parthenon served as Christian church, then mosque, then Venetian-bombarded ammunition dump (1687).

question: Phidias's chryselephantine statue of Zeus at Olympia was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. How tall was it (approximately)?
context: Made of gold and ivory on a wooden frame. Destroyed by fire after being moved to Constantinople. The temple at Olympia was sacked in late antiquity; only the foundations remain.

question: The ferryman who carried souls across the river Styx to the underworld required a coin under the tongue to make the crossing. Who?
context: Greeks were buried with an obol (coin) beneath the tongue for the fare. Those without a coin had to wander the shore for a hundred years. He appears in Dante's Inferno.

question: The underworld in Greek myth had five rivers: Styx (hate), Acheron (woe), Lethe (forgetting), Phlegethon (fire), and which fifth — the river of wailing?
context: Cocytus — from Greek 'wailing'. The dead drank from Lethe to forget their former lives. Souls awaiting reincarnation in the Orphic-Platonic system drank again.

question: The blessed dead and heroes lived after death in a paradise of meadows and music in the underworld. What was it called?
context: Or 'Elysium'. The Champs-Elysees in Paris bears the name. Most of the dead went to the neutral Asphodel Meadows. The wicked went to Tartarus.

question: Where the Titans were imprisoned and where the wicked were punished — Sisyphus, Tantalus, Ixion — the deepest level of the underworld was called what?
context: Hesiod placed it as far below earth as earth is below heaven. Plato in the Republic and Phaedo elaborated the picture of judgment and punishment.

question: A king bound forever to a fiery wheel for attempting to seduce Hera was called what?
context: Zeus made a cloud-image of Hera (Nephele); Ixion's union with the cloud produced the first centaur. His punishment was eternal rotation on a flaming wheel.

question: The mystery religion teaching purification and rebirth, based on the myth of a singer's descent to the underworld, was called what?
context: Orpheus was its founder. Orphic gold tablets buried with initiates gave instructions for the journey. Plato's myths in the Republic and Phaedo draw on Orphic eschatology.

question: A collection of 33 hexameter poems addressed to various Olympian gods, traditionally attributed to Homer but probably composed by various poets, is called what?
context: Composed 7th-5th centuries BC. The Hymn to Demeter is our chief source for the Eleusinian myth; the Hymn to Hermes for the infant Hermes's exploits.

question: Athena's protective goatskin shield — bearing the Gorgon's head and given by Zeus — was called what?
context: From Greek 'aix' (goat). The word now means 'sponsorship' or 'protection' ('under the aegis of'). Hephaestus made the shield of Achilles for the Iliad's set-piece description.

question: The half-horse, half-human creatures of Greek myth, mostly wild and savage but with at least one wise exception (Chiron), were called what?
context: Born from Ixion's union with a cloud-image of Hera. The wedding of Pirithous was the famous centauromachy — drunk centaurs tried to abduct the bride; the Lapiths fought them off.

question: One centaur was wise and just, tutor to Achilles, Asclepius, and Jason. Who?
context: Son of Cronus, not Ixion's line. Wounded accidentally by Heracles's poisoned arrow; immortal but in agony, he traded his immortality for Prometheus's freedom. Became Sagittarius.

question: The mostly-male, lecherous, drunken companions of Dionysus, often depicted with goat features, were called what?
context: Their leader Silenus was Dionysus's tutor. Later Roman art gave them goat legs and tails. Satyr plays followed Greek tragedies as ribald comic relief.

question: Minor female nature-divinities of springs, woods, and caves, often pursued by gods and heroes, were called what?
context: Naiads (springs), Oreads (mountains), Dryads (trees), Nereids (seas), Hamadryads (specific trees). Generally long-lived but not immortal — they died when their tree or spring died.

question: The three avenging goddesses who pursued wrongdoers — especially murderers of kin — were called the Erinyes or what alternative euphemism?
context: Born from Uranus's blood. Aeschylus's Eumenides ends Orestes's trial with their transformation into protectors of Athens — euphemism becoming reality.

question: The three Fates of Greek myth spin, measure, and cut the threads of human lives. Their Greek name is what?
context: Clotho spun; Lachesis measured; Atropos cut. Roman Parcae. Older even than the Olympians. Zeus could persuade but not overrule them.

question: The three Graces — handmaidens of Aphrodite, embodiments of beauty and charm — were called the what in Greek?
context: Aglaea (splendor), Euphrosyne (joy), Thalia (good cheer). Daughters of Zeus. Botticelli's Primavera depicts them. Roman Gratiae.

question: The Horai — daughters of Zeus and Themis — personified order and the seasons. They guarded the gates of where?
context: Eunomia (good order), Dike (justice), Eirene (peace). Roman Horae. The word 'hour' comes from them — they parceled the day as well as the year.

question: The god of medicine, son of Apollo and a mortal, was depicted with a staff and serpent. His name is what?
context: His staff (rod of Asclepius) is the modern medical symbol. He was so good a healer he raised the dead; Zeus killed him with a thunderbolt for upsetting cosmic order.

question: Hephaestus's smithy was traditionally located on which volcanic Aegean island?
context: Roman Vulcan's forges were beneath Mount Etna in Sicily. Hephaestus had landed on Lemnos when Zeus threw him from Olympus. The Sintians (locals) nursed him.

question: Odysseus received the winds tied in a sack from a wind-keeping king on a floating island. Who?
context: The Aeolian Islands off Sicily bear his name. His sack of winds blew Odysseus's ship within sight of Ithaca — until the crew opened it thinking it was gold.

question: Three judges decided the fate of dead souls in the underworld: Minos, Aeacus, and which third?
context: All three were sons of Zeus. Minos, the Cretan king of myth; Rhadamanthys his brother; Aeacus, ancestor of Achilles. Plato's Apology has Socrates eager to meet them in death.

question: The first word of Homer's Iliad in Greek announces its central theme: 'menin' — which means what?
context: 'Sing, goddess, the wrath of Peleus's son Achilles, ruinous wrath that brought countless griefs upon the Achaeans...'. Achilles's anger drives the action of the poem.

question: The first word of Homer's Odyssey in Greek is 'andra' — which means what?
context: 'Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns...'. The Iliad announces wrath; the Odyssey announces a man. The two-poem symmetry of the Greek epic tradition.

question: A mythical tribe of warrior women, said to live near the Black Sea, fought against Greek heroes including Heracles and Theseus. Who?
context: Their queen Hippolyta lost her belt to Heracles. Their queen Penthesilea died at Troy by Achilles's hand — he fell in love with her dying face. Often identified with Scythian women warriors.

question: Heracles's ninth labor was to fetch the belt of an Amazon queen. Which queen?
context: Hera disguised herself among the Amazons and stirred war. Heracles killed Hippolyta. Theseus carried off her sister Antiope and married her — leading to the Athenian amazonomachy.

question: A Titan was condemned by Zeus to hold up the sky on his shoulders forever. Who?
context: His name gave 'atlas' (book of maps), the Atlas Mountains, and the Atlantic Ocean. Heracles briefly took the burden while Atlas fetched the Hesperides' apples.

question: A blind Theban prophet appears in many myths — he had lived as both man and woman, had been blinded for seeing Athena bathe (or for siding with Hera), and prophesied for Odysseus in the underworld. Who?
context: Sophocles's Oedipus Rex and Antigone feature him. He told Odysseus how to return home. Eliot puts him at the center of The Waste Land.

question: Jason was sent on the quest for the Golden Fleece by his usurping uncle, who hoped he would not return. Who was the uncle?
context: Pelias had killed Jason's father Aeson. Medea later tricked Pelias's daughters into chopping him up and boiling him, expecting him to be rejuvenated. He was not.

question: At the wedding feast of Pirithous king of the Lapiths, drunken centaurs tried to abduct the bride and her women. The resulting battle is called what?
context: Theseus, friend of Pirithous, fought beside the Lapiths. The Parthenon's south metopes depict the battle. A symbol of Greek civilization defeating chaotic barbarism.

question: The son of the sun-god Helios tried to drive his father's chariot and lost control, scorching the earth until Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt. Who?
context: Greek 'shining one'. The Sahara desert, the dark skin of African peoples, and the rivers of the world were said to derive from his disaster. Ovid's Metamorphoses 2 is the source.

question: Hesiod's second great poem, addressed to his brother Perses on farming, justice, and the seasons, was called what?
context: c. 700 BC. Includes the Pandora myth, the five ages of man, and practical agricultural advice — the first 'farmer's almanac' in Western literature.

question: Pandora's container — for most of Western art history called a 'box' — was originally what kind of vessel in Hesiod's Greek?
context: Erasmus translated 'pithos' as 'pyxis' (box) in his 1508 Adagia. The mistranslation stuck. A pithos was a large storage jar — the same kind in which Diogenes lived.

question: Hesiod opens the Theogony with the nine Muses singing on a mountain. Which mountain?
context: Sacred to the Muses, in Boeotia. Hesiod was tending sheep there when they appeared and gave him a laurel staff and the gift of song. He wrote two great poems thereafter.

question: Zeus blasted a monstrous hundred-headed son of Gaia and buried him beneath which Sicilian volcano?
context: Typhon was the last great challenge to Zeus's rule. His thrashing under Etna explains its eruptions. He fathered most of Greek myth's monsters with Echidna.

question: Zeus turned a mortal princess into a white cow to hide her from Hera; Hera demanded the cow and tormented her with a gadfly. Who was the princess?
context: She wandered from Greece to Egypt, where Zeus restored her shape. Their son Epaphus founded the line that produced the kings of Egypt (in Greek mythology).

question: Artemis's nymph Callisto was seduced by Zeus, banished by Artemis, transformed into a bear by Hera, and placed in the sky as which constellation?
context: Her son by Zeus, Arcas, became the Little Bear (Ursa Minor) — or her arc-aiming hunter, depending on the version. Arcadia was named for him.

question: Heracles's twelve labors began with the strangling of an invulnerable lion. From which place?
context: The Nemean Lion's skin became his cloak. The constellation Leo memorializes it. Set as the first labor by King Eurystheus of Mycenae, who hid from Heracles in a bronze jar.

question: Heracles's third labor was to capture a golden-horned deer sacred to Artemis. He pursued it for how long?
context: The Ceryneian Hind. He caught it in Hyperborea and brought it alive to Eurystheus. Artemis met him on the way and demanded its release; he negotiated her acceptance.

question: Heracles's fourth labor was to capture alive a giant boar from which mountain?
context: Eurystheus hid in his bronze jar when Heracles arrived with the boar over his shoulders. Heracles fought Pholus and other centaurs in the same labor.

question: Heracles's sixth labor was to drive off birds with bronze beaks from a marsh. He used a bronze rattle gifted by which goddess?
context: The bronze rattle (krotala) was forged by Hephaestus. The Stymphalian Birds, man-eating, had been bred by Ares. They fled to the island of Aretias, where the Argonauts later met them.

question: Heracles's seventh labor was to capture a rampaging bull from which Greek island?
context: The same bull was father (with Pasiphae) of the Minotaur. Heracles brought it back; Eurystheus released it. It wandered to Marathon, where Theseus killed it as a labor of his own.

question: Heracles's eighth labor was to capture the man-eating mares of which Thracian king?
context: He fed Diomedes himself to the mares to tame them. Heracles's friend Abderus was eaten before that solution presented itself; the city of Abdera was founded in his memory.

question: Heracles's tenth labor was to fetch the red cattle of a three-bodied giant on the island Erythia. Whose cattle?
context: Geryon's herdsman was Eurytion and dog Orthrus. Heracles killed all three and drove the cattle across Europe — Hesperia. Cacus stole some near future Rome; Heracles killed him.

question: Theseus negotiated the labyrinth using a thread given by Minos's daughter Ariadne. What was the thread tied to?
context: He played it out as he went, then followed it back. The story is the original 'Ariadne's thread' for solving complex problems.

question: The Minotaur was the offspring of Queen Pasiphae of Crete and which animal, by a curse of Poseidon?
context: Daedalus crafted a wooden cow for Pasiphae to hide in. The Minotaur — 'bull of Minos' — was kept in the labyrinth and fed Athenian youths every nine years.

question: Theseus's father — king of Athens — threw himself into the sea when he saw Theseus's ship returning under black sails instead of white. Who was the king?
context: Theseus had forgotten to change the sails after killing the Minotaur. The Aegean Sea bears his father's name.

question: After his accidental wounding by Heracles's poisoned arrow, the wise centaur Chiron asked Zeus for what?
context: He was immortal but in agony. He swapped his immortality with Prometheus, who was thus freed. Zeus set Chiron in the sky as Sagittarius — the archer-centaur.

question: The Pythia at Delphi inhaled vapors rising from a chasm beneath the temple before prophesying. Modern geology suggests the vapor was probably what?
context: A 2001 study by de Boer and colleagues found ethylene seeping from a fault beneath the adyton. Ethylene was used as an anesthetic in the early 20th century — known to produce euphoric trance.

question: When Croesus of Lydia asked the Delphic oracle if he should attack Persia, the response was: 'if you cross the river, you will destroy a great empire'. Whose empire?
context: Croesus crossed the Halys, was crushed by Cyrus the Great in 547 BC, and lost Lydia. Herodotus's account makes the story the archetype of an ambiguous oracle.

question: The Delphic oracle reportedly told Chaerephon that no man in Athens was wiser than which philosopher?
context: Plato's Apology — the source. Socrates spent years checking the oracle by interrogating those who thought themselves wise. He concluded the oracle meant he alone knew that he knew nothing.

question: Alexander the Great consulted an oracle of Zeus-Amun in 331 BC, where he was reportedly hailed as a god's son. In which Egyptian desert oasis?
context: Eight days west of Memphis through the Western Desert. Alexander was greeted as son of Amun (Egyptian) / Zeus (Greek). The vision shaped his later self-presentation as god-king.

question: The Eleusinian Mysteries promised initiates a blessed afterlife. Their central revelation has remained largely unknown because they were sworn to do what?
answer: Reveal nothing on pain of death
choices: Reveal nothing on pain of death
context: Lasted from c. 1500 BC to 392 AD — over 1,800 years. The secrecy held remarkably. Among initiates: Pythagoras, Sophocles, Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Augustus, Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius.

question: The Greek myth explaining the cycle of seasons holds that the earth is barren during the months Persephone spends where?
context: Demeter's grief and search for her daughter give the Eleusinian Mysteries their narrative core. Persephone returns each spring; harvests come; she descends each autumn; winter follows.

question: Dionysus was born twice — first from his mortal mother Semele, killed by Zeus's lightning when she insisted on seeing him in glory, and then from where?
context: Hera had tricked Semele into asking. Zeus rescued the unborn child by sewing him into his thigh until he came to term. Hence 'twice-born' — and the cult title Dimetor.

question: King Midas grew donkey ears as a punishment for judging which god's music better than Apollo's?
context: He had hidden the ears under a turban; his barber whispered the secret into a hole, but reeds grew up and whispered 'King Midas has ass's ears'. Ovid's Metamorphoses 11.

question: A satyr who challenged Apollo to a music contest and lost was flayed alive — his skin hung in a cave as warning. Who?
context: He played the aulos (double flute); Apollo played the lyre. The Muses judged. The flayed Marsyas became a Renaissance symbol of artistic suffering; Titian painted it in his old age.

question: Most of the dead in the Greek underworld went to a neutral region of pale flowers, neither rewarded nor punished. What was it called?
context: Asphodel — a Mediterranean lily-like plant. Achilles in Homer's Odyssey would rather be a slave on earth than king of the asphodel meadows. Most of the dead did not rate Tartarus or Elysium.

question: The Argonauts' ship was built with sacred oak from which oracle's grove?
context: Dodona — the oldest Greek oracle, sacred to Zeus. A talking timber from the grove was set in the prow. Athena helped build the ship. The Argo became the constellation Argo Navis.

question: The Argonauts passed two great rocks that smashed together. They sent which bird through first to test the timing?
context: The Symplegades — the 'clashing rocks' — were at the Bosphorus. The dove lost a tail-feather; the Argo lost a stern ornament. After the Argo passed, the rocks were fixed in place.

question: After Orpheus was torn apart by maenads, his head floated down which river singing?
context: His head was washed to Lesbos, where it became an oracle until Apollo silenced it. The Hebrus is now the Maritsa, flowing through Bulgaria, Greece, and Turkey to the Aegean.

question: Aphrodite set Psyche four impossible tasks to win back her husband Eros. The first was to sort a vast pile of mixed seeds before nightfall. Who helped?
context: The ants felt pity. Other tasks: fetching golden fleece; filling a jar from the Styx; bringing back beauty in a box from Persephone. She failed only the last by opening the box.

question: Phrixus reached Colchis and gave its king the Golden Fleece. The king's name was what?
context: Aietes was the son of Helios; brother of Circe; father of Medea. Jason — sent by Pelias of Iolcus to fetch the fleece — won Medea's help, betrayal of her father, and her flight.

question: Perseus accidentally killed his grandfather Acrisius with a discus throw, fulfilling the prophecy Acrisius had tried to prevent by locking up Perseus's mother Danae. The death occurred at games in which city?
context: Acrisius had been visiting Larissa. Perseus, traveling through, competed in funeral games. The discus deflected and struck Acrisius. He afterward refused to take the throne of Argos in remorse.

question: Perseus founded which Greek city — capital of the Mycenaean civilization?
context: According to legend. Mycenae was a real Bronze Age citadel, c. 1600-1100 BC. Excavated by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 — who claimed to have found the gold death-mask of Agamemnon.

question: On Agamemnon's return from Troy, his wife murdered him in his bath. Who was she?
context: Aeschylus, Oresteia. She wove a robe to entangle him, then struck with an axe. She had two motives: avenging Iphigenia and her own affair with Aegisthus during his ten-year absence.

question: Agamemnon's son avenged his father by killing his own mother Clytemnestra. The Furies then pursued him. Who?
context: Apollo had ordered the matricide. Athena established the first murder trial in Athens to acquit him. Aeschylus's Eumenides turns the Furies into protectors of the city.

question: At Aulis, just as Agamemnon's blade was about to fall on his daughter, Artemis snatched her away and substituted what?
context: Euripides's Iphigenia in Aulis and Iphigenia in Tauris. She became a priestess of Artemis among the Taurians on the Black Sea — eventually rescued by her brother Orestes.

question: Theseus's son was killed when his stepmother falsely accused him of attempting her, and Poseidon sent a sea-monster to spook his chariot-horses. Who was the son?
context: Phaedra, the stepmother, hanged herself after writing the false accusation. Euripides's Hippolytus (428 BC) tells the story. The young hero had sworn celibacy to Artemis.

question: A wife agreed to die in her husband's place when no one else would — Heracles wrestled Death and brought her back. Who was she?
context: Wife of King Admetus of Pherae. Euripides's Alcestis (438 BC) tells the story. The first 'wife dies for husband' tale that has become a Western pattern.

question: How many gods are traditionally counted as the Olympian pantheon?
context: The standard twelve: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, and either Dionysus or Hestia. Hades is not counted — he stayed below.

question: Hades is generally not counted among the Twelve Olympians because his realm is what?
context: Brother of Zeus and Poseidon, the three divided the cosmos: Zeus got the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the dead. Hades rarely left his realm — and was generally avoided when he did.

question: The goddess of witchcraft and crossroads, often depicted with three faces or bodies, was called what?
context: Pre-Olympian; honored by all the Olympians. The triple form may relate to her power over earth, sea, and sky. Medea was her priestess. Roman Trivia ('three ways').

question: The moon-goddess fell in love with a beautiful shepherd whom Zeus put into perpetual sleep so she could visit him each night. Who was the shepherd?
context: On Mount Latmos in Caria. They had fifty daughters. The story is in Apollonius's Argonautica. Selene and Artemis were sometimes identified, though originally distinct.

question: The dawn-goddess of Greek myth is described by Homer with what famous epithet?
context: Greek 'rhododaktulos'. Eos (Roman Aurora). Sister of Helios and Selene. Mother of the four winds and the stars. Lover of Tithonus, Cephalus, Orion, and others.

question: The north wind in Greek myth carried off an Athenian princess (Orithyia) to Thrace and fathered Argonauts on her. Who was the wind?
context: The four winds: Boreas (north), Notus (south), Eurus (east), Zephyrus (west). Boreas's sons were the winged Argonauts Zetes and Calais.

question: The west wind in Greek myth married a flower-goddess. Who was the goddess?
context: Roman Flora. Zephyrus was the gentlest wind, harbinger of spring. He had also loved Hyacinthus — his jealousy turned the discus to kill the youth, in some versions of the myth.

question: The Argonauts rescued the blind prophet Phineus from winged half-women who snatched his food. Who were they?
context: Boreas's sons Zetes and Calais — themselves winged — drove the Harpies off. Phineus then prophesied for the Argonauts the way through the Symplegades.

question: The Greek goddess who personified divine retribution against hubris was called what?
context: Daughter of Nyx (Night). She was Helen's mother in some accounts (Zeus pursued her as a goose). She punished those who enjoyed undeserved good fortune as well as the merely overweening.

question: The Greek goddess of fortune and the chance fall of lots was called what?
context: Roman Fortuna. Rose to prominence in the Hellenistic period as old certainties dissolved. Patron of cities — every major Hellenistic city had its Tyche statue with mural crown.

question: The Greek personification of inevitability — a primordial force older than the Olympians — was named what?
context: Mother of the Moirai (Fates). Plato in the Myth of Er has her spindle at the cosmos's center. Even Zeus could not overrule her. Roman Necessitas.

question: In Greek thought, the inevitable comeuppance for overweening pride was called what?
context: Hubris is the offense; Nemesis is the punishment. Ate is the delusion that drives a person to hubris. Sophrosyne (moderation, self-control) is the virtue opposite to hubris.

question: Seven sisters pursued by Orion were turned by Zeus into a star-cluster in Taurus. They were daughters of which Titan?
