question: Odin rode an eight-legged horse, the swiftest of all steeds, who could travel between worlds — down to Hel, up to Asgard, across air, fire, and water. The horse was the offspring of Loki (transformed into a mare) and what stallion?
context: Sleipnir. The improbable conception was Loki's escape from a contract: he had promised the gods that a giant builder could not finish a wall in one season. The giant's horse hauled stones too fast, so Loki distracted it as a mare. Sleipnir resulted.

question: Slain warriors chosen by the Valkyries were brought to Odin's hall, where they feasted on the inexhaustible boar Sahrimnir, drank mead from the goat Heidrun, and fought daily — those killed in practice revived for the evening feast. They were called what?
context: Einherjar. They would fight beside the gods at Ragnarok. Odin sought them: he needed warriors for the final battle. The Valkyries ('choosers of the slain') flew over battles selecting half the dead for Valhalla; Freyja chose the other half for Folkvangr.

question: The thunder god's hammer was the most powerful weapon in the Nine Worlds — forged by dwarves with a flaw (a short handle, because Loki as a fly bit the dwarf at the forge). What was the hammer named?
context: Mjolnir ('grinder' or 'lightning'). It always returned to Thor's hand. It could shrink small enough to be hidden in his clothing. Thor wore iron gloves (Jarngreipr) and a belt that doubled his strength (Megingjord). The hammer-amulet was a popular Viking talisman.

question: When the giant Thrym stole Thor's hammer and demanded Freyja as bride for its return, Loki proposed that Thor disguise himself as Freyja in bridal veil and ride to Jotunheim. At the wedding, when the hammer was brought out to bless the bride, Thor seized it and what?
answer: Killed Thrym and all the giants
choices: Killed Thrym and all the giants
Threw the hammer at his bride-stealer
context: Thrymskvida (one of the funniest Eddic poems). Thor ate an ox, eight salmon, and three vats of mead at the wedding — Loki explained Freyja was hungry. Thrym suspected nothing. Thor slaughtered everyone. The myth combines high drama and broad comedy.

question: Thor and Loki traveled to the hall of the giant Utgarda-Loki, who challenged them to contests. Thor drank from a horn but could not empty it; he tried to lift a gray cat from the floor but could only raise one paw; he wrestled an old crone to a knee. What were they actually?
answer: The ocean, Jormungandr, and Old Age
choices: The ocean, Jormungandr, and Old Age
context: Gylfaginning. The horn touched the world-encircling sea; the cat was actually the Midgard Serpent in disguise; the old woman was Elli ('Old Age'). Even Thor cannot defeat Old Age — but he had shaken the world. The giant Skrymir's snoring made the mountains tremble.

question: Thor went fishing with the giant Hymir, using an ox's head as bait. He hauled up the world-encircling serpent and was about to strike it dead when Hymir, terrified, cut the line. What is the serpent's name?
context: Jormungandr, child of Loki and Angrboda. Thor and the serpent's mutual destiny — Thor kills him at Ragnarok, then dies of his venom nine paces later. The two are the world's destined enemies.

question: Loki's shape-shifting included becoming a mare to distract the giant Svadilfari and prevent a wall being built in time. From this union Loki bore an eight-legged foal — which he gave to Odin. What was the foal?
context: Sleipnir. Loki's parentage of a horse he himself bore is one of mythology's strangest moments. Loki also fathered the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jormungandr, and the goddess Hel with the giantess Angrboda — and Helblindi and Byleist with Laufey.

question: Frigg secured oaths from everything in creation not to harm her beautiful son — except one plant deemed too young to swear. The gods threw weapons at the invulnerable Baldr for sport. Loki tricked the blind god Hodr into throwing what at him?
context: Mistletoe. Baldr died — the most beloved of the gods. Hermod rode to Hel to ransom him; she said yes if all creation wept for him. Only one giantess Thokk (Loki in disguise) refused — Baldr stayed in Hel until after Ragnarok.

question: After Baldr's death and his insults to all the gods at Aegir's feast (Lokasenna), Loki fled. The gods caught him, bound him over three sharp rocks with the entrails of his own son turned to iron. A serpent dripped venom on his face. Who held the bowl?
context: Sigyn. When she emptied the bowl to pour out venom, drops fell on Loki and his writhing caused earthquakes. He stayed bound until Ragnarok, when he broke free and led the giants and dead against the gods.

question: When Baldr dreamed his own death, his mother went out and asked an oath of every thing in creation — fire, water, metal, stone, every creature — not to harm her son. She missed one small plant. What was her name, and what plant?
context: Frigg. Mistletoe ('mistilteinn'). Loki extracted from Frigg her admission of the oversight. Mistletoe's modern Christmas associations were possibly imported by Norse Yule traditions. The 'kiss under the mistletoe' may originate in the gods' guilt over Baldr's death.

question: After Baldr was killed by mistletoe, the gods bore his body to his ship Hringhorni for cremation. They could not push it out to sea until the giantess Hyrrokin came — and her giant-wolf mount terrified the gods. Who lit the pyre?
choices: Heimdall blew his horn over it
context: Hyrrokin pushed the ship; Thor blessed (or struck) it. His pregnant wife Nanna died of grief and was placed on the pyre with him. Even Baldr's horse was burned with him. Odin laid the gold ring Draupnir on the pyre as parting gift.

question: When the Aesir tried to bind the growing wolf Fenrir, who they knew would devour Odin at Ragnarok, he agreed only if a god placed a hand in his mouth as pledge. He bit it off when he found himself bound. Whose hand?
context: Tyr. The god of justice and oath-keeping sacrificed his sword-hand to bind the world's enemy. The dwarven chain Gleipnir held Fenrir — made from six impossible things including the footfall of a cat and the breath of a fish.

question: After Fenrir broke two normal chains (Leyding and Dromi), the gods commissioned the dwarves of Svartalfheim to forge an unbreakable cord. They made it from six impossible things. Name three.
answer: Cat's footfall, woman's beard, fish's breath
choices: Cat's footfall, woman's beard, fish's breath
Stone's blood, hare's tail, wolf's mercy
Sun's shadow, moon's heat, snow's sound
Tree's tear, dragon's pity, eagle's silence
context: Gleipnir's six ingredients: footfall of a cat, beard of a woman, roots of a mountain, sinews of a bear, breath of a fish, spittle of a bird. Smooth as a silken ribbon. The dwarves of Svartalfheim were the great craftsmen of Norse cosmology.

question: The Vanir fertility god sat on Odin's throne Hlidskjalf (forbidden to others) and saw a giantess of such beauty he despaired of love. His servant Skirnir went to woo her, taking Freyr's magical self-fighting sword. What was lost?
context: Skirnismal. Freyr won Gerd but lost his sword. At Ragnarok he must fight Surt without it — and dies because of the lack. The god's choice: love now versus survival at the world's end. The sword was made by dwarves and fought of its own accord.

question: The Vanir god received from the dwarves a ship that could be folded up small enough to fit in a pouch, always sailed with a fair wind, and could carry all the gods. What was the ship?
context: Skidbladnir, made by the sons of Ivaldi. Freyr also received the boar Gullinbursti ('Golden-bristled') from the dwarves Brokk and Eitri — same competition that produced Mjolnir and Sif's golden hair.

question: The Vanir love-and-war goddess obtained her most prized necklace from four dwarven smiths by sleeping with each of them in turn. Loki later stole it from her. What was the necklace?
context: Brisingamen ('necklace of the Brisings'). Loki transformed into a flea to enter Freyja's chamber. Heimdall caught him by transforming into a seal; their fight prefigured the deeper destiny — Heimdall kills Loki at Ragnarok, and Loki kills Heimdall.

question: Half the slain warriors went to Odin's Valhalla; the other half went to a hall belonging to the Vanir love goddess, where she rode in a chariot drawn by two great cats. What was her hall, and what cats?
context: Folkvangr ('field of the host') and her hall Sessrumnir ('roomy-seat'). The cats are unnamed but were probably Norwegian Forest Cats. Freyja got first pick of the battle-slain — Odin took the second half. She also taught the Aesir 'seidr' magic.

question: Goddess of youth who kept golden apples in her ash-wood box. The gods ate them and stayed young. When Loki betrayed her to the giant Thiazi, the gods began to age and grow gray. Who?
context: Idunn. Loki had to rescue her, becoming a falcon (with Freyja's cloak) and carrying her back as a nut. Thiazi pursued as an eagle and was burned in fires the gods set on Asgard's walls. His daughter Skadi later married Njord in compensation.

question: The white god guarded Bifrost, slept like a bird (needed less sleep than any other god), could see for hundreds of leagues, and heard grass growing. At Ragnarok he would sound his horn to call the gods to battle. What horn?
context: Gjallarhorn ('resounding horn'). Heimdall was also called Rig — and per the Rigsthula fathered the three Norse social classes: Thrall (slave), Karl (free farmer), Jarl (noble). At Ragnarok Heimdall and Loki kill each other.

question: When the giant Thiazi was killed by the gods, his daughter came to Asgard for vengeance, armed and armored. The gods placated her with reparations: the right to marry one of them, but choosing only by his feet. She chose the most beautiful feet — and got the wrong god. Why?
answer: She thought beautiful feet meant Baldr, got Njord
choices: She thought beautiful feet meant Baldr, got Njord
She thought ugly feet meant Loki, got Heimdall
She thought hairy feet meant Thor, got Tyr
She thought scarred feet meant Tyr, got Odin
context: Skadi. Njord's feet were beautiful from sea-water. Their marriage failed — she missed mountains and wolves, he missed the sea and gulls. They divorced. Skadi married Ullr or Odin in later sources; she became goddess of skiing, hunting, and winter.

question: At Ragnarok, the wolf Fenrir would swallow Odin. The all-father's son — known for silence and great strength — would avenge him by stepping on Fenrir's lower jaw with a magical shoe and tearing his upper jaw apart. Who?
context: Vidar. His shoe was made from all the leather scraps that humans had ever cut from their shoes — a centuries-long accumulation. Norse pieties may have called for cutting shoe-leather mindfully to contribute to Vidar's shoe.

question: After Baldr died, his brother rode Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir down to Hel to ransom him back. Hel said she would release him if all the world wept for him. Who was the brother?
context: Hermod. He rode nine nights through deep dark valleys, crossed the Gjallarbru bridge over the Gjoll river (guarded by the giantess Modgudr), and addressed Hel. Hermod returned with the golden ring Draupnir as token but without Baldr.

question: The brother of Baldr — born blind — was tricked by Loki into throwing a dart of mistletoe that killed his beloved kinsman. Who was the blind god?
context: Hodr (Hod). After Baldr's death, Vali (newborn but grown to manhood in a day) avenged Baldr by killing Hodr. The Baldr-Hodr cycle anticipates the death-and-return Christian Christology that early Christianizers found in Norse myth — useful for syncretism.

question: The Aesir god of poetry and eloquence, husband of the youth-keeping goddess Idunn. His name became a Norse word for poetic skill and Icelandic skald-craft. Who?
context: Bragi. His name shares root with 'brag' in English. He greeted Loki at Aegir's feast and was insulted; he greeted brave warriors entering Valhalla. The 'bragarfull' (Bragi's cup) was the cup oaths were sworn over in Viking-age feasts.

question: The end of the Norse cosmos: a fierce three-year winter (Fimbulwinter), Loki freed, the giants and dead marching on Asgard, sun and moon swallowed by wolves, the world tree shaken, gods and giants dying together, the world burned and sunk — then reborn. What is it called?
context: Voluspa ('Prophecy of the Seeress') gives the fullest account. Wagner's 'Ragnarok' / 'Twilight of the Gods' (Gotterdammerung — German cognate). Two humans (Lif and Lifthrasir) survive in a wood; Baldr returns from Hel; the world is reborn green.

question: Three winters without summer in a row — preceding the gods' doom. Wolves swallow the sun and moon; brothers slay brothers; cosmic moral order collapses. What is this prelude to Ragnarok called?
context: Fimbulwinter has been speculatively associated with the 535-536 climate anomaly (likely a volcanic dust veil) that devastated Scandinavia. Cosmic violence in myth may have echoed climatic memory. The world's seasons themselves break before the gods fall.

question: From Muspelheim at Ragnarok will come a fire-giant wielding a flaming sword brighter than the sun. He will fight Freyr (who lost his sword for love), kill him, and then set the whole world ablaze. Who?
context: Surt ('the swarthy'). His sword is brighter than the sun. After the gods are all dead, his fire consumes the nine worlds, the seas rise, the world sinks. Then a new world rises green from the sea — fertile and clean.

question: At Ragnarok a great ship will set sail from Helheim bearing the dead against the gods. It is made entirely from the untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead. What is its name?
context: Naglfar ('nail-farer'). Norse custom: trim the nails of the dead before burial to slow the ship's completion. Loki captains it. The ferryman is the giant Hrym (or in another version Loki himself). Cosmic horror: even your nail clippings might fight the gods.

question: At Ragnarok, two great wolves who had been chasing the sun and moon across the sky finally caught and devoured them. The world turned dark. Who are the wolves?
context: Skoll ('treachery') chased Sol the sun; Hati ('hate') chased Mani the moon. They were sons of Fenrir. Their kin Fenrir himself swallowed Odin. Vidar avenged Odin by tearing Fenrir's jaws. The Norse cosmos was always racing toward its end.

question: When the world burns at Ragnarok, two human survivors hide in a wood called Hoddmimis Holt (the holly of Hod's memory). They eat the morning dew. When the new earth rises, they emerge and repopulate. Who are they?
context: Lif ('life') and Lifthrasir ('eager for life'). The Norse cosmos ends and begins again — cyclical eschatology rather than linear. Baldr also returns from Hel. A new generation of gods (Vidar, Vali, Modi, Magni — sons of Odin and Thor) rules.

question: Around 1220 in Iceland, a Christian poet, politician, and historian compiled a handbook of Norse mythology for aspiring skalds, organizing the tradition systematically (Gylfaginning, Skaldskaparmal, Hattatal). Without this our Norse myth would be fragments. Who?
context: Snorri (1179-1241). Murdered in his cellar at Reykholt by orders of King Hakon IV of Norway. His Prose Edda became the main systematized source. His Heimskringla (sagas of Norwegian kings) is also priceless. Pagan myth preserved by a Christian.

question: A 13th-century Icelandic manuscript (the Codex Regius, 'King's Book') preserved roughly 31 anonymous Old Norse poems on mythology and heroic legend — including Voluspa, Havamal, Thrymskvida, Volundarkvitha. What is the collection called?
context: The Codex Regius (c. 1270). Lost from view, rediscovered 1643. Gifted to the King of Denmark; returned to Iceland 1971 as national treasure. The Poetic Edda preserves mythology in its rawest poetic form — without Snorri's systematic editing.

question: The greatest poem of the Poetic Edda — a prophetess raises herself from the dead at Odin's command and reveals to him the world's creation, the rise of the gods, the murder of Baldr, the coming of Ragnarok, and the rebirth. What is the poem?
context: Voluspa ('the seeress's prophecy'). 66 stanzas — 1,000 years of Norse cosmological thought condensed. Probably composed late 10th century when Norse paganism was meeting Christianity. The volva (seeress) is the Norse equivalent of the Pythia.

question: Approximately 165 stanzas of Norse wisdom literature attributed to Odin: gnomic verses on hospitality, friendship, women, drinking, the impermanence of wealth, the impermanence of self ('cattle die, kindred die...'). What is it called?
context: Havamal ('Sayings of the High One'). The famous lines on death: 'Cattle die, kindred die / Every man is mortal. / But the good name never dies / Of one who has done well.' Practical wisdom shaped by Viking-age values.

question: In one of the most acidic Eddic poems, Loki crashes a feast at Aegir's hall and insults every god and goddess in turn — exposing their cuckoldries, cowardices, and incests. Thor finally drives him out. What is the poem?
context: Lokasenna ('Loki's quarrel'). The poem may be a late composition by a Christian skald sending up the old gods — or it may preserve genuinely scandalous traditions. The gods' moral untidiness, comparable to Greek Olympians.

question: Court poetry of the Viking age used elaborate metaphorical substitutions — 'whale-road' for sea, 'gore-sweat' for blood, 'wave-horse' for ship, 'feeder of the ravens' for warrior. What are these metaphors called?
context: Kennings. Skalds were the court poets; their compositions praised kings, recorded battles, and demanded technical virtuosity. Egil Skallagrimsson is the most famous skald. Kennings can be many-layered: 'feeder of ravens' = warrior; 'feeder of feeders of ravens' = king.

question: In 930 AD Icelandic settlers gathered annually at Thingvellir to make laws, settle disputes, and elect a lawspeaker who recited the law from memory. This was the oldest continuously existing what?
context: Althing. Met at the edge of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge — Eurasian and North American plates literally pulling apart there. The 1944 republic was founded at Thingvellir. The site remains symbolic of Icelandic democracy and independence.

question: In 1000 AD at the Althing, Iceland faced civil war over religion. The lawspeaker Thorgeir Thorkelsson lay under a cloak for a day, then proposed a compromise: all would accept Christianity outwardly, but pagan practices could continue in private. What practices were kept private?
answer: Horse meat, exposure of infants, sacrifice
choices: Horse meat, exposure of infants, sacrifice
context: Thorgeir's compromise allowed gradual Christianization without civil war. Within decades the private exceptions were also abandoned. Iceland's conversion was one of the most peaceful in Europe — and Christian Iceland uniquely preserved the pagan tradition through Snorri.

question: Every nine years at the great pagan temple of Uppsala in Sweden, mass sacrifices were held to Odin, Thor, and Frey. Adam of Bremen (c. 1075) recorded that nine males of every species — including humans — were sacrificed and hung in a sacred grove. What kind of sacrifice?
context: Adam of Bremen's account of human sacrifice at Uppsala is widely accepted, though some scholars question particulars. Norse paganism's underbelly: ritual slavery, human sacrifice, raiding as religious vocation. The Christianization of Sweden was largely complete by c. 1100.

question: A form of magic associated with Freyja and Odin — divination, fate-weaving, prophecy. The volva carried a staff (vand) and chanted from an elevated seat. Men who practiced it were considered effeminate ('ergi'). What was this practice?
context: Seidr. Freyja taught seidr to Odin — who learned it despite the gender associations. The volva (seeress) practiced seidr; Eric the Red's saga preserves a vivid description of a volva visiting a Greenland farm. Seidr involved trance, song, and fate-shaping.

question: One of the greatest Icelandic family sagas — about a 10th-century farmer, warrior, and skald who killed his first man at age seven, served kings and feuded with them, and composed some of the greatest skaldic poetry. Who?
context: Egil's Saga. Probably written by Snorri Sturluson c. 1230s. Egil's grandson. Captures the Norse poet-warrior ideal — ferocity, treasure-quest, and verse alike. His poem 'Sonatorrek' ('Loss of Sons') is one of medieval literature's great elegies.

question: The longest and arguably greatest Icelandic family saga — a 10th-11th century tale of feud and friendship in southern Iceland ending in the burning of a wise man and his family in their hall. Who was burned?
context: Njal's Saga, c. 1280. Anonymous. The summit of saga literature. Njal's lawyerly wisdom could not save him from blood-feud's logic. His friendship with Gunnar (Gunnar of Hlidarendi) and their tragedies illuminate Iceland's culture as it was leaving the heroic age.

question: Between 200 and 500 AD, rabbis in Palestine and Babylonia compiled the oral law (Mishnah) and surrounding commentary (Gemara) into a vast collection of legal discussion, ethics, lore, and biblical interpretation. Together they form what?
context: Two Talmuds: the Babylonian (more authoritative, completed c. 500 AD) and the Jerusalem (Palestinian, completed c. 400 AD). The Talmud became the foundation of rabbinic Judaism, replacing temple sacrifice with law-study after the temple's 70 AD destruction.

question: A 12th-century Andalusian-born Jewish philosopher, physician, and rabbi codified Jewish law in the Mishneh Torah (1180), reconciled Aristotle with Judaism in the Guide for the Perplexed (1190), and formulated 13 principles of Jewish faith. Who?
context: Maimonides (1135-1204). Born in Cordoba, fled Almohad persecution to Fez and then Egypt. Court physician to Saladin. His 13 principles became the basis of the daily prayer 'Yigdal'. His tomb in Tiberias remains a pilgrimage site.

question: Around 1280 in Castile, Moses de Leon began circulating manuscripts of a mystical commentary on the Torah in Aramaic, attributed to the 2nd-century Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. The book systematized the Sefirot — the ten emanations of God. What is it called?
context: The Zohar ('splendor'). Foundational text of Kabbalah. Scholem's modern scholarship attributed it to de Leon's composition. The 16th-century Lurianic Kabbalah of Safed (Isaac Luria) added the concepts of tzimtzum (divine contraction), shevirat ha-kelim (breaking of vessels), and tikkun olam (repair).

question: Nazi Germany's systematic murder of European Jewry from 1941-1945 killed approximately 6 million — two-thirds of European Jewry. The plan was finalized at the Wannsee Conference in January 1942. What Hebrew term names the catastrophe?
context: Shoah ('catastrophe' or 'utter destruction') — preferred by many Jewish writers over 'Holocaust' (Greek 'whole burnt offering') because it does not religiously frame the killing as sacrifice. Yom HaShoah (April-May) commemorates the dead. Yad Vashem in Jerusalem is the memorial.

question: Captured by Mossad agents in Buenos Aires in 1960 and brought to Israel for trial, the Nazi logistics chief of the Holocaust was hanged in 1962 — the only person Israel has ever judicially executed. Hannah Arendt covered the trial and coined the phrase 'the banality of evil'. Who?
context: (1906-1962). Eichmann had organized the trains. Arendt's 1963 book 'Eichmann in Jerusalem' argued his evil was not demonic but bureaucratic — a thesis fiercely debated since. He was tried in glass booth and convicted; his ashes were scattered at sea outside Israeli waters.

question: In 622 AD, persecuted in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers migrated to Yathrib (later renamed Medinat al-Nabi, 'City of the Prophet'). This migration begins the Islamic calendar. What is it called?
context: Hijra. AH 1 = 622 AD. The Hijri calendar is lunar (354-355 days), so Islamic festivals (Ramadan, Hajj) drift through the Gregorian seasons. From Medina Muhammad fought the Meccans (Badr 624, Uhud 625, Trench 627), then conquered Mecca in 630.

question: The five obligatory acts of Sunni Islam: shahada (declaration of faith), salat (prayer five times daily), zakat (alms), sawm (fasting in Ramadan), and what fifth?
context: The Five Pillars. Hajj is obligatory once in a lifetime if physically and financially able. Shia Islam adds further pillars (e.g., walaya — loyalty to the Imams). Some Khariji and other small groups add jihad as a sixth pillar.

question: A 12th-century Andalusian Muslim philosopher (1126-1198 AD) wrote definitive commentaries on Aristotle, defending philosophy against the religious skepticism of al-Ghazali. His Latinized name. Who?
context: Averroes. Born in Cordoba, served as qadi (judge) of Seville and Cordoba. Court physician to the Almohad caliphs. His Aristotle commentaries dominated Latin scholastic philosophy — Aquinas spent decades engaging him. Latin Averroists at Paris read him heterodoxly.

question: An 11th-century Persian Sunni theologian and philosopher (1058-1111 AD) wrote 'The Incoherence of the Philosophers' (Tahafut al-Falasifa, c. 1095), arguing that Aristotelian philosophy as practiced by Avicenna contradicted Islam. He turned to Sufism. Who?
context: Al-Ghazali's critique of causation — denying necessary cause-effect relations — was central to the Asharite turn that closed the Islamic Golden Age's openness to natural philosophy. Averroes answered with 'The Incoherence of the Incoherence' but al-Ghazali won the long argument inside Islam.

question: A 13th-century Persian Sufi poet (1207-1273 AD) settled in Konya, Anatolia, wrote the six-volume 'Mathnawi' — a treasury of mystical love-poetry — after his transformative friendship with the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz. Who?
context: Rumi. His followers became the Mevlevi order — the 'Whirling Dervishes' who spin in mystical dance. Rumi is the best-selling poet in America today (Coleman Barks's free translations). 'I died as mineral and became a plant...' captures the Sufi vision of transformation.

question: In 1324 the emperor of Mali — perhaps the richest man in human history — made the Hajj from West Africa to Mecca with a caravan of 60,000 (including 12,000 slaves carrying gold). His spending in Cairo crashed the Egyptian gold economy for a decade. Who?
context: Mansa Musa (r. 1312-1337). His Hajj put Mali on European maps for the first time — the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows him on a gold throne. He built mosques in Timbuktu and brought scholars back. Mali was a major center of Islamic learning into the 16th century.

question: In 1979 the Pahlavi monarchy in Iran was overthrown by a popular revolution led by a Shia clergyman who had spent 14 years in exile. He returned to Tehran in February and established the Islamic Republic. Who?
context: Khomeini (1902-1989). 'Velayat-e-Faqih' (guardianship of the jurist) became the regime's organizing principle — the supreme leader is a cleric, not just an elected president. The 1979 revolution marked a watershed in modern Islamism. Iran-Iraq War 1980-88 killed perhaps a million.

question: After conquering Kalinga with hideous bloodshed in 261 BC, an Indian emperor was so horrified by the suffering he caused that he converted to Buddhism, renounced violent conquest, and erected pillars and rock edicts proclaiming Buddhist ethics across his empire. Who?
context: Ashoka (r. 268-232 BC). His pillars, carved with edicts on dharma and tolerance, survive — the Lion Capital at Sarnath became modern India's emblem. He sent Buddhist missionaries throughout Asia and to the Hellenistic Mediterranean. Buddhism transformed under his patronage from regional sect to world religion.

question: Buddhism divided over the centuries into major schools. The southern school (Sri Lanka, Thailand, Burma) emphasizes individual liberation through monastic practice and the Pali Canon. What is it called?
context: Theravada ('teaching of the elders'). Mahayana ('greater vehicle') spread to East Asia (China, Korea, Japan) and emphasizes bodhisattvas who postpone nirvana to help others. Vajrayana ('diamond vehicle') developed in Tibet from Mahayana with tantric practices.

question: The Tibetan Buddhist tradition holds that one of its highest spiritual leaders is reincarnated repeatedly. The current incarnation, the 14th, was born in 1935 and fled to India in 1959 after the Chinese Communist suppression. Who?
context: Tenzin Gyatso. The Gelugpa school's leader. Nobel Peace Prize 1989. China's Cultural Revolution destroyed roughly 6,000 of Tibet's 6,000+ monasteries. The 'Tibetan question' remains a sore point in Chinese international relations.

question: Philosophical texts (c. 900-500 BC) at the end of the Vedic corpus turned from external ritual to internal meditation, exploring the ultimate reality (Brahman) and its identity with the individual self (Atman). 'Tat tvam asi' — what is the famous phrase?
context: The Chandogya Upanishad's 'Tat tvam asi'. Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism) — Brahman alone is real; the individual self's separateness is illusion (maya). Shankara (c. 800 AD) systematized this; Ramanuja (12th c.) gave a qualified non-dualist alternative.

question: Set on the eve of the great Mahabharata battle at Kurukshetra, this 700-verse poem records a dialogue between a doubting prince refusing to fight his kinsmen and his charioteer (revealed to be God incarnate). What is the text?
context: The Gita teaches the paths of karma yoga (action without attachment), bhakti yoga (devotion), and jnana yoga (knowledge). Krishna reveals his cosmic form (Vishvarupa) — the source of Oppenheimer's quotation ('I am become Death, destroyer of worlds') at the first atom bomb.

question: One of two great Hindu epics — composed by the sage Valmiki — tells of a king of Ayodhya exiled to the forest with his wife and brother, his wife abducted by a demon king of Lanka, and rescue by an army of monkeys led by the devoted minister Hanuman. Whose story?
context: Ramayana. 24,000 verses. Rama as ideal king, Sita as ideal wife, Hanuman as ideal devotee. Ravana, the ten-headed demon king of Lanka. Diwali commemorates Rama's return. The Ramayana remains foundational in Indian and Southeast Asian cultures — performed across Java, Bali, Thailand.

question: The eighth (in some lists) avatar of Vishnu — the divine cowherd of Vrindavan whose flute called the gopis (cowgirls), the dark prince of the Mahabharata who taught Arjuna at Kurukshetra, the playful child who stole butter from his mother's house. Who?
context: Krishna. His name means 'dark' or 'all-attractive'. His consort is Radha (in Vrindavan tradition) or Rukmini (in dynastic tradition). The Bhagavad Gita is his teaching. Krishna's devotional cult (bhakti) became one of Hinduism's central streams.

question: The elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati — patron of beginnings, remover of obstacles, scribe of the Mahabharata. He lost his head when Shiva (not recognizing him) decapitated him; Parvati demanded restoration; Shiva grafted the first animal's head he could find. What head?
context: Ganesha (Ganapati). The most beloved deity in India. Invoked before any undertaking. His mount is a mouse. He broke his own tusk to use as a pen for the Mahabharata. The Ganesh Chaturthi festival features mass clay images submerged in water on the tenth day.

question: The dark mother goddess, depicted with four arms — holding a sword, a severed head, a bowl of blood, and making a fear-not gesture. Garlanded with skulls, dancing on the corpse of Shiva. A goddess of destruction and liberation. Who?
context: Kali ('the black one'). Particularly worshipped in Bengal. Ramakrishna Paramahamsa was her devotee. The British misunderstood the Thuggee cult (early 19th c.) as Kali-worshippers — colonial-era exaggeration. Kali appears in Tantra, in Krishnamurti, in the Beatles. Her cult mixes fear and intimate love.

question: The Hindu social system divides humanity into four hereditary classes (varnas) — Brahmin (priests), Kshatriya (warriors), Vaishya (merchants), and Shudra (laborers) — plus those outside the system. The outcaste group was traditionally subject to extreme discrimination. What did B.R. Ambedkar call them?
context: 'Dalit' is the preferred self-designation, used since Ambedkar. 'Harijan' ('children of God') was Gandhi's term — now considered patronizing. India's 1950 Constitution outlawed untouchability; reality persisted. Ambedkar himself converted to Buddhism in 1956 to escape caste, taking 500,000 followers with him.

question: The holiest shrine of Sikhism, built by Guru Arjan in the early 17th century in the city he founded (literally 'Pool of Nectar'), is a marble building covered in gold leaf, surrounded by a sacred reflecting pool. What city, and what is the temple's Punjabi name?
context: Harmandir Sahib (Darbar Sahib). Sikhism's spiritual center. Damaged in Operation Blue Star (June 1984) when Indian troops stormed it to remove militants. Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards in revenge that October. Anti-Sikh riots followed, killing thousands.

question: The Egyptian sun god sailed across the sky each day in his solar barque, then descended into the underworld each night where he fought the serpent Apep (Apophis) before being reborn at dawn. Who?
context: Ra. Centered at Heliopolis. Often combined with Atum (creator) and Amun (Theban god) — Amun-Ra became the empire god of New Kingdom Egypt. Akhenaten in 1350 BC declared the solar disk (Aten) the sole god — Egypt's brief and unsuccessful experiment with monotheism.

question: Egyptian god of the dead and rebirth, murdered and dismembered by his jealous brother. His wife-sister gathered the pieces (all but his phallus, which a fish ate), reassembled and reanimated him long enough to conceive their son. Who is the jealous brother?
context: Osiris. Isis the wife. Set the brother. Horus the son who eventually avenged Osiris by defeating Set. Osiris became judge of the dead — every Egyptian aspired to identify with him after death. His green skin signified regeneration like the Nile flood.

question: In the Egyptian Book of the Dead, the deceased's heart was weighed against the feather of truth on a balance scale before forty-two judges and Osiris. If lighter than the feather, the soul passed to paradise. If heavier — what?
choices: It was burned in the lake of fire
It was returned to the body for another life
It was sent to wander as a shade
context: Ammit, 'the devourer of the dead'. The heart had to be unburdened of sin. Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead has the deceased declaring before each judge 'I have not committed [specific sin].' Ma'at — truth, order, balance — was the central Egyptian moral concept.

question: The 18th-dynasty pharaoh (r. 1353-1336 BC) abandoned the traditional Egyptian pantheon, declared the solar disk Aten the sole god, moved the capital to a new city Amarna, and changed his own name. His reforms barely outlived him. Who?
context: Akhenaten ('servant of Aten'). His wife Nefertiti, his son Tutankhamun. Amarna art is strikingly naturalistic, breaking from millennium-old conventions. After his death, the priests restored the old gods, dismantled Amarna, and erased his name. Tutankhamun's tomb was famously found by Howard Carter in 1922.

question: The oldest surviving substantial literary work in human history, written in cuneiform around 2100 BC (with earlier oral antecedents), concerns a Sumerian king of Uruk who befriends the wild man Enkidu, defies the goddess Ishtar, and seeks immortality after Enkidu's death. Who?
context: The Epic of Gilgamesh. Recovered from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (7th c. BC), translated by George Smith in 1872. Tablet XI contains a flood narrative strikingly parallel to Noah — Utnapishtim survives by building a great boat. Gilgamesh learns immortality belongs only to the gods.

question: The Babylonian creation epic — 'When on high' (the opening words) — narrates how the chief god of Babylon slew the chaos-monster Tiamat and from her body made the cosmos. Read aloud each year at the new year festival. Who is the chief god?
context: Marduk. Tiamat (primordial salt waters) had been the mother of the older generation of gods. Marduk split her body to form heaven and earth. He created humans from the blood of her commander Kingu to serve the gods. The epic became the founding text of Babylonian theology.

question: The chief god of the Aztecs — god of war and the sun — was born from the goddess Coatlicue, fully grown and armed. He slew his sister Coyolxauhqui and his 400 brothers. He required human hearts to sustain the sun. What was his name?
context: Huitzilopochtli ('hummingbird of the south'). His twin temple atop Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan was matched by Tlaloc's. Aztec religion held that the sun required human blood to continue rising — generating the mass-sacrifice imperative. Estimates: 20,000 sacrifices per year at peak.

question: At the Great Temple in Tenochtitlan, Aztec priests cut out human hearts and lifted them still beating to feed the sun. The 1487 rededication may have sacrificed 80,000 captives in four days. The empire's organizing logic was procuring captives. What was the system?
answer: The Flower Wars and tribute warfare
choices: The Flower Wars and tribute warfare
context: Flower wars (xochiyaoyotl) were ritualized battles with neighboring states whose explicit purpose was capturing victims for sacrifice. Aztec religion was not optional ritual — it was the regime's organizing principle. Cortes's success owed much to Mesoamerican peoples who hated the sacrifice imperative.

question: A Mesoamerican god worshipped widely — feathered serpent — patron of priests, learning, calendar. Aztec legend held he had departed eastward but would return. Some have argued Moctezuma briefly thought Cortes might be his return. Who?
context: Quetzalcoatl. The Maya called him Kukulkan; the Mixtec Coo Dzaui. His pyramid at Cholula is the largest by volume in the world. Some scholars now doubt the Moctezuma-Cortes story; it may be a Spanish post-conquest narrative imposed on Aztec memory.

question: The K'iche' Maya creation epic narrates the descent of the Hero Twins (Hunahpu and Xbalanque) into the underworld Xibalba to play ball-games against the lords of death and avenge their father. Recovered by a Dominican priest in the 18th century. What text?
context: Popol Vuh ('council book'). Originally hieroglyphic (mostly destroyed in colonial book-burnings); preserved in colonial-era K'iche' alphabetic text by Francisco Ximenez. The Mesoamerican ball-game appears here in cosmic-significance form. The Hero Twins eventually defeat Xibalba.

question: The priestly caste of pre-Christian Celtic societies — across Gaul, Britain, and Ireland — practiced their rituals in sacred groves (often of which tree?), prophesied, judged disputes, and conducted human sacrifices according to Roman sources (probably exaggerated). Who?
context: Druids ('oak-knowers' — disputed etymology). Caesar's Gallic War provides the main account. Druidic memorization was extensive — 20 years of training, all oral. Roman emperors banned druids. They survived longest in Ireland; Christianized in 5th-6th c. The modern 'Druid' revival is 18th-c. invention.

question: The Shinto sun goddess and ancestress of the Japanese imperial family. After a fight with her brother the storm god, she hid in a cave, plunging the world into darkness. The other gods lured her out with a mirror and a lewd dance. Who is the brother?
context: Amaterasu Omikami. Her shrine at Ise is Shinto's holiest. The Japanese emperor traditionally claimed descent from her. The sacred mirror (Yata no Kagami) is one of the Three Imperial Regalia. Susanoo, after his exile, slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi and recovered the sacred sword Kusanagi.

question: When the storm god Susanoo's outrages drove the Shinto sun goddess into a cave, plunging the world into darkness, the other gods devised a stratagem: the goddess Ame-no-Uzume danced lewdly, the gods laughed, and the sun goddess peeked out curious. What lured her fully out?
answer: Her own reflection in a mirror
choices: Her own reflection in a mirror
A promise of her brother's exile
context: Yata no Kagami (sacred mirror) became one of Three Imperial Regalia. Ame-no-Uzume is the goddess of laughter, dance, and revelry. The myth foundationally links Japanese sovereignty, dawn, mirrors, and joyful absurdity. Ise Shrine houses the mirror still.

question: A culture-hero across Polynesia — Hawaii, Tahiti, Maori — who lassoed the sun to slow its passage, fished up the islands from the sea, stole fire for humanity, and died trying to grant humans immortality by entering the goddess of death. Who?
context: Maui. New Zealand's North Island is 'Te Ika-a-Maui' (Maui's fish). His attempt at immortality: crawling into the sleeping death-goddess Hine-nui-te-po. A bird laughed at the absurdity. She woke and crushed him. Death entered the world.

question: The Hawaiian goddess of fire, lightning, dance, volcanoes, and violence. Sister of the shark god, the wind god, and others. She lives in Kilauea's crater. Tourists who take volcanic rocks from Hawaii report bad luck and mail them back. Who is she?
context: Pele. Her sister Hi'iaka is patron of dance (hula) and healing. Pele's modern cult is alive — sacrifices and prayers still offered. Mark Twain wrote of her devotees. Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop's 19th-c. legacy preserved Pele lore at Bishop Museum.

question: The trickster spider-god of West African (especially Akan/Ashanti) tradition, carried by enslaved Africans to the Caribbean and Americas. Hero of countless folktales of cunning over strength. Who?
context: Anansi. Often portrayed as having stolen all stories from the sky god Nyame. His tales spread to Jamaica ('Anansy stories'), the American South (he became Brer Rabbit in part), and modern children's literature (Eric Kimmel, Neil Gaiman). The trickster motif unites world cultures.

question: Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, defended the Nicene faith against Arianism for nearly fifty years. He was exiled five times by emperors shifting position. A Latin phrase summarizing his lonely stance became proverbial. What does it say?
context: Athanasius's *On the Incarnation*, written before age thirty, remains a classic of patristic theology. His phrase 'God became man so that man might become God' (*theosis*) became central to Eastern Orthodox spirituality.

question: The Council of Chalcedon in 451 AD produced a definition that has bounded mainline Christology for fifteen centuries — describing the union of divine and human in Christ using four adverbs (without confusion, without change, without division, without separation). What did it call the union?
answer: The hypostatic union — two natures, divine and human, in one person.
choices: The hypostatic union — two natures, divine and human, in one person.
The communicatio idiomatum — sharing of attributes between the natures, defined later by Cyril of Alexandria.
The kenotic union — a self-emptying of divinity into humanity, drawn from Philippians 2.
The theandric union — a single divine-human energy, the formula later condemned as Monothelitism.
context: Chalcedon's definition split Christianity. The Oriental Orthodox churches (Copts, Armenians, Syrians, Ethiopians) rejected it, holding to a single 'Miaphysite' nature. The split has not fully healed in fifteen centuries.

question: Augustine, bishop of Hippo for two decades, began a massive work in 413, three years after Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome. Pagans blamed Christianization for the catastrophe. Augustine's answer contrasted two cities. What does he name them?
answer: The City of God and the City of Man — two communities defined by what their members love.
choices: The City of God and the City of Man — two communities defined by what their members love.
The City of Spirit and the City of Flesh — two communities defined by where their members set their treasure.
The City of Light and the City of Shadow — two communities defined by what their members can see.
The City of Saints and the City of Strangers — two communities defined by who their members welcome.
context: *De Civitate Dei*, written over thirteen years, runs to 22 books. Augustine argued earthly Rome was never the eternal one Christians sought. The book grounded Western political theology for a millennium, from Charlemagne to Aquinas.

question: Around 410 the British monk Pelagius arrived in Africa teaching that humans could keep God's commands by their own free will, without special grace. Augustine attacked Pelagianism for two decades. What was his central counter-claim?
answer: Original sin — a corruption of the will inherited from Adam, which only divine grace can heal.
choices: Original sin — a corruption of the will inherited from Adam, which only divine grace can heal.
Soteriological monergism — that God alone saves and humans contribute nothing whatever.
Synergism — that grace and will cooperate, with the human side stronger than Pelagius admitted.
Theosis — that the goal of salvation is divinization, which only divine action could effect.
context: Carthage 418 and Ephesus 431 condemned Pelagianism. Augustine's view became Western orthodoxy. Luther and Calvin renewed and intensified Augustinian themes — total depravity, election, irresistible grace — a thousand years later.

question: On November 27, 1095, Pope Urban II preached at Clermont calling Christian knights to march east — the Byzantine emperor had asked for mercenary help against the Seljuks; Urban turned the appeal into holy war. What was the reported response?
answer: *Deus vult!* — 'God wills it!' — the rallying cry of the First Crusade.
choices: *Deus vult!* — 'God wills it!' — the rallying cry of the First Crusade.
*Pax Romana!* — 'Roman peace!' — invoking the imperial idea Urban hoped to revive.
*Sanctus, Sanctus!* — 'Holy, Holy!' — the liturgical acclamation continued in the field.
*Christus regnat!* — 'Christ reigns!' — the proclamation used at later papal coronations.
context: The First Crusade reached Jerusalem in 1099 and took the city with a massacre — Muslim and Jewish inhabitants slaughtered. The Crusades remained a defining and contested chapter. Modern Catholic teaching has acknowledged the abuses without disowning the original defensive impulse.

question: Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican friar who joined the order against his noble family's wishes, wrote the *Summa Theologica* — a systematic synthesis of Christian doctrine on Aristotelian foundations. He never finished it. What stopped his writing on December 6, 1273?
answer: A mystical experience during Mass after which he said all he had written seemed 'like straw.'
choices: A mystical experience during Mass after which he said all he had written seemed 'like straw.'
An order from the master of the Dominicans forbidding further work on Aristotelian themes.
A condemnation by the bishop of Paris placing his Aristotelian propositions under suspicion.
A fall from a horse that left him unable to dictate to his secretary Reginald of Piperno.
context: Aquinas died March 7, 1274 on the way to the Council of Lyon. The *Summa* was finished by disciples from his earlier writings. Canonized 1323 and declared Doctor of the Church; Leo XIII made Thomism the official Catholic philosophy in 1879.

question: Hildegard of Bingen (d. 1179), a Benedictine abbess in the Rhineland, wrote theology, composed liturgical music, illustrated visionary cosmologies, and corresponded with popes and emperors. She called her visionary work by a Latin name. What was it?
answer: *Scivias* — 'know the ways' (of the Lord), her most famous theological work.
choices: *Scivias* — 'know the ways' (of the Lord), her most famous theological work.
*Speculum* — 'mirror,' the standard title for medieval encyclopedias.
*Itinerarium* — 'journey,' the title later used by Bonaventure for his mystical text.
context: Hildegard was named Doctor of the Church by Benedict XVI in 2012 — only the fourth woman so titled. Her music — the *Symphonia* — has been recovered and recorded; her cosmological diagrams are reproduced everywhere. Medieval Christianity preserved more women's voices than caricature suggests.

question: On October 31, 1517, a young Augustinian friar in Wittenberg posted ninety-five propositions on indulgences for academic debate. Thesis 1 has been remembered ever since. What did it say?
answer: When our Lord said 'repent,' he willed the whole life of believers to be one of repentance — not a single act.
choices: When our Lord said 'repent,' he willed the whole life of believers to be one of repentance — not a single act.
The papacy has no power over the dead, since purgatory is a doctrine without scriptural foundation.
Indulgences are a fraud invented by Pope Leo X to fund the building of the new St. Peter's Basilica.
The treasury of merit on which indulgences draw is empty, since only Christ's merit can be applied.
context: Luther had not broken with Rome in 1517; the Theses were a call to reform. The break came over the next four years as Rome refused negotiation. Quickly printed and spread across Germany — the printing press made the Reformation possible.

question: John Calvin, a French reformer in Geneva, wrote a systematic exposition of Protestant doctrine first at age 26 and revised through five editions; it established Reformed Protestantism. What is it called?
answer: *Institutes of the Christian Religion* — *Institutio Christianae Religionis* in Latin.
choices: *Institutes of the Christian Religion* — *Institutio Christianae Religionis* in Latin.
*The Christian Faith* — *De Fide Christiana*, a title later borrowed by Schleiermacher.
*Loci Communes* — 'Common Places,' the title Melanchthon used for his Lutheran systematic theology.
*The Geneva Catechism* — a series of question-and-answer formularies for Reformed children.
context: The *Institutes* runs to four books, 80 chapters in its final 1559 edition. Calvinist theology — predestination, the sovereignty of God, the regulative principle of worship — shaped Scotland, the Netherlands, Puritan New England. The Geneva consistory provided the institutional model.

question: In 1553 the Spanish anti-Trinitarian Michael Servetus, author of *Restitution of Christianity*, was burned in Geneva on Calvin's authority. He had been condemned by Catholic and Protestant tribunals alike. The result for Calvin's reputation?
answer: Damaged it for centuries — even in his own time, Sebastian Castellio attacked it as religious tyranny.
choices: Damaged it for centuries — even in his own time, Sebastian Castellio attacked it as religious tyranny.
Strengthened it in Geneva, since the consistory had finally established its authority over civic life.
Was forgotten until the 19th century, when liberal Protestantism rediscovered the case as embarrassing.
Won him Rome's reluctant approval — burning an anti-Trinitarian was something both sides could share.
context: Castellio's 1554 *Concerning Heretics, Whether They Should Be Persecuted* is one of the earliest serious defenses of religious toleration. Calvin defended the execution to his death. Modern Reformed Christians have largely acknowledged it as a stain; a Servetus memorial stands in Geneva today.

question: In 1611 King James I authorized publication of an English Bible by a committee of 47 scholars working in three companies over seven years. It drew heavily on Tyndale, with revisions toward more elevated style. What is this Bible called?
answer: The King James Bible — also known as the Authorized Version.
choices: The King James Bible — also known as the Authorized Version.
The Bishops' Bible — an earlier English Protestant translation revised by Anglican bishops.
The Geneva Bible — favored by Puritans and the Pilgrim Fathers in New England.
The Douay-Rheims Bible — the Catholic English version completed in 1609.
context: The KJV dominated English-speaking Protestantism for three centuries. Its cadences shaped English literature from Bunyan to Lincoln to King's 'I Have a Dream.' Modern translations have largely supplanted it for accuracy, but its influence on English prose is permanent.

question: The Scottish Reformation's leader spent nineteen months as a French galley slave after Cardinal Beaton's assassination. He returned in 1559, preached crowds into tearing apart Catholic churches, and confronted Mary Queen of Scots. Who?
answer: John Knox — author of *History of the Reformation in Scotland* and the *First Book of Discipline*.
choices: John Knox — author of *History of the Reformation in Scotland* and the *First Book of Discipline*.
George Wishart — the preacher Beaton had burned in 1546, whose execution triggered the cardinal's killing.
Patrick Hamilton — the first Scottish Protestant martyr, burned in 1528 at age twenty-four.
Andrew Melville — Knox's successor and the leading Scottish Presbyterian theologian of the next generation.
context: Knox established Presbyterianism — a polity governed by elders rather than bishops — as the Scottish national church. His tradition spread through Ulster, into America (where Presbyterians were prominent in the Revolution), and worldwide. He died in Edinburgh in 1572.

question: Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury under Henry VIII and Edward VI, composed the *Book of Common Prayer* (1549, revised 1552) — the liturgical foundation of Anglicanism. Under Mary I he was condemned for heresy. At his execution he did something unexpected. What?
answer: Thrust his right hand — the one that had signed recantations — into the fire first, saying it had offended.
choices: Thrust his right hand — the one that had signed recantations — into the fire first, saying it had offended.
Refused to speak from the platform, having said all he could say in his recantations.
Sang a Te Deum in Latin as the flames rose, baffling the crowd with his appropriation of Catholic worship.
Embraced his executioner and the bishop who oversaw the burning, asking forgiveness for his enemies.
context: Cranmer had recanted under pressure, then recanted his recantations at the stake. The *Book of Common Prayer* set the rhythms of English religious life for centuries — 'till death us do part,' 'ashes to ashes, dust to dust,' 'speak now or forever hold your peace' all enter English from Cranmer's liturgy.

question: After the Council of Trent (1545–1563) and the Counter-Reformation, a Spanish soldier named Iñigo López de Loyola, wounded by a cannonball at Pamplona, founded a new religious order during a long convalescent reading of Christian classics. Its motto: 'to the greater glory of God.' What is its name and motto in Latin?
answer: The Society of Jesus — *Ad maiorem Dei gloriam*. Founded 1540, approved by Paul III.
choices: The Society of Jesus — *Ad maiorem Dei gloriam*. Founded 1540, approved by Paul III.
The Theatines — *Soli Deo gloria*. Founded 1524 by Cajetan and Pietro Carafa.
The Capuchins — *Pax et bonum*. Founded 1525, a stricter branch of Franciscans.
The Oratorians — *Ad Iesum per Mariam*. Founded by Philip Neri in 1564.
context: The Jesuits became the spearhead of Counter-Reformation Catholicism. Their schools educated Catholic elites worldwide; their missions reached Japan (Francis Xavier), China (Matteo Ricci), and the Americas. The order was suppressed by Clement XIV in 1773, then restored in 1814.

question: Teresa of Ávila, a Spanish Carmelite nun, undertook reform of her order, founding seventeen 'discalced' convents across Spain against opposition from her superiors and the Inquisition. She wrote great mystical texts of the Catholic tradition. What is her most famous one?
answer: *The Interior Castle* — describing the soul as a crystal castle with seven mansions leading inward.
choices: *The Interior Castle* — describing the soul as a crystal castle with seven mansions leading inward.
*The Dark Night of the Soul* — written by her younger collaborator John of the Cross, not Teresa.
*The Ascent of Mount Carmel* — also John of the Cross, the climbing companion to *Dark Night*.
*The Spiritual Exercises* — the Jesuit retreat manual by Ignatius of Loyola, not Teresa.
context: Teresa was named Doctor of the Church by Paul VI in 1970 — the first woman so named. Her younger colleague John of the Cross, who wrote *Dark Night* and *Ascent of Mount Carmel*, was already a Doctor. Spanish Catholic mysticism reached its peak in their generation.

question: an Oxford-educated curate attended a Moravian meeting on Aldersgate Street in London. As Luther's preface to Romans was read, he felt his heart 'strangely warmed' — the experiential moment launching a movement of itinerant field preaching across Britain and America. Who?
answer: John Wesley — founder of the Methodist movement with his brother Charles and George Whitefield.
choices: John Wesley — founder of the Methodist movement with his brother Charles and George Whitefield.
George Whitefield — the great evangelist of the First Great Awakening who preached to crowds of 30,000.
Jonathan Edwards — Northampton, Massachusetts pastor whose 'Sinners' sermon in 1741 became famous.
Howell Harris — the Welsh Methodist evangelist who founded the Trefeca community in mid-Wales.
context: Wesley rode an estimated 250,000 miles on horseback and preached over 40,000 sermons in his lifetime. Methodism's emphasis on field preaching, personal holiness, and lay leadership reshaped popular Christianity. By Wesley's death in 1791, Methodism had spread across England and America.

question: In 1692 the Salem Village panic killed twenty people. Nineteen were hanged. The twentieth was something else — uniquely in American legal history. What happened to Giles Corey?
answer: He was pressed to death under heavy stones — the only American so executed — for refusing to enter a plea.
choices: He was pressed to death under heavy stones — the only American so executed — for refusing to enter a plea.
He was burned at the stake — the only victim so executed — for the more serious charge of consorting with the devil in person.
He was drowned in the Connecticut River after a 'swimming' test that returned a positive verdict for witchcraft.
He died in custody before sentencing of a fever, and was buried in unconsecrated ground at the church's edge.
context: Corey's *peine forte et dure* (rarely used in English law) lasted three days. His reported last words — 'more weight' — became proverbial. Governor Phips halted the trials in October 1692. Twenty deaths is small compared to European witch panics that killed ~40,000–60,000 across the early modern period.

question: On April 4, 1968, an American Baptist minister was assassinated on a Memphis motel balcony where he had come in support of striking sanitation workers. He had organized the civil rights movement as a Christian moral campaign for thirteen years. Who?
answer: Martin Luther King Jr. — pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church and head of the SCLC.
choices: Martin Luther King Jr. — pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church and head of the SCLC.
Ralph Abernathy — King's deputy at the Southern Christian Leadership Conference who succeeded him.
Fred Shuttlesworth — Birmingham pastor whose church was repeatedly bombed by Klan members.
C. T. Vivian — King's lieutenant who was beaten in Selma trying to register Black voters.
context: King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (1963), written in response to white clergy who called his campaign 'unwise and untimely,' is a classic of Christian political ethics. His sermons grounded the civil rights movement in Christian moral theology — *agape* love, prophetic confrontation, the beloved community.

question: The schism between Eastern and Western Christianity was sealed on July 16, 1054, when papal legates marched into Hagia Sophia during the Divine Liturgy and laid a bull of excommunication on the altar. The patriarch responded in kind. What was the chief theological dispute?
answer: The *Filioque* — whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or 'from the Father and the Son.'
choices: The *Filioque* — whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or 'from the Father and the Son.'
Iconoclasm — whether images of Christ and the saints could be venerated in churches.
The date of Easter — whether Eastern or Western calculations of Pascha should be authoritative.
The use of leavened or unleavened bread in the Eucharist — a smaller dispute settled at Florence in 1439.
context: Papal authority and the *Filioque* (added by the West to the Nicene Creed) were the chief disputes. The mutual excommunications were not formally lifted until 1965 (Paul VI and Athenagoras I). Eastern Orthodoxy remains the second-largest Christian communion after Catholicism.

question: On Maundy Thursday 988 a grand duke of Kievan Rus was baptized in the Crimean port of Chersonesus, having rejected Islam, Judaism, and Western Christianity. His emissaries had reported about Constantinople: 'we knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth.' Who?
answer: Vladimir the Great — who imposed Orthodox Christianity on the population of Kievan Rus.
choices: Vladimir the Great — who imposed Orthodox Christianity on the population of Kievan Rus.
Boris of Bulgaria — whose conversion a century earlier had set the precedent for Slavic Orthodoxy.
Stefan Nemanja — founder of medieval Serbia, who founded the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos.
Mieszko I of Poland — whose baptism in 966 had brought Poland into the Western (Latin) church instead.
context: Vladimir's baptism made Kievan Rus part of Orthodox civilization. After Constantinople fell in 1453, Moscow claimed the title 'third Rome' — the new center of Orthodox Christianity. Russian Orthodoxy was suppressed under the Soviets but revived dramatically after 1991.

question: a Black preacher named William J. Seymour began holding services on Azusa Street in Los Angeles. The interracial meetings featured speaking in tongues and direct experiences of the Holy Spirit. What movement traces its origin to Azusa Street?
answer: Pentecostalism — now the second-largest Christian tradition globally, with over 600 million adherents.
choices: Pentecostalism — now the second-largest Christian tradition globally, with over 600 million adherents.
Adventism — already established by the William Miller movement and Ellen White decades earlier.
Dispensationalism — the prophetic system codified by John Nelson Darby and the Scofield Reference Bible.
The Holiness movement — the 19th-century Wesleyan tradition Pentecostalism partly grew out of, but distinct.
context: Azusa Street ran continuously for three years and drew visitors from around the world. Pentecostalism grew explosively, especially in Latin America, Africa, and Asia. The global Christian map of the early 21st century looks very different from the early 20th — and Pentecostalism is the main reason.

question: Mother Teresa, born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje, entered the Loreto Sisters in Ireland at 18, taught in Calcutta, and in 1948 received what she called her 'call within a call' to leave the school and work among the poorest of the poor. What congregation did she found in 1950?
answer: The Missionaries of Charity — eventually expanded to 139 countries by the time of her death.
choices: The Missionaries of Charity — eventually expanded to 139 countries by the time of her death.
The Sisters of Calcutta — a regional order under the local archdiocese, with no plans to expand.
The Daughters of the Bengali Poor — a secular institute that admitted Hindu and Muslim members.
The Servants of the Sacred Heart of Calcutta — affiliated with the existing Loreto Sisters' constitution.
context: Teresa was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979; canonized in 2016. Her published private letters revealed long decades of spiritual darkness — feeling God's absence acutely — which her supporters cite as Christian witness and her critics treated as evidence of doubt.

question: The doctrine that emerged from the controversies of the 4th and 5th centuries holds that there is one God in three 'persons' — Father, Son, Holy Spirit — of one substance, distinct in their relations but not divisible. What is this doctrine called?
answer: The Trinity — *Trinitas* in Latin, the term Tertullian coined in the early 3rd century.
choices: The Trinity — *Trinitas* in Latin, the term Tertullian coined in the early 3rd century.
Modalism — the rejected view that the three are masks the one God wears in turn, not distinct persons.
Subordinationism — the view that the Son and Spirit are real but lesser than the Father, condemned with Arius.
Tritheism — the rejected view that the three persons are three gods, working in close cooperation.
context: The Trinity is the central distinctive doctrine of Nicene Christianity, separating it from Judaism, Islam, and from Christian groups (Unitarians, JWs, Christadelphians) that have rejected it. Augustine's *De Trinitate* and the Cappadocian Fathers shaped its classic articulation.

question: The five doctrinal points known by the acronym TULIP — total depravity, unconditional election, limited atonement, irresistible grace, perseverance of the saints — were codified in a 1618–1619 Dutch confessional response to a softening of Calvinist soteriology. What synod produced this?
answer: The Synod of Dort (Dordrecht) — convened in response to the Remonstrant movement of Jacobus Arminius.
choices: The Synod of Dort (Dordrecht) — convened in response to the Remonstrant movement of Jacobus Arminius.
The Synod of Heidelberg — which had produced the 1563 Heidelberg Catechism.
The Synod of Geneva — convened by Calvin's successor Theodore Beza to harmonize Reformed practice.
The Synod of Emden — the founding 1571 synod of the Dutch Reformed Church under William of Orange.
context: Arminius had argued for conditional election (God elects those he foreknows will believe) and resistible grace. The Synod of Dort condemned the Arminian Remonstrance. Arminian theology survived through Methodism, the Anglican via media, and most Pentecostal traditions; Calvinist Reformed theology dominates Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist confessions.

question: The Marian dogmas — distinctive Catholic doctrines about Mary — include the Theotokos (defined at Ephesus 431) and three others. Which dogma, defined by Pius IX in 1854, holds that Mary herself was conceived without inheriting original sin?
answer: The Immaculate Conception — confused in popular imagination with the Virgin Birth of Jesus.
choices: The Immaculate Conception — confused in popular imagination with the Virgin Birth of Jesus.
The Perpetual Virginity — Mary remained a virgin before, during, and after the birth of Jesus.
The Assumption — Mary was assumed bodily into heaven at the end of her earthly life.
The Co-Redemptrix — a proposed but undefined dogma about Mary's cooperation in redemption.
context: Pius IX's *Ineffabilis Deus* (1854) preceded the dogma of papal infallibility (1870) but became the chief example of an *ex cathedra* definition. Pius XII's *Munificentissimus Deus* (1950) defined the Assumption — the only other formal *ex cathedra* definition.

question: The Spanish Inquisition was established in 1478 by Ferdinand and Isabella with papal authorization, distinct from the older medieval (papal) Inquisition. Its first Grand Inquisitor became a byword for fanatical severity, conducting an estimated 100,000 trials before his retirement in 1494. Who was he?
answer: Tomás de Torquemada — the Dominican friar appointed Grand Inquisitor in 1483.
choices: Tomás de Torquemada — the Dominican friar appointed Grand Inquisitor in 1483.
Bernardo Gui — the 14th-century French Dominican whose inquisitor's manual survives.
Robert le Bougre — the 13th-century French inquisitor of Cathars in Languedoc.
Konrad von Marburg — the 13th-century German inquisitor killed by enraged Hessian nobles.
context: Modern historiography (e.g., Henry Kamen) has revised the maximalist death tolls: the Spanish Inquisition executed approximately 3,000–5,000 people over its 350-year existence — appalling but smaller than older Protestant polemic claimed. Abolished in 1834.

question: Pope Alexander VI (1492–1503), born Rodrigo Borgia, fathered at least four children before his election. His son Cesare and daughter Lucrezia became Renaissance Italy's most notorious siblings. What did Alexander do with the papacy?
answer: Used it to enrich his family — purchasing his election with bribes and granting his children lavish offices.
choices: Used it to enrich his family — purchasing his election with bribes and granting his children lavish offices.
Drew up the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) — dividing the New World between Spain and Portugal.
Patronized Pinturicchio to decorate the Borgia Apartments in the Vatican with extraordinary frescoes.
All of the above — Alexander VI did all three, and was a complex figure beyond simple caricature.
context: Alexander VI is the locus classicus of Renaissance papal corruption — though he was also a capable administrator and patron. The Borgia papacy is unsparingly named in honest Christian history. Savonarola, the Dominican preacher of Florence who denounced the corruption, was excommunicated by Alexander and burned in 1498.

question: On the night of December 6, 343 AD (traditional date), in the Lycian town of Myra, the bishop reportedly threw bags of gold through the window of an impoverished family to provide dowries for three daughters and save them from being sold into prostitution. Who was this bishop, later patron of children?
answer: Saint Nicholas of Myra — eventually transmuted via Dutch *Sinterklaas* into Santa Claus.
choices: Saint Nicholas of Myra — eventually transmuted via Dutch *Sinterklaas* into Santa Claus.
Saint Basil of Caesarea — Cappadocian Father whose feast is January 1 in Eastern tradition.
Saint John Chrysostom — the 'golden-mouthed' Constantinople patriarch known for his preaching.
Saint Gregory Nazianzen — Cappadocian theologian known as 'the Theologian' in Eastern usage.
context: Nicholas's relics were stolen from Myra by Italian sailors in 1087 and taken to Bari, where they remain. The Santa Claus figure of secular Christmas descends from Dutch Protestant settlers' *Sinterklaas* in New Amsterdam, reshaped in the 19th century by Clement Clarke Moore's poem and Thomas Nast's cartoons.

question: Saint Patrick was not Irish — he was a Romano-British Christian taken to Ireland as a slave at sixteen, escaped after six years, returned later as a missionary, and used a common Irish plant to explain the Trinity to his audiences. What was the plant?
answer: The shamrock — three leaves on one stem, illustrating three persons in one God.
choices: The shamrock — three leaves on one stem, illustrating three persons in one God.
The clover — four leaves on one stem, with the fourth representing the unity of the three.
The thistle — used by Patrick to illustrate the harshness of pre-Christian Irish religion.
The reed — woven by Patrick into crosses still bearing his name and given to converts.
context: Patrick's *Confessio* — a short autobiographical letter, one of the earliest documents of medieval Western Christianity — survives. The shamrock story is medieval rather than from Patrick's own writings. Patrick's mission Christianized Ireland in a generation; Irish monastic learning later preserved classical and Christian texts.

question: The Hagia Sophia ('Holy Wisdom') in Constantinople was rebuilt by Emperor Justinian and dedicated in 537 AD. On entering it Justinian is reported to have exclaimed, comparing it to Solomon's temple. What did he say?
answer: 'Solomon, I have surpassed you!' — *Nenikēka se Solōmōn!* in Greek.
choices: 'Solomon, I have surpassed you!' — *Nenikēka se Solōmōn!* in Greek.
'Solomon's temple was a shadow; this is the substance.' — comparing the architectures of the two covenants.
'Behold, the dwelling of God is with men!' — quoting Revelation 21.
'I have built a house worthy of the wisdom of God.' — in Aramaic, the architects' liturgical language.
context: Hagia Sophia was the largest Christian church in the world for nearly a thousand years. It became a mosque after Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453; a museum under Atatürk in 1934; reverted to a mosque under Erdoğan in 2020. Its dome — 31 meters wide, 56 meters above the floor — remains an architectural marvel.

question: In 726 AD, the Byzantine Emperor Leo III began the first wave of iconoclasm — ordering the destruction of religious images on the grounds they were idolatrous. The controversy raged for over a century. What council in 787 reversed it and defined legitimate icon veneration?
answer: The Second Council of Nicaea — the seventh ecumenical council, restoring icon veneration.
choices: The Second Council of Nicaea — the seventh ecumenical council, restoring icon veneration.
The Quinisext Council (in Trullo, 692) — predating the iconoclast period.
The Council of Constantinople IV (869–870) — a later council on the Photian schism.
The Council of Chalcedon — the fourth ecumenical council, of 451, on the natures of Christ.
context: John of Damascus (676–749), writing safely under Muslim rule outside Byzantium, was the chief theological defender of icons. The 'triumph of Orthodoxy' is celebrated each year on the first Sunday of Lent in Orthodox churches. The veneration of icons (proskynesis) is carefully distinguished from worship (latria) reserved for God alone.

question: Ethiopian Orthodoxy — one of the oldest continuous Christian traditions — became state religion in 330 AD under King Ezana of Aksum. It preserves a unique biblical canon. What book — canonical in Ethiopia, excluded elsewhere — does it preserve?
answer: 1 Enoch — quoted in the New Testament Epistle of Jude, but absent from the Catholic, Protestant, and Greek Orthodox canons.
choices: 1 Enoch — quoted in the New Testament Epistle of Jude, but absent from the Catholic, Protestant, and Greek Orthodox canons.
The Gospel of Thomas — a Coptic sayings gospel found at Nag Hammadi in 1945.
The Didache — an early Christian church order recovered only in 1873 by Patriarch Bryennios.
The Shepherd of Hermas — an early Christian apocalyptic work circulated widely in the patristic era.
context: Ethiopia's Solomonic dynasty (ending in 1974 with Haile Selassie) claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. The Kebra Nagast tells the story. Ethiopia's continuous Christian history — including resistance to Muslim and Italian invasions — is one of the great African Christian inheritances, predating Constantine's empire.

question: Hebrews, an anonymous letter to Jewish Christians tempted to revert under persecution, argues that Christ is greater than angels, greater than Moses, greater than the levitical priesthood. Christ is high priest 'after the order of' a mysterious Genesis figure. Who?
answer: Melchizedek — king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham in Genesis 14.
choices: Melchizedek — king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham in Genesis 14.
Aaron — the brother of Moses and first high priest, traditionally seen as the head of the levitical line.
Phinehas — grandson of Aaron whose zeal at Shittim earned him an everlasting priesthood.
Zadok — David's high priest, whose line dominated the Jerusalem priesthood until the Maccabean era.
context: Hebrews 7 develops the Melchizedek typology: a priest without recorded genealogy or end of life, greater than Levi (since Levi 'paid tithes through Abraham'). Christ's eternal priesthood, unlike the levitical, does not pass to a successor — he ever lives to make intercession.

question: On April 6, 1830, a 24-year-old American named Joseph Smith founded the Church of Christ in Fayette, New York, having published the previous month a translation he claimed to have made of golden plates given him by an angel. What was the translation called?
answer: The Book of Mormon — 'another testament of Jesus Christ' — covering events in pre-Columbian America.
choices: The Book of Mormon — 'another testament of Jesus Christ' — covering events in pre-Columbian America.
The Doctrine and Covenants — Smith's later compilation of his ongoing revelations to the church.
The Pearl of Great Price — Smith's translation of an Egyptian funerary papyrus and other texts.
The Book of Abraham — a portion of the Pearl of Great Price treated as scripture by Mormons.
context: Smith led his followers west through Ohio, Missouri, and Illinois under persecution; he was lynched at Carthage Jail in 1844. Brigham Young led the church to Utah in 1847. Mormons (now The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) have grown to about 17 million, with global headquarters in Salt Lake City.

question: On October 31, 1517 — coincidentally the same day as Luther's Theses — was 280 years before another religious founding. In 1879 a Massachusetts woman, after recovering from a serious fall, published *Science and Health*. She founded what religion?
answer: Christian Science — Mary Baker Eddy's First Church of Christ, Scientist, headquartered in Boston.
choices: Christian Science — Mary Baker Eddy's First Church of Christ, Scientist, headquartered in Boston.
Seventh-day Adventism — Ellen White's church, dating from the 1860s, not the 1870s or 1880s.
Theosophy — Madame Helena Blavatsky's syncretic movement, founded in New York in 1875.
New Thought — a broader movement of which Christian Science is one strand, not founded by any one figure.
context: Christian Science teaches that sickness is an error of mortal mind that prayer can cure; medical treatment is discouraged. The Christian Science Monitor newspaper, founded 1908, won several Pulitzer Prizes. Eddy's followers built distinctive 'Christian Science reading rooms' in cities across America. Membership has declined dramatically since mid-20th century.

question: Søren Kierkegaard, a Danish Lutheran philosopher writing in the 1840s, attacked the comfortable 'Christendom' of Copenhagen's state church as systematic betrayal of the New Testament. He argued faith requires a 'leap' beyond rational demonstration — using one Old Testament figure as his exemplar. Who?
answer: Abraham — whose binding of Isaac, in *Fear and Trembling* (1843), is the paradigm of faith.
choices: Abraham — whose binding of Isaac, in *Fear and Trembling* (1843), is the paradigm of faith.
Job — whose dialogues, in *Repetition* (1843), are the paradigm of suffering trust.
Moses — whose hesitations at the burning bush, in Kierkegaard's later work, paradigm of vocation.
Solomon — whose Ecclesiastes Kierkegaard cited as the paradigm of existential despair.
context: Kierkegaard's pseudonymous works — including *Either/Or*, *Sickness Unto Death*, and *Concluding Unscientific Postscript* — invented what would become 20th-century existentialism. Karl Barth, Heidegger, Sartre, and Tillich all read him. Kierkegaard died in 1855 attacking the established Lutheran church.

question: Fyodor Dostoevsky's *The Brothers Karamazov* (1880) features a long chapter inside the novel set in 16th-century Seville. An old cardinal interrogates a returning Christ for offering humans freedom they cannot bear. What is the chapter called?
answer: The Grand Inquisitor — Ivan Karamazov's parable to his believing brother Alyosha.
choices: The Grand Inquisitor — Ivan Karamazov's parable to his believing brother Alyosha.
The Confession of Zossima — the old monk's deathbed teaching to the novices.
The Marriage of Marya — Dmitri's drunken account of his betrothal to Katerina.
