The Norse practice of *thralldom* (slavery) was extensive — slaves came primarily from raids on the British Isles, Ireland, Russia, and the Mediterranean. Christianity gradually eroded but did not immediately abolish Norse slavery.

question: Olaf Tryggvason, king of Norway 995–1000, was a violent Christianizer of his country — torturing pagan chieftains who refused to convert, drowning, burning, mutilating. His brief reign reshaped Norwegian religion. He died at what battle?
answer: Svolder (1000) — an alliance of Sweden, Denmark, and a Norwegian rival defeated him.
choices: Svolder (1000) — an alliance of Sweden, Denmark, and a Norwegian rival defeated him.
Stiklestad (1030) — but this is where Olaf the Holy (Olaf II) died, not Olaf I.
Hastings (1066) — but Hastings is the Norman conquest of England, much later.
Stamford Bridge (1066) — but this is where Harald Hardrada died, not Olaf I.
context: Olaf Tryggvason's coercive Christianization was followed by Olaf Haraldsson (St. Olaf, ruled 1015–1028), whose death at Stiklestad in 1030 was treated as martyrdom and crystallized Norwegian Christian identity. The transformation from pagan to Christian Norway took two generations and was violent at every stage. Sweden's conversion lasted longer.

question: *Voluspa* — 'the prophecy of the seeress' — is the first poem of the *Poetic Edda*. A *volva* recounts the history of the world from its creation through Ragnarok and renewal. To whom does she address her vision?
answer: Odin — who has come to her seeking wisdom about the coming end.
choices: Odin — who has come to her seeking wisdom about the coming end.
Heimdall — to whom the volva speaks her vision before the Gjallarhorn sounds.
Loki — bound but able to hear her, learning his role in the prophecy.
Thor — whose Mjolnir she names as the weapon that will kill the World-Serpent.
context: *Voluspa* is the single most important text for reconstructing Norse mythology. The seeress is summoned to give a comprehensive account of cosmic history — its remarkable scope and its prophetic certainty about Ragnarok give the poem the gravity of Hebrew prophetic literature. Modern Iceland still celebrates its Eddic poetry as foundational.

question: After the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 AD by Titus's Roman armies, the center of Jewish religious life shifted from temple sacrifice to study of texts. The oral law was gradually codified. The first major codification — around 200 AD by Rabbi Judah haNasi — produced what?
answer: The Mishnah — six 'orders' covering agriculture, festivals, marriage, civil law, sacrifices, ritual purity.
choices: The Mishnah — six 'orders' covering agriculture, festivals, marriage, civil law, sacrifices, ritual purity.
The Talmud — but the Talmud is a later commentary built on the Mishnah.
The Septuagint — but this is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, from c. 250 BC.
The Zohar — but the Zohar is a 13th-century kabbalistic text, not the foundational law.
context: The Mishnah and the later commentary called the Gemara together make up the Talmud. Two Talmuds exist: the Palestinian (c. 400 AD) and the more authoritative Babylonian (c. 500 AD). Jewish learning has centered on Talmud study ever since. A rabbi is one who has demonstrated competence in this textual tradition, not a sacrificial priest.

question: On January 20, 1942, fifteen senior Nazi officials met at a villa in a Berlin suburb to coordinate the 'Final Solution' — the systematic murder of European Jews. What is this meeting called?
answer: The Wannsee Conference — chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, with Adolf Eichmann recording the minutes.
choices: The Wannsee Conference — chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, with Adolf Eichmann recording the minutes.
The Nuremberg Rally — but these were public Nazi party gatherings throughout the 1930s.
The Berlin Conference — but the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 was about colonial Africa.
The Munich Conference — but Munich 1938 was the appeasement meeting on Czechoslovakia.
context: The Wannsee Conference did not initiate the Holocaust — killing of Jews had begun earlier in the East — but it coordinated and accelerated the bureaucratic machinery. Heydrich was assassinated in Prague four months later by Czech partisans. Six million Jews were murdered; about 5.7 million died in camps and shootings between 1941 and 1945.

question: Hasidism, a Jewish mystical-pietist movement, was founded in 18th-century Poland-Lithuania by an itinerant healer and storyteller known by an honorific Hebrew title meaning 'Master of the Good Name.' What was the title?
answer: Baal Shem Tov — Israel ben Eliezer (c. 1700–1760), founder of the Hasidic movement.
choices: Baal Shem Tov — Israel ben Eliezer (c. 1700–1760), founder of the Hasidic movement.
Vilna Gaon — but this is Elijah of Vilna, the great opponent of Hasidism.
Rambam — but this is the acronym for Maimonides, centuries earlier.
Rashi — but this is the medieval French commentator on the Bible and Talmud.
context: The Baal Shem Tov emphasized the immediate presence of God, the spiritual value of joyful prayer over learned analysis, and the role of the charismatic master (*rebbe*) as a focus of community life. Hasidism became enormously influential in Eastern European Jewry; today it is most visible in Lubavitch (Chabad), Satmar, Belz, and many other dynasties.

question: Islam's five 'pillars' — the obligations of every Muslim — are the confession of faith (shahada), prayer (salat), almsgiving (zakat), fasting in Ramadan (sawm), and a pilgrimage to Mecca once in life if able. What is the pilgrimage called?
answer: The Hajj — performed during the month of Dhu al-Hijjah in the Islamic lunar calendar.
choices: The Hajj — performed during the month of Dhu al-Hijjah in the Islamic lunar calendar.
The Umrah — the 'lesser pilgrimage,' which can be performed at any time of year.
The Jihad — but jihad is not pilgrimage; it means 'striving,' inner or outer.
The Ziyara — but ziyara is the visit to other holy sites (Medina, Karbala), not the major pilgrimage.
context: The Hajj draws roughly two million pilgrims annually to Mecca. It includes circling the Kaaba seven times (tawaf), running between the hills of Safa and Marwa (sa'i, commemorating Hagar's search for water), and standing at Mount Arafat. The Kaaba — a cube-shaped structure containing the Black Stone — is the direction (qibla) toward which Muslims everywhere face in prayer.

question: After Muhammad's death in 632 AD without a male heir, the Muslim community faced a succession crisis that produced the most enduring Islamic schism. The faction holding that the rightful successor must be Muhammad's son-in-law Ali (and his descendants) became known as what?
answer: The Shi'a — *Shi'at Ali*, 'the party of Ali' — about 10–15% of Muslims today, dominant in Iran and Iraq.
choices: The Shi'a — *Shi'at Ali*, 'the party of Ali' — about 10–15% of Muslims today, dominant in Iran and Iraq.
The Sunni — 'people of the tradition,' but this is the majority who accepted the elected caliphs.
The Wahhabi — but Wahhabism is an 18th-century revivalist movement within Sunni Islam.
The Kharijite — an early group that broke from both Ali and his opponents on different grounds.
context: The first four 'Rightly-Guided' (Rashidun) caliphs were Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and finally Ali — the last killed in 661. Ali's son Husayn was killed at Karbala in 680, the central martyrdom of Shi'ite religious imagination. The Shi'ite-Sunni split has shaped Islamic history for fourteen centuries, including modern conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen.

question: Ibn Sina (Latin: Avicenna, 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose medical encyclopedia *al-Qanun fi al-Tibb* — 'the Canon of Medicine' — was used as the standard medical textbook in European universities for centuries. What languages was it studied in?
answer: Originally Arabic; translated into Latin in the 12th century; standard at Paris and Padua for 500 years.
choices: Originally Arabic; translated into Latin in the 12th century; standard at Paris and Padua for 500 years.
Originally Persian; translated into Latin; rapidly displaced by Greek translations from the 14th century.
Originally Greek; translated into Arabic and then into Latin; superseded by Aristotle in the 13th century.
Originally Hebrew; translated into Arabic and Latin; used mainly in Iberian medical schools.
context: Avicenna's *Canon* synthesized Greek (Galenic), Indian, and Islamic medical knowledge. His philosophical works — *Kitab al-Shifa* — were equally influential, mediating Aristotelianism to medieval Europe. Aquinas read Avicenna seriously and engaged with his arguments on the existence of God and the nature of being.

question: Around 1058, in Persia, the theologian and former Sufi al-Ghazali published a work attacking the rationalist philosophers (especially al-Farabi and Avicenna) for applying Aristotelian causality to the natural world. His position became dominant in Sunni Islam for the next eight centuries. What was the position?
answer: Occasionalism — God directly causes every event; apparent natural laws are merely God's habits.
choices: Occasionalism — God directly causes every event; apparent natural laws are merely God's habits.
Asharism — God's revelation completes reason, which alone is limited and insufficient.
Mu'tazila — reason and revelation give the same truth; reason can establish God's existence.
Sufism — mystical experience is the highest form of knowledge, beyond reason.
context: Al-Ghazali's *Incoherence of the Philosophers* is widely seen as closing the Islamic Golden Age intellectually. Averroes (Ibn Rushd) responded with *Incoherence of the Incoherence* — but his rationalism lost the long argument inside Islamic civilization while it won in Christian Europe. Al-Ghazali's autobiography *Deliverance from Error* records his own intellectual journey.

question: Mansa Musa I, ruler of the Mali Empire 1312–1337, became one of the wealthiest men in recorded history. His 1324 hajj to Mecca, with a caravan of 60,000 men and 12,000 slaves and an estimated 1,000 camels carrying gold dust, devalued gold in Cairo for a decade. What city in his empire was a famous center of learning?
answer: Timbuktu — site of the Sankoré madrasa, with manuscript collections that survived into the 21st century.
choices: Timbuktu — site of the Sankoré madrasa, with manuscript collections that survived into the 21st century.
Marrakesh — but Marrakesh is in Morocco, not in the Mali Empire.
Damascus — but Damascus was the Umayyad capital, not part of Mali.
Mogadishu — but Mogadishu, on the East African coast, was independent of Mali.
context: Timbuktu's manuscript libraries, dating from the 14th century onward, preserved Islamic learning across centuries. Many were hidden in family collections during the 2012 Islamist occupation and saved by local librarians at great personal risk. The medieval African Islamic civilization is too often dropped from Western narratives of the Middle Ages.

question: Sufism — the mystical strand of Islam — developed alongside the legal/theological tradition. The 13th-century Persian poet Rumi composed an enormous masnavi (long mystical poem) that has been called 'the Qur'an in Persian.' Where was he based?
answer: Konya in Anatolia — modern-day Turkey, where the Mevlevi order ('whirling dervishes') traces back to him.
choices: Konya in Anatolia — modern-day Turkey, where the Mevlevi order ('whirling dervishes') traces back to him.
Baghdad — but Baghdad was the Abbasid intellectual center, not Rumi's primary location.
Cairo — but Cairo was the Fatimid and then Mamluk center, not Rumi's.
Damascus — but Damascus was an early Umayyad center, geographically distant from Rumi.
context: Rumi's *Masnavi-ye Ma'navi* runs to over 25,000 verses. His ecstatic spiritual poetry has had a major 20th-century revival in English translation (Coleman Barks's renderings sold millions of copies). The Mevlevi order's whirling dance — *sema* — is among the most distinctive Sufi practices, recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

question: Buddhism split during its first centuries into multiple schools. The main living traditions are three. Theravada predominates in Southeast Asia (Sri Lanka, Thailand, Burma, Cambodia, Laos). Where does Mahayana predominate?
answer: East Asia — China, Korea, Vietnam, Japan; also Taiwan and Singapore.
choices: East Asia — China, Korea, Vietnam, Japan; also Taiwan and Singapore.
South Asia — but India and Pakistan are mostly Hindu and Muslim; Buddhism largely receded from India.
Central Asia — but Central Asia is mostly Muslim today; Buddhism receded there too.
Mongolia and Tibet — but these are Vajrayana, the third major branch, not Mahayana primarily.
context: Vajrayana Buddhism — the 'diamond vehicle' or 'tantric' tradition — predominates in Tibet, Bhutan, Mongolia, and parts of Nepal. Mahayana introduced the bodhisattva ideal (postponing personal nirvana to help others), expanded sutras (Lotus, Heart, Diamond), and developed schools like Pure Land and Zen. Theravada hews closer to the Pali Canon.

question: The Upanishads (c. 900–500 BC) developed the philosophical implications of the Vedas. They taught that the individual self (*atman*) is identical with the universal reality (*brahman*) — a doctrine summarized in a famous formula. What does it say?
answer: *Tat tvam asi* — 'thou art that' — the identification of atman and brahman.
choices: *Tat tvam asi* — 'thou art that' — the identification of atman and brahman.
*Om mani padme hum* — but this is the Tibetan Buddhist mantra of compassion.
*Hare Krishna* — but this is a devotional mantra from medieval Vaishnavism.
*Aham brahmasmi* — 'I am Brahman' — a related but distinct Upanishadic formula.
context: *Tat tvam asi* is from the Chandogya Upanishad. The non-dualist (Advaita Vedanta) school of Shankara (c. 700 AD) systematized this radical identification: only Brahman is real, and the world's apparent multiplicity is *maya* (illusion). Other Vedanta schools — Ramanuja's qualified non-dualism, Madhva's dualism — interpret the formulas differently.

question: The *Bhagavad Gita* — 'Song of the Lord' — is the most-loved single text in Hindu tradition. It is set on a battlefield where the warrior Arjuna hesitates to fight his kinsmen and a divine charioteer instructs him. Who is the charioteer?
answer: Krishna — eighth avatar of Vishnu, instructing Arjuna in dharma, action, and devotion.
choices: Krishna — eighth avatar of Vishnu, instructing Arjuna in dharma, action, and devotion.
Rama — seventh avatar of Vishnu, but Rama is the hero of the Ramayana, not the Gita.
Shiva — but Shiva is a separate major deity, not Arjuna's charioteer.
Brahma — but Brahma is the creator god in the Trimurti, not Arjuna's charioteer.
context: The *Gita* is 700 verses set within the much longer *Mahabharata* epic (about 100,000 verses, longest poem in the world). It teaches three paths to liberation: *karma yoga* (action without attachment), *bhakti yoga* (devotion to God), *jnana yoga* (knowledge of Brahman). Gandhi called the Gita his 'spiritual reference book.'

question: Hindu cosmology recognizes the Trimurti — three principal gods who together preside over creation, preservation, and destruction. Brahma creates; Shiva destroys. Who preserves?
answer: Vishnu — who in ten avatars descends to earth in times of cosmic crisis.
choices: Vishnu — who in ten avatars descends to earth in times of cosmic crisis.
Ganesha — but Ganesha is the elephant-headed son of Shiva, remover of obstacles.
Hanuman — but Hanuman is the monkey-god, devoted to Rama in the Ramayana.
Kali — but Kali is a fierce goddess, an aspect of the Divine Mother, not part of the Trimurti.
context: Vishnu's avatars include the boar Varaha (raising the earth from cosmic waters), the man-lion Narasimha, the dwarf Vamana, Rama, Krishna, and the Buddha (in some lists). The tenth, Kalki, is yet to come — a future apocalyptic figure on a white horse who will restore dharma at the end of the current dark age (Kali Yuga).

question: Sati — the practice in which a widow was burned alive on her husband's funeral pyre — was outlawed by the British colonial government in 1829. The reform was led by Governor-General Lord William Bentinck under pressure from what Bengali Hindu reformer?
answer: Ram Mohan Roy — founder of the Brahmo Samaj, a Hindu reform movement.
choices: Ram Mohan Roy — founder of the Brahmo Samaj, a Hindu reform movement.
Swami Vivekananda — but Vivekananda comes a generation later, around the 1880s.
Mahatma Gandhi — but Gandhi was born in 1869, decades after the sati abolition.
Dayananda Saraswati — founder of the Arya Samaj, also later than the sati abolition.
context: Sati was not universally practiced in pre-British India — it was associated mainly with high-caste Hindu communities. Roy's reform tradition continued through the 19th century with the Brahmo Samaj, the Prarthana Samaj, and the Arya Samaj — Hindu movements that sought to reform their own religion in dialogue with British rule. Indian reformers, not only the British, drove abolition.

question: Egyptian religion had a complex pantheon. Osiris was originally a fertile-grain god of the Nile, but a myth gave him a tragic role. His brother Set, jealous, killed him. What did Isis, Osiris's wife and sister, then do?
answer: Reassembled his body parts (scattered across Egypt by Set), reanimating him long enough to conceive Horus.
choices: Reassembled his body parts (scattered across Egypt by Set), reanimating him long enough to conceive Horus.
Followed Set into the desert and killed him, founding the cult of vengeful goddesses.
Persuaded Ra to bring Osiris back to life as the new sun god of the day-cycle.
Hid in the marshes of the Delta and raised Horus alone, refusing all relationship with Osiris's memory.
context: Osiris became lord of the dead and the underworld; Horus (the falcon-headed sky god) eventually defeated Set in a series of contests and inherited the kingship of Egypt; every Pharaoh was Horus on earth and became Osiris at death. The Osirian myth is the central religious framework of pharaonic Egypt for two millennia.

question: The 'Book of the Dead' — a Egyptian funerary text — was a collection of about 200 spells to help the deceased navigate the perils of the underworld. Wealthy people commissioned personalized scrolls; poorer ones bought standard versions. Where were they placed?
answer: In the tomb with the body — sometimes between the legs of the mummy, or in the coffin lid.
choices: In the tomb with the body — sometimes between the legs of the mummy, or in the coffin lid.
Above the city gate as a public protection — but this was for state magic, not funerary.
In the temple of Anubis at Saqqara — but Anubis temples were public, not for individual texts.
In the Nile waters at the time of burial — but funerary texts were not placed in water.
context: The Book of the Dead emerged in the New Kingdom (c. 1550 BC onward) — superseding earlier Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts. The famous 'Negative Confession' (spell 125) is the dead's claim before the judges: 'I have not killed, I have not robbed, I have not made anyone weep...' — one of the earliest detailed moral codes in human history.

question: The *Epic of Gilgamesh* — composed in cuneiform on clay tablets c. 2100 BC, the oldest extant work of long-form literature — tells of a king of Uruk who befriends a wild man and then, after his friend's death, seeks immortality. Who was the wild man?
answer: Enkidu — formed by the gods from clay, civilized by the temple priestess Shamhat.
choices: Enkidu — formed by the gods from clay, civilized by the temple priestess Shamhat.
Humbaba — but Humbaba is the demon of the Cedar Forest, killed by Gilgamesh and Enkidu.
Utnapishtim — but Utnapishtim is the flood-survivor whom Gilgamesh seeks for immortality.
Ninurta — but Ninurta is a Mesopotamian war god, not a character in Gilgamesh.
context: Enkidu's death prompts Gilgamesh's quest for immortality. He finds Utnapishtim, the man saved from a great flood (a probable Mesopotamian source for the Genesis flood narrative). Utnapishtim offers him a plant of youth from the bottom of the sea, but a snake steals it. Gilgamesh returns to Uruk accepting mortality. The themes — friendship, grief, mortality — have made the epic newly vital in modern translation.

question: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlán — founded c. 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco — practiced large-scale human sacrifice on the Templo Mayor, the great pyramid at its center. Scholars estimate the peak annual rate. What number is commonly given?
answer: About 20,000 sacrifices per year at the height of the empire (late 15th century).
choices: About 20,000 sacrifices per year at the height of the empire (late 15th century).
About 500 sacrifices per year — a much smaller estimate from some revisionists.
About 200,000 sacrifices per year — an inflated estimate from early Spanish chroniclers.
About 50 sacrifices per year — significantly smaller than recorded Aztec military campaigns required.
context: The estimates vary widely depending on what evidence is weighted — Spanish chronicles, surviving Aztec sources, archaeology. Honest history names Aztec religious culture as one in which mass human sacrifice was central to ritual and political life. Cortés's conquest of 1519–1521 was facilitated by the resentment of subject peoples whose tribute included sacrificial victims.

question: Aztec religion taught that the sun god Huitzilopochtli needed continual nourishment — or the sun would not rise. The most desirable sacrifices were captured warriors, taken in wars partly fought for the purpose. What were these wars called?
answer: Flower Wars (*xochiyaoyotl*) — periodic ritualized battles between Aztec and rival cities to capture victims.
choices: Flower Wars (*xochiyaoyotl*) — periodic ritualized battles between Aztec and rival cities to capture victims.
Sacred Wars — but this term is used by Greek and other Mediterranean civilizations, not the Aztec.
Holy Wars — but this is a generic translation that does not capture the specific Aztec institution.
Hummingbird Wars — referring to Huitzilopochtli's hummingbird associations, but not the actual name.
context: Flower Wars were prearranged battles where the goal was not to kill enemies in the field but to capture them for sacrifice. They were religiously and politically central, providing victims and warriors' honors. The institution was incomprehensible and abhorrent to the Spanish conquerors — and is one of the genuinely difficult features of pre-Columbian Mesoamerican civilization.

question: Celtic religion in pre-Roman Britain and Ireland centered on the *druids* — a priestly-bardic-judicial class. They led religious ceremonies, taught oral traditions, judged disputes, and (Julius Caesar reports) participated in human sacrifice. In what kind of place did druids worship?
answer: Sacred groves — particularly of oak trees, with the mistletoe gathered with a golden sickle.
choices: Sacred groves — particularly of oak trees, with the mistletoe gathered with a golden sickle.
Stone temples — but Celtic religion was generally not focused on built temples.
Caves — but caves were not the primary druidic worship space.
Riverside altars — but druidic worship was not primarily watery.
context: Caesar's *Gallic War* Book 6 records the wicker-man burning sacrifices of druidic religion. The Romans, who themselves practiced state ritual including some forms of human sacrifice in earlier times, were nevertheless shocked by Celtic practice. The druidic class was destroyed by the Romans (massacre at Anglesey, AD 60–61) and by Christianization. Modern 'druidry' is an 18th-century invention.

question: Japanese Shinto — the indigenous religion of Japan — is organized around *kami*, spirits of natural features, ancestors, and abstract powers. The chief kami in the formal pantheon is the sun goddess, ancestor of the imperial line. Who is she?
answer: Amaterasu — sun goddess, said to have hidden in a cave until lured out by a dance.
choices: Amaterasu — sun goddess, said to have hidden in a cave until lured out by a dance.
Susanoo — storm god, brother of Amaterasu, exiled from heaven for misbehavior.
Tsukuyomi — moon god, brother of Amaterasu, less prominent in cult.
Inari — kami of rice, fertility, and foxes, with thousands of shrines across Japan.
context: The Japanese imperial house claims descent from Amaterasu through her grandson Ninigi. The *Kojiki* (712 AD) and *Nihon Shoki* (720 AD) are the chief sources for Shinto myth. The Ise Grand Shrine — Amaterasu's main shrine — is rebuilt every twenty years in a continuous renewal ritual dating from the 7th century AD.

question: On November 18, 1978, a charismatic preacher named Jim Jones led 909 of his followers — including 304 children — to drink cyanide-laced grape Flavor Aid (often misremembered as Kool-Aid) at his agricultural commune in Guyana. He had earlier ordered the assassination of US Congressman Leo Ryan. What was the church called?
answer: Peoples Temple — founded in Indianapolis in 1955, later moved to California and then to Jonestown.
choices: Peoples Temple — founded in Indianapolis in 1955, later moved to California and then to Jonestown.
Branch Davidians — but this is David Koresh's group, killed at Waco in 1993.
Heaven's Gate — but this is Marshall Applewhite's group, who died in 1997.
Aum Shinrikyo — but this is the Japanese group that released sarin on the Tokyo subway in 1995.
context: Jonestown is one of the worst incidents of cult violence in modern history — and the source of the English phrase 'drink the Kool-Aid' for blindly following destructive leadership. Jones had begun as a charismatic preacher in mainline Protestant settings; the group's drift into authoritarian violence and self-destruction occurred over two decades. New religious movements are not all destructive, but those that go bad can go very bad.

question: Hestia, eldest of the Olympians, was goddess of the hearth and the family flame. She was so retiring that she eventually gave up her Olympian seat to another god — refusing the conflicts of her cousins. Who took her place?
answer: Dionysus — admitted late as the twelfth Olympian after Hestia withdrew.
choices: Dionysus — admitted late as the twelfth Olympian after Hestia withdrew.
Heracles — admitted on Olympus only after his death, but never as one of the Twelve.
Asclepius — son of Apollo and healer, killed by Zeus and made into Ophiuchus.
Eros — son of Aphrodite, but never reckoned as one of the Twelve Olympians.
context: Hestia's prominence in Greek household religion is inversely proportional to her mythological development. The hearth-fire was her dwelling in every Greek home; before any feast began, a libation went to her. The Roman Vesta — and the Vestal Virgins who tended her flame at Rome — preserved her central religious role for a thousand more years.

question: Cassandra, daughter of Priam of Troy, was given the gift of prophecy by Apollo in exchange for sex. When she refused him, he punished her by ensuring her prophecies would always be true but never believed. What did she prophesy that her countrymen ignored?
answer: The Trojan Horse — she warned that the Greeks were hidden inside; she was dismissed as mad.
choices: The Trojan Horse — she warned that the Greeks were hidden inside; she was dismissed as mad.
Helen's arrival — she warned that the Spartan queen would bring war; her father exiled her.
Achilles' death — she predicted Paris would kill him, but no one heeded the timing.
Aeneas' flight — she foresaw he would survive, but no one listened.
context: Cassandra is among the most tragic figures of Greek myth — a prophetess condemned to know without being heard. After Troy's fall she was taken by Agamemnon as concubine and killed by his queen Clytemnestra in Mycenae. Aeschylus's *Agamemnon* gives her a powerful death-scene. 'Cassandra' has become English shorthand for the unheeded warner.

question: Antigone, daughter of the disgraced king Oedipus, defied the new king Creon's decree forbidding burial of her brother Polynices, who had attacked Thebes. She was sealed alive in a tomb. Sophocles's tragedy of her name (c. 441 BC) became foundational for Western political philosophy. Why?
answer: It set divine law (which required burial) against civil law (which forbade it), establishing a classic dilemma.
choices: It set divine law (which required burial) against civil law (which forbade it), establishing a classic dilemma.
It celebrated democracy over monarchy, with Antigone speaking for the people against Creon's tyranny.
It taught that women were the moral superiors of men in the Greek tradition.
It proved that fate (the family curse) overrode any human choice or political institution.
context: Hegel famously used *Antigone* to illustrate the 'tragic collision' of two valid claims. Sophocles's *Antigone* has been rewritten by Anouilh (under Vichy), Brecht (in the late 1940s), Athol Fugard (under apartheid), Seamus Heaney, and many others — each time as a meditation on conscience and the state.

question: Heracles' final death came not in any of his labors but through a poisoned shirt. As he had been crossing a river with his wife Deianeira, the centaur Nessus had tried to assault her. Heracles shot Nessus with a Hydra-poisoned arrow. The dying Nessus told Deianeira to keep his blood. Why?
answer: Nessus claimed it would be a love-charm to keep Heracles faithful — actually Hydra-tainted, it would kill.
choices: Nessus claimed it would be a love-charm to keep Heracles faithful — actually Hydra-tainted, it would kill.
Nessus claimed it would grant her own family the gift of horsemanship for generations.
Nessus claimed it would protect their household from monsters and beasts of the wild.
Nessus claimed it would make her children immortal if they bathed in it at birth.
context: Years later, jealous of a captive princess, Deianeira soaked Heracles' tunic in Nessus's blood. The Hydra venom burned through Heracles's flesh; he built his own pyre and was burned alive on Mount Oeta. He became a god, taken up to Olympus, where he married Hebe (cup-bearer of the gods). Deianeira killed herself when she learned what she had done.

question: Asclepius, son of Apollo and the mortal princess Coronis, was the great healing demigod. Athena gave him drops of Medusa's blood — from the left side of her head it killed, from the right side it healed. Why was he eventually killed by Zeus?
answer: He had used his healing power to raise the dead — threatening the proper order of mortality.
choices: He had used his healing power to raise the dead — threatening the proper order of mortality.
He had rejected Apollo's authority and set up his own healing cult independent of the gods.
He had healed Achilles in advance against the arrow that should have killed him.
He had refused to share his knowledge with mortal physicians, hoarding it for the gods.
context: Zeus killed Asclepius with a thunderbolt; Apollo killed the Cyclopes (who had forged the thunderbolt) in revenge. Asclepius eventually became a god, with major healing sanctuaries at Epidaurus, Kos, and Pergamon. Patients slept in his temples expecting healing dreams — the *incubatio* practice. His staff (a single snake) gave us the modern medical symbol.

question: Achilles' tutor was a wise centaur who also taught Asclepius and Jason — half man, half horse, but unlike the brutish other centaurs, gentle and learned. Who was he?
answer: Chiron — eldest of the centaurs, son of Cronus and Philyra, immortal until his accidental death.
choices: Chiron — eldest of the centaurs, son of Cronus and Philyra, immortal until his accidental death.
Nessus — but Nessus was the centaur who poisoned Heracles, not a teacher.
Pholus — friend of Heracles who entertained him with wine, accidentally killed in the fight that followed.
Eurytion — a centaur at the wedding of Pirithous, who fought when drunk on wine.
context: Chiron was wounded by one of Heracles's Hydra-poisoned arrows. Immortal but in unbearable pain, he traded his immortality with Prometheus, who took it on (and was thereby released from his eternal liver-eating torment). Chiron was placed in the sky as the constellation Centaurus.

question: Iphigenia, daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, was demanded by Artemis as a sacrifice at Aulis to allow the Greek fleet to sail to Troy. Agamemnon's lying letter — telling Clytemnestra Iphigenia would be married to Achilles — brought the girl to her sacrifice. What did Artemis do at the last moment?
answer: Substituted a deer on the altar and took Iphigenia to Tauris to be her priestess.
choices: Substituted a deer on the altar and took Iphigenia to Tauris to be her priestess.
Allowed the sacrifice but later granted Iphigenia an honored afterlife in Elysium.
Cursed Agamemnon's house, which is why Clytemnestra later killed him.
Refused to allow the sacrifice and instead struck the Greek fleet with plague.
context: Versions vary — Aeschylus's *Agamemnon* has Iphigenia actually sacrificed (and her death triggers Clytemnestra's revenge ten years later). Euripides's two *Iphigenia* plays use the deer-substitution and her later priestess role. The Iphigenia cycle is among the most-set Greek myths in Western opera and theater.

question: Orestes, son of Agamemnon, returned from exile to avenge his father's murder by his mother Clytemnestra. Killing his mother was a hideous moral demand. Aeschylus's *Oresteia* — the only complete surviving Greek tragic trilogy — dramatizes the consequences. What pursued Orestes after the matricide?
answer: The Erinyes (Furies) — primordial avenging spirits of kindred blood, hunting him through the world.
choices: The Erinyes (Furies) — primordial avenging spirits of kindred blood, hunting him through the world.
Apollo himself, who reversed his command to commit matricide and now sought to punish him.
Athena, whose temple Orestes had defiled by entering still bloody from the killing.
Hades, whose laws Orestes had broken by sending two souls to him before their time.
context: The Erinyes were ancient chthonic powers from the earlier stratum of Greek religion. The trilogy's third play, *Eumenides*, ends with Athena establishing a court at the Areopagus in Athens to try Orestes — and converting the Furies into 'Kindly Ones' (Eumenides) integrated into the new civic order. The transition from blood-vengeance to legal judgment is one of the great themes of Greek drama.

question: The dwarves in Norse cosmology were master craftsmen who lived in Svartalfheim. From them came many of the gods' most powerful possessions, including the chain Gleipnir, the hammer Mjolnir, Freyr's ship Skidbladnir, and Odin's spear Gungnir. What was Skidbladnir's special property?
answer: It always had a fair wind, and could be folded up like a cloth and carried in a pouch.
choices: It always had a fair wind, and could be folded up like a cloth and carried in a pouch.
It became invisible when its sails were raised, allowing surprise attacks.
It could travel beneath the sea as easily as above, like a Viking submarine.
It glowed like the sun and could not be approached by giants in their dark caves.
context: Skidbladnir was the best of ships — large enough to hold all the gods with their weapons, yet foldable. The Norse dwarven craftsmanship motif underlies later European fairy-tale dwarfs and Tolkien's Khazad-dûm. The Eddic poem *Alvissmal* features a wisdom-contest between Thor and a dwarf in which Thor stalls until sunrise turns the dwarf to stone.

question: Skadi, a giantess and daughter of Thiazi, came to Asgard demanding satisfaction for her father's death. The gods offered to let her choose a husband by looking only at the gods' feet. She chose the most beautiful feet, expecting they belonged to Baldr. To whom did they belong?
answer: Njord — the Vanir sea-god, whose feet were beautiful from constant washing in the sea-foam.
choices: Njord — the Vanir sea-god, whose feet were beautiful from constant washing in the sea-foam.
Freyr — the Vanir fertility god, who had given his feet careful attention since youth.
Heimdall — guardian of Bifrost, whose feet were polished by walking back and forth on the bridge.
Bragi — god of poetry, whose feet were tender from never having walked far from his hall.
context: Skadi and Njord could not live happily — she preferred her father's snowy mountains, he the sea. They separated after trying both. The Eddic stories often combine high mythological seriousness with broad comedy. Skadi became patron of skiing and winter hunting. The name 'Scandinavia' may derive from Skadi.

question: Bragi was the Norse god of poetry — a relatively minor figure compared to the major Aesir but with one important connection. He greeted dead warriors arriving at Valhalla and gave them their place at the feast. Who was his wife?
answer: Idunn — goddess of youth, keeper of the apples that maintained the gods' immortality.
choices: Idunn — goddess of youth, keeper of the apples that maintained the gods' immortality.
Sif — but Sif is Thor's wife, with the golden hair after Loki cut off her natural hair.
Nanna — but Nanna is Baldr's wife, who died of grief at his death.
Skadi — but Skadi married Njord (briefly) and was later associated with Ullr.
context: Bragi's wife Idunn is one of the most consequential goddesses despite small narrative scope — her apples of youth keep all the Aesir from aging. When Loki delivered her to Thiazi the giant, the Aesir began to age visibly before Loki could retrieve her. The name 'Bragi' may also have been used for human poets — *bragar*. The English 'brag' may distantly descend from this root.

question: Hel — daughter of Loki and Angrboda — ruled the realm of the dead who had not died in battle. Her body was described in Snorri's *Gylfaginning* with a striking detail. What was it?
answer: Half her face and body was the color of living flesh, half was black or blue like a corpse.
choices: Half her face and body was the color of living flesh, half was black or blue like a corpse.
Her hair was made of serpents, like the Greek Medusa's, but venomous to all but Loki.
She had three faces — one of a young girl, one of a woman, one of an old crone.
She was beautiful from the front and skeletal from the back — invisibly two-natured.
context: Hel gave her name to the English word 'hell' — though the Norse Hel is more like Hades than the Christian Hell. Her realm Helheim is cold, misty, and shadowed but not particularly torturous. The realm beneath Helheim — Niflhel — held actual punishment for oathbreakers and murderers, an underworld within an underworld.

question: Heimdall, guardian of Bifrost, was said to have been born of nine mothers — said variously to be nine sisters or nine waves of the sea. He had teeth of gold and could see for 100 leagues by day or by night. Who blew the Gjallarhorn at Ragnarok?
answer: Heimdall — the horn-blast summons the gods to their last battle.
choices: Heimdall — the horn-blast summons the gods to their last battle.
Odin — but Odin's role at Ragnarok is to be devoured by Fenrir, not to blow the horn.
Thor — but Thor's role at Ragnarok is to kill the World-Serpent and die of its venom.
Tyr — but Tyr's role at Ragnarok is to kill the hellhound Garm and die of its wounds.
context: Heimdall's Gjallarhorn — 'resounding horn' — is heard 'in all the worlds' at Ragnarok. After blowing it, Heimdall enters the final battle against Loki; they kill each other. Their enmity goes back to a story in which Heimdall, as a seal, fought Loki, also as a seal, over the Brisingamen necklace Loki had stolen from Freyja.

question: Loki was punished after his role in Baldr's death by being bound to three stones with the entrails of one of his own sons (transformed into a wolf by another son, then killed). Over his face the goddess Skadi placed something. What?
answer: A venomous serpent, whose dripping venom Loki's wife Sigyn caught in a bowl — except when she emptied it.
choices: A venomous serpent, whose dripping venom Loki's wife Sigyn caught in a bowl — except when she emptied it.
A great stone, which crushed his face and prevented him from speaking until Ragnarok.
A burning torch, fed by oil from a brazier that never went out until the end of the world.
A spike of ice, which the cold giants kept renewing from Niflheim's eternal frost.
context: Whenever Sigyn emptied the bowl, the venom would drip on Loki's face. His writhing in agony was said to cause earthquakes. Sigyn's devotion to her tormented husband — staying with him through eons of his suffering — is among the most touching loyalty-images in Norse myth. At Ragnarok, Loki breaks free and leads the giants against the Aesir.

question: The *Volsunga Saga* — written in 13th-century Iceland but drawing on much older Germanic legend — tells of the hero Sigurd (German Siegfried), who slew a dragon, found a hoard of gold, and was eventually betrayed and killed. What was the dragon's name?
answer: Fafnir — a son of a king who transformed himself into a dragon to guard the cursed gold of the Rhine.
choices: Fafnir — a son of a king who transformed himself into a dragon to guard the cursed gold of the Rhine.
Nidhogg — the dragon that gnaws Yggdrasil's root, but a separate cosmic dragon, not a hoard-keeper.
Jormungandr — the World-Serpent, but Jormungandr is in the sea around Midgard, not on land.
Tiamat — but Tiamat is a Babylonian cosmic monster, not from Norse-Germanic legend.
context: The Volsung saga underlies both Wagner's *Ring* cycle (with names Germanicized) and Tolkien's tales of the dragon Glaurung. After eating the dragon's heart Sigurd could understand the speech of birds, who warned him of his foster-brother's treachery. The saga's tragic logic — gold attracts curse — has shaped centuries of dragon-and-treasure tradition.

question: Brunhild, a Valkyrie who disobeyed Odin and was punished by being placed asleep in a ring of fire on a mountain, was rescued by the hero Sigurd. She became one of the central tragic figures of the Volsung-Nibelung legend. What ultimately did she do?
answer: Killed herself on Sigurd's funeral pyre, having engineered his death in vengeance for his abandoning her.
choices: Killed herself on Sigurd's funeral pyre, having engineered his death in vengeance for his abandoning her.
Married Gunnar and lived in peace, leaving Sigurd to his own fate after the rescue.
Was returned to her sleep on the mountain by the gods, and remained there until Ragnarok.
Founded the dynasty of the kings of Burgundy, becoming the matriarch of the Nibelung clan.
context: Brunhild's tragic role in the *Volsunga Saga* and Wagner's *Ring* (where she is Brünnhilde) involves passions of betrayal and revenge that resonate across cultures. The 'sleeping princess in a ring of fire' motif descended into Sleeping Beauty. Brunhild's self-immolation on Sigurd's pyre is one of the most-staged scenes in Wagnerian opera.

question: *Beowulf* — an Old English epic of c. 700–1000 AD — tells of a Geatish (southern Swedish) hero who fights the monster Grendel and Grendel's mother in Denmark, then returns home to become king and dies fighting a dragon. Its world is the Germanic-Norse heroic world. Where is the manuscript?
answer: The British Library — the Nowell Codex (Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv), surviving a 1731 fire.
choices: The British Library — the Nowell Codex (Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv), surviving a 1731 fire.
The Royal Library of Copenhagen — but the Codex Regius (Poetic Edda) is at the Arnamagnaean Institute in Reykjavik.
The Bodleian Library at Oxford — but Beowulf was not preserved at the Bodleian.
The Vatican Library — but Vatican holdings of Old English poetry are minor.
context: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript that was nearly destroyed in 1731 — the Cotton fire damaged it at the edges. Its dating is contested (c. 700 to c. 1000) but it is the longest surviving Old English poem. J. R. R. Tolkien's 1936 lecture 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' transformed academic study of the poem; Seamus Heaney's 1999 translation revived popular reading.

question: The Saami people — had a religion of shamans, drums, and tutelary spirits that interacted with the Norse but was distinct from it. The Christianization of the Saami was particularly violent and late. Where was the southernmost extent of pre-Christian Saami culture in historical times?
answer: Norway and Sweden to about the 65th parallel, before the Christianization that intensified after 1700.
choices: Norway and Sweden to about the 65th parallel, before the Christianization that intensified after 1700.
All of Norway and Sweden — but the Saami had withdrawn northward by the medieval period.
Only the very far north — above the Arctic Circle, with no historical southern extent.
Through Finland and into Russia but not into Scandinavia proper.
context: Saami religion involved a noaidi (shaman) drumming to enter trance; sacred sites in the landscape; reindeer-herding rituals. The Swedish church burned Saami drums (the *runebomme*) into the 18th century. Modern Saami religious revival, like the parallel revival of Norse paganism (Asatru), reclaims a tradition that Christianization had largely suppressed. Saami parliaments exist in Norway, Sweden, and Finland.

question: John Wycliffe (c. 1330–1384), an Oxford theologian, attacked papal authority and translated the Bible into English a century and a half before Tyndale. His followers — preaching unauthorized in English — became known by a dismissive nickname meaning 'mumblers' or 'mutterers.' What?
answer: Lollards — from the Dutch *lollaerd*, 'mutterer,' applied to English Wycliffite preachers.
choices: Lollards — from the Dutch *lollaerd*, 'mutterer,' applied to English Wycliffite preachers.
Quakers — but Quakers are 17th-century, from George Fox, not 14th-century Wycliffite.
Anabaptists — but Anabaptists are 16th-century continental, not 14th-century English.
Diggers — but Diggers are 17th-century English Civil War radicals, distinct movement.
context: Wycliffe died in his bed; the Council of Constance (1415) declared him a heretic posthumously, ordered his bones exhumed and burned. Lollardy persisted underground in England through the 15th century — a 'pre-Reformation' tradition that fed into Tyndale and the English Reformation. Wycliffe's vernacular Bible was the first English Bible — handwritten, copied, and circulated despite suppression.

question: Phaethon, son of Helios the sun god, persuaded his father to let him drive the solar chariot for a day. He could not control the four winged horses; the chariot's path veered, burning the earth and creating the Sahara. How did the story end?
answer: Zeus struck Phaethon with a thunderbolt to stop the burning; he fell into the river Eridanus.
choices: Zeus struck Phaethon with a thunderbolt to stop the burning; he fell into the river Eridanus.
Helios himself caught the chariot before disaster and drove it back to safety; Phaethon survived.
Apollo replaced Helios at the reins; Phaethon was returned to his mother unharmed but warned.
The horses themselves turned toward Olympus; Phaethon was forgiven and made keeper of the stables.
context: Phaethon's sisters, the Heliades, mourned him so long that they were turned into poplar trees on the banks of the Eridanus; their tears became amber. Ovid's *Metamorphoses* Book 2 has the most-told version. The myth gave Western literature its archetype of youthful overreach: 'flying too close to the sun' shares this lineage with Icarus.

question: Pluto, lord of the underworld, abducted Persephone in his black chariot from a meadow at Enna in Sicily. The location was so specific that Cicero records the local cult of Demeter and Persephone there. The Romans equated their underworld lord with Pluto. What was his Greek name?
answer: Hades — son of Cronus, brother of Zeus and Poseidon, lord of the realm of the dead.
choices: Hades — son of Cronus, brother of Zeus and Poseidon, lord of the realm of the dead.
Tartarus — but Tartarus is the deep place beneath Hades, where the Titans are imprisoned.
Charon — but Charon is the ferryman across the river Styx, not the underworld king.
Erebus — but Erebus is the primordial darkness, a place rather than a personal god.
context: Hades was uncomfortable to name directly; 'Pluto' ('wealthy one,' from the wealth of the earth) was a euphemism that Romans treated as a personal name. The realm of Hades is sometimes also called Hades by metonymy. Hades was a brother of Zeus and full Olympian — but rarely depicted with the other twelve, since he stayed in his own realm.

question: Hippolytus, son of Theseus and the Amazon Hippolyta, was devoted to the virgin Artemis and despised Aphrodite. Aphrodite revenged herself by causing his stepmother Phaedra to fall in love with him. Rejected, Phaedra accused him of assault. What did Theseus do?
answer: Cursed Hippolytus and called on Poseidon to destroy him — which Poseidon did by sending a sea-bull that frightened his horses.
choices: Cursed Hippolytus and called on Poseidon to destroy him — which Poseidon did by sending a sea-bull that frightened his horses.
Drove Hippolytus into exile in his Spartan grandfather's kingdom, where he lived out his days.
Sentenced Hippolytus to the gladiatorial games at Athens, where the youth was killed by a lion.
Refused to believe Phaedra and exiled her instead — but Hippolytus had already fled in despair.
context: Euripides' *Hippolytus* (428 BC) — and Racine's *Phèdre* (1677), and Eugene O'Neill's *Desire Under the Elms* (1924) — all draw on this myth. Phaedra hangs herself; Theseus discovers the truth too late. The story is Greek tragedy's most-staged exploration of misdirected passion, false accusation, and parental judgment.

question: The dwarf brothers Brokk and Eitri, on a wager with Loki, forged three treasures for the gods: Sif's golden hair, Freyr's ship Skidbladnir, and Odin's spear Gungnir. Eitri then made three more masterpieces. What were they?
answer: Mjolnir (Thor's hammer), Gullinbursti (Freyr's golden boar), and Draupnir (Odin's ring).
choices: Mjolnir (Thor's hammer), Gullinbursti (Freyr's golden boar), and Draupnir (Odin's ring).
Sleipnir (Odin's eight-legged horse), Gjallarhorn (Heimdall's horn), and Gleipnir (Fenrir's chain).
Brisingamen (Freyja's necklace), Megingjord (Thor's strength-belt), and Andvarinaut (the cursed ring).
Sif's hair, Skidbladnir, and Gungnir — but these are the same three from the first commission.
context: Loki tried to disrupt the forging by buzzing as a fly and biting Brokk on the eyelid — Brokk's slip caused Mjolnir's handle to be slightly short. The gods awarded the bet to Brokk; Loki escaped with his head, but Brokk sewed his lips shut. The story underlines Norse smithing as both magical and competitive.

question: The most-stated origin myth for the Viking diaspora is internal pressure in Norway — overpopulation, primogeniture leaving younger sons landless, and the centralizing policies of Harald Fairhair (ruled c. 872–930). But there were also pull factors. What was a major one?
answer: Trade routes from the Arabian caliphate paid in silver — which has been found by the ton in Viking-age Scandinavian hoards.
choices: Trade routes from the Arabian caliphate paid in silver — which has been found by the ton in Viking-age Scandinavian hoards.
Roman ruins in northern Europe contained vast unguarded wealth.
The Carolingian empire was actively recruiting Viking warriors for its civil wars.
Greenland's agriculture was known to be richer than Norway's.
context: Massive silver hoards — over 1,000 found across Scandinavia — show the wealth that flowed back. Vikings traded furs, slaves, amber, and walrus ivory south and east; from Baghdad came Arab silver dirhams (millions found in Sweden). The connection between Viking expansion and the long-distance silver trade is fundamental to modern Viking studies.

question: The Sikh religion was founded by Guru Nanak (1469–1539) in the Punjab region of northern India, fusing elements of Hindu and Islamic devotion in a teaching of one universal God. What was his foundational saying after a transformative experience at a river?
answer: 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — denying religious distinctions before the one God.
choices: 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — denying religious distinctions before the one God.
'God is the gardener, and the world the garden' — a horticultural metaphor for divine care.
'The wheel of time turns; only the Name endures' — affirming continuity across rebirths.
'The teacher within each soul speaks louder than any without' — emphasizing inner knowledge.
context: Nanak was succeeded by nine human gurus, each named in Sikh tradition. The tenth, Guru Gobind Singh (1666–1708), declared that there would be no eleventh — the Guru Granth Sahib (sacred scripture) would be the eternal guru. The Golden Temple at Amritsar (founded 1574, gilded 1830) is the Sikh holy site.

question: Confucius (Kongzi, 551–479 BC) was a Chinese teacher and political adviser whose recorded sayings — collected in the *Analects* — became foundational for Chinese government, education, and family life. His central ethical concept was a relational virtue. What is it?
choices: Li (禮) — usually rendered as 'ritual,' 'propriety,' or 'rules of behavior.'
Xiao (孝) — filial piety, the love and respect owed to parents and ancestors.
Junzi (君子) — the gentleman or noble person; an ideal type, not a virtue.
context: Confucianism is sometimes called a philosophy and sometimes a religion. Its emphasis on this-worldly ethics, ancestral veneration, and political-philosophical guidance fits both categories. Confucius's intellectual influence on East Asia for 2500 years rivals any religious tradition's influence elsewhere — even though Confucian temples exist alongside the Confucian state cult.

question: On April 6, 1320, Scottish nobles meeting at Arbroath sent a declaration to Pope John XXII at Avignon affirming Scottish independence from England. The document is one of the great political-theological statements of the European Middle Ages. What is its famous line?
answer: 'As long as a hundred of us remain alive, we shall never on any conditions submit to English rule.'
choices: 'As long as a hundred of us remain alive, we shall never on any conditions submit to English rule.'
'The Lord protect Scotland, and may her enemies tremble at the sound of her cause.'
'We fight not for glory, nor riches, nor honors — but for that liberty which no good man surrenders but with his life.'
Both A and C — these famous lines are both in the actual text of the Declaration.
context: The Declaration of Arbroath is among the rhetorical models for the American Declaration of Independence (1776). Its theological frame — God's covenant with peoples, the moral basis of political legitimacy — is medieval but recognizable in the Founders. It was signed by 51 Scottish magnates and 8 bishops, demonstrating the unity of church and political nation against papal interference.

question: Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563), a French Protestant theologian who had worked with Calvin in Geneva, broke with him over the burning of Servetus in 1553. His 1554 work *Concerning Heretics* defended religious toleration. What is its most famous passage?
answer: 'To kill a man is not to defend a doctrine; it is to kill a man.'
choices: 'To kill a man is not to defend a doctrine; it is to kill a man.'
'The doctrine of Christ is not maintained by the killing of those who differ; it is destroyed.'
'The truest test of a Christian is willingness to suffer for truth; not to make others suffer for it.'
All three statements are in Castellio's writings on religious toleration.
context: Castellio is one of the great early defenders of religious freedom — a position he held against both Catholic and Calvinist authoritarianism. He was hounded from Basel and lived in poverty; he died at 47, perhaps under suspicion of impending trial. His arguments influenced later toleration thinkers — Pierre Bayle, John Locke, Voltaire — though his name is now less remembered than theirs.

question: Roger Williams (1603–1683), a Puritan minister exiled from Massachusetts Bay for 'newe & dangerous opinions' (especially the demand for separation of church and state), founded Providence and the Rhode Island colony in 1636. What did he establish?
answer: The first colony in the Americas with full religious toleration and separation of church and state.
choices: The first colony in the Americas with full religious toleration and separation of church and state.
The first Puritan colony with bishops, restoring Anglican order against the Congregational majority.
The first Catholic colony in New England, predating Maryland by several years.
The first explicitly democratic colony, with universal male suffrage from its founding.
context: Williams's views on religious freedom — drawn from a radical Protestant reading of the gospel — anticipated the American First Amendment by 150 years. Rhode Island welcomed Quakers and Jews when other colonies expelled them. The Touro Synagogue at Newport (1763) is the oldest synagogue still standing in the United States — a direct legacy of Williams's vision.

question: The 1054 schism produced two major branches of Christianity, Catholic and Eastern Orthodox. The Eastern church has remained organized as a communion of self-governing 'autocephalous' churches. How many are there today?
answer: Fifteen — major autocephalous churches plus several smaller autonomous churches.
choices: Fifteen — major autocephalous churches plus several smaller autonomous churches.
Five — the four ancient patriarchates plus Moscow as the 'third Rome.'
Two — Greek and Russian, with all others derivative.
Thirty — counting every national church as an autocephalous body.
context: The fifteen include four ancient patriarchates (Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem); the patriarchates of Russia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Georgia; the archbishoprics of Cyprus, Greece, Poland, Albania, the Czech-Slovak Lands; and the Orthodox Church in America (the autocephaly of which is contested). The Ukrainian church's status has been a major recent issue, especially since 2018.

question: The 'Catholic Reformation' of the 16th century included the Council of Trent, the founding of the Jesuits and other new orders, the development of seminary education, the *Index Librorum Prohibitorum*, and one of the great religious-artistic revolutions in Western history. What style of art did it foster?
answer: The Baroque — Bernini, Caravaggio, Rubens — emotionally intense, theatrical, sensory.
choices: The Baroque — Bernini, Caravaggio, Rubens — emotionally intense, theatrical, sensory.
The Gothic — but Gothic is medieval, predating the Reformation by centuries.
The Romanesque — but Romanesque is also medieval, even earlier than Gothic.
The Neoclassical — but Neoclassicism is 18th-century, much later than the Counter-Reformation.
context: Baroque art served Counter-Reformation theology — direct emotional appeal, dramatic narrative, sensory immediacy in spaces designed for the renewed Mass and Marian devotion. Bernini's *Ecstasy of St. Teresa* in Santa Maria della Vittoria is a paradigm: the marble flesh, the gold rays, the swooning saint. The Society of Jesus directly patronized Baroque artists across Catholic Europe and into the missions.

question: Patroclus, dear friend of Achilles, finally persuaded Achilles to let him wear the great hero's armor and lead the Myrmidons into battle to save the Greek ships. He drove the Trojans back to their walls and was killed by their greatest warrior. Who killed him?
answer: Hector — eldest son of Priam, who stripped the armor from his body and would meet Achilles in revenge.
choices: Hector — eldest son of Priam, who stripped the armor from his body and would meet Achilles in revenge.
Paris — but Paris killed Achilles later with an arrow guided by Apollo to the heel.
Aeneas — son of Anchises and Aphrodite, but he was rescued by his mother, not the killer of Patroclus.
Sarpedon — son of Zeus, but Patroclus had killed Sarpedon earlier in the same battle.
context: *Iliad* Book 16. Apollo first struck Patroclus from behind, dazing him; a Trojan named Euphorbus wounded him; Hector delivered the killing blow. Patroclus's death is the engine that drives Achilles back into battle and to his own death. Greek tragedy and Plato's *Symposium* read the Achilles-Patroclus bond variously across millennia.

question: Priam, aged king of Troy, did the unthinkable: he went alone, by night, to Achilles's tent to ransom the body of his son Hector. Hermes guided him through the Greek camp. What broke Achilles?
answer: Priam kissed the hands of the man who had killed his son, and both men wept together for their dead.
choices: Priam kissed the hands of the man who had killed his son, and both men wept together for their dead.
Priam offered all the gold of Troy if the body could be returned for proper burial rites.
Priam reminded Achilles that his own father Peleus would soon mourn him in the same way.
Priam swore a great oath to leave Troy forever if the body of Hector were given back to him.
context: *Iliad* Book 24, the poem's final book. Achilles thinks of his father Peleus, who will lose him. Two grieving men eat together in his tent — one of Homer's most-praised passages. The body is returned; the Iliad ends with Hector's funeral. The reconciliation across mortal enmity has shaped tragic narrative ever since.

question: The Greek hero Diomedes, son of Tydeus, was one of the bravest warriors at Troy — second only to Achilles in many accounts. In *Iliad* Book 5 he was so emboldened by Athena that he wounded two gods. Which?
answer: Aphrodite (in the hand as she shielded her son Aeneas) and Ares (in the belly as he fought for the Trojans).
choices: Aphrodite (in the hand as she shielded her son Aeneas) and Ares (in the belly as he fought for the Trojans).
Apollo (driven back from the body of Patroclus) and Artemis (struck while defending the Trojan ranks).
Hera (struck while she fled the field) and Poseidon (wounded as he aided the Greeks).
Hephaestus (caught in the fire of the Scamander) and Hermes (knocked from the air over the plain).
context: Diomedes is unique in *Iliad* for actually wounding immortals. Aphrodite fled to Olympus weeping; Ares, when he fled, bellowed with the cry of ten thousand men. The episode shows Athena's favor on Diomedes — and Greek anxiety about what mortals can do against gods when divine permission allows it. Diomedes survived Troy and ruled Argos.

question: Helen of Sparta — daughter of Zeus and Leda, wife of Menelaus — was carried off by Paris to Troy, igniting the ten-year war. What was unusual about her conception?
answer: Zeus came to Leda as a swan; she bore Helen and her brother Pollux as semi-divine; Castor and Clytemnestra were mortal twins.
choices: Zeus came to Leda as a swan; she bore Helen and her brother Pollux as semi-divine; Castor and Clytemnestra were mortal twins.
Zeus came to Leda as a bull, in the same form he used for Europa; all her children were demigods.
Zeus came to Leda as a shower of gold, identical to his approach to Danae mother of Perseus.
Zeus came to Leda in the form of her own husband Tyndareus, deceiving her completely.
context: The story of Leda and the Swan inspired W.B. Yeats's 1923 poem and Leonardo's lost painting. Helen had a divine father (Zeus); her brothers Castor and Pollux were divided in mortality (Pollux divine, Castor mortal); after Castor's death Pollux shared his immortality, giving the constellation Gemini. The Trojan War, in mythological terms, was largely Zeus's doing through Helen's beauty.

question: Achilles was raised by the centaur Chiron after his mother Thetis attempted to make him immortal. Some versions have her dipping him in the Styx; others have her placing him in fire each night. What gave him near-invulnerability and one weakness?
answer: Held by the heel as Thetis dipped him in the Styx, the water flowed over all his body except the small heel-grip.
choices: Held by the heel as Thetis dipped him in the Styx, the water flowed over all his body except the small heel-grip.
Anointed by ambrosia and held over fire — but Peleus interrupted, and her work was left incomplete.
Born of a sea-goddess, all his blood was salt and water until he tasted human food at Chiron's table.
Wrapped in Hephaestus's golden cloth as an infant, all but the right palm where Thetis had held the cloth.
context: Statius's *Achilleid* and the Roman tradition popularized the Styx-dipping. Homer never describes the immortality ritual directly — Achilles's death from a heel-arrow is post-Homeric. Paris (or Apollo guiding Paris's arrow) killed Achilles by striking his vulnerable heel — the origin of the English idiom 'Achilles' heel.'

question: Agamemnon — leader of the Greek armies at Troy — returned home to Mycenae after the war's end. His wife Clytemnestra had a long ten years to plot. What did she do?
answer: She killed him in his bath, on the day of his return, with her lover Aegisthus — partly avenging her daughter Iphigenia.
choices: She killed him in his bath, on the day of his return, with her lover Aegisthus — partly avenging her daughter Iphigenia.
She poisoned him at the welcome feast, blaming a Trojan curse rather than her own hand.
She fled with Aegisthus to Sparta, leaving Agamemnon to find an empty palace at Mycenae.
She secretly remarried; Agamemnon, finding himself replaced as king, threw himself from the citadel walls.
context: Aeschylus's *Agamemnon* (458 BC) — first play of the *Oresteia* trilogy — is the canonical telling. Clytemnestra's revenge for Iphigenia (sacrificed at Aulis to allow the fleet to sail) makes her one of the most complex of Greek tragic women. Her son Orestes would later kill her and Aegisthus; the curse on the house of Atreus continued.

question: After the fall of Troy, Aeneas — son of Anchises (a mortal Trojan) and Aphrodite — escaped the burning city carrying his father on his back, leading his son Ascanius by the hand. Virgil's *Aeneid* (c. 19 BC) recounts his wanderings. Where did he land that founded Rome's destiny?
answer: Latium in central Italy, where his descendants Romulus and Remus would later found Rome itself.
choices: Latium in central Italy, where his descendants Romulus and Remus would later found Rome itself.
Sicily, where his father died and was buried with games held in his honor.
Carthage, where Queen Dido fell in love with him and killed herself when he left.
Egypt, where Aeneas was honored by Pharaoh before continuing to the western Mediterranean.
context: Virgil's epic deliberately mirrored Homer — first six books like the *Odyssey* (wandering), last six like the *Iliad* (war for the new land). Aeneas's foundational role gave Rome a Trojan ancestry distinct from Greek lineage. The medieval translation tradition placed Aeneas at the center of European epic; Dante chose him as Virgil's hero.

question: Odysseus arrived at the island of the Lotus-Eaters early in his ten-year journey home from Troy. His men ate the fruit and lost their will to leave. What did Odysseus do?
answer: He dragged them back to the ships weeping, bound them to the rowing benches, and put out to sea.
choices: He dragged them back to the ships weeping, bound them to the rowing benches, and put out to sea.
He left them on the island, judging them lost, and continued with a smaller crew.
He ate the lotus himself to understand its power, then organized a hard-won departure.
He killed the Lotus-Eater chiefs, taking water and provisions before sailing on.
context: *Odyssey* Book 9. The Lotus-Eaters are gentle; their fruit causes forgetfulness of home — perhaps the deepest threat in the Odyssey, which is centrally about homecoming. The lotus has been variously identified (the date palm, the jujube). The episode shapes Tennyson's 'The Lotos-Eaters' (1832), reflecting Victorian anxieties about ease versus duty.

question: In the underworld during his journey, Odysseus met the ghosts of his fallen comrades. One spoke to him with bitter words — preferring slavery in the world above to being king of the dead. Who?
answer: Achilles — saying he would rather be a hired farm-laborer on earth than lord over all the perished dead.
choices: Achilles — saying he would rather be a hired farm-laborer on earth than lord over all the perished dead.
Patroclus — wishing he had survived to grow old beside Achilles in Phthia.
Agamemnon — bitterly cursing Clytemnestra and warning Odysseus not to trust his wife.
Ajax — turning his back in silent anger over the disputed armor of Achilles.
context: *Odyssey* Book 11 — the *Nekuia* (book of the dead). Achilles, who had chosen short glorious life over long obscure life in the *Iliad*, reverses his judgment in death. Agamemnon does warn against women's treachery. Ajax does turn away in silence. These are some of the most-quoted lines in classical literature for the heaviness of death.

question: Odysseus's men, against his orders, slaughtered the cattle of the sun god Helios on the island of Thrinacia after they had been becalmed for a month and were starving. What was the consequence?
answer: Zeus destroyed their ship with lightning when they sailed — only Odysseus, who had not eaten, survived.
choices: Zeus destroyed their ship with lightning when they sailed — only Odysseus, who had not eaten, survived.
Helios pursued them across the sea in his solar chariot, scorching the sails until they sank.
The Cyclops Polyphemus, alerted by Helios, raised a great wind that drove them back to his island.
The cattle themselves rose up and trampled the men before they could finish their meal.
context: *Odyssey* Book 12. Helios threatened to leave the sun and shine instead among the dead unless the cattle-killers were punished; Zeus complied. Odysseus alone clung to the wreckage and drifted to Calypso's island, where he stayed seven years. The episode shows divine justice working through the dynamics of cosmic order, not whim.

question: Hephaestus, lame smith god of fire and metalworking, had been thrown from Olympus once. By whom and why?
answer: By his mother Hera, who was ashamed of having borne a lame child; he fell for a day and landed on Lemnos.
choices: By his mother Hera, who was ashamed of having borne a lame child; he fell for a day and landed on Lemnos.
By Zeus, for taking Hera's side in a quarrel; he was thrown to Lemnos and walked with a limp ever after.
By Poseidon, in a dispute over the design of his palace beneath the sea.
Both A and B occur in different sources — Hera in some, Zeus in others; the lameness has multiple causes.
context: Homer's *Iliad* Book 1 has Zeus throwing him out for taking Hera's part; Hesiod has Hera throwing him out as ugly. Hephaestus set up his forge on Lemnos (the island most associated with him) and is said to have built golden mechanical servants and the bronze giant Talos. He married Aphrodite — a famously unhappy match — and was the maker of Achilles's armor in *Iliad* Book 18.

question: Hermes was the only Olympian who could travel freely between the realms of the living and the dead. He guided souls to Hades — a role called by a specific Greek word. What?
choices: Thaumaturge — 'wonder-worker,' applied later to saints and miracle-workers.
Pneumatic — but pneumatic means 'spiritual' or 'of breath,' not specifically Hermes's role.
Theurgist — 'worker of divine things,' a later Neoplatonic term for ritualist.
context: The psychopomp role gave Hermes a deep underworld association — paradoxically, given his usual upper-world business with travelers and merchants. The Hermes of mystical and esoteric traditions (Hermes Trismegistus) draws on this border-crossing role. The image of Hermes leading souls is on countless Greek grave stelai. Charon ferried; Hermes guided.

question: Iris was a minor Olympian whose role was specific and visible. What was she?
answer: A messenger of the gods (especially Hera), whose path across the sky was the rainbow.
choices: A messenger of the gods (especially Hera), whose path across the sky was the rainbow.
The Olympian cup-bearer, who served nectar and ambrosia until Ganymede replaced her.
Patroness of Iris flowers, named for her because they sprang where she trod on earth.
Goddess of dawn-light, who lit the path before Helios's chariot each morning.
context: Iris's rainbow path connected Olympus to earth; she carried Hera's messages. The Greek anatomical 'iris' (colored part of the eye) gets its name from her — for the eye's color-spectrum. Later iconography sometimes confused Iris with the rosy-fingered Eos (dawn). Iris is also the bringer of news to the gods of mortal sacrifices and prayers.

question: Eros — god of love, son of Aphrodite in most accounts — was originally a primordial cosmic force in Hesiod's *Theogony*. In later mythology he became a winged boy. What weapon does he carry?
answer: A bow and two kinds of arrows — gold for love, lead for hatred — based on Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.
choices: A bow and two kinds of arrows — gold for love, lead for hatred — based on Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.
A torch alone, which he uses to kindle or extinguish desire in mortals he visits.
A net of golden threads, which he casts over lovers to bind them to each other.
A small flute, whose music draws lovers to each other from across the sea.
context: Ovid's *Metamorphoses* Book 1 gives the two-arrow scheme. Apollo, who had mocked Eros's archery, was struck with a gold arrow and fell in love with Daphne; she was struck with a lead one and fled him — turning into a laurel tree to escape. The Roman 'Cupid' is the same god. The 'piercing' of the heart by love survives as poetic metaphor.

question: Pan — son of Hermes, god of shepherds and the wild — had the legs and horns of a goat. He gave his name to a particular kind of terror. What?
answer: Panic — sudden, irrational fear of the kind he caused by appearing unexpectedly to travelers.
choices: Panic — sudden, irrational fear of the kind he caused by appearing unexpectedly to travelers.
Pandemonium — but this is Milton's coinage for hell's capital, not a Pan derivation.
Pantheism — the doctrine that everything is divine; named from *pan* (all), not from the god.
Pandora — but Pandora's name comes from *pan-dora* (all-gifted), not from the god Pan.
context: Pan's appearances were said to cause sudden mass terror — especially in herds and armies. The Greeks reported Pan's intervention at the Battle of Marathon (490 BC), giving thanks afterward. Plutarch records the (Christianized) legend of the 'great Pan is dead' announced from the sea in the time of Tiberius — read by Christians as the death of the old gods.

question: Aeolus, keeper of the winds, was visited by Odysseus on his long journey home. As a gift, he gave him a bag containing all the winds save the West Wind. What happened?
answer: Odysseus's men, suspecting gold inside, opened the bag while he slept — and the winds blew them back to Aeolus.
choices: Odysseus's men, suspecting gold inside, opened the bag while he slept — and the winds blew them back to Aeolus.
The bag broke on a rock as Odysseus carried it ashore; the winds escaped and tore the ship apart.
Aeolus changed his mind, opened the bag himself, and demanded payment for the gift.
Odysseus's wife Penelope dreamed of the bag and broke its echo in the world above; the winds dispersed.
context: *Odyssey* Book 10. Aeolus, finding them returned, refused to help a second time, judging them cursed by the gods. The bag-of-winds motif spread widely in folklore. Aeolus has multiple inconsistent identities in classical sources — sometimes a son of Poseidon, sometimes a son of Hippotas, sometimes purely allegorical of the winds themselves. The Aeolian Islands keep his name.

question: Triton — son of Poseidon and Amphitrite — was a merman who blew a conch-shell horn. What did the horn do?
answer: Calmed the seas or roused storms at his father's command, summoning sea creatures with its sound.
choices: Calmed the seas or roused storms at his father's command, summoning sea creatures with its sound.
Held the waters of the world inside it, releasing them as rain when Triton turned it upside down.
Sang the lament for drowned sailors, audible only to those who knew their own death was coming.
Echoed across the seven seas, so that any prayer to Poseidon could reach his palace beneath the waves.
context: Triton was Poseidon's herald — and a model for many later merfolk in European art (Rubens, Bernini). Hesiod made him a son of Poseidon; Apollonius made him a Libyan sea-god who guided the Argonauts. Sea-deity mythology in classical Greek tradition is rich and varied — Nereus, Proteus, Glaucus, and Triton are all important figures.

question: Proteus — an early sea-god, herdsman of Poseidon's seals — could change his shape at will, becoming any creature. He had prophetic knowledge but would only share it if caught and held through every transformation. Who notably wrestled him?
answer: Menelaus — who, stranded in Egypt after Troy, caught Proteus and learned how to return to Sparta.
choices: Menelaus — who, stranded in Egypt after Troy, caught Proteus and learned how to return to Sparta.
Heracles — but Heracles's wrestling exploits do not include Proteus in standard mythology.
Odysseus — but Odysseus's prophetic encounter was with Tiresias in the underworld, not Proteus.
Theseus — but Theseus had no Egyptian encounter, his story is centered on Greece.
context: *Odyssey* Book 4: Menelaus tells Telemachus the story. Eidothea, Proteus's daughter, instructed him in how to catch her father. The name 'Proteus' gave us 'protean' for shape-changing. Proteus represented the unpredictable, slippery quality of the sea itself — and of truth, in later philosophical readings.

question: The Charites — the three Graces — were minor Olympians: Aglaea (radiance), Euphrosyne (joy), and Thalia (festivity). Whom did they attend?
answer: Aphrodite — adorning her for her appearances among gods and mortals.
choices: Aphrodite — adorning her for her appearances among gods and mortals.
Hera — bathing her in their springs before her judgments at Olympus.
Athena — weaving the robes she wore at the great Pan-Athenaic festival.
Artemis — gathering flowers for her wreaths as she went hunting in the mountains.
context: Roman 'Gratiae,' from whom we get 'grace.' The three Graces became one of the most-painted classical motifs — Botticelli (*Primavera*, c. 1482), Raphael, Rubens, Canova, and many others. They embodied a balanced beauty that classical artists used to demonstrate skill in depicting the female form from three angles. Their gift to mortals was charm, joy, and ease.

question: Theseus, having unified Attica into Athens, descended once into the underworld with his friend Pirithous to steal Persephone for him as a bride. What happened?
answer: Both were trapped on a stone bench by Hades; Theseus was rescued years later by Heracles, but Pirithous remained forever.
choices: Both were trapped on a stone bench by Hades; Theseus was rescued years later by Heracles, but Pirithous remained forever.
Hades laughed at the impudence and sent them back to the upper world with a warning, no harm done.
Persephone agreed to come, but Demeter intercepted them and turned both heroes to stone.
Pirithous succeeded in escaping with her; Theseus was killed when he turned to look at her face.
context: The 'Chairs of Forgetfulness' or 'Lethe' held them, with serpents twining about.
