He replied 'Woman, mine hour is not yet come.' Mary, undeterred, told the servants 'whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.' Six stone waterpots stood by, each 20-30 gallons. What did Jesus instruct?
answer: Fill the waterpots with water; draw out and bear to the governor — water had become wine of better quality than the first
choices: Fill the waterpots with water; draw out and bear to the governor — water had become wine of better quality than the first
Empty the waterpots into the well; the water would draw up wine for the bridegroom to taste and to discern
Crush the grapes outside the gate; the new wine would be aged in a single hour to match the best vintage
Hide the waterpots under the table; the bridegroom would find skins of new wine where they had stood
context: John 2 records the first 'sign' (semeion) — water made wine, perhaps 120-180 gallons of it. The governor, not knowing the source, called the bridegroom and remarked that normally the good wine is served first; here the best had been kept till last. John presents the signs not as marvels but as windows onto Christ's identity.

question: In John 4, Jesus came to a Samaritan city called Sychar near Jacob's well. Wearied, he sat at the well at noon while his disciples were off buying food. A Samaritan woman came to draw water. He asked for a drink. She was startled — Jews and Samaritans had no dealings. The conversation touched on living water, her five husbands, the place to worship. She asked about the coming Messiah. What did Jesus say?
answer: 'I that speak unto thee am he' — the first explicit Messianic self-disclosure in the Fourth Gospel, given to a Samaritan woman
choices: 'I that speak unto thee am he' — the first explicit Messianic self-disclosure in the Fourth Gospel, given to a Samaritan woman
'Behold the day cometh' — postponing the disclosure to Jerusalem and the Festival of Tabernacles three months later
'Believe in the Father' — refusing the Messianic title at this point and pointing her instead to general theism
'Thou art the Messiah' — turning the disclosure back to the woman as a prophetic riddle she must solve herself
context: John 4:26. The woman left her water jar, ran into the city, and brought back many Samaritans who believed. The episode is striking — Jesus's longest recorded one-on-one conversation, given to a woman, a Samaritan, of disreputable marital history, with a Messianic claim he gave to almost no one else.

question: When Jesus heard of John the Baptist's death, he departed by ship to a desert place. The multitude followed on foot. He had compassion and healed their sick. As evening drew on, the disciples urged him to send them away. He refused. He asked Philip 'Whence shall we buy bread?' Andrew brought a lad with five barley loaves and two fishes. Jesus told the people — about 5,000 men plus women and children — to sit. What happened?
answer: He blessed and brake, distributed by the disciples; all ate and were filled; twelve baskets of fragments remained
choices: He blessed and brake, distributed by the disciples; all ate and were filled; twelve baskets of fragments remained
He multiplied only the loaves and the fish appeared transformed into wine for the elders of the assembly
He commanded an angel to fly to Jerusalem and return with loaves from the Temple altar of shewbread
He sent the disciples to a Roman supply caravan a mile distant which surrendered its provisions without protest
context: The feeding of the 5,000 is the only miracle (besides the Resurrection) in all four Gospels. The twelve baskets — one for each disciple — became a symbol of Eucharistic abundance. John 6 follows it with the 'Bread of Life' discourse, the most explicit Eucharistic teaching in the Gospels.

question: After the feeding, Jesus sent the disciples ahead by boat across the Sea of Galilee while he went alone into a mountain to pray. About the fourth watch (3-6 AM) the boat was in mid-sea, wind contrary. Jesus came walking on the sea. They cried out, supposing it a ghost. He said 'Be of good cheer; it is I.' Peter answered 'Lord, if it be thou, bid me come.' Jesus said 'Come.' What happened?
answer: Peter walked on the water toward Jesus, then saw the wind, was afraid, began to sink, cried 'Lord, save me'; Jesus caught his hand
choices: Peter walked on the water toward Jesus, then saw the wind, was afraid, began to sink, cried 'Lord, save me'; Jesus caught his hand
Peter took a step onto the water, looked down, and sank to his waist; Jesus called him back to the boat from a distance
Peter declined to step out, recognizing his lack of faith; Jesus boarded the boat and the storm immediately ceased
Peter ran across the water to Jesus, embraced him, and the two walked together to the boat without any incident
context: Matthew 14:22-33. The rebuke 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' became a refrain for Christian discipleship — the call is always to fix the eyes on Christ rather than the wind. Mark 6 and John 6 contain the walking on water without Peter's failed attempt.

question: In John 11, Mary and Martha of Bethany sent word that their brother Lazarus was sick. Jesus deliberately delayed two days. When he arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days. Martha met him: 'Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.' Jesus said he was the resurrection. At the tomb he ordered the stone removed. Martha protested — by now he stinketh. Jesus prayed aloud, then cried with a loud voice. What was the cry?
answer: 'Lazarus, come forth' — and Lazarus came out bound hand and foot with graveclothes and a napkin over his face
choices: 'Lazarus, come forth' — and Lazarus came out bound hand and foot with graveclothes and a napkin over his face
'Lazarus, awake' — and the dead man rose up walking, the graveclothes falling away of themselves outside the cave
'Spirit, return' — and Lazarus stood breathing inside the tomb, calling for his sisters before he came out
'Talitha cumi' — and Lazarus was lifted from the slab by an angel; his sisters dressed him and led him out
context: John 11:43-44 — the seventh and climactic sign in John's Gospel, immediately precipitating the Sanhedrin's decision to put Jesus to death. 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35) is the shortest verse in the English Bible. Lazarus appears once more in John 12, eating at table with Jesus.

question: After the Last Supper, Jesus went with his disciples to a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives called Gethsemane ('oil press'). He took Peter, James, and John apart and began to be sorrowful. 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death; tarry ye here, and watch with me.' He went a stone's throw, fell on his face, and prayed. Three times he returned and found the disciples asleep. What did he pray?
answer: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt'
choices: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt'
'O my Father, take me up to the bosom of Abraham, lest the cup overwhelm thy servant in the hour of weakness'
'O my Father, behold the cup is heavy: send me twelve legions of angels to support me in the bearing of it'
'O my Father, the disciples sleep, they know not the cup: turn aside the cup, and let Peter taste it instead'
context: Matthew 26, Mark 14, Luke 22 all record the agony. Luke adds his sweat was as great drops of blood (hematidrosis, a real if rare phenomenon under extreme stress). The 'cup' is the prophets' figure for the wrath of God (Jeremiah 25, Isaiah 51). The acceptance is the hinge of the Passion.

question: At the Last Supper, Jesus had warned Peter: 'before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.' Peter protested he would die first. After the arrest in Gethsemane, Peter followed afar off into the courtyard of Caiaphas the high priest. Three times he was challenged — by a maid, by another, by bystanders. Three times he denied. What broke him?
answer: The cock crew the second time; Jesus, being led across the courtyard, turned and looked at him; Peter went out and wept
choices: The cock crew the second time; Jesus, being led across the courtyard, turned and looked at him; Peter went out and wept
The maid herself was Mary Magdalene, who recognized him from his denials and rebuked him by name before the soldiers
A soldier struck him with the flat of his sword and recognized the wound he had given Malchus by the same blade
John the Beloved, also in the courtyard, called Peter's name from across the fire, and Peter realized he had been seen
context: Luke 22:61-62 records 'the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter,' the look that broke him. Peter's denial — and Christ's later threefold restoration in John 21 ('Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?') — became foundational for Catholic doctrine of the papacy. The church of St. Peter in Gallicantu commemorates it.

question: Friday morning, the chief priests delivered Jesus bound to Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect of Judea. Pilate examined him and found no fault. He sought to release him by Passover custom. The crowd, stirred by the priests, demanded Barabbas — a robber — instead. Pilate offered Jesus repeatedly; each time they shouted 'Crucify him.' He took water and washed his hands. What did he say?
answer: 'I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it' — and the people answered 'His blood be on us, and on our children'
choices: 'I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it' — and the people answered 'His blood be on us, and on our children'
'I have judged him not guilty of capital crime: take ye him' — and the crowd seized Jesus and dragged him out themselves
'I am bound by the law of Caesar: my hands are tied' — and the soldiers led him out without further inquiry from the prefect
'Crucify your king then, if such be your demand' — taunting them with the title before granting the death sentence
context: Matthew 27:24-25. Hand-washing was a Jewish ritual gesture (Deuteronomy 21:6-9); Pilate, knowing the custom, appropriated it. The phrase 'his blood be on us' was tragically misused for centuries to justify Christian violence against Jews; Vatican II's Nostra Aetate (1965) repudiated that reading.

question: Hanging on the cross from about 9 AM to 3 PM, Jesus spoke seven recorded sayings. To the Father: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.' To the repentant thief: 'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.' To his mother and John: 'Woman, behold thy son; behold thy mother.' The fourth, in the ninth hour, was a cry with a loud voice. What was it?
answer: 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' — 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the opening line of Psalm 22
choices: 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' — 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the opening line of Psalm 22
'Maranatha, maranatha' — 'Come, O Lord' — the Aramaic prayer that became a closing of early Christian letters
'Hosanna in excelsis Deo' — 'Glory to God in the highest' — taken up later by the angels at the empty tomb
'Berakhah, berakhah' — 'Blessed, blessed' — the priestly blessing he had received as a child in the Temple
context: Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34. Whether read as despair or as the trustful opening of Psalm 22 (which ends in vindication), it remains the most theologically charged of the seven words. The other three: 'I thirst,' 'It is finished' (tetelestai), 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.'

question: On the evening of the first day, the disciples gathered in a locked room. Jesus came and stood in the midst, showing his hands and side. Thomas (Didymus, the Twin) was absent. The others told him: 'We have seen the Lord.' Thomas refused — 'except I shall put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.' Eight days later, with Thomas present, Jesus appeared. What did he say?
answer: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; thrust thy hand into my side: and be not faithless, but believing'
choices: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; thrust thy hand into my side: and be not faithless, but believing'
'Stand back, thou doubter; the others have believed and so shalt thou: keep thy hands at thy side until the morn'
'Thomas, twin of my own thought; thou shalt see when thou hast first taught the others' doubt away from them'
'Bring forth the centurion's spear; pierce me again, and prove to thy own hand that I am no spirit of the night'
context: John 20:24-29. Thomas's response — 'My Lord and my God' — is the highest Christological confession in the Gospel. Jesus's reply — 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' — became the touchstone for all later faith. Caravaggio's painting (c. 1601) captures the moment with shocking physicality.

question: On the same first day, two disciples (Cleopas and a companion) walked the seven miles from Jerusalem to Emmaus. A stranger joined them; they did not recognize him. They told him about Jesus's crucifixion and the women's empty-tomb report. Beginning at Moses and the prophets, he expounded what scripture said of the Christ. At Emmaus they urged him to stay. He sat at meat. What happened?
answer: He took bread, blessed and brake, and gave to them; their eyes were opened, they recognized him, and he vanished
choices: He took bread, blessed and brake, and gave to them; their eyes were opened, they recognized him, and he vanished
He drew from his side and showed them the wound; they fell at his feet; he laid hands on them and disappeared
He drank the cup and said 'Peace be unto you'; they recognized his voice; he ascended through the ceiling above
He told the parable of the Good Samaritan once more; they recognized his teaching style and he was taken away
context: Luke 24:13-35 — the disciples saying 'did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?' The moment of recognition 'in the breaking of bread' became foundational for Eucharistic theology. The two returned to Jerusalem that same night to tell the eleven.

question: Luke 15 contains three parables of lost things. The Lost Sheep — shepherd leaves ninety-nine. The Lost Coin — woman sweeps her house. The longest: a man had two sons. The younger demanded his portion, took his journey into a far country, wasted his substance in riotous living. A famine arose; he was reduced to feeding swine. He came to himself and resolved to return as a hired servant. While he was yet afar off, what did his father do?
answer: Saw him afar off, had compassion, ran, fell on his neck, kissed him; called for the best robe, ring, fatted calf
choices: Saw him afar off, had compassion, ran, fell on his neck, kissed him; called for the best robe, ring, fatted calf
Sent the elder son to meet him; demanded restitution; received him only after a year of laboring as servant
Stood at the gate and made the younger son walk the last mile on his knees through the gathered village
Refused to see him; the mother received him secretly; only after seven years was the father reconciled
context: Luke 15:11-32. Rembrandt's painting (c. 1668) and Nouwen's book Return of the Prodigal Son made the parable resonant in modern devotional literature. The elder son's complaint — 'these many years do I serve thee' — and the father's reply ('Son, thou art ever with me') give the parable its dual structure.

question: A lawyer asked Jesus 'who is my neighbour?' Jesus answered with a parable. A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among thieves who stripped, wounded, and left him half dead. A priest passed by on the other side. A Levite likewise. Then a Samaritan — a despised group — had compassion, bound his wounds, set him on his beast, brought him to an inn, paid for his care. Jesus asked the lawyer which was neighbor. What was the answer?
answer: 'He that shewed mercy on him' — at which Jesus replied 'Go, and do thou likewise'
choices: 'He that shewed mercy on him' — at which Jesus replied 'Go, and do thou likewise'
'He that paid the innkeeper most generously' — refusing to name the Samaritan even in confession of mercy
'He that was nearest by ethnicity, were he Hebrew' — failing to grasp the parable's substantive force
'He that bound up the wounds in the prescribed manner' — naming only the action and not the man himself
context: Luke 10:25-37. The parable inverted ethnic and religious assumptions — the despised heretic outdoes the religious establishment in love of neighbor. The term 'good Samaritan' entered English; 'Good Samaritan laws' protect rescuers from liability. The road from Jerusalem to Jericho descends 3,300 feet through wilderness, still a robbery hotspot in Jesus's day.

question: Near Caesarea Philippi at the foot of Mount Hermon — a region famous for its pagan shrines, including a great cave to Pan — Jesus asked the disciples 'whom do men say that I the Son of man am?' They answered: some say John the Baptist; some, Elias; others, Jeremias, or one of the prophets. He pressed: 'But whom say ye that I am?' Simon Peter answered. What did he say, and what was Jesus's reply?
answer: 'Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God' — and Jesus replied 'thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church'
choices: 'Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God' — and Jesus replied 'thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church'
'Thou art the prophet greater than Moses' — and Jesus replied 'thou hast spoken from the Spirit; tarry yet a season'
'Thou art the king of Israel come from David' — and Jesus replied 'the kingdom is not yet; speak not of it openly'
'Thou art the Logos that was with the Father' — and Jesus replied 'the Father hath revealed his Word to thee'
context: Matthew 16:13-19. The wordplay — Petros (Peter, stone) and petra (rock) — became the foundation of Catholic papal theology: Peter as first pope, the rock on which the Church is built. Protestants typically read 'this rock' as Peter's confession rather than Peter himself. The episode marks a turning point — from public ministry to the journey to the cross.

question: Per Acts 2, fifty days after Passover — the Jewish feast of Shavuot — the disciples were gathered in one place in Jerusalem. Suddenly there came a sound as of a rushing mighty wind. Cloven tongues like fire sat on each of them. They were filled with the Holy Ghost. Devout Jews from every nation under heaven heard the noise and gathered. What perplexed them?
answer: Each heard the disciples speaking in his own native language — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Cretans, Arabians, all understood
choices: Each heard the disciples speaking in his own native language — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Cretans, Arabians, all understood
Each saw the same tongue of flame standing over Peter alone — the others appeared invisible from outside the upper room
Each tasted unleavened bread and wine on his tongue without having eaten — a sensory miracle without spoken words
Each felt himself rising above the ground — the entire upper room was levitating two cubits in plain sight
context: Acts 2 records Pentecost, traditionally the birthday of the Church. Peter's sermon — citing Joel 2 and Psalm 16 — added about 3,000 souls that day. The reversal of Babel (Genesis 11: languages divided) is deliberate: in Christ the nations are gathered. Western Christians commemorate Pentecost the seventh Sunday after Easter.

question: Around 60 AD, having appealed to Caesar following his arrest in Jerusalem, Paul was being shipped to Rome as a prisoner under centurion Julius. The voyage proved disastrous. Despite Paul's warning at Fair Havens on Crete, the captain pushed on. A typhoon-like 'Euroclydon' wind drove the ship for fourteen days. The crew gave up hope. Paul prophesied no loss of life, only the ship. Where did they finally make landfall?
answer: Malta — they ran the ship aground; all 276 souls reached land; Paul was bitten by a viper but suffered no harm
choices: Malta — they ran the ship aground; all 276 souls reached land; Paul was bitten by a viper but suffered no harm
Sicily — they put in at Syracuse where Paul healed the governor's father of fever and dysentery for three days
Cyprus — they were driven back east; Paul preached three months in Salamis before continuing to Rome by overland route
Sardinia — they landed near Cagliari; Paul was held by the Roman garrison for forty days before sailing on to Rome
context: Acts 27-28 records the shipwreck. The Maltese chief Publius received them; Paul healed his father; many came for healing. They wintered three months on Malta, then sailed via Syracuse and Rhegium to Puteoli, and walked the Appian Way to Rome. Paul spent two years in Rome under house arrest awaiting his hearing.

question: William Tyndale (c. 1494-1536) was first to translate the New Testament from Greek into English and print it. He fled England for the Continent (1524); his NT was smuggled in from 1526; copies were burned at St. Paul's. He continued with parts of the OT from Hebrew. Betrayed in Antwerp, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde Castle (October 1536). What were his famous last words?
answer: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes' — within months Henry VIII authorized an English Bible largely drawn from Tyndale
choices: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes' — within months Henry VIII authorized an English Bible largely drawn from Tyndale
'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' — taking up Christ's own cry of dereliction at his execution
'Now Lord, I depart in peace' — Simeon's Nunc Dimittis from his own English New Testament translation
'Forgive them, Father' — taking up Christ's words of forgiveness toward his persecutors at the stake
context: Tyndale's prayer was answered: within a year, the King's Great Bible (1539) drew heavily on his translation. The King James Version (1611) reportedly retains 75-85% of Tyndale's New Testament phrasing — making him arguably the chief architect of English religious vocabulary. 'My brother's keeper,' 'salt of the earth,' 'fight the good fight,' 'a stranger in a strange land' — all Tyndale.

question: In summer 325 AD Emperor Constantine convened roughly 250-318 bishops at Nicaea. The controversy: the Alexandrian priest Arius had been teaching the Son was a created being — 'there was a time when he was not.' Bishop Alexander and his deacon Athanasius opposed him fiercely. The council produced a creed and condemned Arius. The decisive Greek term meant 'of the same substance.' What was the term?
answer: Homoousios — declaring the Son of one substance with the Father, rejecting Arian Christology and establishing the Trinitarian orthodoxy of later catholic Christianity
choices: Homoousios — declaring the Son of one substance with the Father, rejecting Arian Christology and establishing the Trinitarian orthodoxy of later catholic Christianity
Homoiousios — declaring the Son of similar substance with the Father, the moderate compromise that papered over the disagreement for several decades after Nicaea
Hypostasis — declaring the Son a distinct personhood from the Father, the term later central in the Cappadocian formula of one ousia in three hypostases
Theotokos — declaring Mary the Mother of God, the term that became the test of Christological orthodoxy at the Council of Ephesus a century later
context: The single Greek iota between homoousios and homoiousios gave us 'not an iota of difference.' Arianism persisted under Constantius II and dominated among Germanic tribes for centuries. Athanasius was exiled five times defending the Nicene formula.

question: On October 27, 312 AD two Roman armies converged on a bridge over the Tiber north of Rome. On one side was Maxentius; on the other Constantine. The night before, according to Eusebius, Constantine saw a cross of light over the sun with the words 'In this sign, conquer.' He ordered the Chi-Rho painted on his soldiers' shields. He won; Maxentius drowned. What was the lasting result?
answer: The Edict of Milan in 313 legalized Christianity throughout the empire, ending three centuries of persecution and beginning the path to Theodosius making it official in 380
choices: The Edict of Milan in 313 legalized Christianity throughout the empire, ending three centuries of persecution and beginning the path to Theodosius making it official in 380
Christianity was established at once as sole legal religion, ending paganism by decree within a decade and confiscating the temples of the old gods
The first ecumenical council was convoked at once, producing the Nicene Creed in 313 and establishing the doctrinal unity the church had lacked for three centuries
The imperial capital was transferred to Constantinople at once, splitting the empire into eastern and western halves never again ruled as a single unit
context: Historicity of the vision is debated; Constantine's coins featured Sol Invictus for years. The Edict of Milan in early 313 with Licinius did legalize Christianity. Constantine convened Nicaea in 325, founded Constantinople (330), and was baptized on his deathbed by an Arian bishop in 337.

question: On October 6, 1536, at Vilvoorde near Brussels, a 42-year-old English priest was strangled and his body burned. His crime: translating the New Testament into English from Erasmus's Greek (1526 Worms edition) and part of the Old Testament from Hebrew. His final reported words: 'Lord! Open the King of England's eyes.' The King James (1611) drew 75-83% of its New Testament from his phrasings. Who was he?
answer: William Tyndale — whose translation gave English 'let there be light,' 'salt of the earth,' 'fight the good fight,' shaping English as much as any writer except Shakespeare
choices: William Tyndale — whose translation gave English 'let there be light,' 'salt of the earth,' 'fight the good fight,' shaping English as much as any writer except Shakespeare
Miles Coverdale — whose 1535 translation of the entire Bible was the first complete printed English Bible, his Psalms remaining standard in the Book of Common Prayer
John Rogers — who under the pseudonym Thomas Matthew published the Matthew Bible in 1537, the first authorized English Bible, before being burned at Smithfield in 1555
John Wycliffe — whose Lollards produced English translations of the Latin Vulgate in the 1380s, prompting Arundel's Constitutions of 1409 against vernacular Bibles
context: Wycliffe's translation was from the Vulgate, not Greek. Tyndale's was from Greek and Hebrew. He coined or popularized 'Jehovah,' 'Passover,' 'atonement,' and 'scapegoat.' David Daniell's biography (1994) is the standard modern account. The King James translators acknowledged his foundational work.

question: On October 16, 1978, cardinals elected the 58-year-old archbishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła. He took the name John Paul II — first non-Italian pope in 455 years, first Slavic pope ever. He had grown up under Nazi occupation, entered an underground seminary in 1942. In June 1979 he made his first papal visit to Poland — three million at the Kraków Mass. What was the strategic effect?
answer: It catalyzed Solidarity in 1980 — first independent labor union in the Eastern Bloc — beginning the chain leading to the 1989 collapse of communism in Eastern Europe

question: On July 8, 1741, in the meetinghouse at Enfield, Connecticut, a 37-year-old Northampton minister rose to preach a sermon. As he read in his flat delivery, the congregation began to weep, then cry out, then grip the pews in terror that the floor would open beneath them. He had to pause and ask for silence. The sermon became the most famous in American religious history. Who was he?
answer: Jonathan Edwards — a Calvinist holding humans hang over hell by a slender thread; his theology fused Enlightenment philosophical sophistication with Reformed orthodoxy
choices: Jonathan Edwards — a Calvinist holding humans hang over hell by a slender thread; his theology fused Enlightenment philosophical sophistication with Reformed orthodoxy

He died of a smallpox inoculation as president of Princeton.

question: On May 24, 1738, at about a quarter before nine in the evening, a 34-year-old Church of England priest reluctantly attended a small Moravian society meeting on Aldersgate Street in London. He had been a missionary to Georgia (1736-37), had returned in failure. Someone was reading aloud from Luther's preface to Romans. The priest later wrote: 'I felt my heart strangely warmed. question: On June 8, 793 AD, a small fleet of longships from Norway appeared off the coast of Northumbria in northeast England. They beached at the island of Lindisfarne, a Celtic Christian monastic center founded by St. Aidan from Iona in 635. The raiders killed monks, smashed altars, and carried off treasures and slaves. The English scholar Alcuin of York, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote in horror: 'Never before has such terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a pagan race.' What did the raid mark?
answer: The traditional beginning of the Viking Age — three centuries of Scandinavian raiding, trading, and settlement across Britain, Ireland, France (Normandy), Russia

question: Among the most widely-copied texts in ancient Egypt — from the New Kingdom (c. 1550 BC) onward, written on papyrus rolls placed in tombs to guide the dead through the afterlife — was a collection of spells, prayers, and instructions. At the climactic moment, the deceased's heart was weighed on a scale against a single object. If the heart was lighter, the deceased proceeded to the field of reeds (Egyptian paradise). If heavier, the heart was eaten by the demon Ammit. What was on the other pan of the scale?
answer: The feather of Maat — the goddess of truth, justice, and cosmic order — embodying the principle of righteousness against which the moral life was weighed; the deceased
choices: The feather of Maat — the goddess of truth, justice, and cosmic order — embodying the principle of righteousness against which the moral life was weighed; the deceased

context: The 'Weighing of the Heart' is depicted in many surviving papyri (the Papyrus of Hunefer at the British Museum is famous). Maat — order, truth, justice — is one of the deepest Egyptian theological concepts: the gods themselves are bound by maat, and pharaoh's principal duty was to maintain it against chaos (isfet).

question: On July 6, 1415, in a field outside the city of Constance (Konstanz) on the south shore of Lake Constance, a Czech reformer was led to a stake. He had been promised imperial safe-conduct by Sigismund of Luxembourg. He was given a final chance to recant. He refused. As the fire was lit, he was reportedly heard to pray, 'Lord Jesus, son of the living God, have mercy on me.' His ashes were thrown in the Rhine to prevent their veneration. Who was he, and what was the wider impact?
answer: Jan Hus (c. 1369-1415) — and the Hussite Wars (1419-1434) followed, with the Czech Hussites under Jan Žižka and Prokop the Bald defeating five papal crusades; Hus's followers eventually compromised with Rome

question: At Horeb the 80-year-old former Egyptian prince now shepherding his father-in-law Jethro's flock saw a thornbush blazing yet unconsumed. From the fire a voice called him by name. He asked: when the Israelites ask who sent me, what is your name? The answer became foundational for Jewish, Christian, and Islamic theology. What name did the voice give?
answer: Ehyeh asher ehyeh — I AM that I AM, rendered YHWH in the consonantal tetragrammaton, the name so holy later Jews substituted Adonai or HaShem when reading aloud

question: Late one afternoon King David walked his palace roof and saw a woman bathing. He sent for her. She conceived. Her husband Uriah the Hittite was at the siege of Rabbah; David recalled him hoping he would mask the paternity. Uriah slept at the palace gate refusing comfort while comrades fought. David sent him back with sealed orders to die. How did the prophet Nathan confront David?

question: Around 870 BC the prophet Elijah challenged 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel before Ahab and Jezebel. Each side would prepare a bull; whichever god answered by fire was God. The Baal prophets cried from morning to noon, gashing themselves; nothing. Elijah mocked them: perhaps Baal is sleeping. He drenched his altar with twelve jars of water. What happened next?

question: Commanded to preach repentance to the Assyrian capital Nineveh, the prophet Jonah fled the opposite direction, boarding a ship for Tarshish (somewhere west, perhaps Spain). question: In Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, Lazarus had been dead four days and was already in the tomb when Jesus arrived. question: Six days after Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain (traditionally Mount Tabor, possibly Hermon). question: Around 33-35 AD a young Pharisee from Tarsus named Saul, trained under Gamaliel and consenting to Stephen's stoning, obtained letters authorizing arrests in Damascus. question: On August 24, 410 AD Alaric and the Visigoths sacked Rome for three days — the first time in 800 years the city had fallen. question: In late 1224 a man dying of stomach cancer, near-blind from trachoma, having received the stigmata at La Verna, dictated a Umbrian-Italian hymn from his sickbed at San Damiano. question: Around 1078 a 45-year-old Benedictine prior at Bec in Normandy spent a sleepless night on a single argument. He wrote it as a prayer to God: faith seeking understanding. question: In 1535 a 57-year-old Lord Chancellor of England was executed by Henry VIII for refusing to swear the Oath of Supremacy. On the scaffold he reportedly said he died 'the king's good servant, but God's first.' Twenty years earlier (1516) he had published in Latin a satirical fiction set on a fictional island. answer: Utopia — Greek for 'no place'; a fictional traveler's account describing an ideal commonwealth and (more cuttingly) satirizing English abuses; the word became the genre

question: At sunset on a day in May or June 399 BC, after a trial in spring and a delay during the Athenian sacred mission to Delos, a 70-year-old philosopher sat with his friends in the state prison. He had been convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth. The Eleven brought the cup of hemlock. He drank. He walked. He felt his legs grow cold. What were his last words?

question: From 995 to 1000 a Viking-king turned Christian missionary forcibly converted Norway. question: Around 1000 AD Leif Eriksson (son of Eirik the Red, who had founded Greenland in 985-986) sailed west and discovered three lands. The first was a rocky waste (Helluland, probably Baffin Island). The second was forested (Markland, probably Labrador). The third had wild grapes. What did he call this third land, and what was found in 1960?
answer: Vinland — the wine-land; L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland was excavated by the Ingstads from 1961, confirming a Norse outpost of c. 1000 AD with longhouses, ironworks, and characteristic artifacts

question: On September 25, 1066, on the Derwent in Yorkshire, the last great Viking invasion of England met its end. Harald Sigurdsson Hardrada ('hard ruler') of Norway, who had served in the Varangian Guard, had landed with 300 ships claiming the English throne. Harold Godwinson marched 185 miles in four days to surprise him. What was the result?
answer: Harald Hardrada was killed by an arrow to the throat; Tostig Godwinson (allied with Harald) also fell; the Viking survivors departed in only 24 ships; Harold marched south to face William

question: Around 520 AD a south Indian Buddhist monk traveled to China and was granted audience with Emperor Wu of Liang. Wu boasted of his merit; the monk replied 'no merit.' Asked the highest holy truth, the monk said 'vast emptiness, nothing holy.' Asked who stood before him, he said 'don't know.' He left for the north. What did he reputedly do at Shaolin?
answer: He sat facing a wall meditating for nine years — the founder of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China; his transmission to Huike (the second patriarch) became the founding lineage of all Zen schools
choices: He sat facing a wall meditating for nine years — the founder of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China; his transmission to Huike (the second patriarch) became the founding lineage of all Zen schools
He compiled the Diamond Sutra in Chinese translation — the foundational Mahayana text Huineng would later hear and be enlightened by, but not Bodhidharma's actual work
He established the Pure Land school by chanting Amitabha's name — actually the practice of Honen and Shinran centuries later, mistakenly attributed to Bodhidharma in popular accounts
He founded Shaolin temple itself — actually founded by Batuo about 30 years before Bodhidharma's arrival; he taught martial arts to existing monks in later (disputed) tradition
context: Bodhidharma is the 28th patriarch of Indian Buddhism and the 1st Chinese Chan patriarch. The 'nothing holy' exchange with Emperor Wu is the famous case 1 of the Blue Cliff Record. The line of transmission — Bodhidharma to Huike to Sengcan to Daoxin to Hongren to Huineng — runs through the formative period of Chinese Chan.

question: In 1935 a child was born in Amdo (northeastern Tibet). At 2 he was identified as the rebirth of the 13th Dalai Lama. At 4 he was enthroned in Lhasa. At 15 he assumed authority (November 17, 1950) as Chinese troops crossed the eastern border. On March 17, 1959, during the Lhasa uprising, he fled across the Himalayas in disguise. What was his name, and where did he settle?
answer: Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama — settled at Dharamsala in Himachal Pradesh, India, establishing the Tibetan government-in-exile; awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his nonviolent resistance
choices: Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama — settled at Dharamsala in Himachal Pradesh, India, establishing the Tibetan government-in-exile; awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his nonviolent resistance
Tashi Namgyal, the 14th Dalai Lama — settled at Kalimpong before moving to Lhasa-in-exile in Sikkim under the protection of the Chogyal until the 1975 Indian annexation
Karmapa Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, the 16th Karmapa — head of the Karma Kagyu school, who actually fled with the Dalai Lama in 1959 but settled at Rumtek in Sikkim
Lobsang Yeshe, the 14th Dalai Lama — settled in Switzerland under UN refugee status before relocating to India in 1962 after the Sino-Indian War made Dharamsala viable
context: Tibet lost about 1.2 million people to Chinese rule between 1950 and 1980 by some estimates (contested figure). About 6000 monasteries were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976). The 14th Dalai Lama has said the office may end with him.

question: In the oldest substantial literary work (Sumerian fragments from c. 2100 BC, full Akkadian version c. 1200 BC), the king of Uruk was 2/3 divine, 1/3 mortal and oppressed his subjects. The gods created a wild man as his match. They fought, became inseparable friends, and set out for the cedar forest to win fame. They killed its guardian. Who was the friend and who was the guardian?
answer: Enkidu (the wild man, civilized by the priestess Shamhat) was the friend; Humbaba (the monstrous guardian, slain after Shamash sent the winds to subdue him) was the guardian killed
choices: Enkidu (the wild man, civilized by the priestess Shamhat) was the friend; Humbaba (the monstrous guardian, slain after Shamash sent the winds to subdue him) was the guardian killed
Adapa (the first sage) was the friend; Asakku (the rock-demon) was the guardian; the alternative Babylonian myth-cycle frequently confused with Gilgamesh in popular surveys
Etana (the earlier shepherd-king) was the friend; Anzu (the storm-bird who stole the tablets of destiny) was the guardian; again a separate myth-cycle from Gilgamesh's
Atrahasis (the flood-survivor) was the friend; Mummu (Tiamat's vizier) was the guardian; the flood-narrative myth mistakenly conflated with Gilgamesh by some early scholarship
context: Gilgamesh's grief at Enkidu's death (the gods killed Enkidu for hubris) drives the second half of the epic — Gilgamesh seeks immortality from Utnapishtim the flood-survivor, fails, and returns to Uruk to find peace in walls and city-pride. The epic's Tablet XI gives the Mesopotamian flood story behind Genesis 6-9.

question: In late March 1997, in a rented mansion in Rancho Santa Fe, California, 39 members of a UFO religious group died in three groups (March 22-26). They wore matching black shirts and black Nike sneakers; each had a 5-dollar bill and three quarters in their pocket. They had eaten phenobarbital in applesauce and put plastic bags over their heads. What did they believe they were doing?
answer: Boarding a spacecraft following the Hale-Bopp comet — leaving their 'vehicles' (bodies) for the Next Level, the higher evolutionary kingdom from which Applewhite (Do) and Nettles (Ti) claimed to come
choices: Boarding a spacecraft following the Hale-Bopp comet — leaving their 'vehicles' (bodies) for the Next Level, the higher evolutionary kingdom from which Applewhite (Do) and Nettles (Ti) claimed to come
Awaiting the Second Coming of Christ — a different cult-suicide pattern from earlier and later groups including the Branch Davidians, not Heaven's Gate's specific UFO eschatology
Returning to the divine realm through dissolution — Aum Shinrikyo theology adapted to a Western Christian-Buddhist syncretism, mistakenly applied to Heaven's Gate
Greeting the end of the millennium two years early — a chronology not connected to Heaven's Gate's UFO doctrine that did not depend on millennial dating
context: Marshall Applewhite (1931-1997, son of a Presbyterian minister, music teacher fired for homosexuality) and Bonnie Nettles (1928-1985, nurse-astrologer) had founded the group in the mid-1970s as 'The Two' from Revelation 11. Applewhite had himself castrated; six other male members also did. The website (with the 'red alert' banner) remained online for years after their deaths.

question: Jesus said, 'Blessed are the pure in heart.' What will they see?
context: Matthew 5:8: 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.'

question: What food did the prodigal son end up eating while feeding pigs?
answer: the pods that the pigs ate
choices: the pods that the pigs ate
context: Luke 15:16. He longed to fill his belly with the pods the pigs ate, but no one gave him anything. This was the low point before he returned home.

question: In one parable, a king forgave a servant a huge debt. What did the servant do to a fellow servant?
answer: threw him in prison for a small debt
choices: threw him in prison for a small debt
context: The Parable of the Unforgiving Servant (Matthew 18:21-35). Jesus told it after Peter asked how many times to forgive a brother.

question: Jesus said the kingdom of God is like a mustard seed. The seed is tiny but grows into what?
answer: a great tree where birds nest
choices: a great tree where birds nest
context: Mark 4:30-32. Small beginnings can lead to great endings. The mustard seed is among the smallest of seeds.

question: What word means God's free gift of love that we cannot earn?
context: Grace is unmerited favor. The whole Bible turns on this: God gives what people could never deserve.

question: Jesus said that whatever you do for the least of these, you do it to whom?
context: Matthew 25:40. The Parable of the Sheep and the Goats: feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the prisoner are done to Christ himself.

question: How many spies did Moses send into the Promised Land in Numbers 13?
context: Numbers 13. One spy from each tribe. Only two — Joshua and Caleb — brought back a good report.

question: A hunter who stumbled on Artemis bathing was transformed into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds. Who?
context: Cadmus's grandson. Ovid's account in Metamorphoses 3 dwells on his realization, his vain attempt to call off the hounds, and his fate. A favorite Renaissance painting subject.

question: Sophocles's play features a sister who defies a royal edict to bury her brother and is sentenced to die in a tomb. Who is she?
context: Daughter of Oedipus. King Creon refused burial to her brother Polynices for attacking Thebes. The play is the founding text of the conflict between divine and civil law.

question: A king of Corinth who twice cheated death was condemned to push a boulder eternally up a hill, only to watch it roll down. Who?
context: Camus's essay 'The Myth of Sisyphus' takes him as the symbol of the absurd. 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' Hesiod and Homer first record the punishment.

question: A beautiful youth fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and pined away beside it. Who?
context: A flower sprang up where he died. Echo the nymph had loved him in vain. From his name come 'narcissism' and the narcissus flower. Ovid's Metamorphoses tells the fullest version.

question: Asclepius's most famous temple, where the sick slept hoping for dreams of cure, was at which Peloponnesian site?
context: The temple complex had baths, gymnasia, a famous theater, and an abaton (dormitory). Inscriptions record thousands of healings. The medical school of Cos developed alongside.

question: Eos the Dawn won immortality but not eternal youth for her mortal lover; he shriveled into a grasshopper. Who was he?
context: Trojan prince. Tennyson's poem 'Tithonus' is the famous English meditation: 'after many a summer dies the swan'. The grasshopper detail comes from the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite.

question: Orestes's sister, who urged on his vengeance against their mother, was the subject of plays by both Aeschylus and Sophocles. Who?
context: She had nursed her brother's hatred for ten years. Freud's 'Electra complex' (female counterpart to the Oedipus complex) takes her name.

question: The sun-god Helios drove his chariot across the sky each day. The chariot was drawn by what?
context: His son Phaethon's attempt to drive them ended in disaster. The horses were named Pyrois, Eoos, Aethon, and Phlegon. Helios was distinct from Apollo, though later sometimes identified.

question: The cornucopia — horn of plenty — was a horn broken off from which mythical animal?
context: She had nursed the infant Zeus on Mount Ida. He broke off one of her horns; it gave forth endless food. After her death he set her in the sky as the constellation Capra.

question: The Golden Fleece hung in a sacred grove in which Black Sea kingdom?
context: Roughly modern Georgia. A sleepless dragon guarded it. Medea — daughter of King Aietes of Colchis — drugged the dragon so Jason could seize the fleece.

question: Souls awaiting reincarnation drank from a river to forget their previous lives. The river was called what?
context: Greek 'forgetfulness'. Drinking induced oblivion of one's previous life. Plato in the Myth of Er describes the procedure. The opposite of Lethe is Aletheia — Greek 'truth' as 'unforgetting'.

question: Winners of the ancient Olympic Games received not money but a crown made of what?
context: The kotinos — olive branch from the sacred grove of Zeus at Olympia, cut with a golden sickle by a boy whose parents were both alive. Other Panhellenic games gave different crowns.

question: The Nemean Games, fourth of the Panhellenic games, gave victors crowns of which plant?
context: Held at Nemea, where Heracles killed the lion. Sacred to Zeus. Held in years one and three of the Olympic cycle. Adult victors got a green celery crown; boys got a yellow one.

question: The world of humans in Norse cosmology lies in the middle, surrounded by the great sea. It is called what?
context: Old Norse 'middle enclosure'. Tolkien borrowed 'Middle-earth' as its English translation. Surrounded by an ocean in which lurks the Midgard Serpent (Jormungandr).

question: The dark and freezing realm of mist and ice in Norse cosmology, where the dead who did not die in battle go to Hel, was called what?
context: Old Norse 'mist-home'. Birthplace of frost. Hvergelmir spring boils up here. Sometimes equated with Helheim or treated as a distinct prior realm — sources vary.

question: The realm of fire to the south of the cosmos, ruled by the fire-giant Surt, was called what?
context: Existed before the gods. From the meeting of Muspelheim's heat and Niflheim's cold in the Ginnungagap, the first being Ymir was formed. Surt will burn the world at Ragnarok.

question: The home of the light-elves was given to which god as a tooth-gift when his first tooth came?
context: Snorri's Prose Edda. Light-elves (ljosalfar) dwelt there; dark-elves (dökkalfar) — sometimes identified with dwarves — dwelt below. Freyr's hall stood at its center.

question: The white god who guards the rainbow bridge against intruders, with hearing sharp enough to catch grass growing, was called what?
context: His horn is Gjallarhorn — to be blown at Ragnarok. He needs less sleep than a bird. His teeth are gold. He will fight Loki at Ragnarok; the two will kill each other.

question: Alongside Ymir there formed a primordial cow who fed him with her milk and licked the ice. She licked a god out of the ice. What was her name?
context: She licked Buri from the ice — grandfather of the gods. Buri's son Bor married a giantess; their sons were Odin, Vili, and Ve. Audhumla represents primordial nourishment.

question: Freyr's magical ship, the best of all ships, could carry all the gods yet be folded up and put in a pocket. What was it called?
context: Made by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi. It always had a fair wind. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda lists it among the great treasures of the gods.

question: The Norse end of the world — when most of the gods die in battle against the giants and the cosmos burns — is called what?
context: Old Norse 'doom of the powers'. Wagner's Götterdämmerung translates the term as 'twilight of the gods' — based on a variant Ragnarøkr ('twilight') used by Snorri. Both forms appear in the sources.

question: The first major Viking raid in the historical record fell on a Northumbrian monastery on Holy Island in 793 AD. Which monastery?
context: Founded by Aidan in 635 AD; home to Cuthbert. Alcuin of York wrote a horrified letter about the attack. Conventionally the start of the Viking Age.

question: After the Lindisfarne raid of 793, an English scholar at Charlemagne's court wrote of the horror: 'never before in Britain has such terror appeared as this we have now suffered'. Who?
context: He wrote to King Aethelred of Northumbria and to the surviving monks. The Vikings would return many times — to Iona, Jarrow, the Wessex coast, Ireland, France, Spain, and the Caspian Sea.

question: The two most famous Viking ship burials, excavated in southern Norway, are named for the farms where they were found. They are Gokstad and what?
context: Oseberg (c. 834 AD) contained two women, perhaps a queen and her servant, along with a beautifully carved oak ship now in Oslo's Viking Ship Museum. Gokstad (c. 900 AD) contained a man and a magnificent ship.

question: Wealthy Vikings were often buried in great earthen mounds. What did they often include?
context: Sometimes ships under the mounds. Sometimes slain slaves. Ibn Fadlan, an Arab traveler on the Volga in 922, witnessed and recorded a Rus chieftain's funeral including a slave's sacrifice.

question: Norse berserkers were said to do what with their own shields before battle, in the trance state?
context: Old Norse texts describe biting the shield's rim, howling like animals, foaming at the mouth. The Hrafnsmal of Thorbjorn Hornklofi (c. 900) describes them as 'wolf-coats' at the Battle of Hafrsfjord.

question: In Norse cosmology, oathbreakers, murderers, and adulterers were tormented in a hall whose walls were of woven snakes that dripped venom. The hall was called what?
context: Old Norse 'shore of corpses'. The Voluspa describes it. The dragon Nidhogg sucks the bodies of the dead there. A vivid hellscape that may have been influenced by — or influenced — Christian descriptions of Hell.

question: The dwarves Brokkr and Sindri forged Freyr's boar Gullinbursti and which other two great treasures?
context: Made for the gods. The sons of Ivaldi made the rival set: Sif's hair, Skidbladnir, Gungnir. Loki bet his head on which set was best; the gods chose Brokkr and Sindri's.

question: The Old English (Anglo-Saxon) concept of fate — cognate with Old Norse 'urdr' — was called what?
context: Etymologically related to 'weird'. The phrase 'wyrd bid ful araed' ('fate is wholly inexorable') in the Old English poem The Wanderer captures it. The Weird Sisters of Macbeth and Norse Norns are cognates.

question: One of the great Icelandic family sagas tells of a wise lawyer burned to death in his house, along with his family, after a long blood-feud. Whose saga?
context: Written c. 1280, set in 10th-11th century Iceland. The masterpiece of the saga literature. Halfdan the Black and Olaf Tryggvason appear. Njal and his sons die when Flosi and his men burn down their farmhouse.

question: Around 1000 AD a Norse explorer reached the North American mainland — five centuries before Columbus. He named the new land 'Vineland' (Vinland). Who?
context: Son of Erik the Red, who had founded the Greenland colony. The L'Anse aux Meadows site in Newfoundland (excavated 1960) confirmed Norse settlement c. 1000 AD. The Vinland Sagas tell the story.

question: The Icelandic Volsunga Saga (c. 1270) tells of a hero who slew a dragon and was betrayed by a love triangle, providing the source for Wagner's Ring Cycle. Who slew the dragon?
context: Norse 'Sigurd' becomes German 'Siegfried' in the Nibelungenlied. The dragon Fafnir guarded a cursed treasure-hoard. Wagner's four operas — Das Rheingold, Die Walkure, Siegfried, Götterdämmerung — adapt the legend.

question: The dragon slain by Sigurd guarded a cursed treasure-hoard. Originally he was a dwarf (or giant) who transformed into a dragon out of greed. What was his name?
context: The story: the gods stole the dwarf Andvari's gold; Andvari cursed it; Fafnir killed his father Hreidmar to keep it; the hoard then doomed all who held it. The curse drives the Nibelung saga.

question: An Arab traveler witnessed a Rus chieftain's ship funeral on the Volga in 922 AD and wrote a vivid account including the sacrifice of a slave girl. Who was he?
context: Ahmad ibn Fadlan, secretary of an Abbasid embassy to the Volga Bulgars. His Risala is one of the most important external sources for Viking-age practice and a major source for Ibn Fadlan's account.

question: The boar — Freyr's sacred animal — was traditionally sacrificed at midwinter. The Norse name for the midwinter festival was what?
context: Yule was a 12-day festival. Boar sacrifices, mead drinking, and oaths sworn over the slaughtered boar are recorded. Christianized as Christmastide. 'Yule log' and 'Yuletide' preserve the term in English.

question: After Sigurd killed the dragon Fafnir, he tasted the dragon's blood while roasting its heart. What new ability did he gain?
context: The birds warned him that Regin (Fafnir's brother, Sigurd's tutor) planned to kill him for the treasure. Sigurd killed Regin first and rode away with the hoard on his horse Grani.

question: The dwarf whose cursed treasure-hoard fueled the entire Volsung saga was named what?
context: Loki caught him in fish-form and forced him to give up his hoard, including a magic ring. Andvari cursed the gold. Hreidmar took it as wergild; Fafnir killed Hreidmar; Sigurd killed Fafnir; doom followed all.

question: In the Volsung legend, Gunnar was killed in a snake-pit at the court of which historical Hunnic king?
context: The historical Attila (d. 453 AD) is the basis. Gunnar played his harp (with his feet, as his hands were bound) until all snakes slept — except one, his mother in disguise, who killed him.

question: The oldest surviving Germanic heroic epic — about a Geatish hero who fights three monsters — is an Anglo-Saxon poem in Old English. What is the hero's name?
context: c. 700-1000 AD. The poem is set in pre-Christian Scandinavia but composed by a Christian Anglo-Saxon. Beowulf kills Grendel, Grendel's mother, and a dragon — dying of his wounds in the third fight.

question: After Beowulf killed Grendel, Grendel's mother came to the mead-hall to avenge her son. Beowulf killed her in her underwater lair with what?
context: Hrunting failed against her. Beowulf found an old sword in the mere-hall — possibly a giant's. The blade melted from her venomous blood, leaving only the hilt — which Beowulf brought back as proof.

question: A legendary Danish king of the 6th century, mentioned in Beowulf and the subject of his own Icelandic saga, was famed for his twelve berserker champions. Who?
context: The Hrolfs saga kraka. He scattered gold on the plain to slow his pursuers — a magical scene. The Danish royal line was traced from him. Tolkien drew on his story for Beorn and Hrothgar.

question: Russian tradition traces the dynasty that ruled Russia until 1598 to a 9th-century Norse warlord invited to bring order. Who?
context: Possibly identifiable with Rorik of Dorestad (a Norse warlord in Frisia). The Rus took their name from him — or from a Finnish word for the Swedes. Founded Novgorod c. 862 AD.

question: The Vikings settled in northern and eastern England — the Danelaw — and added many words to English. 'Skirt', 'sky', 'window', 'egg', 'they', 'them' are all Old Norse loanwords. They sat alongside what?
context: English 'shirt' (native) and 'skirt' (Norse) are doublets — same original Germanic word, different developments. 'Sky' replaced 'heaven' as the everyday word. The pronouns are unusually deep grammatical borrowings.

question: The part of England that came under Norse law after the great army of 865 AD — the eastern half — was called the what?
context: From the Wash to the Mersey. Alfred the Great's treaty with Guthrum (c. 880) recognized the division. The English kings reconquered it during the 10th century. Place-names ending '-by', '-thorpe' mark its extent.

question: The tribute paid by Anglo-Saxon kings to buy off Viking armies was called what?
context: The kings of Wessex resorted to massive payments under Aethelred the Unready in 991-1014. Rudyard Kipling's poem 'Dane-Geld': 'It is wrong to put temptation in the path of any nation, / By paying it cash to go away'.

question: William the Conqueror — invading England in 1066 — was descended from Norse settlers in northern France. Their territory was called what?
context: Old Norse 'Northmen' — the Vikings under Rollo had been granted the land by Charles the Simple in 911. By 1066 they spoke French. William's invasion was the Vikings reaching England — by another path — five generations later.

question: Iceland's open-air parliament met annually on a plain where two tectonic plates meet (the only place on land where the Mid-Atlantic ridge surfaces). What was it called?
context: Old Norse 'parliament-plains'. Iceland's national park since 1928. The Althing met there from 930 AD until 1798 — over 850 years of continuous use as a meeting-place.

question: The horse that pulls the chariot of Day across the sky has a glowing mane that lights the air. What is the horse called?
context: Old Norse 'shining mane'. Hrimfaxi ('rime mane') pulls the chariot of Night — frost dripping from his mane is the morning dew. Day and Night were giant siblings made gods.

question: Some Viking-age swords found in graves bear an inlaid signature that has puzzled scholars — 'Ulfberht'. What was distinctive about these swords?
context: Tested examples show crucible steel with very low slag — comparable to Damascus steel from the Islamic world. The Ulfberht trade may have been a branded Carolingian-Frankish workshop's product.

question: Late Anglo-Saxon and Norse kings kept a personal bodyguard of professional warriors — distinct from the levied troops. They were called what?
context: Old Norse 'house-men'. Cnut the Great brought them to England. The huscarls who died around King Harold at Hastings were the last great battle of this institution. They fought on foot with two-handed axes.

question: The Byzantine emperor's elite guard from the late 10th century onward was famously composed of Norsemen. They were called what?
context: Old Norse 'sworn companions'. Vladimir of Kiev sent 6,000 to Emperor Basil II in 988 AD. Norsemen could grow rich in the guard and return home to Iceland. Harald Hardrada served before becoming king of Norway.

question: Adam of Bremen's description (c. 1075) of the great pagan temple at Uppsala in Sweden lists three principal idols. The most prominent — central in the temple — was which god?
context: Adam's account: 'Thor presides in the middle, as the most powerful'. Odin and Freyr flanked him. Sacrifices of nine humans (alongside animals) hung in the sacred grove every ninth year — pagan Scandinavia's premier temple.

question: An early Norse settler of Iceland is said to have used what to find the island?
context: Hrafna-Floki Vilgerdarson — 'Raven Floki' — in the Landnamabok. The first raven flew back; the second flew to the ship; the third flew on toward Iceland and Floki followed. He gave Iceland its modern name.

question: Before any world existed, there was only the great void between the realms of fire and ice. In Old Norse it was called what?
context: Old Norse 'yawning gap' or 'magical chasm'. The meeting of the heat from Muspelheim and the frost from Niflheim in Ginnungagap brought forth the first being Ymir from the dripping ice.

question: After the gods killed Ymir, his body became the world — but he had earlier produced offspring from his own body. Mostly which beings?
context: From Ymir's armpit came a male and female giant; his legs sired more. After his death, his blood drowned all the giants except Bergelmir and his wife — from whom the later giants descend.

question: When the gods killed Ymir, his blood drowned all the giants except one couple, who escaped in a hollowed-out log (or 'mill'). The husband's name was what?
context: He fled with his wife in a 'ludr' — sometimes translated 'box' or 'mill' (a hollowed-out wooden chest). All later giants descend from them. A Norse parallel to Noah and Deucalion.

question: Saturday is the one day of the English week whose name does not preserve a Germanic god. Whose name does it preserve?
context: Latin dies Saturni — day of Saturn. The Germanic peoples kept the Roman name rather than naming a god of their own. Possibly because they had no obvious equivalent of Saturn — the god of time, harvest, exile.

question: Norse and Anglo-Saxon law systems used a system of monetary compensation paid for killings — graduated by the social rank of the slain. What was it called?
context: Old English 'wer' (man) + 'geld' (payment). Norse 'mangjald'. An attempt to channel revenge into legal compensation. The killing of a king might cost more than an entire kingdom could pay.

question: Norse legal disputes were sometimes settled by a formal duel on an island or a small marked piece of ground. What was the duel called?
context: Old Norse 'island-going'. Three shields per fighter; the loser paid up or yielded. Outlawed in Iceland in 1006 after Gunnlaug Wormtongue lost his life over a woman to his rival Hrafn.

question: Norse legal assemblies — meetings of free men to make law and settle disputes — were called what?
context: Local 'things' and regional 'allthings' across the Norse world. Iceland's Althing, Norway's Frostathing and Gulathing, the Tynwald on the Isle of Man (still in session). The Tinwald in Scotland's Orkney.

question: An Icelandic merchant led a major settlement attempt at Vinland c. 1010 AD. His son Snorri was born there — the first European born in the Americas. Who was the merchant?
context: Married to Gudrid (widow of Erik the Red's son Thorstein). Three years in Vinland, then back to Iceland. Snorri's descendants include three early bishops of Iceland — and his mother Gudrid made a pilgrimage to Rome.

question: The Norse colony of Greenland — founded by Erik the Red c. 985 AD — eventually died out in the 15th century. Causes are debated. The two settlements were called the Eastern and the what?
context: Both on the southwestern coast — neither was geographically 'eastern' in modern terms. The Western Settlement died first (c. 1350); the Eastern Settlement vanished by c. 1450. The Little Ice Age, the Black Death, and Inuit competition are competing explanations.

question: A great marble lion at the harbor of Athens (now in Venice) bears Norse runic graffiti — proof of the Vikings' Mediterranean reach. What is the lion called?
context: Carved in the 4th century BC. The runes were probably carved by a Varangian Guard contingent in 1040 AD during Harald Hardrada's service. Venetian Francesco Morosini took the lion to Venice in 1687.

question: A vast amount of Arabic silver — Abbasid dirhams from Samarkand to Baghdad — found its way to Viking Scandinavia. Through what trade network?
answer: The Volga and Dnieper river routes
choices: The Volga and Dnieper river routes
context: The Rus carried slaves and furs east; brought silver back. Hoards of Arabic dirhams found in Sweden number in the hundreds of thousands. Vikings minted no coins of their own — they weighed silver to pay.

question: Norse society had three classes — jarls (nobles), karls (free farmers), and thralls. What were the thralls?
context: The Rigsthula in the Poetic Edda derives the three classes from visits by Heimdall (as Rigr) to three couples. Slaves were captured in raids or born to slave parents. They could be freed; freed slaves were called leysingjar.

question: The Prophet Muhammad's first revelation, around 610 AD, came in a cave on Mount Hira where he was meditating. The angel commanded him to do what?
context: Arabic 'iqra' — the first word of the first revelation, opening Sura 96. The Arabic word for the revelations he received is 'Qur'an' — 'recitation'. Muhammad was about 40 years old.

question: Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD marks the start of the Islamic calendar. What is the migration called?
context: Threatened with assassination in Mecca, Muhammad fled with Abu Bakr. The Islamic year is dated AH (Anno Hegirae) from this event. The lunar Islamic calendar is about 11 days shorter than the solar Gregorian year.

question: In 630 AD Muhammad returned to Mecca at the head of an army of 10,000 and accepted its peaceful surrender. He then cleansed which sacred building of its idols?
context: The Kaaba — said by Islam to have been built by Abraham and Ishmael. Muhammad reportedly destroyed 360 idols. The Black Stone in the Kaaba's eastern corner is kissed by pilgrims during the Hajj.

question: The Quran was compiled into the official form used today around 650 AD by the third Caliph. Who?
context: The Uthmanic codex. Earlier variant collections were destroyed to prevent dispute. The Arabic text has remained essentially stable since. About 78,000 words, 114 chapters (suras).

question: The first of Islam's Five Pillars is the profession of faith — 'there is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger'. What is it called in Arabic?
context: To convert to Islam, one needs only sincerely recite the Shahada before two Muslim witnesses. The other four pillars: salat (prayer five times daily), zakat (alms), sawm (Ramadan fasting), hajj (pilgrimage).

question: Muslims pray five times daily, facing Mecca. The five prayer times are dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset, and night. What is this practice called?
context: Each prayer involves prescribed words and movements (rakaa). The call to prayer (adhan) is given five times daily from the mosque's minaret. Friday noon prayer is communal; other prayers can be individual.

question: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset throughout which lunar month?
context: Ninth month of the Islamic calendar. No food, drink, smoking, or sex during daylight. The month commemorates the first revelation of the Quran. Eid al-Fitr (Festival of Breaking the Fast) follows.

question: The Kaaba — the cube-shaped building at the center of Mecca's Great Mosque — has a sacred stone set in its eastern corner. What is the stone called?
context: Possibly meteoric in origin. Said by Islamic tradition to have been given to Abraham by Gabriel. Pilgrims kiss or touch it during the Hajj. Once stolen by Qarmatian Shia in 930 AD; returned 22 years later.

question: The dispute over who should succeed Muhammad split Islam into Sunni and Shia branches. The fourth Caliph (Sunni view) or first Imam (Shia view) was Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law. Who?
context: Murdered in 661 AD. His son Husayn died at the Battle of Karbala in 680 AD — the defining tragedy of Shia Islam. The Shia hold that Ali was Muhammad's designated successor; the Sunni hold for elected caliphate.

question: A 9th-century Persian mathematician at the House of Wisdom gave us both 'algebra' (from his book Al-Jabr) and 'algorithm' (from a Latinized version of his name). Who?
context: c. 780-850. Also developed the Hindu-Arabic numeral system into European use. His algorithm-name (Algoritmi) gave us our central computing term over a thousand years later.

question: An 11th-century Persian polymath wrote the Canon of Medicine — a standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries. Who?
context: 980-1037. Born near Bukhara. Wrote on medicine, philosophy, astronomy, alchemy. His Book of Healing was a 4-volume philosophical encyclopedia. His arguments influenced Thomas Aquinas.

question: A 13th-century Sufi mystic and Persian poet wrote the six-volume Mathnawi — a vast spiritual epic of stories, parables, and divine longing. Who?
context: 1207-1273. The Whirling Dervishes (Mevlevi Order) trace to him. His tomb in Konya is a major pilgrimage site. In recent decades the best-selling poet in English translation in America.

question: The historical Buddha was born around the 5th century BC in a garden grove in what is now southern Nepal. Where?
context: His mother Mahamaya gave birth standing, holding a sal tree branch. Ashoka erected a pillar at Lumbini in 249 BC that still survives. UNESCO World Heritage Site. Tradition: he was born from his mother's side.

question: The young Prince Siddhartha left his palace and saw four sights that drove him to renounce his life. Three were an old man, a sick man, and a dead man. The fourth was what?
context: The first three showed him suffering as the universal human condition. The fourth showed him the possibility of renunciation. He left his wife and infant son that night to begin his spiritual quest.

question: After six years of asceticism, Siddhartha sat under a fig tree and vowed not to rise until he had attained enlightenment. He attained it at dawn. Where did this occur?
context: In modern Bihar, India. The Bodhi Tree (a descendant of the original) still stands there. Buddhists from all over the world make pilgrimage. Buddha was 35 years old.

question: After his enlightenment, Buddha gave his first sermon in a deer park near Varanasi. He taught the Four Noble Truths to his five former companions. Where?
context: The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta — 'Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dhamma'. Ashoka built a stupa at Sarnath. The site is now one of Buddhism's four most sacred places (with Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, and Kushinagar).

question: Buddha's first sermon presented Four Noble Truths. The first is that all existence is characterized by what?
context: Pali 'dukkha' — unsatisfactoriness, not just gross pain. The others: dukkha has a cause (craving); it can cease (nirvana); the path to cease it is the Eightfold Path.

question: The fourth Noble Truth gives the path beyond suffering. It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right what?
context: The eight folds are grouped into wisdom (the first two), ethics (the next three), and concentration (the last three). The Eightfold Path is depicted as the Dharmachakra — the eight-spoked wheel of dharma — central in Buddhist iconography.

question: The Buddha died at age 80 at Kushinagar, lying on his right side between two sal trees. The event is called the what?
context: His death is called 'parinirvana' or 'mahaparinirvana' — final passing into nirvana. His relics were divided among eight kingdoms. Last words (paraphrased): 'all conditioned things are impermanent — strive on with diligence'.

question: The Dalai Lamas are believed to be reincarnations of the bodhisattva of compassion. What is the bodhisattva's name?
context: Chinese 'Guanyin' (often female in Chinese Buddhism); Tibetan 'Chenrezig'. The Dalai Lama lineage began in the 14th century. The current Dalai Lama is the 14th. Lineage continuation is currently in question due to Chinese state interference.

question: Hinduism's oldest scriptures — the four Vedas — were composed in Sanskrit by Indo-Aryan migrants into northern India. The oldest, dating to c. 1500-1200 BC, is the what?
context: 1,028 hymns to various gods (Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma). Composed in early Vedic Sanskrit. The Sama Veda is mostly drawn from the Rig Veda for liturgical chanting; the Yajur Veda and Atharva Veda followed.

question: Later Vedic texts shifted from ritual hymns to philosophical dialogues on the nature of self and ultimate reality. They are called what?
context: Sanskrit 'sitting down near' — pupil-by-teacher transmission. Around 200 Upanishads; thirteen 'principal' ones from c. 900-500 BC. Schopenhauer regarded them as the consolation of his old age.

question: Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions all teach that the soul (or stream of consciousness) is reborn into successive lives in a cycle. What is the cycle called?
context: Sanskrit 'wandering, flowing along'. The quality of rebirth is determined by karma (action). Release from samsara is moksha (Hindu) or nirvana (Buddhist).

question: In Egyptian belief, the dead person's heart was weighed against a feather. If lighter than the feather, the soul went to a paradise; if heavier, it was eaten by a monster. The feather was that of which goddess?
context: Ammut — 'devourer of the dead', part lion, part hippo, part crocodile — ate hearts that failed the weighing. Anubis weighed; Thoth recorded. The Book of the Dead provided spells to ensure passage.

question: In November 1978, a cult leader in Guyana ordered his followers to drink cyanide-laced beverage; 909 died, including 304 children. The leader was who?
context: Peoples Temple. Jones started his ministry in Indiana, moved to California, then established 'Jonestown' in remote Guyana. The phrase 'drinking the Kool-Aid' (originally Flavor Aid) preserves the event.

question: In March 1995 a Japanese cult released sarin gas in the Tokyo subway, killing 13 and injuring thousands. The cult was led by who?
context: Aum Shinrikyo. Syncretic doomsday cult drawing on Buddhism, Hindu Tantrism, Christian apocalyptic, and Nostradamus. Asahara and twelve followers were executed in 2018. The group renamed itself Aleph and continues in reduced form.

question: On the road to Hel, Hermod crossed a river called Gjoll over a bridge guarded by a maiden. Who guarded the bridge?
context: Old Norse 'furious battler'. The bridge had a golden roof. She told Hermod that five battalions of dead had recently crossed — yet his single rider made more noise than all of them.

question: Hel's hall in the realm of the dead was called what?
context: Old Norse 'misery'. Her plate was Hunger, her knife was Famine, her servants Slow-and-Languid, her bed Sickness, her doormat Stumbling-Block. A grim Norse vision of the realm of the natural dead.

question: The Norse lament-poem composed for a dead lord or king was called what?
context: Old Norse 'lord's lament'. 'Erfikvaedi' (memorial poem) was the broader term. Egil Skallagrimsson composed Sonatorrek for his drowned sons — one of the great lyric poems of Old Norse literature.

question: Snorri Sturluson's great chronicle of the Norwegian kings — covering legendary times through the 12th century — is named for its first two words: 'kringla heimsins', 'the circle of the world'. What is it called?
context: 16 sagas. Written c. 1230. The principal source for Norway's medieval history. Sigvat Thordarson, Stuf, and other 11th-century skalds are extensively quoted as eyewitnesses.

question: Snorri Sturluson served Iceland's Althing as Lawspeaker — head legal officer — for two separate terms. He was murdered in his cellar at Reykholt in 1241 on whose orders?
context: Killed by King Hakon's agents (led by his son-in-law Gissur Thorvaldsson) for opposing Norway's takeover of Iceland. The country submitted to Norway in 1262, ending the Commonwealth. Snorri's last words: 'do not strike!'

question: Muhammad's closest companion, his father-in-law, and the first caliph after Muhammad's death in 632 AD was who?
context: Caliph 632-634. Defended Islam against the Ridda (apostasy) wars. Father of Muhammad's wife Aisha. Designated his successor Umar. His brief reign held the young Islamic state together.

question: The Islamic calendar dates years from Muhammad's hijra (migration) from Mecca to Medina. In which Gregorian year does year 1 AH fall?
context: Established under Caliph Umar (c. 638 AD). The Islamic year is purely lunar — about 354 days. Each year drifts about 11 days earlier in the Gregorian calendar. Ramadan rotates through the seasons.

question: When her daughter was taken, the harvest goddess wandered the earth grieving, refusing her divine office. The fields lay barren; humanity starved. Disguised as an old woman she was welcomed in Eleusis, where she founded what mysteries?
context: The Greek world's most prestigious mystery cult — initiates kept secrets for 2,000 years (we still don't know fully what happened in the telesterion). Demeter taught Triptolemus how to plant grain; he became culture-hero of agriculture.

question: Sailors kidnapped a beautiful youth on a Greek island, planning to sell him into slavery. The mast sprouted grape vines; wine flowed across the deck; a lion appeared. The pirates leapt into the sea — and became dolphins. Who was the captive?
context: Homeric Hymn 7. Dionysus, god of wine, madness, and theater, son of Zeus and Semele. He was twice-born — first from Semele's burning body, then from Zeus's thigh. His worship spread from Thrace; Pentheus of Thebes resisted and was torn apart by Maenads.

question: The most prestigious mystery cult of the Greek world, held annually at a town fourteen miles from Athens. Initiates fasted, processed, drank a barley-mint potion (kykeon), and saw something in the telesterion. For 2,000 years initiates kept the secret. What town?
context: Initiates ('mystai') promised better fates in the afterlife. The cult dramatized Demeter's search for Persephone. Cicero, Plutarch, and many emperors were initiates. Even Christian writers refer to it. The cult was finally shut down c. 392 AD by Theodosius.

question: The most famous Greek temple, built 447-432 BC on the Athenian Acropolis to house Phidias's 40-foot gold-and-ivory statue of the patron goddess. Designed by Ictinus and Callicrates; sculpture supervised by Phidias. Whose temple?
context: Pericles commissioned it after the Persian Wars. The Doric temple's sculpture (pediments, metopes, frieze) is dispersed today — the Parthenon Marbles in the British Museum, others in the Acropolis Museum. Phidias's statue is lost; copies in Roman art survive.

question: One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: a 40-foot gold-and-ivory statue of the king of the gods, enthroned in his temple at Olympia. The sculptor's workshop has been excavated; the statue is lost. Who carved it?
