context: Phidias of Athens (5th c. BC). The chryselephantine technique (gold over ivory on a wooden core) was Phidias's specialty — same method as his Athena Parthenos. The Zeus Olympios statue stood until c. 5th c. AD and was lost in fire (in Constantinople, where it had been moved).

question: The all-father sent two ravens out across the worlds each dawn and gathered news from them at dusk. They sat on his shoulders and whispered to him. They symbolized thought and memory. What are their names?
context: Huginn ('thought') and Muninn ('memory'). Odin worried — confessed Havamal — more about Muninn than Huginn, suggesting memory is more easily lost than thought. The two ravens are heraldic in Viking iconography.

question: The Germanic runic alphabet originally had 24 letters (the Elder Futhark, from c. 200 AD). In the Viking age it was reduced to 16 letters. What was the reduced form called?
context: Younger Futhark, c. 800 AD. Runes were primarily epigraphic — carved on stone, wood, weapons, ornaments. They served both writing and divination. Christianization gradually replaced them with Latin script, though runic survived as folk-script into the early modern period.

question: In 874 AD Norse settlers fleeing the unification of Norway under Harald Fairhair colonized a North Atlantic volcanic island. They founded an unusual republic without a king. What island?
context: Iceland. By 930 AD the Althing was meeting at Thingvellir — the world's oldest continuous parliament. Iceland Christianized voluntarily in 1000 AD (Thorgeir's compromise). Iceland preserved Norse myth uniquely because of its remote conversion.

question: The 'Viking Age' is conventionally dated from one specific raid: June 8, 793, when Norse warriors descended on an island monastery off Northumbria, slaughtering monks and carrying off treasures. Alcuin wrote that 'such terror had not before been seen in Britain'. Where?
context: Lindisfarne. The raid shocked Christian Europe. Within a generation Vikings were raiding from Ireland to Spain to Russia. By the 9th-10th centuries they had founded the Danelaw in England, settled Iceland, raided Paris, and Rurik's dynasty in Kievan Rus.

question: The central Norse pagan ritual: an animal (or in greater offerings, a human) was sacrificed, its blood sprinkled on the altar, idols, and worshippers. The meat was boiled and eaten in a communal feast. Toasts (skalir) were drunk to the gods. What was this called?
context: Blot ('blood-letting' / 'sacrifice'). The word is the etymological cognate of English 'bless'. Three great annual blots: Winter Nights (October), Yule (December), Sigrblot (April). Blot is still practiced by modern Heathen / Asatru communities — without animal sacrifice.

question: Norse warriors who fought in trance-fury, biting their shields, immune to pain, possibly drugged or possessed. Their name means 'bear-shirts' from the wolf or bear skins they wore. Who?
context: Berserkers. Ulfhednar (wolf-coats) were a related class. Trance was sometimes achieved with amanita muscaria or other psychoactives, though this is debated. Outside battle the trance-state made them dangerous to friends. Banned by King Eirik I of Norway in the 11th c.

question: In 1904 archaeologists in Norway excavated a magnificent ship burial dating to 834 AD. Two women — one elderly, one younger — were interred with rich grave goods including a wagon, sleds, and textiles. What is the site called?
context: Oseberg, Norway. The ship is on display at the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo. Ship burials were reserved for the highest-status dead — possibly a queen and her companion (servant, slave, or relative — debated). Gokstad nearby contained a male warrior in 890 AD.

question: Around 1000 AD, an Icelander sailed from Greenland to North America — at a place he called 'Vinland' for the wild grapes (or 'meadowland'). He had a brief Norse settlement in what is now Newfoundland. Who, and what archaeological site confirms it?
context: L'Anse aux Meadows (excavated 1960s by Anne Stine Ingstad and Helge Ingstad). Confirmed Norse occupation c. 1000 AD — 500 years before Columbus. The Vinland Sagas (Saga of Erik the Red, Saga of the Greenlanders) record the voyages.

question: In the early 18th century in Ukraine and Poland, an unlettered mystic preached a Judaism of joy, song, dance, and direct experience of God available to the simplest peasant — not only to scholars. He inspired a movement. Who?
answer: Israel ben Eliezer (the Baal Shem Tov)
choices: Israel ben Eliezer (the Baal Shem Tov)
context: (c.1700-1760). The Baal Shem Tov ('master of the good name'). Hasidism spread rapidly across Eastern Europe — opposed by the 'mitnagdim' (Vilna Gaon's Lithuanian Talmudists). Today's Lubavitcher, Satmar, Belz, Breslov, and other dynasties descend from his movement.

question: Around 610 AD, a 40-year-old Meccan merchant in the habit of retreating to a cave on Mount Hira for contemplation received what he experienced as a vision of the angel Gabriel commanding him 'Recite!' (Iqra). His wife Khadija believed him. Who?
context: Muhammad (570-632 AD). The Quran ('recitation') was given over 23 years. Khadija was the first convert. The first Muslim community emerged in Mecca, then moved to Medina in the Hijra (622 AD) — the start of the Islamic calendar.

question: The cube-shaped building at the center of the Great Mosque of Mecca, draped in black silk embroidered with gold Quranic verses, is the qibla (direction of prayer) for all Muslims worldwide. A black stone in one corner is venerated. What is the building?
context: The Kaaba. Pre-Islamic Arabs had used it for centuries — Muhammad cleared the idols when Mecca surrendered in 630. The Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad) is believed to date from Abraham and Ishmael's building of the original sanctuary. Muslims circumambulate it (tawaf) during Hajj.

question: After Muhammad's death in 632 AD, Muslims divided over succession. The majority accepted Abu Bakr (the prophet's friend and father-in-law) as first caliph; the minority backed his cousin and son-in-law as the rightful first imam. Who was the minority's choice?
context: Ali. Ali was eventually the fourth Rashidun caliph, but assassinated in 661. His son Husayn was killed at Karbala in 680 — the foundational tragedy of Shia identity. Sunni-Shia division shapes modern Iran (Shia), Saudi Arabia (Sunni), Iraq (mixed), and the wider Middle East.

question: Under the Abbasid caliphs in 8th-9th century Baghdad, a great translation and research institute gathered Greek, Persian, and Indian texts and rendered them into Arabic. It became the center of the Islamic Golden Age. What was it?
context: Founded under Caliph al-Mansur (754-775), expanded by Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun. Aristotle, Galen, Hippocrates, Euclid, Ptolemy, and others translated. Sacked by the Mongols in 1258 when they took Baghdad — the books cast in the Tigris ran black for days.

question: A 9th-century Persian mathematician working in Baghdad's House of Wisdom wrote 'al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala' (c. 820 AD), establishing algebra as a discipline. His Latinized name gives us another word. What word?
context: 'Algorithm' is the Latinized form of his name. 'Algebra' comes from 'al-jabr' (restoration) in his book's title. He also introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals (and zero) to the Islamic world; from there they reached medieval Europe via Spain.

question: A Persian polymath (980-1037 AD) wrote 'The Canon of Medicine' (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb) — used as a standard medical textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for 600 years. He also wrote 'The Book of Healing' (philosophy). Latin-renamed for short. Who?
context: Avicenna's metaphysics — 'essence' versus 'existence', the necessary existent, the proof from contingency — deeply influenced Aquinas, Duns Scotus, and others. The Canon was used in Padua and Bologna medical schools into the 17th century.

question: A Sakya prince in northern India, shielded from suffering in his palace, ventured out as a young man and saw four sights: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a serene wandering ascetic. He renounced his life of luxury at age 29. Who?
context: Siddhartha. Born c. 563 BC at Lumbini (modern Nepal). His father had tried to fulfill prophecy that he would either be a great king or a great teacher by hiding suffering. The Four Sights triggered the Great Renunciation. He left wife Yashodhara and son Rahula.

question: After six years of severe asceticism that nearly killed him, Siddhartha sat under a tree at Bodh Gaya determined not to rise until he understood. Through the night he wrestled with Mara (the tempter). At dawn he attained enlightenment. What tree?
context: Bodh Gaya in Bihar, India. The current Mahabodhi Temple complex is a UNESCO site. The tree is supposedly a descendant of the original (Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta carried a cutting to Sri Lanka c. 250 BC where it still grows at Anuradhapura).

question: After his enlightenment, Siddhartha (now the Buddha — 'the awakened') walked to Sarnath near Varanasi and preached his first sermon to five ascetic companions in the Deer Park. He set in motion 'the wheel of dharma'. What were the contents?
context: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. The Four Noble Truths: suffering exists (dukkha); suffering arises from craving (samudaya); suffering can cease (nirodha); the way to cessation is the Eightfold Path (magga). The five ascetics became the first Buddhist monks.

question: The foundation of Buddhist teaching, set forth in the Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath. The first truth: dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness) is universal. The second: it arises from craving (tanha). The third: cessation is possible. What is the fourth?
answer: The Eightfold Path leads to cessation
choices: The Eightfold Path leads to cessation
context: Magga — the Noble Eightfold Path. Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. Often grouped into three: wisdom (view, intention), ethics (speech, action, livelihood), meditation (effort, mindfulness, concentration).

question: In Mahayana Buddhism, a being who has attained the verge of nirvana but vows to remain in samsara to help all sentient beings reach liberation. What is this figure called?
context: The bodhisattva vow is foundational to Mahayana. Avalokiteshvara (Chinese Guanyin / Japanese Kannon) — the bodhisattva of compassion — became enormously popular across East Asia. Tibetan Buddhism considers the Dalai Lama an emanation of Avalokiteshvara.

question: The oldest sacred texts of Hinduism — four collections of hymns, mantras, and ritual instructions in archaic Sanskrit, composed in the late Bronze Age in northern India (c. 1500-1200 BC). What are they called?
context: Four Vedas: Rigveda (oldest, hymns to gods like Indra, Agni, Soma), Yajurveda (sacrificial formulas), Samaveda (chants), Atharvaveda (later, household and magical formulas). Transmitted orally with extraordinary precision before being written. Foundational scripture of Hinduism.

question: The three great Hindu deities: creator, preserver, and destroyer. The Vedas privilege the second; the Puranas elevate the third. The first has only a few temples in all of India. What are they?
context: Trimurti (sometimes spelled Trimurthi). Brahma (creator) has only one major temple (Pushkar). Vishnu (preserver) has Krishna and Rama as major avatars. Shiva (destroyer/transformer) is worshipped in linga form. Each has a consort: Saraswati, Lakshmi, Parvati.

question: The Hindu practice of widow self-immolation on her husband's funeral pyre — sometimes voluntary, often coerced. Roop Kanwar's 1987 case showed it had not fully ended. When was it formally abolished by the British in Bengal?
context: Banned by Governor-General William Bentinck and Raja Ram Mohan Roy's reform campaign. Sati was always rare — but powerful symbolically. Modern reform Hinduism (Vivekananda, Roy, Tagore) rejected it firmly. Hindu reform from within ran parallel to colonial pressure.

question: Born in 1469 near Lahore, this Punjabi spiritual teacher had a revelatory experience while bathing in a river — he was, he said, taken to God's presence and given a mission to teach. His central message: 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.' Who?
context: Nanak (1469-1539). Founder of Sikhism. He synthesized elements of Hindu bhakti and Sufi Islam, rejecting both ritual and caste. The nine subsequent gurus refined the tradition. The tenth, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa in 1699. After his death, the eternal Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib.

question: On Baisakhi day 1699 at Anandpur, the tenth Sikh guru challenged the assembly: 'Who will give his head for God?' Five volunteers were taken behind a curtain (and emerged alive). They became the first Khalsa, initiated by the guru, then they initiated him. Who?
context: Guru Gobind Singh (1666-1708). The Khalsa ('pure') were Sikh warriors — bearing the Five Ks: kesh (uncut hair), kangha (comb), kara (steel bracelet), kachera (cotton breeches), and kirpan (sword). All male Khalsa Sikhs take the surname Singh ('lion'); female Khalsa take Kaur ('princess').

question: An 81-chapter Chinese classic from the 4th-6th century BC, attributed to an obscure figure who supposedly wrote it down at the request of a gatekeeper before riding west on a water buffalo. The founding text of Taoism. Title and traditional author?
context: Daodejing ('Classic of the Way and Virtue'). Possibly composite. The Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao. Wuwei (non-action) — flowing with rather than against the natural order. Yin-yang complementarity. Modern philosophical Taoism distinguishes from religious Taoism with temples and rituals.

question: A Taoist sage in the 4th century BC dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering happily. He woke and wondered: was he a man dreaming he was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming he was a man? Who?
context: Zhuangzi (Zhuang Zhou, c. 369-286 BC). His book is the second great Taoist classic. The butterfly dream raises classic questions of identity and reality. Zhuangzi mocked Confucians; embraced paradox; preferred fishing in a stream to ruling a kingdom.

question: Around 1754 BC, a Babylonian king inscribed 282 laws on a basalt stele — including the famous 'eye for an eye' (lex talionis). The stele is now in the Louvre. Who was the king?
context: Hammurabi (r. c. 1792-1750 BC). His code distinguishes punishments by class — a free man's eye costs more than a slave's. Not the oldest code (Ur-Nammu's code, c. 2100 BC, precedes it), but the most preserved and influential. The Mesopotamian legal tradition.

question: The Yoruba orisha of thunder, lightning, and justice. A historical fourth king of Oyo, deified after his death. His thunderbolt-stones (neolithic axe-heads) were collected by his priests. Sacred to him: the double-axe. Who?
context: Shango. The Yoruba pantheon (orishas) traveled with the slave trade — Santeria (Cuba), Candomble (Brazil), Vodou (Haiti) all preserve orisha worship. Olokun, Yemoja, Oshun, Ogun, Obatala are major orishas. Yoruba religion has perhaps 100 million adherents worldwide.

question: On November 18, 1978 in a Guyanese jungle compound, more than 900 American followers of a Bay Area preacher died by cyanide poisoning at his order — most coerced, some forced. The preacher shot himself. Who?
context: Jonestown massacre — 909 dead including 304 children. The phrase 'drink the Kool-Aid' enters English from this event (the cyanide was in Flavor-Aid, not Kool-Aid). Congressman Leo Ryan was murdered the same day investigating. The largest deliberate loss of American civilian life until 9/11.

question: On March 20, 1995, members of a Japanese new religion released sarin nerve gas on five Tokyo subway lines during morning rush hour, killing 13 and injuring thousands. The cult leader was executed in 2018. Who founded the cult?
context: Shoko Asahara (Chizuo Matsumoto). Aum Shinrikyo had perhaps 50,000 followers worldwide before the attack — many were highly educated. Their attempts to acquire nuclear weapons and produce VX gas alarmed counterproliferation experts. Asahara and 12 others executed July 2018.

question: The Eleusinian Mysteries — secret rites celebrated near Athens for nearly two millennia (c. 1500 BC to 392 AD) — initiated thousands of Greeks and later Romans into knowledge said to remove the fear of death. Which deity was the central figure?
answer: Demeter and her daughter Persephone — the rites reenacted the mother's search for the kidnapped daughter.
choices: Demeter and her daughter Persephone — the rites reenacted the mother's search for the kidnapped daughter.
Dionysus — the Eleusinian rites were sometimes confused with Dionysian, but were distinct.
Apollo at Eleusis — but Apollo had no shrine at Eleusis; this is the Delphic confusion.
Asclepius — the healing god at Eleusis was a later, separate cult.
context: The Mysteries were so secret that the death penalty applied to revealing them — and almost nothing survives of what was actually said and done. Initiates included Cicero, Augustus, Hadrian, and Marcus Aurelius. The cult ended when Theodosius I closed the shrine and the Goths sacked it in 396.

question: The Olympic Games — held every four years at Olympia from 776 BC — were one of four Panhellenic games. Athletes competed naked, anointed with oil, and the prize was an olive wreath rather than money. What god were the Olympic games dedicated to?
answer: Zeus — the chief Olympian, with the games held at his sanctuary at Olympia in the western Peloponnese.
choices: Zeus — the chief Olympian, with the games held at his sanctuary at Olympia in the western Peloponnese.
Apollo — the patron of the Pythian Games at Delphi, but not the Olympic.
Poseidon — the patron of the Isthmian Games at Corinth, but not the Olympic.
Heracles — sometimes identified as the founder of the Olympic Games, but not their dedicatee.
context: The Olympic Games ran continuously from 776 BC to 393 AD — nearly twelve centuries — when Theodosius I shut down all pagan festivals. The modern revival began with Coubertin's 1894 IOC and the 1896 Athens games. The original site is preserved and the Olympic flame is still lit there for each modern games.

question: Animal sacrifice was central to Greek religion. The animal was led to the altar (a *bomos*), water was sprinkled on it (when it nodded, this was taken as consent), the throat was cut, and blood was caught in a bowl. What was traditionally done with the inedible parts — the thigh bones and fat?
answer: Burned on the altar for the gods, while the meat was roasted and shared among the worshippers.
choices: Burned on the altar for the gods, while the meat was roasted and shared among the worshippers.
Buried in pits beside the altar, kept from the gaze of common eyes by the priests.
Thrown into the sea or river closest to the temple, returning to the elements that birthed them.
Returned uncut to the herd, releasing the surviving animals back to their pastures.
context: Hesiod tells how Prometheus tricked Zeus at Mecone into accepting the bones-and-fat portion for the gods, leaving the meat for humans — the etiology of the standard sacrificial division. Greek temples were essentially butcher shops where meat consumption coincided with worship. Vegetarianism (Pythagoreans, some Orphics) was a self-conscious break with religion.

question: Viking-age religion practiced animal and (occasionally) human sacrifice — *blot* — to the gods. The major sanctuary at Uppsala in Sweden was described by the German chronicler Adam of Bremen (c. 1075) as the site of nine-yearly festivals. What did Adam report?
answer: Nine male animals of every kind — including humans — sacrificed and hung in a sacred grove.
choices: Nine male animals of every kind — including humans — sacrificed and hung in a sacred grove.
Nine ships burned with their crews aboard at the temple's pier each ninth midsummer.
Nine virgins drowned in the spring beside the temple, with their bodies cast into a pit.
Nine bulls slaughtered together with nine horses, the meat distributed to all worshippers.
context: Adam of Bremen's account is contested — he was a hostile Christian source — but archaeological evidence supports a major pagan cult center at Uppsala. The grove with hanging sacrifices may reflect actual practice. Honest historiography of Norse religion does not flinch from naming human sacrifice as part of the picture; Christianization in the 11th century ended such practices.

question: The runes — the angular Norse alphabet — were used for writing inscriptions on stone, wood, bone, and metal. There were two main forms. What characterized them?
answer: The Elder Futhark (24 runes, c. 150–800 AD) and the Younger Futhark (16 runes, c. 800–1100 AD).
choices: The Elder Futhark (24 runes, c. 150–800 AD) and the Younger Futhark (16 runes, c. 800–1100 AD).
The North Futhark and the South Futhark — but these are not Norse distinctions.
The Pagan Futhark and the Christian Futhark — but rune use predated and outlasted Christianization.
The Royal Futhark and the Common Futhark — but rune use was not class-restricted.
context: Rune-carving spread with Viking trade and conquest — runic inscriptions have been found from Greenland to Constantinople. The Younger Futhark, used during the Viking Age (793–1066), was a 16-letter simplified form. Anglo-Saxon Futhorc (33 runes) is a separate Germanic development. Runes had both writing and divinatory uses.

question: Iceland was settled by Norwegians fleeing the centralizing rule of King Harald Fairhair around 874 AD. By 930 the new society had created what may be the world's oldest continuously functioning parliament. What is it called?
answer: The Althing — convened annually at Thingvellir, where the law-speaker recited the laws aloud.
choices: The Althing — convened annually at Thingvellir, where the law-speaker recited the laws aloud.
The Storting — but Storting is the modern Norwegian parliament, not the Icelandic.
The Folketing — but Folketing is the modern Danish parliament, not Icelandic.
The Riksdag — but Riksdag is the modern Swedish parliament, not Icelandic.
context: The Althing met annually at Thingvellir — a dramatic site of cliffs and fissures where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates pull apart. The Althing legislated, judged, and arbitrated. It accepted Christianity peacefully in 1000 by a single decision of the law-speaker — perhaps the most remarkable conversion in European history.

question: Around 1000 AD, an Icelandic expedition reached the coast of North America — five centuries before Columbus. The leader was the son of Erik the Red (founder of the Greenland colony). What was he called, and what did he name his discovery?
answer: Leif Eriksson — who named the new land Vinland for the wild grapes he found growing.
choices: Leif Eriksson — who named the new land Vinland for the wild grapes he found growing.
Bjarni Herjolfsson — who had first sighted the coast but did not land; his story is in the *Saga of the Greenlanders*.
Thorfinn Karlsefni — who led the largest follow-up expedition with about 160 settlers.
Thorvald Eriksson — who explored further but was killed in a skirmish with the Skraelings.
context: L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, excavated 1960–68, confirmed Norse presence in North America with structures and artifacts dating to c. 1000 AD. The colonization attempts failed because of conflict with native peoples (Skraelings) and the small size of the Norse population in Greenland. The discovery was forgotten outside Iceland until the 20th century.

question: *Njal's Saga* — among the greatest of Icelandic sagas, written c. 1280 — tells of a long feud culminating in the burning of an old wise man in his own house with his entire household. Who is the burned man?
answer: Njal of Bergthorsknoll — whose foreseeing of his fate is one of the saga's tragic notes.
choices: Njal of Bergthorsknoll — whose foreseeing of his fate is one of the saga's tragic notes.
Egil Skallagrimsson — but Egil is the protagonist of *Egil's Saga*, not Njal's.
Gunnar of Hlidarendi — Njal's friend, whose earlier killing is part of the cycle of revenge.
Skarphedin — Njal's son, who in fact died in the burning along with his father.
context: Icelandic family sagas (the *islendingasogur*) — composed in the 13th century about events of the 10th and 11th — are among medieval Europe's great prose achievements. They develop characters with psychological depth, narrative subtlety, and a strong sense of fate. Njal, the burned lawyer, faces his death with characteristic stoicism.

question: The Viking-age raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne on the coast of Northumbria in 793 AD is often dated as the opening of the 'Viking Age.' The Northumbrian scholar Alcuin, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote of the attack in shock. What did he find most remarkable?
answer: That God had allowed his church and the saints' relics to be desecrated by pagans.
choices: That God had allowed his church and the saints' relics to be desecrated by pagans.
That the Viking ships had reached the British Isles at all, without prior warning.
That the monks had been unable to defend themselves with the relics of their saints.
That the Vikings had taken so few prisoners and so much treasure in a single raid.
context: Alcuin's letters to King Æthelred of Northumbria and Bishop Higbald of Lindisfarne treat the raid as God's judgment on a sinful England. Viking raids became regular over the next two centuries, with major incursions into Frankia, Ireland, Russia, and the Mediterranean. The 'Viking Age' is conventionally dated 793–1066.

question: Muhammad (c. 570–632 AD) of Mecca received his first revelation in a cave on Mount Hira around 610. Tradition records that the angel Gabriel pressed him and commanded him to recite. What was the first word?
choices: *Bismillah* — 'in the name of God' — the opening of every Quranic chapter after the first revelation.
*Allahu akbar* — 'God is greatest' — the *takbir*, central to Muslim worship.
*Shahada* — 'witness' — the confession of faith, but a later codification.
context: Muhammad fled Mecca for Medina in 622 — the *hijra*, the start of the Islamic calendar. Within ten years he had unified most of the Arabian peninsula under Islam. He returned to Mecca in 630, cleansed the Kaaba of its idols, and consolidated the new religion. He died at Medina in 632.

question: The Abbasid 'House of Wisdom' in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian, and Indian works and originated original research. One scholar there gave his name to 'algorithm' and a branch of mathematics. Who?
answer: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850) — whose name gave us 'algorithm' and whose book gave us 'algebra' (*al-jabr*).
choices: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850) — whose name gave us 'algorithm' and whose book gave us 'algebra' (*al-jabr*).
Al-Kindi (c. 800–873) — the first Arab philosopher, who wrote on metaphysics, mathematics, and music.
Al-Razi (c. 865–925) — physician, philosopher, and alchemist; the European 'Rhazes.'
Al-Battani (c. 858–929) — astronomer who refined Ptolemy's calculations.
context: Al-Khwarizmi's *Kitab al-Jabr wa-l-Muqabala* (c. 830) systematized algebraic methods. His work was translated into Latin in the 12th century and became the foundation of European algebra. The transmission of Greek learning through Arabic translation was essential to the later European recovery of classical science.

question: In February 1979 an exiled cleric returned to Tehran. Within months the Shah had fled, the army had stood down, and the cleric had been installed as Supreme Leader of a new Islamic Republic. Who?
answer: Ruhollah Khomeini — Grand Ayatollah whose 1979 revolution founded the Islamic Republic of Iran.
choices: Ruhollah Khomeini — Grand Ayatollah whose 1979 revolution founded the Islamic Republic of Iran.
Hassan Banna — but he is the founder of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, in 1928, not the Iranian revolutionary.
Sayyid Qutb — Egyptian Brotherhood ideologue executed by Nasser in 1966; influenced jihadist thought.
Mawlana Mawdudi — Pakistani Islamist thinker, founder of Jamaat-i Islami, not the Iranian revolutionary.
context: The Iranian Revolution of 1979 was the first successful Islamist revolution in the modern world. Khomeini's doctrine of *velayat-e faqih* (guardianship of the jurist) gave political authority to clerics — a major innovation in Shi'ite thought. The post-1979 regime executed political opponents, crushed dissent, and engaged in regional proxy conflicts.

question: Siddhartha Gautama was born a prince of the Shakya clan in Lumbini. Tradition records that his father, warned that the boy might become either a great king or a religious renunciant, kept him in the palace to prevent his seeing four things outside. What were the four?
answer: An old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — together prompting his Great Renunciation.
choices: An old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — together prompting his Great Renunciation.
A beggar, a soldier, a king, and a priest — the four classes of the broader Indian society.
Fire, water, wind, and earth — the four elements that the young Siddhartha had to recognize.
Joy, grief, fear, and hope — the four passions the young prince was protected from until age 29.
context: The 'Four Sights' broke through his protected upbringing. The first three revealed suffering, age, and death; the fourth offered a path. At 29 he left wife, son, and palace to seek the cause of suffering. After six years of austere asceticism, he sat under a Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya and attained enlightenment, becoming the Buddha ('awakened one').

question: The Buddha's first sermon, given at the Deer Park in Sarnath near Varanasi, set out the foundational doctrine of Buddhism — the Four Noble Truths. The first truth is that life is *dukkha* (suffering, unsatisfactoriness). What is the second?
answer: *Samudaya* — the origin of suffering is craving (*tanha*) and attachment.
choices: *Samudaya* — the origin of suffering is craving (*tanha*) and attachment.
*Anicca* — all things are impermanent, which is a related but distinct truth.
*Anatta* — there is no permanent self, which is a third related teaching.
*Nirvana* — the cessation of suffering, which is in fact the third Noble Truth.
context: The Four Noble Truths: *dukkha* (suffering exists), *samudaya* (its origin is craving), *nirodha* (its cessation), and *magga* (the path to cessation — the Eightfold Path). The Eightfold Path covers right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. Buddhism's first sermon — the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* — codifies all this.

question: Ashoka, emperor of the Maurya dynasty in India (ruled c. 268–232 BC), conquered the kingdom of Kalinga in eastern India around 261 BC. The carnage of the war reportedly converted him. To what?
answer: Buddhism — after which he spread Buddhist ideas across India and beyond through stone edicts.
choices: Buddhism — after which he spread Buddhist ideas across India and beyond through stone edicts.
Hinduism — but Ashoka came from a Hindu background; the conversion was away from violence.
Jainism — but Jainism, like Buddhism, taught nonviolence; Ashoka's specific conversion was Buddhist.
Christianity — Christianity reached India only centuries later, with Thomas tradition.
context: Ashoka's edicts, inscribed on pillars and rocks across his empire, are among the earliest deciphered Indian texts. They promote tolerance, animal welfare, public works, and Buddhist *dhamma*. His missions reached Sri Lanka, Greece, and likely beyond. Ashoka's reign is conventionally celebrated as Buddhism's transformation from a small monastic movement into a major civilizational force.

question: Zen Buddhism — the East Asian meditation tradition — was traced traditionally to a southern Indian monk who is said to have come to China around 520 AD and meditated in a cave for nine years. Who?
answer: Bodhidharma — first patriarch of Chan (Chinese) Buddhism, ancestor of Japanese Zen.
choices: Bodhidharma — first patriarch of Chan (Chinese) Buddhism, ancestor of Japanese Zen.
Padmasambhava — but he is the foundational figure of Tibetan Buddhism (8th century).
Nagarjuna — but he is the 2nd-century founder of the Madhyamaka school of Mahayana philosophy.
Hui Neng — but he is the sixth Chan patriarch (638–713 AD), much later than Bodhidharma.
context: Zen ('Chan' in Chinese) emphasizes direct experience, the use of *koans* (paradoxical questions), and lineage transmission from master to student. It spread to Japan in the 12th–13th centuries (Eisai for Rinzai, Dogen for Soto). Bodhidharma is the figure typically depicted with a fierce, bearded face in Zen iconography — often without eyelids, said to have torn them off to prevent sleep.

question: The four Vedas — *Rig*, *Sama*, *Yajur*, *Atharva* — are the oldest layer of Hindu scripture, composed in Sanskrit between c. 1500 BC and 500 BC. The oldest is which?
answer: The Rig Veda — 1,028 hymns to the Vedic gods, the oldest text of Hindu tradition.
choices: The Rig Veda — 1,028 hymns to the Vedic gods, the oldest text of Hindu tradition.
The Sama Veda — derived from the Rig, set to melodies for liturgical chant.
The Yajur Veda — formulas for sacrificial rituals, later than the Rig.
The Atharva Veda — folk magic and incantations, often dated latest of the four.
context: Vedic Sanskrit — the language of the Rig Veda — is one of the oldest attested Indo-European languages, sharing roots with Greek, Latin, Celtic, and Germanic. Comparative philology has used the Rig Veda extensively to reconstruct Proto-Indo-European. The hymns address Indra (storm-warrior), Agni (fire), Soma (sacred drink), Varuna (sky-judge), and many others.

question: Egyptian eschatology held that the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of Ma'at (truth) in the Hall of Judgment. A specific deity oversaw the weighing. Who was it?
answer: Anubis — jackal-headed god of embalming and the underworld guide.
choices: Anubis — jackal-headed god of embalming and the underworld guide.
Ra — the sun god, who traveled through the underworld each night.
Thoth — but Thoth was the recorder of the verdict, not the weigher.
Set — but Set was the chaos god, not associated with the judgment.
context: If the heart proved heavier than the feather (weighed down by sin), it was eaten by the crocodile-hippopotamus-lion monster Ammit, and the soul ceased to exist. If lighter or equal, the dead entered the blessed afterlife — the 'Field of Reeds.' The Book of the Dead provided spells to help the deceased pass the test. Egyptian afterlife was earned through both ritual and moral conduct.

question: On March 20, 1995, members of a Japanese new religious movement released sarin nerve gas on five trains of the Tokyo subway during the morning rush hour. Twelve people were killed and over 5,500 injured. What was the group called?
answer: Aum Shinrikyo — led by the partially-blind self-proclaimed prophet Shoko Asahara.
choices: Aum Shinrikyo — led by the partially-blind self-proclaimed prophet Shoko Asahara.
Soka Gakkai — but this is a large legitimate Nichiren Buddhist movement, not violent.
Mahikari — but this is a Japanese new religion focused on light healing, not violence.
Tenrikyo — but this is a 19th-century Japanese new religion, not violent.
context: Asahara had cultivated a syncretic theology drawing on Hindu, Buddhist, and apocalyptic Christian sources, predicting an imminent end of the world. Aum had infiltrated university science departments to develop biological and chemical weapons. Asahara and twelve disciples were executed in 2018. The subway attack remains the worst terrorist attack on Japanese soil and a landmark case in the study of modern cult violence.

question: Empedocles of Acragas was a religious teacher as well as a natural philosopher. He claimed prior lives as fish, bird, girl. His doctrine: all things are four elements held by Love and Strife. What did legend say of his death?
answer: He leaped into the crater of Mount Etna, leaving one bronze sandal at the edge to mark his ascent as a god.
choices: He leaped into the crater of Mount Etna, leaving one bronze sandal at the edge to mark his ascent as a god.
He vanished without trace from a religious festival, his disciples taking it as his apotheosis.
He died in old age and was buried at Athens with the lawgiver Solon as his tomb-mate.
He drowned crossing from Sicily to Italy and his body was returned by dolphins to Acragas.
context: Matthew Arnold's poem 'Empedocles on Etna' (1852) imagines the philosopher's last hours. Empedocles' four-element doctrine (earth, water, air, fire) became standard in Western thought through Aristotle. His distinctive contribution — that Love and Strife (cosmic forces) alternately combine and separate the elements — has interested modern thinkers from Freud to Heidegger.

question: Egil Skallagrimsson (c. 904–995 AD), an Icelandic warrior-poet and one of the protagonists of *Egil's Saga*, composed the long lament *Sonatorrek* ('the irreparable loss of sons') after his sons died. The poem helped him survive his grief. Sons by whom?
answer: His wife Asgerd, with whom he had several children whom he outlived.
choices: His wife Asgerd, with whom he had several children whom he outlived.
His brother's widow, whom he took into his house after his brother's death.
His Norwegian mistress, whom he could not bring back to Iceland.
His sister Thora — but no incestuous relationships are recorded in the saga.
context: *Egil's Saga* may have been composed by Snorri Sturluson. Egil is the model Viking-age warrior-poet — a violent man and a tender father. His poetry survives across his career, much of it in skaldic stanzas embedded in the saga. *Sonatorrek* is one of the most-praised personal poems in Old Norse and gave the saga its psychological depth.

question: Norse women in Viking-age society had more legal rights than their counterparts in much of medieval Europe — including the right to inherit property, divorce, and own land. They also had a particular role at one type of social occasion. What?
answer: Pouring the mead at the feast — a ritualized act of welcome and authority over the hall.
choices: Pouring the mead at the feast — a ritualized act of welcome and authority over the hall.
Negotiating peace between feuding clans — a role traditionally outside their authority.
Leading raids in the absence of male warriors — a role they did not normally hold.
Determining the inheritance of male children — fathers normally made these decisions.
context: The *valkyrja* mythological figure descends from this ritual role — the woman with the cup. Viking-age women's status was certainly not modern feminism, but it was distinctively strong by medieval European standards. The conversion to Christianity actually weakened some legal rights of Norse women, though others gained protections.

question: Snorri Sturluson's *Heimskringla* — 'circle of the world' — is a saga history of the kings of Norway from legendary origins through the 12th century. It opens with a euhemerist explanation of the gods. What does it claim?
answer: The Aesir were originally human migrants from Troy in Asia, deified by their descendants in error.
choices: The Aesir were originally human migrants from Troy in Asia, deified by their descendants in error.
The Aesir were created at the same time as humans, by a parallel act of the Christian God.
The Aesir were demons, sent by Satan to deceive the peoples of the north before the gospel.
The Aesir were spirits of natural features (sky, sea, fire) personalized in religious imagination.
context: Snorri's euhemerism (treating gods as deified humans) was a way to preserve and explain pagan mythology in a Christian context. The 'Troy connection' echoes medieval royal genealogies that traced everyone back to Trojan refugees. Snorri's preservation of Norse mythology in Christian framing is the great paradox: without his work, Norse pagan lore would be vastly poorer.

question: Norse settlers in Greenland (c. 985–1450 AD) eventually died out — the most southerly settlement abandoned around 1450, the more northerly Western Settlement by c. 1350. Recent climate research, archaeology, and pollen analysis suggest the causes were multiple. What was a central factor?
answer: The Little Ice Age — climate cooling reduced agricultural viability and lengthened sea ice.
choices: The Little Ice Age — climate cooling reduced agricultural viability and lengthened sea ice.
Bubonic plague — but plague reached Iceland only in 1402, and Greenland not at all certainly.
Conflict with the Inuit (Thule) — possible, but no archaeological evidence of major violence.
Religious schism — false; Greenland Christianity remained tied to Trondheim, with no schism.
context: The Norse failed to adapt their farming-and-cattle economy to the cooling climate while the Inuit successfully did adapt their hunting culture. The 'Greenland disaster' is now an active research area in archaeology, climate history, and adaptive failure. The Norse cattle-cellars and farm sites are preserved in the Greenlandic landscape.

question: Laozi, traditional founder of Daoism, is said to have ridden west from China on a water buffalo around the 6th century BC. At the western gate, the gatekeeper Yinxi recognized him as a sage and asked him to leave a teaching. What is the result?
answer: The Daodejing — 81 short chapters of poetic-philosophical reflection on the Dao and natural living.
choices: The Daodejing — 81 short chapters of poetic-philosophical reflection on the Dao and natural living.
The Analects — but the Analects is Confucian and was compiled by Confucius's disciples.
The Mencius — but this is the work of the Confucian thinker Mencius (c. 372–289 BC).
The Zhuangzi — but the Zhuangzi is by Zhuangzi (c. 369–286 BC), not Laozi.
context: The historicity of Laozi is debated — the *Daodejing* probably formed gradually from multiple sources. Its central idea is the Dao ('Way') — the natural pattern of the universe, with which the sage harmonizes by *wu-wei* ('non-coercive action'). Religious Daoism developed alongside the philosophical tradition, with temples, priesthood, and ritual.

question: The Orphic mysteries taught a particular afterlife doctrine that differed from the standard Greek view. What did the Orphics teach?
answer: The soul reincarnates many times; through ritual purity it may eventually be released from the cycle.
choices: The soul reincarnates many times; through ritual purity it may eventually be released from the cycle.
There is no afterlife — the body decays and the soul scatters into the elements.
All souls go immediately to the Elysian Fields, regardless of conduct in life.
The soul becomes a star in the night sky, watching over its descendants on earth.
context: Orphic teaching shaped early Pythagorean and Platonic thought — Plato's myths of the soul's journey owe much to Orphic ideas. The gold tablets buried with Orphic initiates (small inscribed laminae found in graves across Italy and Greece) instructed the soul on what to say to gatekeepers in the underworld. Their content is among the closest evidence we have of actual Orphic doctrine.

question: Greek sacrifice (*thysia*) followed a standard procedure: the animal was led to the altar, sprinkled with water and grain, then killed. Specific parts of the animal had specific destinations. What did the gods receive?
answer: The thigh bones wrapped in fat and burned — the smoke rising to Olympus; humans ate the meat.
choices: The thigh bones wrapped in fat and burned — the smoke rising to Olympus; humans ate the meat.
All the internal organs, burned whole on the altar as the gods' portion.
The choicest cuts of meat, with the leftover offal eaten by the worshippers.
Just the smoke — no part of the actual animal was reserved for the gods.
context: Hesiod's *Theogony* explains the practice via Prometheus, who tricked Zeus into accepting the bones-and-fat portion at Mecone — establishing the worship-arrangement that humans got the better food. The smoke from the altar 'fed' the gods. Greek temples did not hold the worshippers; the sacrifice happened at the open-air altar, and the meal followed nearby.

question: The Greek concept of *hubris* — overreaching pride — has shaped Western moral thought. What was the standard divine response?
answer: *Nemesis* — divine vengeance, sometimes personified as a goddess of the same name.
choices: *Nemesis* — divine vengeance, sometimes personified as a goddess of the same name.
*Ate* — but ate is the delusion that leads to ruin, not the response to it.
*Tyche* — but tyche is fortune or luck, not divine vengeance.
*Kairos* — but kairos is the right or critical moment, not response to hubris.
context: Nemesis is both a concept and a goddess of retribution. The temple at Rhamnous in Attica was her main shrine. Herodotus describes Persian king Xerxes whipping the Hellespont in arrogance, then losing the war — a paradigmatic hubris story. The hubris-nemesis pattern shapes Greek tragedy and historical writing alike. It does not require explicit divine action; nemesis can come through the structure of events.

question: Norse cosmology held that the sky was formed from Ymir's skull, held up at the four corners by what?
answer: Four dwarves — Austri (east), Vestri (west), Nordri (north), Sudri (south) — each holding a corner.
choices: Four dwarves — Austri (east), Vestri (west), Nordri (north), Sudri (south) — each holding a corner.
Four giants chained to the corners by Odin's command at the dawn of the cosmos.
Four mountains, one in each cardinal direction, on which the skull rested.
Four pillars of fire from Muspelheim, transformed into the corners of the sky-roof.
context: The four dwarves of the directions are named in *Gylfaginning*. The Norse image of the universe is dense with personified support — every part of the cosmos is the body of a slain primordial being, held in shape by named beings. The sky as Ymir's skull is one of many such body-of-the-world cosmologies (compare the Indian *Purusha-sukta* in the Rig Veda; the Babylonian Marduk-Tiamat).

question: *Laxdaela Saga* — a great Icelandic family saga — tells a love triangle between Kjartan, Bolli, and Gudrun. How does it end?
answer: Gudrun goads Bolli into killing Kjartan; Bolli is killed in revenge; Gudrun in old age says 'I was worst to him I loved most.'
choices: Gudrun goads Bolli into killing Kjartan; Bolli is killed in revenge; Gudrun in old age says 'I was worst to him I loved most.'
Kjartan kills Bolli in a duel in Norway, brings Gudrun back, and lives the rest of his life in peace at the family estate.
Gudrun chooses Bolli openly at the local thing assembly; Kjartan accepts the loss and remains close friends with both.
All three die in a Viking raid on Norway during a feud with the local jarl, leaving the family farm in ruin.
context: *Laxdaela* (c. 1245) follows several generations of Icelandic family history through the Christianization period. Gudrun ends her days as a nun. Her final cryptic remark — 'Thaeim var ek verst, er ek unna mest' — is one of the most haunting endings in medieval prose. The Norse saga tradition's psychological complexity often exceeds even what classical Greek and Roman authors achieved.

question: *Eirik's Saga* and *The Saga of the Greenlanders* both tell of Norse voyages to North America around 1000 AD. What did the Norse call the people they encountered?
answer: Skraelings — a generic term, possibly meaning 'wretches' or 'screamers.'
choices: Skraelings — a generic term, possibly meaning 'wretches' or 'screamers.'
Vinlanders — but Vinlanders would be settlers of Vinland, not natives.
Northmen — but Northmen is a self-description of the Norse, not for natives.
Karls — but karls means 'freemen,' the Norse middle class, not natives.
context: The Skraelings of the sagas were probably Beothuk or Inuit peoples encountered in Newfoundland or Labrador. The encounters were sometimes friendly (initial trade) and sometimes hostile (deaths on both sides). The 'failure' of Norse North American settlement is partly traceable to Skraeling resistance — Norse populations in Greenland were too small to maintain a colony in territory contested by natives.

question: *Egil's Saga* — likely by Snorri Sturluson — tells of Egil Skallagrimsson saving his life through poetry. He had been condemned by King Eirik Bloodaxe in York. What did he do?
answer: Composed a praise poem *Hofudlausn* ('Head-ransom') overnight, and won his freedom.
choices: Composed a praise poem *Hofudlausn* ('Head-ransom') overnight, and won his freedom.
Killed his guards and fled across the moors to the Scottish border.
Swore an oath to convert to Christianity if the king spared him.
Promised to surrender all his lands in Norway as payment for his life.
context: *Egil's Saga* is among the great works of medieval Icelandic prose. *Hofudlausn* — Egil's praise poem to Eirik — saved his head from the axe. The episode captures the central Norse value: skilled poetry is worth more than gold; a brilliant skald can save his life with the right verses. Egil's career mixes raid, slaughter, love, and the production of *Sonatorrek* — his great lament for his dead sons.

question: Norse seasonal cycles had three main religious festivals (or *blot*). At what time of year was the most important?
answer: Yule — at midwinter, marking the sun's return; gave the English word 'Yule' for Christmas season.
choices: Yule — at midwinter, marking the sun's return; gave the English word 'Yule' for Christmas season.
Beltane — at midsummer, though Beltane is properly Celtic, not Norse.
Imbolc — at early spring, but again Celtic rather than Norse.
Equinox — at March and September, balanced festivals though less elaborate than Yule.
context: Yule (Norse *jol*) was the great winter festival — feasting, drinking, sacrifices to ensure the sun's return and the spring's coming. The Christianization of Scandinavia adapted Yule into Christmas-season traditions; many modern Christmas customs (the Yule log, the boar's head, the Yule goat) descend from pre-Christian Norse practice. *Jol* persists as the Scandinavian word for Christmas today.

question: Norse slavery — *thralldom* — was extensive and central to Viking-age society. From where did most thralls come?
answer: Raids on Ireland, Scotland, England, and the Slavic lands east of the Baltic.
choices: Raids on Ireland, Scotland, England, and the Slavic lands east of the Baltic.
Internal Scandinavian conflicts; nearly all thralls were ethnic Norse.
Trade with North African Muslim slave markets, which supplied most Norse households.
Captured in battle on the Russian steppes from Cumans, Mongols, and Khazars.
context: Norse slavers raided the British Isles repeatedly through the 9th and 10th centuries; Dublin (founded by Norse) was a major slave entrepôt. Slavs sold across Eurasia gave the word 'slave' to multiple European languages. Norse legal codes distinguished thralls from freemen and from aristocrats sharply. The Christianization of Scandinavia slowly eroded but did not immediately abolish slavery.

question: Norse *holmgang* — formal duel — followed specific rules. What was the typical staging?
answer: Both fighters stood on a cloak or marked-out square; stepping off forfeited the duel.
choices: Both fighters stood on a cloak or marked-out square; stepping off forfeited the duel.
Both fighters were tied to a post by one ankle, with three feet of slack chain.
Both fighters were stripped to the waist; armor was forbidden by Norse honor.
Both fighters had their swords sealed in scabbards until a horn sounded.
context: *Holmgang* (literally 'island-going,' since duels were often fought on small islands) was a formal way of settling disputes in Norse society. The Icelandic *Althing* abolished it in 1006 because too many disputes were being settled by ritual murder. The rules — cloaks marking the dueling space, three blades per fighter, blood-shedding signaling the end — were specific. *Holmgang* features in many of the family sagas.

question: The Norse concept of *wyrd* (Anglo-Saxon) or *urdr* (Old Norse) gave English which modern word?
answer: Weird — originally meaning 'fated' or 'concerned with destiny,' as in Shakespeare's 'weird sisters.'
choices: Weird — originally meaning 'fated' or 'concerned with destiny,' as in Shakespeare's 'weird sisters.'
Wert — but wert is the archaic second-person of 'to be,' not from wyrd.
Word — but word descends from a different Germanic root.
World — from Old English *weorold*, a separate compound meaning 'age of man.'
context: *Wyrd* is the Germanic concept of fate — a network of causation more than predestination. *Beowulf*'s phrase 'gæð a wyrd swa hio scel' — 'goes ever fate as it must' — captures the worldview. The 'weird sisters' in *Macbeth* are the three Norns/Fates. The modern English 'weird' for 'strange' is a semantic drift through the spookiness of fate-encounters; the original meaning was strictly 'fated.'

question: Norse honor centered on a concept called *drengskapr*. What was its essence?
answer: Manly courage and integrity — keeping one's word, facing fate without flinching, supporting kin.
choices: Manly courage and integrity — keeping one's word, facing fate without flinching, supporting kin.
Wealth and generosity — providing for one's household and gifts at feasts.
Political acumen — managing disputes and alliances in the assembly.
Christian humility — borrowed from the conversion period and superseding pagan virtues.
context: *Drengskapr* (or *drengr* as the man who has it) was Norse aristocratic ethics' core — keeping promises, fighting bravely, not abandoning friends, dying well. It does not map perfectly onto Christian virtue or modern 'honor' but is essential to reading the sagas. Norse heroes are often morally complex by modern standards (raiders, slavers) yet rigorous in their personal code. The tension is real and worth confronting honestly.

question: Norse views on the afterlife distinguished several destinations. Where did a person who died of old age in their bed go?
answer: Hel — the realm of the cold misty dead, neither punished nor rewarded but in dim half-existence.
choices: Hel — the realm of the cold misty dead, neither punished nor rewarded but in dim half-existence.
Valhalla — but Valhalla was for those who died in battle, not in bed.
Folkvangr — but Folkvangr was Freyja's hall, also for the battle-slain.
Vanaheim — but Vanaheim was the realm of the Vanir gods, not the human dead.
context: Norse afterlife geography preferred battle-death. Hel's realm was the default for natural death — not torturous, but dim, cold, and joyless. Niflhel — beneath Hel — was the punishment realm for oath-breakers, murderers, and the genuinely evil. The Norse strongly encouraged dying with weapon in hand, even sick old men sometimes 'marking themselves' with a sword-point to claim warrior-death.

question: Norse religious practice in the 9th-10th centuries included *blot* (sacrifice). Where would it typically take place?
answer: Sacred groves or at temples — the Uppsala temple was the most famous, but small local shrines were widespread.
choices: Sacred groves or at temples — the Uppsala temple was the most famous, but small local shrines were widespread.
Mostly at sea — sacrifices were thrown overboard from ships to honor Aegir and the wave-daughters.
Only at major royal cult sites — common Norse households did not perform sacrifices.
In private bedrooms — Norse religion had no public element until Christianization made it visible.
context: Norse religious practice spread across multiple contexts — household shrines for daily piety, regional temples for community festivals, royal cult sites (like Uppsala) for the largest celebrations. Adam of Bremen's late 11th-century description of Uppsala — nine male animals of every kind including humans sacrificed in a sacred grove every nine years — is hostile but probably substantially accurate. Norse religion was practiced; it was not merely a belief system.

question: Buddhism reached China in the 1st-2nd centuries AD via the Silk Road. Two early texts particularly mattered for its Chinese adaptation. What are they?
answer: The Lotus Sutra and the Heart Sutra — both translated multiple times across centuries.
choices: The Lotus Sutra and the Heart Sutra — both translated multiple times across centuries.
The Diamond Sutra and the Pali Vinaya — the latter never widely used in China.
The Tibetan Book of the Dead and the Bardo Thodol — but these are Tibetan, not Chinese.
The Dhammapada and the Sutta Nipata — important in Theravada but less so in Chinese Mahayana.
context: The Diamond Sutra (translated by Kumarajiva c. 401 AD) is short enough to be inscribed on walls and printed — the British Library's 868 AD Chinese Diamond Sutra is the world's earliest dated printed book. The Lotus Sutra became foundational for Tiantai and (in Japan) Nichiren Buddhism. The Heart Sutra, even shorter, is the most-chanted Buddhist text in East Asia today.

question: Zen Buddhism in Japan split into two main schools by the 13th century. Rinzai emphasized koans and sudden enlightenment. What did Soto Zen emphasize?
answer: *Zazen* — silent sitting meditation as itself the expression of enlightenment, not a means to it.
choices: *Zazen* — silent sitting meditation as itself the expression of enlightenment, not a means to it.
Tantric ritual — sexual yoga and elaborate visualization, but this is Vajrayana, not Soto.
Pure Land recitation — but this is the Jodo school, not Soto Zen.
Devotional study of the Lotus Sutra — but this is Nichiren, not Soto.
context: Dogen (1200-1253), founder of Soto Zen in Japan, was a remarkable figure — his masterwork *Shobogenzo* combined philosophical depth with poetic Japanese prose. His central teaching: zazen is not preparation for enlightenment, it IS enlightenment. Soto became the largest Zen school in Japan. Rinzai (also still major) emphasized koan study under master-direction. Hakuin (1686-1769) revived Rinzai in the 18th century.

question: Polynesian mythology's trickster hero Maui performed many feats across the Pacific. In Hawaiian tradition, what did he do to the sun?
answer: He lassoed it with a rope made of his sister's hair, forcing it to travel more slowly across the sky.
choices: He lassoed it with a rope made of his sister's hair, forcing it to travel more slowly across the sky.
He fished it up from beneath the sea, where it had been sleeping after the world's making.
He stole it from his grandfather, who had kept it in a calabash gourd.
He fought it directly in single combat, winning the right to set its daily course.
context: Maui's feats vary across Polynesian cultures: fishing up the islands of New Zealand, snaring the sun (to lengthen the day), stealing fire from an ancestral mountain. He is sometimes a benefactor of humans, sometimes a self-aggrandizing trickster who falls short. The Polynesian voyaging tradition — settling islands from Hawaii to New Zealand to Easter Island — preserved this rich mythological inheritance over thousands of miles of ocean.

question: Norse seers (*volur* — the singular is *volva*) practiced *seidr* — a magical art. What god in particular learned seidr?
answer: Odin learned it from Freyja — a transgressive act, since seidr was considered effeminate for men to practice.
choices: Odin learned it from Freyja — a transgressive act, since seidr was considered effeminate for men to practice.
Thor learned it from his mother Jord, the earth-goddess.
Tyr learned it from his giant mother, but rarely used it.
Loki invented it and taught the gods, but only Freyja and Odin remained users.
context: *Seidr* — involving trance, prophecy, and shape-shifting — was considered fundamentally a female art. Odin's practice of it was an aspect of his ambiguity and edge-walking — gods of wisdom in Norse tradition were often gender-crossers. Men who practiced seidr were sometimes accused of *ergi* (effeminacy, or worse). The Eddic poem *Lokasenna* has Loki insulting Odin for this very practice — and Odin returning the insult with stories of Loki's own gender ambiguities.

question: The Norse runic alphabet — used for inscriptions on stone, wood, bone, and metal — appears across the Germanic world. What is the oldest version called?
answer: The Elder Futhark — 24 runes, in use c. 150-800 AD, named for its first six characters: f-u-th-a-r-k.
choices: The Elder Futhark — 24 runes, in use c. 150-800 AD, named for its first six characters: f-u-th-a-r-k.
The Younger Futhark — but this is the simpler 16-rune version of c. 800-1100 AD.
The Anglo-Saxon Futhorc — but this is the 33-rune English version, distinct from Norse use.
The Greek-Phoenician — but Norse runes have their own development, not derived from Greek directly.
context: The Elder Futhark's 24 letters are inscribed in various artifacts from across Germanic-speaking Europe — the Kylver stone in Sweden (c. 400 AD) shows the complete sequence. Runes had both writing-system function and divinatory use; *Havamal* preserves much rune-lore. The transition from Elder to Younger Futhark (the simplified 16-letter version) happened in Scandinavia c. 700-800 AD. Anglo-Saxon Futhorc developed independently, adding letters for English vowels.

question: Iceland's Althing — founded 930 AD — met annually at Thingvellir. What geological feature made the site dramatic?
answer: The visible boundary between the Eurasian and North American tectonic plates — a great rift in the rock.
choices: The visible boundary between the Eurasian and North American tectonic plates — a great rift in the rock.
An active volcano whose eruptions punctuated the meetings.
Hot springs that allowed the Althing to meet in any weather.
A circle of standing stones that the settlers had found pre-existing.
context: Thingvellir's tectonic rift is a real geological feature — the Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through Iceland. The site was visually dramatic and politically symbolic — a natural amphitheater where the law-speaker recited the laws aloud. The decision in 1000 to accept Christianity was made here. Modern Iceland's national park at Thingvellir preserves the site; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.

question: Norse legal procedure was sophisticated and oral. What was the *Lawspeaker* (lögsögumadr) required to do annually at the Althing?
answer: Recite from memory one-third of the laws of Iceland — completing the full code every three years.
choices: Recite from memory one-third of the laws of Iceland — completing the full code every three years.
Write down all new laws passed in the previous year for the archive.
Travel to every quarter of Iceland to teach the laws to local assemblies.
Adjudicate every dispute brought during the meeting personally.
context: The Lawspeaker memorized the laws and recited them aloud at the Lögberg ('Law Rock') at Thingvellir over the three-year term. The position was the most prestigious in early Icelandic society. The first Lawspeaker was Ulfljotr (c. 930). Snorri Sturluson held the position twice (1215-1218 and 1222-1231). Iceland did not have written law until 1117-1118 — until then, oral tradition was the only legal record.

question: The Greek philosopher Empedocles (c. 494-434 BC), of Acragas in Sicily, was a religious teacher as well as a natural philosopher. What did he claim about his soul?
answer: He had been a boy, a girl, a bush, a bird, and a leaping fish in previous lives.
choices: He had been a boy, a girl, a bush, a bird, and a leaping fish in previous lives.
His soul was uniquely born of fire and air, distinguishing him from other humans.
He had had no previous lives but was destined to be reincarnated 999 times.
His soul came directly from Apollo and would return there at his death.
context: Empedocles taught reincarnation across multiple species — a doctrine closer to Pythagoras and Plato than to most Greek thinkers. His four-element theory (earth, water, air, fire, joined by Love and divided by Strife) became standard ancient physics. Legend said he jumped into Mount Etna to prove his divinity — only his bronze sandal was left at the rim. Matthew Arnold's poem 'Empedocles on Etna' (1852) is the modern recasting.

question: The Greek concept of *xenia* — host-guest hospitality — was sacred and theologically grounded. What god enforced it?
answer: Zeus, in his epithet Zeus Xenios (Zeus of strangers) — violations of xenia were offenses against Zeus himself.
choices: Zeus, in his epithet Zeus Xenios (Zeus of strangers) — violations of xenia were offenses against Zeus himself.
Hermes, the god of travelers, protected strangers and punished bad hosts.
Apollo, who often appeared incognito to test mortals' hospitality.
Hera, as the protector of households and household propriety.
context: Xenia involved the obligation to offer food, drink, bath, and shelter to a guest before asking their business — and the corresponding obligation of the guest not to abuse hospitality. The Trojan War's mythological origin is a xenia violation: Paris violated Menelaus's hospitality by taking Helen. The Odyssey's suitors are punished partly for their xenia violation. Greek civic life depended heavily on guest-friendship bonds across cities; violations were taken with utmost seriousness.

question: Greek temples did not, generally, hold worshippers — worship happened outside, at the altar. What did the temple's interior hold?
answer: The cult statue of the deity, sometimes massive and made of gold and ivory.
choices: The cult statue of the deity, sometimes massive and made of gold and ivory.
Pews for the priestly hierarchy during sacred rituals.
Storage for the sacrificial animals before their slaughter.
The treasury of the temple's accumulated wealth and offerings.
context: Phidias's gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus at Olympia and Athena Parthenos at Athens were among the most famous in antiquity. Worshippers might enter the temple to view the statue and leave offerings, but the sacrifice itself was at the open-air altar. The architectural focus on the *cella* (chamber housing the cult statue) shaped temple design — pediment, columns, frieze all surrounding the housing of the god's image.

question: The Furies (Erinyes) — primordial Greek deities of vengeance — pursued kin-slayers especially. How many were they?
answer: Three: Alecto (Unceasing), Megaera (Grudging), Tisiphone (Avenger of Murder).
choices: Three: Alecto (Unceasing), Megaera (Grudging), Tisiphone (Avenger of Murder).
Two: Justice and Vengeance, named for their functions rather than as persons.
Twelve: one for each major form of bloodguilt named in Greek law.
Innumerable: every spilled drop of blood produced its own Fury.
context: Aeschylus's *Eumenides* (third play of the *Oresteia*) ends with Athena establishing a court at Athens to judge Orestes — and transforming the Furies into the 'Kindly Ones' (Eumenides), incorporated into Athenian civic religion. The shift from blood-vengeance (the Furies' archaic justice) to civic court (Athena's new order) is one of Greek tragedy's great cultural arguments. The Furies represent older chthonic powers preceding the Olympians.

question: Procrustes — a brigand in the wilds of Attica — robbed and killed travelers in a specific way. What?
answer: He had a bed; he stretched short travelers to fit it, and cut off the limbs of tall travelers.
choices: He had a bed; he stretched short travelers to fit it, and cut off the limbs of tall travelers.
He fed travelers poisoned wine, taking their goods after they slept.
He bound travelers to a tree, leaving them for the wolves of the forest.
He challenged travelers to wrestling, killing them when they tired.
context: Procrustes (literally 'the stretcher') was killed by Theseus, who cleared Attica of brigands as he made his way to Athens. The 'Procrustean bed' has become an English idiom for an arbitrary standard to which everything is forced to fit. Procrustes appears in Plutarch's *Theseus* and in many later sources. His method connects him to a wider Greek mythological motif of monstrous innkeepers (Sinis the Pine-Bender, Sciron, others) whose violations of hospitality (*xenia*) deserve heroic punishment.

question: *Hrafnkel's Saga* — a relatively short Icelandic family saga — turns on the conflict between Hrafnkel (a chieftain) and a shepherd. What had the shepherd done?
answer: Ridden Hrafnkel's horse Freyfaxi, which was sacred to the god Freyr and forbidden to others.
choices: Ridden Hrafnkel's horse Freyfaxi, which was sacred to the god Freyr and forbidden to others.
Insulted Hrafnkel at the local thing assembly, refusing to acknowledge his rank.
Helped a fugitive who had wronged Hrafnkel's family.
Refused to pay a fine for letting his sheep graze on Hrafnkel's land.
context: Hrafnkel killed Einar the shepherd for the horse-riding. Einar's relatives pursued vengeance through the law and through force — eventually defeating Hrafnkel and forcing him into exile. He rebuilt his power, returned, killed his old enemies, and reclaimed his land. The saga is psychologically dense — Hrafnkel's character shifts through the narrative. It is among the most-studied of Icelandic sagas, sometimes cited as the model for the saga form's compression and ethical complexity.

question: *Volsunga Saga* and the German *Nibelungenlied* tell related stories. What is the great cursed object that drives the tragedy?
answer: The treasure of Andvari — a hoard of gold including a magical ring, cursed by its original owner.
choices: The treasure of Andvari — a hoard of gold including a magical ring, cursed by its original owner.
The hammer of Thor, briefly stolen and recovered, with consequences.
The spear of Odin, lost and refound across generations.
The sword Tyrfing, magical but always demanding blood.
context: The hoard had been extracted from the dwarf Andvari by Loki, with the ring as final extraction; Andvari cursed it. The hoard passed through Hreidmar (killed by his sons over it), to Fafnir (turned to dragon for greed), to Sigurd (who slew Fafnir), to the Volsungs and Burgundians, eventually buried in the Rhine. Wagner's *Ring* cycle (1853-1874) reworked the material. Tolkien's *The Lord of the Rings* drew on the cursed-ring motif and on Norse-Germanic atmosphere generally.

question: Norse divination involved several practices. *Hlautteinn* — 'lot-twigs' or 'blood-twigs' — were used in what context?
answer: Determining the gods' will at sacrifices — twigs were dipped in sacrificial blood and read for omens.
choices: Determining the gods' will at sacrifices — twigs were dipped in sacrificial blood and read for omens.
Settling legal disputes at the thing, by lot rather than by judgment.
Marking the seasons in the agricultural calendar.
Identifying witches and sorcerers in the community.
context: Norse divination practices included runic divination (drawing rune-stones), seidr trance, and blot-divination (reading the patterns of sacrificial blood). Tacitus's *Germania* (c. 98 AD) describes Germanic tribes using rune-marked twigs for divination — perhaps the same practice or an ancestor. The Norse worldview did not separate religion, divination, law, and medicine into modern categories; the same practitioners and the same sacred items often spanned all four.

question: Norse food taboos varied. What was the Christianization-era controversy about horse meat?
answer: Eating horse meat was identified with pagan sacrifice; conversion required forswearing it.
choices: Eating horse meat was identified with pagan sacrifice; conversion required forswearing it.
Eating horse meat was a sign of poverty; converts pledged not to do it as a class-marker.
Eating horse meat caused madness, by old Germanic medical theory.
Eating horse meat was forbidden by Norse pagans before Christianization, not by Christians after.
context: Horse meat was associated with pagan sacrifice at Uppsala and elsewhere — the meat of sacrificed horses was eaten by worshippers. Christianization made horse-eating taboo, marking a clean break with pagan practice. The Iceland 1000 conversion compromise actually allowed horse-eating temporarily as a transitional concession to pagans. The taboo persists in some Christian cultures today, sometimes long after its religious meaning was forgotten. Horse remains found in Norse burial sites confirm the religious significance of horses.

question: The Bahai Faith, founded in 19th-century Persia, traces to which founder?
answer: Baha'u'llah (1817-1892) — proclaimed his mission in 1863; sometimes preceded by the Bab (1819-1850).
choices: Baha'u'llah (1817-1892) — proclaimed his mission in 1863; sometimes preceded by the Bab (1819-1850).
Mirza Ali Muhammad of Shiraz (the Bab) — but the Bab's role is precursor; Baha'u'llah is founder.
Both — the Bahai Faith treats both as central, with the Bab as the herald.
Subh-i-Azal — but this is Baha'u'llah's half-brother, a rival rather than founder.
context: Bahai Faith holds that the Bab announced the coming of a 'promised one,' which Baha'u'llah declared himself to be in 1863. The faith teaches the underlying unity of all religions and the progressive revelation of one truth across history. Bahai's universalism made it appealing in Western contexts; the Bahai world center is at Haifa, Israel. Bahai has faced severe persecution in Iran under the post-1979 Islamic Republic — hundreds executed, thousands imprisoned, the faith officially banned.

question: Hyacinth, the flower itself, has a striking feature according to Greek tradition. What is on its petals?
answer: Letters of grief — 'AI AI' or 'Y' for Hyacinthus (and also for Ajax, in another version).
choices: Letters of grief — 'AI AI' or 'Y' for Hyacinthus (and also for Ajax, in another version).
A drop of red dye that never fades, representing Hyacinthus's blood.
Twelve veins, one for each Olympian who mourned him.
A faint perfume of Apollo's tears, audible only to lovers.
context: Greek tradition saw natural objects as bearing the marks of mythological events. The hyacinth's purple petals bore the letters 'AI AI' (the lament cry, 'alas! alas!'). When Ajax, also bewailed, was associated with the flower, the letters were read as 'AI' for his name as well. The reading of nature as inscribed with mythical history shaped Greek poetic imagination — every flower, every spring, every constellation had a story.

question: Norse berserkers and ulfhednar — wolf-warriors — were dedicated to which god?
answer: Odin — who himself wandered as a wanderer, and whose warriors fought in animal-totem frenzy.
choices: Odin — who himself wandered as a wanderer, and whose warriors fought in animal-totem frenzy.
Thor — but Thor's warriors fought with hammers and shields, not in frenzy.
Tyr — but Tyr's warriors fought by law, not by frenzy.
Freyr — but Freyr's warriors fought for prosperity, not in war frenzy.
context: Odin's *Ynglinga Saga* (Snorri) describes berserker warriors who 'rushed forwards without armor, were as mad as dogs or wolves, bit their shields, and were as strong as bears or wild bulls.' The connection to Odin (god of poetry, war, magic, and death) reflects the deep ambiguity of his cult. Berserker-rage may have involved psychedelic mushrooms or other altered-state techniques. The institution was banned in 12th-century Iceland after Christianization.

question: Norse cosmology had a particular description of the sun and moon. What pulled their chariots?
answer: Horses — the sun by Arvak and Alsvid, the moon by Alsvider.
choices: Horses — the sun by Arvak and Alsvid, the moon by Alsvider.
Wolves — but the wolves Skoll and Hati chase the sun and moon, not pull them.
Stags — borrowed from the four stags that eat Yggdrasil.
Hounds — paralleling the wolves that pursue them.
context: Snorri's *Gylfaginning* and the Eddic *Grimnismal* name the horses. The sun and moon are personified as Sol and Mani, brother and sister, driving their respective chariots. The Norse cosmos was crowded with named, specific beings — every part of the visible world had its agents, its riders, its careful arrangements. The mythological richness contrasts with later Christian cosmology's tendency toward more abstract divine action.

question: Norse cosmology had a particular fish — central to one famous story. Whose was it?
answer: Loki's, transformed into a salmon to escape his pursuers.
choices: Loki's, transformed into a salmon to escape his pursuers.
Aegir's, his pet who lived in the great kettle of mead.
Thor's, caught when he fished Jormungandr from the deep.
Heimdall's, transformed into a seal to fight Loki over Brisingamen.
context: After Loki had engineered Baldr's death and revealed himself by being too clever at Aegir's feast, he fled. Loki built a house with four doors so he could see all directions; he turned into a salmon and hid in the river beneath a waterfall. The gods came after him; he leaped over the net they made; finally Thor caught him by the tail. This is why salmon are slim at the tail — Thor's grip. Loki was bound; his punishment with the venomous serpent followed.

question: Norse runes had multiple uses. What was *seidr*-runic magic typically inscribed on?
answer: Wood, bone, or stone — using carved runes for protection, cursing, or healing.
choices: Wood, bone, or stone — using carved runes for protection, cursing, or healing.
Paper — but paper was not widely used in early medieval Scandinavia.
Tattooed on skin — but no evidence supports widespread Norse runic tattooing.
Spoken only — never written down for magical purposes.
context: Runes for magical purposes were typically carved into wooden sticks (rune-staves), bone, or stone. Archaeological finds include rune-sticks from Bergen with curses, love charms, and prayers. *Havamal*'s rune-stanzas warn against badly cast runes harming the user. The Norse practice of using the same alphabet for ordinary writing, monumental inscription, and magical purpose shows the unity of practical and sacred uses — the modern distinction between 'normal writing' and 'magical writing' was not Norse.

question: Four major athletic festivals — the Panhellenic Games — bound the Greek world together. Each was held in honor of a god, on a regular cycle, with sacred truces declared. What were the four games, their gods, and their cycles?
answer: Olympic (Zeus, Olympia, every 4 years); Pythian (Apollo, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Poseidon, Corinth, every 2 years); Nemean (Zeus, Nemea, every 2 years)
choices: Olympic (Zeus, Olympia, every 4 years); Pythian (Apollo, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Poseidon, Corinth, every 2 years); Nemean (Zeus, Nemea, every 2 years)
Olympic (Zeus, Athens, every 4 years); Pythian (Athena, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Apollo, Corinth, every 2 years); Heraion (Hera, Argos, every 2 years)
Olympic (Apollo, Olympia, every 5 years); Pythian (Zeus, Delphi, every 5 years); Isthmian (Hera, Corinth, every 3 years); Nemean (Athena, Nemea, every 3 years)
Olympic (Aphrodite, Olympia, every 4 years); Pythian (Hermes, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Dionysus, Corinth, every 2 years); Nemean (Demeter, Nemea, every 2 years)
context: The Panhellenic Games schedule was staggered so that two of the four occurred every year. The Olympic Games (founded traditionally 776 BC, the year 1 of Greek dating) were the most prestigious. Victors received olive wreaths (or laurel at Pythian, pine at Isthmian, wild celery at Nemean) — material wealth came from their home cities afterward. The sacred truce (ekecheiria) protected athletes and spectators from war.
