question: After the gods created the world from Ymir's body, they walked along the shore of the new world and found two pieces of driftwood — an ash log and an elm log (per the standard version). They breathed life and consciousness into them, creating the first humans. What were the first humans' names?
answer: Ask (ash) and Embla (elm) — the first man and woman; ancestors of all humanity in Norse mythology
choices: Ask (ash) and Embla (elm) — the first man and woman; ancestors of all humanity in Norse mythology
Buri and Bestla — actually a god and a giantess, the grandparents of Odin from earlier in cosmogony
Lif and Lifthrasir — actually the two humans who survive Ragnarok hidden in Yggdrasil, not the first humans
Bor and Borr — variant names of Odin's father; not the first humans but rather the proto-gods
context: Ask (ash tree) and Embla (elm) were given three gifts by three gods: Odin gave breath/spirit (önd), Hoenir (or Vili) gave consciousness/sense, Lóðurr (or Ve) gave warmth/blood. The myth gave Norse humanity a wooden origin — appropriate to a culture so dependent on forests. Compare Hesiod's Pandora (clay) and Genesis's Adam (clay) — the Norse choice of wood is distinctive.

question: The Germanic peoples had a runic alphabet known as the Futhark (named for its first six letters: f, u, þ, a, r, k). The earliest version — Elder Futhark — had how many letters? And what replaced it later?
answer: 24 letters in Elder Futhark (c. 150-800 AD); replaced by 16-letter Younger Futhark (c. 800-1100 AD) used in Viking Age
choices: 24 letters in Elder Futhark (c. 150-800 AD); replaced by 16-letter Younger Futhark (c. 800-1100 AD) used in Viking Age
16 letters in Elder Futhark; expanded to 33 letters in Anglo-Saxon Futhorc, used into the late Middle Ages
33 letters in Elder Futhark; simplified to 16 in Viking-age Younger Futhark for ease of carving on weapons
12 letters in Elder Futhark; doubled to 24 in Younger Futhark for the more elaborate Viking-age inscriptions
context: Elder Futhark (24 runes) → Younger Futhark (16 runes) in Scandinavia (Viking-age). Anglo-Saxon Futhorc (29-33 runes) developed separately in England. Runes were used for inscriptions on stone (runestones), wood, bone, metal — not for everyday writing. They had names (Fehu = cattle/wealth; Uruz = aurochs; Thurisaz = giant; etc.) with phonetic and symbolic meaning. Used into early modern Iceland for inscriptions; survived in Sweden's Dalecarlian runes into the 20th century.

question: Iceland was settled in 874 AD by the Norwegian chieftain Ingólfur Arnarson. Many of the settlers were chieftains fleeing the centralization of power under King Harald Fairhair of Norway. The settlement period (Landnámsöld) lasted from 874 to about 930. What kind of government did the early Icelanders establish?
answer: The Althing in 930 AD — assembly of free men meeting annually at Thingvellir — perhaps the oldest extant parliament
choices: The Althing in 930 AD — assembly of free men meeting annually at Thingvellir — perhaps the oldest extant parliament
A kingdom under Ingólfur's descendants — the Icelanders established a royal line that endured until 1262
A theocracy under the goði (chieftain-priests) — religion and government were inseparable in early Icelandic society
An anarchic federation — no central institutions developed until Norway annexed the island in 1262 AD
context: The Althing — founded 930 at Thingvellir (Þingvellir, 'Assembly Plains') — is the oldest continuously functioning parliament in the world (with some interruptions). It met annually for two weeks in June, with cases heard, laws recited, news exchanged. The Lawspeaker (lögsögumaður) memorized the laws and recited them. Iceland's medieval Commonwealth (930-1262) operated without a king — a unique European experiment that ended when civil wars led to Norwegian rule.

question: On June 8, 793 AD, a fleet of Norse longships appeared off the holy island of Lindisfarne, the great monastery off the coast of Northumbria in northern England. They sacked the monastery, killing monks and seizing treasures. This is traditionally taken as the start of what era?
answer: The Viking Age (c. 793-1066) — three centuries of Norse expansion, raiding, trading, settlement across Europe and beyond
choices: The Viking Age (c. 793-1066) — three centuries of Norse expansion, raiding, trading, settlement across Europe and beyond
The Heptarchy — actually the seven Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of England, predating the Vikings by centuries
The Christianization of Scandinavia — actually a much later event, starting around 960 AD with Harald Bluetooth
The Carolingian Renaissance — actually Charlemagne's cultural revival, happening on the Continent during this period
context: Lindisfarne marks the conventional start of the Viking Age. The shock was enormous — the great churchman Alcuin (in Charlemagne's court) wrote that 'such a horror had never before appeared in Britain.' The Vikings would raid, trade, and settle for three centuries — Norse settlements in Iceland, Greenland (985), Vinland (c. 1000), the Danelaw in England, Normandy in France, Rus in Russia, the Varangian Guard in Constantinople.

question: The most famous pagan Norse temple was at Uppsala in Sweden. Adam of Bremen (writing c. 1075) described the great festival held there every nine years. What did Adam claim happened at these festivals?
answer: Nine of every kind of male animal were sacrificed, including humans; bodies hung in the sacred grove beside the temple
choices: Nine of every kind of male animal were sacrificed, including humans; bodies hung in the sacred grove beside the temple
Only flower offerings — Uppsala was a peaceful sanctuary contrasting with the warlike practices of southern Vikings
Only gold tribute — no living sacrifices; the temple was richly decorated but pacifist in its religious approach
Only the recitation of poems — Uppsala's nine-year ritual was a poetic festival rather than a sacrificial one
context: Adam of Bremen described 72 victims (nine of each of eight kinds of male animal, plus humans) hung in the sacred grove. Modern scholarship debates whether Adam was accurate — he was a hostile Christian source — but the general pattern of Germanic sacrifice (blot) is well-attested. The pagan temple at Uppsala was destroyed when Sweden converted to Christianity in the late 11th century; modern Uppsala Cathedral stands near the original site.

question: The Norse word for sacrificial worship was 'blót' (related to English 'blood'). Blót involved sacrificing animals (sometimes humans) to the gods. What was the basic structure of a blót ritual?
answer: Animals slaughtered with the blood sprinkled on the altar and the participants; meat eaten communally with the gods present
choices: Animals slaughtered with the blood sprinkled on the altar and the participants; meat eaten communally with the gods present
Animals abandoned alive in sacred groves; the gods would either accept them (they vanished) or reject them (they survived)
Animals burned entirely in offering to the gods; no part was eaten by humans, with the smoke being the divine portion
Animals presented at the temple but not killed; only after a year's keeping could the animals be ritually slaughtered
context: Blót shared the basic structure of Greek and Roman sacrifice: the animal was dedicated, killed, the blood used for ritual purposes, the meat cooked and eaten communally with the divine presence assumed. This combined religion and communal feasting — the social and religious functions of sacrifice were inseparable. The transition to Christianity ended public blót but private practices continued in some forms.

question: The volva (plural völur) — Norse seeress, female practitioner of seidr — had a distinctive social and religious role. She wandered between farms, was given hospitality, prophesied for her hosts, and could mediate with the spirit world. What did the volva wear and carry?
answer: A cloak of blue or black; a hood; a staff (vǫlr — same root as her name); often catskin gloves
choices: A cloak of blue or black; a hood; a staff (vǫlr — same root as her name); often catskin gloves
A robe of crimson silk; a golden crown; a sword and shield; a small portable altar of bronze
A linen veil; a wreath of mistletoe; a chalice and a runic tablet; sandals of woven hemp
A long mantle of bear-fur; a copper diadem; nothing else — the volva traveled with no implements of her trade
context: Eiríks saga rauða (Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 4) describes a volva in detail visiting a farmstead in Greenland. She wore a hooded blue cloak, glass beads, catskin gloves with white fur inside, a hammer-shaped pouch with charms, a staff. She sat on a special platform and entered trance for prophecy. The description has helped scholars understand volva practice as an actual social institution, not just literary motif.

question: Norse warrior bands included some who entered a battle-frenzy state — fighting with extraordinary ferocity, ignoring wounds, perhaps believing themselves to embody animal spirits. The Old Norse term for these warriors is the source of the English word 'berserk.' What did the name mean?
answer: Berserkr — perhaps 'bear-shirt' (wearing bear-hide) or 'bare-shirt' (fighting without armor); etymological debate continues
choices: Berserkr — perhaps 'bear-shirt' (wearing bear-hide) or 'bare-shirt' (fighting without armor); etymological debate continues
Berserkr — 'bare-blade' — referring to warriors who fought without sheathed weapons in battle frenzy
Berserkr — 'big-arm' — referring to warriors of exceptional physical size and strength alone
Berserkr — 'broad-shield' — referring to the distinctive large round shields these warriors carried
context: Berserkr's etymology is debated but probably 'bear-shirt' (warriors wearing bear-hides) or possibly 'bare-shirt' (without armor). Related: ulfheðnar ('wolf-coats'), wearing wolf-hides. These warriors were sometimes Odin's special followers, perhaps a kind of religious brotherhood. Modern theories about psychoactive substances (mushrooms, alcohol) inducing the frenzy state are speculative. The phenomenon was real — berserker laws prohibited their excesses in Iceland after Christianization.

question: Vikings of high status were sometimes buried in ships — vessels covered with earth as great burial mounds. The most famous such ships have been excavated in modern times in Norway. Which two ship burials provided the best-preserved evidence?
answer: Oseberg (c. 834 AD, contained two female bodies and rich grave goods) and Gokstad (c. 900 AD, contained a chieftain)
choices: Oseberg (c. 834 AD, contained two female bodies and rich grave goods) and Gokstad (c. 900 AD, contained a chieftain)
Lindholm Høje (Denmark) and Birka (Sweden) — actually both important sites but not principally ship burials
Sutton Hoo (England) and Vendel (Sweden) — Sutton Hoo is actually Anglo-Saxon, slightly earlier than Vikings
Hedeby (Denmark) and Kaupang (Norway) — actually both Viking trading towns rather than burial sites
context: Oseberg (excavated 1904) contained two women and an extraordinary collection of artifacts — carved wooden objects, textiles, a wagon, sleds, kitchen items, animals. Gokstad (excavated 1880) contained a male chieftain about 60 years old. Both ships are now displayed at the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo. They provide unparalleled archaeological evidence of Viking material culture, status burials, and shipbuilding.

question: Wyrd — the Anglo-Saxon word cognate with Norse 'Urd' — was the central concept of Germanic fatalism. It was not exactly 'fate' as the Greeks or Romans conceived it. How was it distinctive?
answer: Wyrd was the active weaving of past acts into future consequences — what one's deeds had made one's destiny
choices: Wyrd was the active weaving of past acts into future consequences — what one's deeds had made one's destiny
Wyrd was absolute predestination — every event fixed from before time, with no human contribution to the pattern
Wyrd was the will of Odin — what the All-Father chose, fate fulfilled, with no objective independent existence
Wyrd was random chaos — nothing was determined; the word marked the unpredictable nature of existence
context: Wyrd's etymology suggests 'that which has become' (from weorþan, to become) — implying the weight of accumulated past acts shaping future possibility. The concept differs from Greek heimarmene or Latin fatum in its weaving/becoming quality. Old English poetry repeatedly invokes wyrd: 'wyrd biþ swiðost' (fate is strongest). Shakespeare's 'weird sisters' in Macbeth are wyrd-sisters — Norn figures.

question: Egil's Saga (Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar) tells the life of Egill Skallagrímsson (c. 904-995) — among the greatest Icelandic skalds and one of the most ferocious figures in saga literature. He composed his first poem at age three (killing his first man at age seven). What were two of his most famous poems?
answer: Höfuðlausn ('Head-Ransom,' composed overnight to save his life at York) and Sonatorrek ('Loss of Sons,' his lament for two dead sons)
choices: Höfuðlausn ('Head-Ransom,' composed overnight to save his life at York) and Sonatorrek ('Loss of Sons,' his lament for two dead sons)
Lokasenna (actually an Eddic mythological poem, not by Egil) and Hávamál (also Eddic, attributed to Odin not Egil)
Beowulf (actually an Old English epic of unknown author, not Icelandic) and Cædmon's Hymn (also Old English)
Heimskringla (actually Snorri Sturluson's history of Norwegian kings) and Edda (also Snorri's prose mythography)
context: Höfuðlausn ('Head-Ransom') was composed in a single night when Egil was captured by King Eric Bloodaxe at York — Egil saved his head by praising the king who hated him. Sonatorrek was composed after his beloved son Bodvar drowned and his other son Gunnar died of fever. The poem alternates grief and resolution. Egil's Saga is traditionally (and probably correctly) attributed to Snorri Sturluson — making one great Icelandic writer the biographer of another.

question: Njal's Saga (Brennu-Njáls saga, 'The Saga of Burnt Njal') is generally considered the greatest of the Icelandic family sagas. It tells the story of two friends — the wise and prophetic Njal and the brave warrior Gunnar — and the long feud that destroys them both. The climax involves what?
answer: Njal and his entire household are burned alive in their farmhouse by enemies who refused to allow them to leave
choices: Njal and his entire household are burned alive in their farmhouse by enemies who refused to allow them to leave
Gunnar dies in defense of his home but Njal survives him by twenty years to old age and natural death
Both Njal and Gunnar reconcile their enemies; the saga ends in a great peace mediated at the Althing assembly
Gunnar is exiled and lives the rest of his life in Norway; Njal mediates the reconciliation of all their old foes
context: Njal's Saga's structure: Part 1 (Gunnar's story) → Part 2 (Njal's story, ending in his burning) → Part 3 (Kari Solmundarson's revenge for the burning). The burning of Bergþórshvoll farm with 24 dead is among the most famous scenes in medieval literature. The saga combines feud, law, prophecy, character study, and tragedy. Its 159 named characters give it an almost-novelistic richness unique in medieval Europe.

question: The two Vinland Sagas — Eirik's Saga and Saga of the Greenlanders — recount Norse voyages to North America around 1000 AD. The Norse encountered the native inhabitants, whom they called 'Skraelings.' What happened?
answer: Trading at first, then conflict; the Norse retreated; the Vinland colony was abandoned within a few years
choices: Trading at first, then conflict; the Norse retreated; the Vinland colony was abandoned within a few years

context: L'Anse aux Meadows confirms a Norse settlement c. 1000 AD in Newfoundland. The Vinland Sagas describe trade, then conflict, with Skraelings. Thorvald Eiriksson (Leif's brother) was killed by an arrow. The Norse retreated. The Greenland colony continued until c. 1450, when climate change (the Little Ice Age) and conflict with Inuit eliminated it. The Norse North American presence was a brief footnote until rediscovered by 20th-century archaeology.

question: Hasidism — a popular Jewish mystical revival movement — was founded in 18th-century Poland-Lithuania by Israel ben Eliezer (c. 1700-1760), known as the Baal Shem Tov ('Master of the Good Name'). What were the movement's distinctive emphases?
answer: Joyful prayer, mysticism for ordinary Jews, the centrality of the tzaddik (righteous leader), study balanced with devotion
choices: Joyful prayer, mysticism for ordinary Jews, the centrality of the tzaddik (righteous leader), study balanced with devotion

Modernization, secular education, abandonment of distinctive Jewish dress and dietary law
context: Hasidism emphasized devekut (cleaving to God) accessible to ordinary Jews, not just scholars. The Baal Shem Tov reportedly said: 'Where a person's thoughts are, there is the whole person.' Different Hasidic 'courts' formed around tzaddikim (charismatic leaders) — Chabad-Lubavitch, Bratslav, Satmar, others continue today. The Vilna Gaon (1720-1797) opposed Hasidism fiercely; the Mitnagdim ('opponents') and Hasidim were bitter rivals.

question: According to Islamic tradition, in 610 AD, the merchant Muhammad ibn Abdullah (c. 570-632) of Mecca was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira during the month of Ramadan. He was about 40 years old, known in Mecca as al-Amin (the trustworthy). The angel Jibril (Gabriel) appeared and commanded him to 'recite.' What did Muhammad say at first, and what was eventually recited?
answer: He said 'I cannot read' (or 'what shall I recite?'); the angel gave him the first verses of Surah 96 (al-Alaq, the Clot)
choices: He said 'I cannot read' (or 'what shall I recite?'); the angel gave him the first verses of Surah 96 (al-Alaq, the Clot)

context: Surah 96:1-5 (al-Alaq) is traditionally the first revelation: 'Recite! In the name of your Lord who created — created man from a clot of blood. Recite! Your Lord is the most gracious, who taught with the pen, taught man what he did not know.' Muhammad initially feared he was possessed; his wife Khadija comforted him. Her cousin Waraqa (a Christian) recognized the experience as prophetic. Revelations continued over 23 years and were compiled into the Quran.

question: After Muhammad's death (632 AD), succession became a divisive issue. The first four caliphs — Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali — are called the Rashidun ('Rightly Guided'). But the fourth caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law) was assassinated in 661 AD. His supporters (shi'at Ali, 'the party of Ali') believed leadership should have stayed in Muhammad's bloodline. What was the eventual outcome?
answer: Permanent split between Sunni (majority, accepting the elected caliphate) and Shia (minority, insisting on Ali's bloodline)
choices: Permanent split between Sunni (majority, accepting the elected caliphate) and Shia (minority, insisting on Ali's bloodline)
Sunni-Shia reconciliation by the 9th century; the modern divisions are political not theological in origin

context: The Sunni-Shia split is the major sectarian division in Islam (Sunni ~85%, Shia ~15%). The killing of Ali's son Hussein at Karbala (680 AD) further cemented the divide; Shia commemorate this annually at Ashura. Shia developed the doctrine of the Imamate (12 Imams in the dominant Twelver tradition; the 12th went into Hidden Occultation in 874). Shia is dominant in Iran, Iraq (since 2003), Bahrain, and Azerbaijan; significant in Lebanon, Yemen, Syria.

question: Under the Abbasid caliphs (especially Caliph al-Ma'mun, r. 813-833) at Baghdad, a great research institution flourished — the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma). What were its principal achievements?
answer: Translation of Greek philosophical, scientific, and medical works into Arabic; original research in mathematics, astronomy, medicine
choices: Translation of Greek philosophical, scientific, and medical works into Arabic; original research in mathematics, astronomy, medicine

Translation of Sanskrit and Chinese texts only; the Greek tradition was actually rejected by the Abbasids
context: The House of Wisdom translated nearly all of Aristotle, Plato, Galen, Hippocrates, Euclid, Ptolemy, and others. Original scholars: al-Khwarizmi (mathematics, the word 'algorithm' from his name), al-Kindi (philosophy), al-Razi (medicine), al-Battani (astronomy), and many others. The Islamic Golden Age (roughly 800-1250) preserved and advanced Greek learning while Europe entered its Dark Ages. Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 destroyed the House of Wisdom; books were thrown in the Tigris until 'the river ran black with ink.'

question: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780-850), Persian polymath at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, is among the most influential scholars in the history of mathematics. His Latinized name became an English word; his book's title became another English word. What were they?
answer: His name → 'algorithm'; his book Kitab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala → 'algebra' (al-jabr = restoration, completion)
choices: His name → 'algorithm'; his book Kitab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala → 'algebra' (al-jabr = restoration, completion)

context: Al-Khwarizmi introduced systematic solutions to linear and quadratic equations in Kitab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala (c. 820). 'Al-jabr' means 'restoration' or 'completion' (moving subtracted terms to the other side of the equation). His treatise on Hindu numerals popularized the decimal positional system (including zero) in the Islamic world; from Latin translation, it eventually reached Europe. The Latinized 'Algoritmi' for his name became 'algorithm.'

question: After six years of severe ascetic practice nearly killed him, Siddhartha accepted milk-rice from the village girl Sujata. Restored, he sat under a peepal tree (Ficus religiosa) at Bodh Gaya determined to find enlightenment or die. Through the night he meditated. What did he attain?
answer: Bodhi (enlightenment) — full understanding of the cycle of birth and death and liberation from it; he became 'Buddha' ('Awakened One')

Samadhi (concentration) — actually a meditative state, not the final goal that Buddha attained
context: Enlightenment came at age 35. Tradition holds Buddha resisted Mara (the demon of death and desire) through the night, attained the Three Knowledges (of his past lives, of all beings' rebirths, of the Four Noble Truths). At dawn he became Buddha. He sat under the Bodhi tree for 49 days experiencing his realization. The Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya (a descendant of the original) is a major Buddhist pilgrimage site. The Mahabodhi Temple complex marks the location.

question: The Noble Eightfold Path — the fourth Noble Truth — is the practical method for ending dukkha. It consists of eight elements traditionally grouped into three divisions. What are the three divisions?
answer: Wisdom (panna/prajna), Ethics (sila), Concentration/Meditation (samadhi) — covering view, action, and mental discipline
choices: Wisdom (panna/prajna), Ethics (sila), Concentration/Meditation (samadhi) — covering view, action, and mental discipline

context: The Eightfold Path's three divisions: Wisdom (panna): right view, right intention. Ethics (sila): right speech, right action, right livelihood. Concentration (samadhi): right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. The Path is not eight steps in sequence but eight aspects to cultivate simultaneously. The 'right' (samma) means proper or skillful — not moralistic perfection but conducive to enlightenment.

question: Ashoka — emperor of the Maurya dynasty (r. 268-232 BC) — ruled most of the Indian subcontinent. After his brutal conquest of Kalinga (c. 260 BC), with massive casualties, he experienced remorse and converted to Buddhism. He spread the religion through what means?
answer: Royal edicts inscribed on rock and stone pillars across his empire — over 30 surviving — and sending missionaries abroad
choices: Royal edicts inscribed on rock and stone pillars across his empire — over 30 surviving — and sending missionaries abroad

Sending armies into Sri Lanka to forcibly convert the inhabitants by military conquest into Buddhism
context: Ashoka's pillar edicts (the Ashokan inscriptions) are among the most important sources for early Buddhism. Written in Prakrit using Brahmi script, they expound dhamma (his term for moral conduct), urge religious tolerance ('all sects deserve reverence'), and proclaim policies of welfare and non-violence. He sent his son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta as missionaries to Sri Lanka (where they planted a cutting from the Bodhi tree, still venerated at Anuradhapura).

question: Hinduism's earliest sacred texts are the Vedas — four collections of hymns, ritual instructions, and theology composed in Sanskrit. The oldest, the Rigveda (c. 1500-1200 BC), contains 1,028 hymns in 10 books. The other three are Samaveda, Yajurveda, and Atharvaveda. What is the relationship between the four Vedas and the Upanishads?
answer: The Upanishads are the philosophical conclusions appended to each Veda — the 'end of the Vedas' (Vedanta) summarizing their teaching
choices: The Upanishads are the philosophical conclusions appended to each Veda — the 'end of the Vedas' (Vedanta) summarizing their teaching

context: Each Veda has four parts: Samhita (hymns), Brahmana (ritual instructions), Aranyaka (forest treatises), Upanishad (philosophical inquiries). The Upanishads (c. 900-500 BC, with later additions) represent the philosophical culmination — Vedanta ('end of the Vedas'). Major Upanishads: Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya, Katha, Isha, Mundaka, Mandukya, Taittiriya, Aitareya, Kena, Prasna. The Upanishads developed concepts like Brahman, Atman, karma, samsara, and moksha.

question: Japan's earliest written mythology is preserved in two 8th-century chronicles. What are they, and what do they record?
answer: Kojiki ('Record of Ancient Matters,' 712 AD) and Nihon Shoki ('Chronicles of Japan,' 720 AD) — both record Shinto mythology and imperial genealogy
choices: Kojiki ('Record of Ancient Matters,' 712 AD) and Nihon Shoki ('Chronicles of Japan,' 720 AD) — both record Shinto mythology and imperial genealogy

context: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki are foundational texts of Japanese culture and Shinto. They recount: the creation of the world by Izanagi and Izanami; the gods of the Plain of High Heaven; Amaterasu's cave episode; the descent of her grandson Ninigi to Japan; the legendary emperors; and historical reign accounts. Most scholars treat them as combining myth, legend, and history. They were politically important in establishing the divine descent of the emperors.

question: On March 20, 1995, members of the Japanese cult Aum Shinrikyo (Supreme Truth) released the nerve agent sarin in five Tokyo subway trains during morning rush hour. Twelve people died (the toll could have been much higher); thousands were injured. What was the cult, and what was its leader's fate?
answer: Doomsday cult founded 1984 by Shoko Asahara — blended Buddhism, yoga, Christian apocalyptic, with paranoia about US plot; Asahara executed July 6, 2018

context: Aum Shinrikyo carried out multiple attacks before 1995, including a 1994 sarin attack in Matsumoto that killed 8. They had recruited scientists, manufactured sarin in their compound, and amassed weapons. The 1995 subway attack — the most notorious chemical-weapons attack on civilians in decades — exposed the cult. Asahara (Chizuo Matsumoto) was arrested, tried over years, executed in 2018 along with 12 other cult leaders. The remaining members reorganized as Aleph.

question: Around 528 BC, after six years of extreme asceticism nearly starving him to death, a prince of the Shakya clan from Lumbini in modern Nepal — about 35 years old — sat down beneath a Ficus religiosa tree near the village of Bodh Gaya in modern Bihar. He resolved not to rise until he had attained enlightenment. He sat through the night while Mara, the lord of desire, sent armies and beautiful daughters to disturb him. At dawn he saw something. answer: The Four Noble Truths — the truth of suffering, its origin in craving, the possibility of cessation, and the eightfold path; he became the Buddha

context: Buddhism spread through India under Ashoka (3rd century BC), then to Southeast Asia, China (1st century AD), Korea, Japan, Tibet (8th century AD), and now globally. The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya marks the site. The Buddha taught for 45 years before dying at Kushinagar around 483 BC of food poisoning.

question: Around 610 AD, a 40-year-old merchant of the Quraysh tribe in Mecca, husband of the wealthy widow Khadija, had retreated for solitary meditation to a cave on Mount Hira above the city. context: Khadija (Muhammad's first wife, 15 years older than him, owner of a caravan trading business in which he had worked) was the first to believe him. Muhammad fled persecution in Mecca for Medina in 622 (the Hijra, year 1 of the Islamic calendar). He returned to Mecca in conquest in 630 and died in 632 at age 62. The Qur'an was compiled under Caliph Uthman c. 650 AD.

question: In 1244 AD at Konya in Anatolia, a respected 37-year-old Islamic scholar and judge from Khorasan met a wandering dervish named Shams of Tabriz. The meeting transformed him. For the next three years they were inseparable. When Shams disappeared (probably murdered by jealous followers in 1247), the scholar began composing the ecstatic Persian poetry that would make him the most popular poet in the modern English-speaking world. Who was he, and what is his great work?
answer: Jalal ad-Din Rumi (1207-1273) — and the Masnavi-ye Ma'navi (Spiritual Couplets), a six-volume work of 25,000+ verses combining Qur'anic exegesis, Sufi theology, and

context: Rumi's tomb at Konya is one of the most visited religious sites in the Islamic world. Coleman Barks's English translations of Rumi (from the 1980s) made him the best-selling poet in America for years. The Mevlevi order's whirling dervish ceremony (sema) is a meditation practice — turning around the heart while keeping it pointed at God.

question: On a day in 399 BC, in the prison of Athens, a 70-year-old philosopher drank a cup of hemlock surrounded by his closest students. He had been convicted by the Athenian democracy on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth. The conversation that day was preserved by his student Plato in the dialogue Phaedo. He discussed the soul, immortality, and the philosophical life. Just before he drank, he sent his weeping wife Xanthippe and their child away. After he drank, what were his last words?
answer: 'Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; pay the debt, and do not neglect it' — the god of healing was owed a sacrifice; the philosopher saw death as a healing from the
choices: 'Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; pay the debt, and do not neglect it' — the god of healing was owed a sacrifice; the philosopher saw death as a healing from the
'I drink to the better part of the city of Athens — even though the city has chosen to execute me, I retain my civic loyalty
'Tell my wife I did not feel any pain in the drinking; the philosophical training of a lifetime has prepared the soul to leave the body without
'Athens has killed many of her best sons; she will kill many more; the philosophical life will continue in the academies of those
context: Socrates wrote nothing himself; we have him through Plato (his philosophical disciple), Xenophon (his admirer), and Aristophanes (his comic critic in the Clouds). His death is the founding scene of Western philosophy — the philosopher choosing death over compromise with the city. Plato's Phaedo is one of the great dialogues.

question: In 1499 in the village of Sultanpur in Punjab, a 30-year-old Hindu accountant of the Khatri caste named Nanak Dev disappeared while bathing in the river Bein. He was assumed drowned. Three days later he emerged with a profound mystical experience: he announced 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.' He spent the next 25 years traveling — to Mecca, to Tibet, to Sri Lanka — teaching a religion that drew on bhakti Hinduism and Sufi Islam. He died in 1539 at Kartarpur. What religion did he found, and what is its central theology?
answer: Sikhism — and its central theology is Ek Onkar ('there is one God'), strict monotheism transcending Hindu and Muslim categories, with no rituals, no caste, no priesthood; the Guru
choices: Sikhism — and its central theology is Ek Onkar ('there is one God'), strict monotheism transcending Hindu and Muslim categories, with no rituals, no caste, no priesthood; the Guru
Brahmoism — and its central theology is the unity of all religions as expressions of one divine reality, the wider
Kabirpanthism — and its central theology is the Sant Mat synthesis of bhakti Hinduism and Sufi Islam through
Theosophism — and its central theology is the perennial wisdom underlying all religions, the wider pattern being late
context: Sikhism has roughly 25 million adherents today, concentrated in Punjab and the global Sikh diaspora. The five Ks (kesh-uncut hair, kangha-comb, kara-bracelet, kachera-undergarment, kirpan-sword) of the Khalsa (military order founded by tenth Guru Gobind Singh, 1699) are distinctive. The Golden Temple at Amritsar (founded 1574) is the central shrine.

question: Pelops, king of Pisa, had cursed his sons Atreus and Thyestes for the killing of their half-brother Chrysippus. The brothers feuded for the throne of Mycenae. Thyestes seduced Atreus's wife Aerope and stole the throne. Atreus regained it, invited Thyestes back under pretense of reconciliation, and served him at a feast a dish he revealed only after Thyestes had eaten. What was the dish?
answer: Thyestes's own sons, slaughtered and cooked — Atreus produced the hands and heads to reveal what had been eaten, an act that extended the curse on the House of Atreus through to Orestes
choices: Thyestes's own sons, slaughtered and cooked — Atreus produced the hands and heads to reveal what had been eaten, an act that extended the curse on the House of Atreus through to Orestes
Pelops's own bones, exhumed from the ancestor's grave — the cannibalistic violation that paralleled what Tantalus had done to Pelops in the previous generation of the family curse
The flesh of Aerope herself, who Atreus had killed in vengeance for the seduction — the brother's gift to the brother that exceeded all previous family violence
The horses of Diomedes, whose flesh was forbidden — the dietary violation that itself was a curse rather than the cannibalism that became standard in retellings
context: The story is dramatized in Seneca's Thyestes and underlies the Oresteia. Atreus's sons Agamemnon and Menelaus inherited the curse. Agamemnon sacrificed Iphigenia at Aulis for the winds; he was killed by Clytemnestra his wife in the bath on his return; Orestes killed Clytemnestra; the Furies pursued him.

question: A remarkable Icelandic-Greenlandic woman crossed the North Atlantic eight times by sea, gave birth to Snorri Thorfinnsson in Vinland (the first European child born in North America, c. 1009-1011), survived two husbands, made pilgrimage to Rome, and ended as a Christian anchoress at Glaumbaer. Two sagas describe her. What was her name?
answer: Gudrid Thorbjarnardottir — wife of Karlsefni, mother of Snorri Thorfinnsson, traveler of unprecedented breadth (some say she walked to Rome from Northern Europe), founder of a great Icelandic line
choices: Gudrid Thorbjarnardottir — wife of Karlsefni, mother of Snorri Thorfinnsson, traveler of unprecedented breadth (some say she walked to Rome from Northern Europe), founder of a great Icelandic line
Aud the Deep-Minded — the earlier Irish-Scottish widow who settled Iceland with freedmen, founded Hvamm in West Iceland and became one of the great matriarchs; predating Gudrid by a century
Freydis Eiriksdottir — Eirik the Red's daughter and Gudrid's contemporary, who also voyaged to Vinland but committed the camp-slaughter that the saga blames for the venture's failure
Thurid Sturludottir — mother of Snorri Sturluson, whose 12th-century pilgrimages and church-building paralleled Gudrid's earlier journeys but in a different geographic theater
context: Snorri Thorfinnsson lived to become a major figure in Northern Iceland. His descendants include the three bishops of medieval Iceland whose lineages descended from Gudrid through Snorri. Gudrid's churches at Glaumbaer were the foundation of an important episcopal seat. She is sometimes called 'the far-traveler.'

question: From the 870s onward, English kings dealt with Viking raids partly by paying tribute. The systematic payment of silver to keep Vikings from raiding was institutionalized as a tax under Ethelred the Unready after the Battle of Maldon (991). What was this tax called?
answer: Danegeld — Danes' gold; about 240,000 pounds of silver was paid out between 991 and 1014; Kipling's poem 'Dane-Geld' (1911) drew the lesson 'if once you have paid him the Dane-geld / You never get rid of the Dane'
choices: Danegeld — Danes' gold; about 240,000 pounds of silver was paid out between 991 and 1014; Kipling's poem 'Dane-Geld' (1911) drew the lesson 'if once you have paid him the Dane-geld / You never get rid of the Dane'
Heregeld — army-money; the related but distinct tax to maintain the standing fleet and the housecarl bodyguard, abolished in 1051 under Edward the Confessor as a separate category
Wergild — man-price; the different Anglo-Saxon institution of compensation paid to the family of a slain man, mistakenly conflated with Viking tribute by post-Norman historians
Geldgafol — the older tax-tribute paid to pre-Christian Saxon kings, the institutional ancestor of Danegeld but predating Viking pressure as a domestic rather than foreign tax
context: The Danegeld continued under Cnut and lasted until 1162. The institutional machinery of tribute-collection became the foundation of the later medieval English tax system. The Battle of Maldon (991) was commemorated in one of the great Old English poems; the loyal retainers fought to the death after Byrhtnoth fell.

question: On February 1, 1979, after 14 years in exile (Najaf, then Paris), an Iranian Shi'ite ayatollah returned to Tehran. The Shah had fled January 16. A March 30-31 referendum approved an Islamic Republic by 98%. Hostages were seized at the US embassy November 4, 1979. What is the technical name for his doctrine of clerical rule?
answer: Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Jurist) — Khomeini's doctrine from Najaf lectures (Islamic Government 1970): rule belongs to qualified Islamic jurists in the absence of the Hidden Imam
choices: Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Jurist) — Khomeini's doctrine from Najaf lectures (Islamic Government 1970): rule belongs to qualified Islamic jurists in the absence of the Hidden Imam
Ijtihad-e Mutlaq (Absolute Independent Reasoning) — the older Shi'ite legal doctrine of fully independent juridical interpretation that Khomeini extended into the political sphere
Marja-e Taqlid (Source of Emulation) — the traditional Shi'ite institution of senior jurists whose rulings ordinary Shi'a follow; not a political doctrine but a religious-legal status
Khilafat al-Rashidin (Caliphate of the Rightly-Guided) — the Sunni concept Khomeini repurposed for his Shi'ite political theology, claiming continuity with the early Islamic caliphate
context: Velayat-e Faqih is contested even within Shi'ism — the senior Najaf school under Sistani has consistently maintained the older 'quietist' view that clerics should advise rather than rule. Iran's modern republic is unique in implementing Khomeini's doctrine constitutionally.

question: After his enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, the 35-year-old Buddha walked about 250 km north to the deer park at Isipatana near Varanasi. There he met the five ascetics he had previously fasted with, who initially scorned him for breaking the fast. He delivered his first sermon — the 'Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma.' What did it teach?
answer: The Four Noble Truths — dukkha (suffering), samudaya (origin in craving), nirodha (cessation), magga (the eightfold path) — and the Middle Way between sensual indulgence and self-mortification
choices: The Four Noble Truths — dukkha (suffering), samudaya (origin in craving), nirodha (cessation), magga (the eightfold path) — and the Middle Way between sensual indulgence and self-mortification
The five aggregates (skandhas) — form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness — and how clinging to them produces the illusion of self; later systematized by Abhidharma
Dependent origination (paticca-samuppada) in its twelve-link form — ignorance through birth-and-death; the deeper formulation taught only to advanced disciples
The Heart Sutra's emptiness teaching (form is emptiness, emptiness is form) — a much later Mahayana development not present in the historical Buddha's first sermon
context: The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is preserved in the Pali Canon. The five ascetics became the first sangha (monastic community). Sarnath remains one of the four chief Buddhist pilgrimage sites (with Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Kushinagar). Ashoka built a stupa and pillar there in the 3rd century BC.

question: In the central narrative of Egyptian religion, a benevolent king was murdered by his brother Set, who dismembered the body into 14 pieces and scattered them. His sister-wife found 13 (one — the phallus — eaten by a Nile fish), reassembled the body, and conceived a son through magic. The son grew up and defeated the murderer. What were the names?
answer: Osiris (killed), Isis (wife who reassembled him), Horus (son who avenged him), Set (murderer-brother) — the foundational myth shaping Egyptian funerary religion for over 2500 years
choices: Osiris (killed), Isis (wife who reassembled him), Horus (son who avenged him), Set (murderer-brother) — the foundational myth shaping Egyptian funerary religion for over 2500 years

Atum (killed), Tefnut (his wife), Shu (their son), Apep (the murderer) — the Heliopolitan creation account, separate from the Osiris-Isis-Horus dying-god narrative
Ptah (killed), Sekhmet (his wife), Nefertem (their son), Khnum (the murderer) — the Memphite theology, a separate parallel cycle that did not feature the dying-and-rising god
context: Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride (c. 100 AD) is the most complete Greek-Latin source. The myth shaped Egyptian afterlife belief — every dead person became an Osiris. The Osiris-Isis cult spread across the Hellenistic and Roman world; Isis temples reached Britain and Germany. Christianity competed with the Isis cult in the 1st-3rd centuries.

question: On the fourth day of the Babylonian New Year festival (Akitu), priests recited a creation epic to the king. The poem begins 'When on high' (Enuma Elish) and narrates the rise of Babylon's chief god from a younger generation of gods. He killed the primordial salt-water mother and split her body to form sky and earth. Who is this god, and who was the primordial mother he killed?
answer: Marduk killed Tiamat — split her body to make sky (upper half) and earth (lower); her saliva became clouds, her tears the Tigris and Euphrates; the poem celebrates Babylon's claim to cosmic supremacy
choices: Marduk killed Tiamat — split her body to make sky (upper half) and earth (lower); her saliva became clouds, her tears the Tigris and Euphrates; the poem celebrates Babylon's claim to cosmic supremacy
Enlil killed Nammu — the older Sumerian creation tradition mistakenly retrojected onto the Babylonian Enuma Elish which was Marduk's mythology specifically
Anu killed Tiamat — actually Anu was the older father-god who delegated the combat to Marduk; the killing was Marduk's, not Anu's, in the Enuma Elish chronology
Ashur killed Tiamat — the Assyrian rewrite (with Ashur replacing Marduk) of the Babylonian myth that surfaces in some later Assyrian recensions of the poem
context: Enuma Elish (c. 1700-1200 BC, on seven clay tablets) was discovered in Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh and first published in 1876. Parallels with Genesis 1 (separation of waters above and below the firmament, week of creation) have been intensely debated. The connection seems likely though specific borrowing direction is contested.

question: From the Ashanti people of Ghana, a trickster figure shaped both pre-colonial folklore and the diasporic stories carried to the Caribbean during the slave trade. He is depicted as a spider who outwits more powerful animals through cunning. He is said to have collected all the world's wisdom in a clay pot but lost it when his son outsmarted him. What is his name?
answer: Anansi — the most famous African trickster god, son of the sky god Nyame; his tales (Anansesem) spread through the Caribbean (Jamaica especially) and into African American folklore as part of the cultural diaspora
choices: Anansi — the most famous African trickster god, son of the sky god Nyame; his tales (Anansesem) spread through the Caribbean (Jamaica especially) and into African American folklore as part of the cultural diaspora
Eshu — the Yoruba trickster who became Papa Legba in Haitian Vodou; a different West African deity
Br'er Rabbit — the African American descendant figure (recorded in Joel Chandler Harris's Uncle Remus, 1881); the inheritor of trickster traditions including those of Anansi
Mantis — the Khoisan San trickster god of southern Africa; a different regional African tradition entirely, not the Ashanti spider trickster of West Africa
context: Anansi tales taught indirect resistance and survival under power-asymmetries — important for enslaved African peoples maintaining identity under chattel slavery. Anansi appears in Neil Gaiman's American Gods (2001) and Anansi Boys (2005). The tales remain a living tradition in Ghana, Jamaica, Curacao, and the African diaspora.

question: On November 18, 1978, in northwest Guyana, members of an American religious-political movement gathered after the killing of US Congressman Leo Ryan at a nearby airstrip. They drank cyanide and tranquilizers in flavored powdered drink. 909 died, including 304 children. About a third may have been forcibly injected. What was the cult, and what is the misnamed product?
answer: The Peoples Temple under Jim Jones — and the drink was Flavor Aid (not Kool-Aid, though 'drinking the Kool-Aid' became permanent shorthand for cult-suicide)
choices: The Peoples Temple under Jim Jones — and the drink was Flavor Aid (not Kool-Aid, though 'drinking the Kool-Aid' became permanent shorthand for cult-suicide)

The Branch Davidians under David Koresh — the 1993 Waco siege resulting in 76 deaths; a different incident from Jonestown though both became symbols of cult-violence
Aum Shinrikyo under Shoko Asahara — the 1995 Tokyo subway sarin attack by a Japanese cult; not American and 13 deaths from the attack, again confused with Jonestown
context: Jim Jones (1931-1978) had earlier been seen as a progressive figure — interracial church-leadership in Indianapolis (1950s), opposition to segregation, antipoverty work in San Francisco. The 1977 New West expose drove the move to Guyana. Jonestown remains the largest single-day deliberate loss of American lives between Pearl Harbor and 9/11.

question: On the morning of March 20, 1995, during Tokyo's rush hour, members of a Japanese new religious movement placed bags of liquid sarin nerve agent on five trains converging on Kasumigaseki station (the government district). They punctured the bags with umbrella tips. 13 commuters died; over 1000 had serious injuries. What was the cult, and who was its leader?
answer: Aum Shinrikyo (Supreme Truth) under Shoko Asahara (Chizuo Matsumoto, 1955-2018) — a syncretic apocalyptic Buddhist-Hindu-Christian cult with about 10,000 Japanese members; Asahara was executed July 6, 2018
choices: Aum Shinrikyo (Supreme Truth) under Shoko Asahara (Chizuo Matsumoto, 1955-2018) — a syncretic apocalyptic Buddhist-Hindu-Christian cult with about 10,000 Japanese members; Asahara was executed July 6, 2018
Soka Gakkai under Daisaku Ikeda — a mainstream Nichiren Buddhist lay organization, not connected to the Aum attacks despite Western confusion about Japanese new religions
Tenrikyo under Nakayama Miki — a 19th-century Japanese new religion centered on Tenri City, peaceful and unrelated to the 1995 subway attacks
Mahikari under Okada Yoshikazu — another 20th-century Japanese new religion centered on True Light spiritual practice, distinct from Aum despite occasional confusion
context: Aum had earlier killed a lawyer (Sakamoto Tsutsumi) and his family in 1989, conducted a smaller sarin attack in Matsumoto in 1994 (8 dead), and accumulated chemical and biological weapons capability. The attack triggered a Japanese rethink of cult regulation and emergency preparedness. The remnant became 'Aleph' in 2000.

question: The fullest version of the Cupid and Psyche story comes from a 2nd-century AD Latin novel. By what title?
context: Apuleius's Metamorphoses, c. 160 AD — the only complete Latin novel surviving. The protagonist is turned into an ass; the Cupid and Psyche tale is told as an interpolated story.

question: A golden ram rescued two children from sacrifice — but the girl fell into the strait that later bore her name. Who fell?
context: Phrixus reached Colchis safely and sacrificed the ram; its fleece became the goal of Jason's quest. The Hellespont — the modern Dardanelles — was named for Helle.

question: The traditional first permanent settler of Iceland — who built his farm at Reykjavik ('smoky-bay') c. 874 AD — is named what?
context: He had been exiled from Norway for blood-feud. He took the high-seat pillars of his hall (his ship's most sacred objects), threw them overboard, and built where they came ashore. They came ashore at Reykjavik.

question: Iceland's Commonwealth had a chief legal officer who recited the law from memory each year at the Althing. He was called what?
context: Logsogumadr in Old Norse. He served a three-year term. Recited a third of the laws each year. Snorri Sturluson held the office twice (1215-1218 and 1222-1231).

question: Genesis 3: the serpent persuaded Adam's wife to eat from the one forbidden tree in Eden, then offer fruit to Adam himself. What was she named?
context: Hebrew 'Chavah' — 'mother of all living'. The expulsion from Eden is the foundational Christian story of original sin.

question: In Genesis 4, Adam's elder son murdered his younger brother in a field after God favored the brother's sacrifice. Who was the murderer?
context: Cain offered grain; Abel offered the firstborn of his flock. The first human murder in Scripture. God marked Cain so no one would kill him.

question: In Genesis, one righteous man built a wooden vessel to save his family and pairs of animals from a global flood. Who built the ark?
context: The flood narrative parallels the Mesopotamian Gilgamesh flood story (Utnapishtim). Genesis frames it as judgment and covenant — the rainbow follows.

question: In Genesis 11, humanity built a great tower to reach the heavens; God scattered them by confusing their speech. What was the tower called?
context: The story explains the origin of different languages. 'Babel' puns on Hebrew 'balal' (to confuse) and the Babylonian city Babili.

question: In Genesis 12, God called a man from Haran to leave his country and become the father of a great nation. Who was called?
context: Originally Abram. He left Ur, then Haran, and went to Canaan. He is revered as patriarch by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

question: In Genesis 22, a father climbed Mount Moriah to sacrifice his only son before an angel stopped his hand and a ram appeared in a thicket. Who was the father?
context: Hebrew tradition calls this the Akedah ('binding'). Jewish, Christian, and Islamic readings all wrestle with what the test meant.

question: Genesis 28: a fugitive grandson of Abraham dreamed of a stairway between heaven and earth with angels ascending and descending. Who dreamed it?
context: Fleeing his brother Esau, Jacob slept with a stone for a pillow at Bethel. The dream was God's covenant renewal with the patriarchal line.

question: In Genesis 32, a man wrestled an unknown being all night at Peniel and was renamed 'Israel' — 'he who strives with God'. Who wrestled?
context: He limped afterward — the angel touched his hip. The name 'Israel' became the name of his twelve sons and the entire nation.

question: In Genesis, a favored son with a many-colored coat was sold into Egyptian slavery by his jealous brothers. Who was he?
context: Son of Jacob and Rachel. He rose to be Pharaoh's second-in-command after interpreting dreams of seven fat and seven lean years.

question: In Exodus 3, a shepherd on Mount Horeb encountered a bush that burned but was not consumed, and God spoke from it. Who was the shepherd?
context: God revealed his name as YHWH ('I AM') and commissioned Moses to lead the Hebrews out of Egyptian slavery.

question: On the night of the tenth plague, Hebrew families marked their doorposts with lamb's blood so the angel of death would pass over their houses. This founding meal is called what?
context: Exodus 12. The unleavened bread and bitter herbs commemorate the haste of flight. Jesus's Last Supper was a Passover seder.

question: After Pharaoh pursued the Hebrews to the shore, Moses raised his staff and the waters parted for Israel to cross dry-shod. What sea parted?
context: Hebrew 'Yam Suph' — possibly 'Sea of Reeds'. Pharaoh's chariots drowned when the waters returned. The defining act of Exodus.

question: On a mountain wrapped in cloud and thunder, Moses received two stone tablets containing ten divine laws. What mountain was it?
context: Exodus 19-20. Also called Horeb. The covenant law — no other gods, no idols, honor parents, no murder, theft, adultery, false witness, coveting.

question: While Moses was on Sinai, his brother yielded to the people and cast a golden idol they worshipped at the foot of the mountain. Who cast the calf?
context: Exodus 32. Moses shattered the tablets in fury, ground the calf to powder, and made the people drink it. Aaron blamed the crowd.

question: After Moses died, a new leader marched Israel around a Canaanite city seven times until trumpet-blasts brought its walls down. Who led the march?
context: Joshua 6. Jericho's fall opened the Canaan campaign. The story is celebrated in the African-American spiritual 'Joshua Fit the Battle'.

question: A Nazirite judge whose strength lay in his uncut hair was betrayed by his Philistine lover to discover the secret. Who was he?
context: Judges 16. Delilah cut his hair, the Philistines blinded him, then he pulled down their temple of Dagon — killing more in death than in life.

question: A young shepherd boy felled a nine-foot Philistine champion with one smooth stone from a sling at the Valley of Elah. Who was the shepherd?
context: 1 Samuel 17. David later beheaded Goliath with the giant's own sword. He would become Israel's greatest king and ancestor of Jesus.

question: King David saw a beautiful woman bathing on a rooftop and arranged the death of her husband Uriah to take her. Who was she?
context: 2 Samuel 11. The prophet Nathan confronted David with the parable of the rich man and the poor man's lamb. Their second son was Solomon.

question: David's son built Israel's first stone temple in Jerusalem and is remembered for asking God for wisdom. Who was he?
context: 1 Kings 6. The First Temple stood until Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC. Solomon's wisdom became proverbial — Proverbs and Ecclesiastes are credited to him.

question: On Mount Carmel a prophet challenged 450 priests of Baal to call down fire; only his sacrifice burned. Who was the prophet?
context: 1 Kings 18. Elijah taunted Baal's silent prophets, then drenched his own altar in water before fire fell. He was taken to heaven in a whirlwind.

question: A reluctant prophet fled God's command to preach to Nineveh and was swallowed by a great fish for three days. Who was he?
context: Jesus called the three days in the fish a sign of his own three days in the tomb. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching — sparing the city.

question: A Hebrew exile who refused to stop praying to his God was thrown into a den of lions, but God shut their mouths. Who was he?
context: Daniel 6. Under King Darius. Daniel also interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dreams and saw the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast.

question: Three Hebrew youths refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and were thrown into a furnace, where a fourth figure walked with them. Whom were they?
context: Daniel 3. The fourth figure 'looked like a son of the gods'. They emerged unsinged. Their Hebrew names: Hananiah, Mishael, Azariah.

question: At a Babylonian feast, a disembodied hand wrote four Aramaic words on the wall and Daniel interpreted them. Which king saw the writing?
context: Daniel 5. 'Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin' — your kingdom is numbered, weighed, divided. Babylon fell to Persia that very night.

question: A Jewish queen of Persia risked her life to expose a court official's plot to exterminate her people. Who was the queen?
context: The Book of Esther — read at the Jewish festival of Purim. Haman the Agagite plotted the genocide; he was hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

question: A Moabite widow refused to leave her Israelite mother-in-law and became the great-grandmother of King David. Who was she?
context: 'Whither thou goest, I will go.' She married Boaz in Bethlehem after gleaning in his fields. Her line led to David — and to Jesus.

question: The Bible's poem of suffering features a righteous man who lost children, wealth, and health in a divine wager with the Accuser, yet refused to curse God. Who is he?
context: The Book of Job — among the oldest in Scripture. His three friends insisted he must have sinned. God answers from the whirlwind.

question: A prophet saw God enthroned in the temple, surrounded by six-winged seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy', and his lips were cleansed with a coal. Who was he?
context: Isaiah 6. The vision came in the year King Uzziah died (c. 740 BC). Isaiah prophesied Immanuel, the suffering servant, and the messianic peace.

question: In a valley vision, a prophet saw a field of scattered dry bones reassemble, take on flesh, and live as a vast army. Who saw the vision?
context: Ezekiel 37. The bones symbolize exiled Israel — 'Can these bones live?' The prophecy promises national restoration after Babylonian captivity.

question: An angel appeared to a young woman in Nazareth and told her she would bear the Son of the Most High. Which angel?
context: Luke 1. Mary's reply 'Let it be done to me according to your word' is called her fiat. The scene fills Christian art from Fra Angelico to the present.

question: Mary and Joseph found no room at the inn and laid the newborn Jesus in a feeding trough in which town?
context: Luke 2. Bethlehem fulfilled Micah's prophecy. The shepherds came at the angel's announcement; the magi followed the star somewhat later.

question: Eastern wise men followed a star to the child Jesus and gave three gifts: gold, frankincense, and what third?
context: Matthew 2. Tradition calls the magi 'three kings' because of the three gifts. Myrrh was a burial spice — Christian readers see it foreshadowing the cross.

question: Warned in a dream that a king sought the infant Jesus's life, Joseph fled with Mary and the child to which country?
context: Matthew 2. Herod's slaughter of Bethlehem's male infants — the Massacre of the Innocents — drove the flight. They returned after Herod's death in 4 BC.

question: A wild-haired prophet in camel-hair clothing baptized people in the Jordan and pointed out Jesus as 'the Lamb of God'. Who was he?
context: Mark 1 and John 1. He ate locusts and wild honey. Herod Antipas beheaded him at Salome's request — the dance and the silver platter.

question: After his baptism Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness and was tempted by the devil with three offers. How many days?
context: Matthew 4 and Luke 4. Bread from stones, leap from the temple, all kingdoms for worship — Jesus answered each with Scripture from Deuteronomy.

question: On a hillside Jesus fed a vast crowd from a boy's lunch of five loaves and two fish. How many men were fed?
context: All four Gospels record this miracle. Twelve baskets of leftovers remained. A separate feeding of four thousand follows in Matthew and Mark.

question: In a night storm Jesus walked toward his disciples' boat across the surface of a lake; one apostle stepped out and began to sink. Who stepped out?
context: Matthew 14. 'Lord, save me!' Jesus caught him and asked why he doubted. The Sea of Galilee — a freshwater lake — is the setting.

question: On a high mountain Jesus's face shone like the sun and Moses and Elijah appeared beside him. Three apostles witnessed it: Peter, James, and which third?
context: Matthew 17. Tradition places it on Mount Tabor. Peter offered to build three booths. A voice from cloud: 'This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.'

question: Four days dead in his tomb, a man emerged still in his graveclothes when Jesus called 'come out'. Who was he?
context: John 11. 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35) is the shortest verse in English Bibles. Lazarus's sisters Mary and Martha had sent for Jesus too late.

question: Jesus entered Jerusalem riding a young donkey while crowds spread their cloaks and palm branches before him. Christians remember the day as what?
context: Fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. The crowds shouted 'Hosanna' — by Friday they would shout 'crucify him'. The week is called Holy Week.

question: Jesus overturned tables and drove out merchants from the temple courts, denouncing them for making God's house what?
context: Matthew 21. Quoting Jeremiah 7:11. The moneychangers traded Roman coinage for temple shekels; sellers offered approved sacrificial doves.

question: At the Passover meal before his arrest Jesus broke bread and shared wine, telling the twelve 'do this in remembrance of me'. What meal?
choices: The Marriage Supper of the Lamb
context: Matthew 26. The institution of the Eucharist — central to Christian worship. Leonardo's Milan fresco freezes the moment Jesus says one will betray him.

question: Jesus's betrayer kissed him in Gethsemane and was paid thirty silver coins by the chief priests. Who betrayed him?
context: Matthew 26. Judas threw the silver back in the temple and hanged himself. The priests bought a potter's field with it — 'Field of Blood'.

question: During Jesus's trial, his chief apostle denied even knowing him three times before the cock crowed. Who denied him?
context: Luke 22. Jesus had predicted it at supper. Peter went outside and 'wept bitterly'. The risen Jesus restored him three times: 'Feed my sheep'.

question: The Roman governor of Judea publicly washed his hands of Jesus's blood and let the crowd condemn him. Who was the governor?
context: Matthew 27. Pilate's wife had warned him from a dream. The crowd shouted 'His blood be on us and on our children'. He is named in the Apostles' Creed.

question: Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem at a hill whose name in Aramaic means 'Place of the Skull'. What is the Latin name?
context: Aramaic 'Golgotha'. Two criminals were crucified beside him. The Gospels record seven 'last words' from the cross before he died at the ninth hour.

question: On the third day after his burial Jesus's tomb was found empty by women who came to anoint the body. Which woman is named first in all four Gospels?
context: John 20 gives the fullest account — Mary Magdalene at first mistook the risen Jesus for the gardener. The Resurrection is Christianity's central claim.

question: An apostle refused to believe Jesus had risen until he could touch the nail wounds and the spear-pierced side. Who?
context: John 20. A week later Jesus invited Thomas to touch — Thomas answered 'My Lord and my God'. Tradition sends him as missionary to India.

question: Two disciples walked with the risen Jesus toward a village without recognizing him until he broke bread at table. What village?
context: Luke 24. 'Did not our hearts burn within us?' Caravaggio painted the moment of recognition twice. The story shapes Christian Eucharistic theology.

question: Fifty days after Easter, tongues of fire descended on the disciples in Jerusalem and they spoke in languages they did not know. What is the day called?
context: Acts 2. Jews from every nation heard the gospel in their own language. Peter's sermon converted three thousand. The traditional birth of the Church.

question: The first Christian martyr was stoned outside Jerusalem while Saul of Tarsus stood approving. Who was he?
context: Acts 7. Stephen forgave his killers as he died, mirroring Jesus on the cross. A young Saul held the coats — soon to become Paul on the Damascus road.

question: A persecutor of Christians traveling to Damascus was blinded by a sudden light and heard Jesus's voice asking 'why do you persecute me?' Who?
context: Acts 9, c. 34 AD. Renamed Paul, he became Christianity's greatest missionary — author of 13 New Testament letters. His epistles defined Christian theology.

question: Paul stood on the Areopagus in Athens and preached to philosophers about an altar he had seen inscribed 'to an unknown god'. What altar inscription?
context: Acts 17. Paul quoted the Greek poets Epimenides and Aratus. A few converted, including Dionysius the Areopagite — patron of Athens.

question: The Book of Revelation was written by John during his exile on a small Aegean island. Which island?
context: Revelation 1:9, c. 95 AD under Domitian. The visions of seven churches, four horsemen, and the new Jerusalem close the Christian Bible.

question: Tradition holds that Christianity's chief apostle was crucified upside-down in Rome, refusing to die as his Lord had. Who?
context: Under Nero c. 64 AD. Peter felt unworthy of the same death. St Peter's Basilica in Rome is built over what tradition holds is his tomb.

question: Peter's brother became patron saint of Scotland and was crucified on an X-shaped cross. Who?
context: The Saltire of Scotland is the white X-cross of St Andrew on blue. Tradition places his martyrdom in Patras, Greece, under Nero or later.

question: A second-century bishop and disciple of John was burned at the stake in Smyrna at age 86, refusing to curse Christ. Who?
context: Martyred c. 155 AD. 'Eighty and six years have I served him, and he has done me no wrong'. The Martyrdom of Polycarp is the earliest non-canonical martyr account.

question: Before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 AD a Roman emperor saw a cross in the sky and the words 'in this sign conquer'. Who?
context: Latin 'in hoc signo vinces'. Constantine defeated Maxentius outside Rome. The following year's Edict of Milan legalized Christianity across the empire.

question: In 313 AD Constantine issued an edict legalizing Christianity throughout the Roman Empire. The edict bears the name of which city?
context: Co-issued with Licinius. Persecution of Christians ended; confiscated church property was restored. The Constantinian shift transformed Christianity into a public faith.

question: A fourth-century Alexandrian presbyter taught that the Son was a created being, not co-eternal with the Father. Who?
context: Arianism. 'There was a time when the Son was not.' Condemned at Nicaea 325. Long survived among the Germanic tribes — Visigoths, Vandals, Lombards.

question: An Alexandrian bishop exiled five times for defending the full divinity of Christ said 'Athanasius against the world'. Who?
context: Bishop of Alexandria 328-373 AD. His On the Incarnation defended Nicene orthodoxy. He also fixed the New Testament canon in his 367 AD Easter letter.

question: In 386 AD a North African rhetorician converted in a Milanese garden after hearing a child's voice say 'tolle, lege' — 'take and read'. Who?
context: He opened Paul's letter to the Romans. Confessions tells the story. He became the most influential theologian in Western Christianity.

question: After Rome's 410 AD sack by the Visigoths, Augustine wrote a massive defense distinguishing the earthly city from the city of God. What title?
context: De Civitate Dei. Written 413-426. Pagans had blamed Christianity for Rome's fall; Augustine answered with a theology of history.

question: In 529 AD a hermit founded a monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy and wrote a rule that became the foundation of Western monasticism. Who?
context: Ora et labora — pray and work. The Rule of St Benedict balanced prayer, manual work, and study. Benedictine houses preserved learning across the so-called 'Dark Ages'.

question: A late-sixth-century pope sent missionaries to Anglo-Saxon England and reformed church liturgy; his name is attached to a style of chant. Who?
context: Pope 590-604. Sent Augustine of Canterbury to convert the Anglo-Saxons in 597. Gregorian chant bears his name. A Doctor of the Church.

question: In 664 AD a synod in northern England settled the dating of Easter, choosing the Roman calculation over the Celtic. Where did it meet?
context: King Oswiu of Northumbria presided. Wilfrid argued Rome; Colman argued Iona. Rome won, and the Celtic church was integrated into Latin Christendom.

question: At a council in Clermont in 1095 a pope preached the First Crusade with the cry 'Deus vult' — 'God wills it'. Which pope?
context: He called Western knights to liberate Jerusalem from Seljuk Turkish rule. The crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 with a massacre of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

question: After a three-year campaign the First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099 and massacred most of its inhabitants. Which leader took the throne as Defender of the Holy Sepulchre?
context: Godfrey refused to be crowned king where Christ was crowned with thorns. His brother Baldwin took the royal title after him. The Crusader Kingdom lasted to 1291.

question: An Italian merchant's son stripped naked in the Assisi square in 1206, returned his clothes to his father, and embraced poverty as his bride. Who?
context: 1182-1226. Founded the Franciscan order in 1209. Received the stigmata at La Verna in 1224. His Canticle of the Sun praises Brother Sun and Sister Moon.

question: Late in his life Francis of Assisi composed an Italian poem praising God through Brother Sun, Sister Moon, and Sister Death. What is it called?
context: Composed c. 1224 in Umbrian Italian — one of the earliest works of Italian vernacular literature. Often regarded as Christianity's first ecological hymn.

question: A Spanish priest founded a preaching order in 1216 to combat the Albigensian heresy in southern France. Who?
context: The Dominicans — Order of Preachers. Soon staffing both universities and the Inquisition. Thomas Aquinas and Meister Eckhart were Dominicans.

question: A fourteenth-century English anchoress wrote the first book in English by a woman — visions in which Christ assured her 'all shall be well'. Who?
context: c. 1342-1416. Revelations of Divine Love. She lived enclosed beside St Julian's Church in Norwich. 'All shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.'

question: A fourteenth-century Italian Dominican tertiary persuaded the pope to return from Avignon to Rome and was later named a Doctor of the Church. Who?
context: 1347-1380. Letter-writer, mystic, peacemaker. She received the stigmata invisibly. Pope Gregory XI returned to Rome in 1377 partly on her urging.

question: In 1307 King Philip IV of France arrested members of a wealthy crusading order on Friday October 13. Which order?
context: The order was dissolved in 1312. Grand Master Jacques de Molay was burned in Paris in 1314. Origin of the Friday-the-13th superstition.

question: A Bohemian reformer was burned at the stake at the Council of Constance in 1415 after being promised safe conduct. Who?
context: His followers — Hussites — rose in revolt and held off five papal crusades. He is regarded as a forerunner of Luther a century later.

question: The first major book printed in Europe with movable type was a Latin Bible produced around 1455 by a Mainz craftsman. Who?
context: About 180 copies printed. The Gutenberg revolution made the Reformation possible — printed pamphlets carried Luther's message across Europe in weeks.

question: On October 31, 1517 an Augustinian friar reportedly nailed 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church protesting indulgences. In which town?
context: Martin Luther, 1483-1546. The theses spread through printed copies within weeks. Pope Leo X excommunicated him in 1521.

question: Summoned in 1521 to recant his teachings before Emperor Charles V, Luther reputedly answered 'here I stand, I can do no other'. At which Diet?
context: Frederick the Wise then 'kidnapped' Luther to the Wartburg Castle for safekeeping. There he translated the New Testament into German in eleven weeks.

question: A Dominican friar's sales of indulgences in Germany — 'as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs' — sparked Luther's protest. Who?
context: Funds raised to rebuild St Peter's Basilica in Rome. The slogan is folk-tradition rather than verbatim, but the practice was real and lucrative.

question: The Swiss Reformation began in Zurich under a priest who eventually died on a battlefield in 1531 fighting for the Reformed cantons. Who?
context: 1484-1531. At the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 he and Luther agreed on 14 points but split on the Eucharist. Killed at the Battle of Kappel.

question: A French reformer settled in Geneva and wrote a systematic theology first published in 1536. By what title?
choices: Book of Common Prayer of Cranmer
context: John Calvin, 1509-1564. Successive editions expanded it from a small catechism into a four-book systematic theology. Foundation document of Reformed Protestantism.

question: In 1553 a Spanish physician and anti-Trinitarian was burned at the stake in Geneva with Calvin's approval. Who?
context: He had also discovered pulmonary circulation. The execution remains a stain on Calvin's legacy; Calvin had hoped for beheading instead. Sebastian Castellio publicly objected.

question: Henry VIII's Archbishop of Canterbury wrote the 1549 prayer book that shaped Anglican worship for centuries. Who?
context: 1489-1556. Burned at the stake by Mary I in Oxford. He thrust the hand that had signed his recantation into the flames first. His prose still shapes English liturgy.

question: An English translator was strangled and burned in 1536 for putting the New Testament into English. Who?
context: His last words: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes.' Within years Henry VIII authorized an English Bible — 90% of Tyndale's text passed into the King James.

question: The English Bible commissioned by a Stuart king and published in 1611 became the standard Protestant translation for three centuries. By which king?
context: 47 translators in six companies. Built heavily on Tyndale. Its rhythms shaped English prose from Milton to Lincoln to Martin Luther King Jr.

question: The 1534 Act of Supremacy made which English king the supreme head of the Church of England?
context: Triggered by Pope Clement VII's refusal to annul Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon. Thomas More and John Fisher were beheaded for refusing the oath.

question: Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor was beheaded in 1535 for refusing to swear that the king was supreme head of the Church. Who?
context: Author of Utopia. 'The king's good servant, but God's first.' Canonized in 1935. His death troubled Henry — More had been a friend.

question: English religious dissenters sailed in 1620 on the Mayflower seeking freedom of worship in the New World. Where did they land?
context: Separatist Pilgrims, mostly from Scrooby. The Mayflower Compact established self-government. Half died the first winter. The First Thanksgiving followed in 1621.

question: A Puritan lawyer leading the Massachusetts Bay colony in 1630 preached that they would be 'as a city upon a hill'. Who?
context: His sermon A Model of Christian Charity drew on Matthew 5:14. The 'city on a hill' phrase has shaped American self-understanding from Reagan to Obama.

question: On May 24, 1738 an Anglican priest felt his heart 'strangely warmed' at a meeting on Aldersgate Street, founding what would become Methodism. Who?
context: He preached outdoors to coal miners and traveled 250,000 miles on horseback. His brother Charles wrote 6,000 hymns including 'Hark! The Herald Angels Sing'.

question: A 1741 Massachusetts sermon describing sinners dangling like spiders over hellfire became the most famous of the First Great Awakening. Who preached it?
context: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God', delivered at Enfield. Edwards was also America's first significant philosophical theologian, later president of Princeton.

question: A former slave-ship captain converted in a storm at sea and wrote 'Amazing Grace' after becoming an Anglican curate. Who?
context: 1725-1807. He mentored Wilberforce. The hymn's line 'saved a wretch like me' refers to his own life as a slave trader. Published 1779 in Olney Hymns.

question: A seventeenth-century English shoemaker founded the Religious Society of Friends, who 'quaked' before the Lord. Who?
context: 1624-1691. Quakers rejected oaths, professional clergy, and military service. They were imprisoned across England. Pennsylvania was their refuge under William Penn.

question: Charles II gave a vast American grant to which Quaker in payment of debts to his father (1681)?
context: Pennsylvania — 'Penn's Woods'. Penn made treaties with the Lenape that held longer than most. His Frame of Government included full religious toleration.

question: An upstate New York teenager reported a vision of God and Jesus in a grove of trees in 1820, founding what became the Latter-day Saints. Who?
context: Smith later said an angel named Moroni directed him to golden plates buried at the Hill Cumorah. Published the Book of Mormon in 1830. Killed by a mob in 1844.

question: After Joseph Smith's murder, the Latter-day Saints trekked west under a successor and settled in the Salt Lake Valley in 1847. Who led them?
context: 'This is the right place'. The Mormons built Salt Lake City. Polygamy was officially abandoned in 1890 to ease Utah's path to statehood (achieved 1896).

question: The modern Pentecostal movement is often traced to a 1906 revival on a Los Angeles street where the Holy Spirit was experienced with speaking in tongues. Which street?
context: Led by William J. Seymour, son of slaves. Black and white worshipers prayed together — extraordinary in Jim Crow America. Pentecostalism is now over 600 million worldwide.

question: A Lutheran pastor and theologian was hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp on April 9, 1945 for resisting the Nazi regime. Who?
context: 1906-1945. He had returned from safety in America in 1939. His books The Cost of Discipleship and Letters and Papers from Prison shaped 20th-century theology.

question: A German Lutheran pastor who survived Dachau wrote a famous postwar confession beginning 'first they came for the socialists, and I did not speak out'. Who?
context: 1892-1984. A submarine commander in WWI who initially welcomed Hitler before turning against him. Imprisoned 1937-1945 as Hitler's 'personal prisoner'.

question: An Oxford literature don and former atheist converted first to theism and then to Christianity in the early 1930s — partly through his friendship with Tolkien. Who?
